‫التقديم‬
‫• فلسفة انشاء الكلیة او البرنامج و المعاییر األكادیمیة المتبناة ‪NARS 2017‬‬
‫منذ أنشئت كلیة طب االسكندریة في عام ‪ 1942‬وهى تتحمل مسئولیة إمداد المجتمع المحلى و العربي واألفریقي و‬
‫الدولي بخریجین یشهد لهم بكفاءتهم في تقدیم خدمات صحیة ممیزة تساهم في االرتقاء بصحة االفراد و المجتمع‪.‬‬
‫ونظرا ألن التعلیم الطبي قد شهد على مدار العقود الماضیة والحالیة تحوال ملحوظا قامت باالستفادة منه العدید من‬
‫كلیات الطب في أنحاء العالم المختلفة وشمل استحداث وتطبیق الكثیر من التغیرات الجوهریة في إدارة وتنظیم‬
‫المناهج ومحتواها‪ ،‬فقد قامت الكلیة بإنشاء لجنة التعلیم الطبي عام ‪ 2003‬ثم قسم التعلیم الطبي عام ‪ 2008‬بحیث‬
‫تتمكن الكلیة من مواكبة التطورات والتغیرات العالمیة في هذا المجال‪ .‬وقد صاحب هذه الخطوات إجراء تقییم ذاتي‬
‫للكلیة یشمل كل مجاالت التعلیم بها وذلك من خالل الدراسة الذاتیة االولى في العصر الحدیث عامي ‪ 2004‬و ‪2005‬‬
‫وتبعها منذ ذلك الوقت كتابة تقاریر سنویة للبرنامج‪ .‬وترتكز الدراسات الذاتیة و التقاریر السنویة للكلیة و للبرنامج‬
‫على استطالع آراء اصحاب المصلحة ‪ Stakeholders‬وهم ممثلو جهات العمل‪ ،‬نقابة االطباء ‪ ،‬ممثلي المجتمع‬
‫المدني ‪ ،‬إدارة الكلیة ‪ ،‬أعضاء هیئة التدریس بالكلیة والفئات المعاونة وطالب وخریجي الكلیة باإلضافة إلى مراجعة‬
‫الوثائق الخاصة بالمناهج والمقررات ومصادر التعلم المتاحة ونتائج االمتحانات وغیرها‪ .‬وقد اتاح كل ذلك التعرف‬
‫على مواطن القوة في األنشطة والخدمات التي تقدمها الكلیة والمجاالت التي تحتاج للتحسین والتطویر والفرص‬
‫المتاحة والتهدیدات التي قد تؤثر في مسیرة التطویر والتي شكلت محاور التحلیل الرباعي ((‪SWOT analysis‬‬
‫وبناء على نتائج هذا التحلیل للخطة االستراتیجیة األولى لكلیة الطب ‪ 2013/2008‬تم تغییر البرنامج التعلیمي من‬
‫النظام التقلیدي "‪ "Discipline Based Program‬إلى النظام التكاملي ‪"Integrated System Based‬‬
‫"‪ Program‬وبدأ تطبیقه منذ عام ‪ 2010/2009‬بعد اعتماد الالئحة الداخلیة لمرحلة البكالوریوس بتاریخ ‪16‬‬
‫أغسطس ‪ 2009‬مع تبني المعاییر القومیة األكادیمیة القیاسیة ‪ NARS‬في نسختها األولى عام ‪ .2009‬ومع إصدار‬
‫النسخة الثانیة من المعاییر القومیة األكادیمیة القیاسیة ‪ NARS‬عام ‪ 2017‬و التي قامت الكلیة بتبنیها و مع التوصیات‬
‫و القرارات الصادرة من لجنة قطاع الدراسات الطبیة بالمجلس األعلى للجامعات وما تبعها من تعدیل نص المادة‬
‫‪ 154‬من الالئحة التنفیذیة لقانون تنظیم الجامعات الصادر بالقانون رقم ‪ 49‬لسنة ‪ 1972‬و الخاصة بأن تكون مدة‬
‫الدراسة لنیل درجة البكالوریوس في الطب و الجراحة خمس سنوات دراسیة بنظام الساعات أو النقاط المعتمدة‬
‫یعقبها دراسة لمدة سنتین تأسیسیتین للتدریب الكلینیكي یلیها عقد امتحان عام كشرط لمزاولة المهنة في جمهوریة‬
‫مصر العربیة من خالل هیئة التدریب اإللزامي‪ ،‬تم إعادة تشكیل لجنة المناهج لوضع الالئحة الجدیدة لمرحلة‬
‫البكالوریوس وبدأت الكلیة في تطبیق الئحة ‪ 2018‬في العام الجامعي ‪.2019/2018‬‬
‫ومع بدایة عام ‪ 2023‬بدأ تقییم البرنامج ورصد التحدیات التي واكبت تطبیق الئحة ‪ 2018‬بالتعاون مع لجنة متابعة‬
‫ودعم مرحلة بكالوریوس الطب والجراحة‪ 2+5-‬المنبثقة عن لجنة قطاع الدراسات الطبیة بالمجلس األعلى للجامعات‬
‫بجمهوریة مصر العربیة‪ ،‬مما استدعى إجراء بعض التطویر والتعدیل في النسخة األخیرة الصادرة في ‪.2023‬‬
‫ویتم تنفیذ أهداف مرحلة البكالوریوس من خالل تطبیق فلسفة تعلیمیة تعتمد على المبادئ التالیة‪:‬‬
‫‪ .1‬التعلیم عملیة مستمرة مدى الحیاة‪.‬‬
‫‪ .2‬الفرد قادر على التعلم بذاته من خالل الجهد المبذول في االتصال بمصادر المعرفة وأعمال عناصر التفكیر‬
‫فیها والتفاعل معها‪.‬‬
‫موجه یرشد طالبه الى مصادر‬
‫‪ .3‬عضو هیئة التدریس لیس مجرد ناقل للمعرفة والمهارة فحسب وإنما هو ِ‬
‫المعرفة ویضرب لهم المثل والقدوة ویعینهم على مواجهة المشكالت المختلفة واالسهام في حلها في ضوء‬
‫ما اكتسبه من خبرات وذلك في ظل مفهوم الریادة على النحو االمثل‪.‬‬
‫‪ .4‬التعلم القائم على تحقق الجدارات المطلوبة من الخریج مع مراعاة تركیز التعلیم الطبي على النتائج المتعلقة‬

• The joint is the point of meeting of two or more bones.

 Classification
• They are classified according to the substance between
the ends of the bones into:
A. Fibrous
- The substance between the bones is "fibrous tissue".
B. Cartilaginous
- The substance between the bones is "cartilage".
C. Synovial joints
- The substance between the bones is "synovial fluid".

• It contains long strand of Hyaluronic Acid attached non-covalently to
Link proteins.
• Link proteins are attached non-covalently to Core proteins.
• Core proteins are attached covalently to GAGs by O-Glycosidic bonds
between Xylose sugar and OH of serine.
• Basic proteoglycan unit is called Aggrecan or Proteoglycan Monomer.
• Proteoglycan Monomer = Core protein + Attached GAGs.
• Aggregation of proteoglycan monomers within collagen meshwork, adding
structural Rigidity to matrix.
• GAGs in proteoglycans are polyanions (-) and can bind greatly with
polycations (+) like Na* & K* which attract HO by osmotic pressure into
ECM.

Globular protein, present inside the living cell, but
they can act independent of the cells.
• They are of high molecular weight, heat labile, non-chalyzable &
colloidal in nature.
• Substrate: The organic substance on which enzyme acts.
• Product: The organic substance produced by the action of the enzyme.
• Co- Enzyme:
• Essential for the activity of enzymes.
• Considered as second substrate or Co- substrates.
:: Terminology of Enzymes:
• Enzymes which were discovered early were given general names still used
as pepsin, Cathepsin, Emulsin, .

of Reaction catalyzed: Aldolase, Mutase,
Transaminase,
Dehydrogenase.

• as name of substrate + type of reaction.
• lactic acid dehydrogenase.
• Glycogen synthetase.

A-Integral Membrane Proteins:
•
•

They are embedded within the lipid bilayer.
Most of these proteins traverse the whole thickness of the
membrane and are called transmembrane proteins while
others are partially embedded within the membrane.

•

There are six functional forms of integral membrane
proteins:

1. Pumps: transport ions (Na+, K+) actively across the membrane.
2. Channels: transport substances passively.
3. Receptors: allow binding of specific molecules e.g., hormone.
4. Enzymes: ATP synthase of the inner mitochondrial membrane and
some types of digestive enzymes in the small intestine.
5. Linkers: anchor the intracellular cytoskeleton to the extracellular
matrix.
6. Structural proteins: form junctions between neighboring cells.

B-Peripheral Membrane Proteins:

•They are not embedded into lipid bilayer, but they are loosely associated with membrane.
•They are usually located on the cytoplasmic surface of the membrane.
•Function: form a link between the cell membrane and the cytoplasmic components.

text:
Histology of the Blood, Immune & Lymphoid system(By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)

• It is a specialized type of connective tissue that composed of:
1. The plasma: represents the matrix.
2. The formed blood elements: represent the cells.
Blood has no fibers.

The formed blood elements:
1- Red blood corpuscles (RBCs).
2- White blood cells (WBCs) or leukocytes including:
 Granular leukocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
 Agranular leukocytes: lymphocytes and monocytes.
3- Blood platelets.

Preparation of a blood smear:
1-Giemsa's stain (methylene blue+ eosin) is used which
differentiate blood cells by their nuclei and cytoplasmic
granules:
• basophilic (violet)
• eosinophilic (pink)
• azurophilic (red purple)
2-Blood count:
• It is the average number of a formed blood element per cubic
millimeter blood.
 RBCs count.
 Total leukocytic count.
 Platelets count.
 Differential leukocytic count: it is the percentage of each type of leukocytes
relative to the total number of WBCs.

Red Blood Corpuscles (RBCs)
• Average RBCs count:
 In males: 5-5.5 millions/mm3.
 In females:4.5-5 millions/mm3.
• Life span of RBCs:
 It is 100-120 days.
 Old & deformed RBCs are phagocytosed by the
macrophages in the spleen & liver.
Function of Red blood corpuscles: Contain
hemoglobin for gas exchange.

Blood & Immune system Module

Page 1

 Histology of the Blood, Immune & Lymphoid system(By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)
LM:
• Shape: eosinophilic biconcave discs.
• Diameter: 7.2-7.8µm (=the size of the smallest blood capillaries).
• Nucleus: absent.
• Cytoplasm: hemoglobin occupies about 33% of the corpuscular
volume & is more concentrated at the periphery.

EM:
• Shape: membranous electron dense biconcave
discs.
• Cell organelles: no nucleus& no organelles.

RBCs Membrane:
1- From outside: It is covered by a well-developed
glycocalyx which is responsible for the blood grouping.
2- From inside: It is supported by a well-developed
cytoskeleton, which is responsible for the flexibility of
RBCs.
 It is formed of microfilaments (actin &spectrin) that
are attached to a peripheral membrane protein
(ankyrin).

How do the RBCs adapt to their function?
1- The biconcave discoid shape increases the
surface area of the RBCs by 20-30% more than if they had a spherical shape.
2- The lack of a nucleus and organelles allows more space in the cytoplasm for carrying the
maximal amount of hemoglobin.
3- The concentration of hemoglobin at the periphery of the cytoplasm facilitates its binding
to oxygen and carbon dioxide.
4- The structure of the cytoskeleton helps the RBCs to be squeezed through the narrowest
blood capillaries without being damaged.
5- The selective permeability of the cell membrane to oxygen and carbon dioxide to
enhance their diffusion rates during gas exchange.

Myeloid tissue
• Sites:
1- The central bone marrow cavity in young long bones.
2- The marrow cavities of cancellous bones.

• Types of bone marrow:

1- Red bone marrow: active in hemopoiesis.
2- Yellow bone marrow:
Blood & Immune system Module

Page 2

 Histology of the Blood, Immune & Lymphoid system(By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)
 inactive bone marrow in which the blood formation has stopped.
 Its yellow color is due to the presence of fat cells.
 It can revert to the red type in hemorrhage & anemia.

• Structure of myeloid tissue:
I-The stroma:

A. Reticular fibers: support the myeloid cells & blood
sinusoids.
B. Stromal cells: the fixed cell population of the bone
marrow. They include:
1- Reticular cells: have 3 functions:
 Produce the reticular fibers.
 Secrete growth factors that stimulate the hemopoietic
stem cells.
 In yellow bone marrow, these cells are changed to fat
cells.
2- Macrophages:
 Phagocytosis of aged RBCs & the malformed blood elements.
 Storage of iron for reuse.
3- Fat cells: One of the largest cells in bone marrow.
II-The blood sinusoids:
 Wide & irregular blood vessel.
 Lined by fenestrated endothelial cells.
III-The myeloid cells:

 Type of immune response

Non specific immune response

Specific immune response

1- Mechanism of action

Acts non specifically by:
1- Surface protection: physical barrier (skin), chemical
defense (low pH), secreted substances(lysozyme)&
ciliated cells lining respiratory epithelium.
2- Innate immunity: complement system, phagocytic
cells, granulocytes & natural killer cells.

Acts specifically by:
1-Humoral immune response: secretion
of antibodies.
2-Cell mediated immune response:
against virally infected cells and cancer
cells.

2- Time of reaction

Rapid response( minutes to hours).

Slow response (days).

3- Memory cells

Absent.

Present.

4- Cells

Phagocytic cells, Natural killer & granulocytes.

B and T lymphocytes.

 Types of
Lymphocytes

T- lymphocytes

B-lymphocytes

1-Origin &
development:

•HPSCs in bone marrow and then their daughter cells migrate to thymus.
•In the thymus: T cells proliferate, mature and acquire T cell receptors on their surface
specific for certain antigen.

In the bone marrow where they
proliferate, mature and acquire
surface immunoglobulins
receptors specific for certain
antigen recognition.

2-Site of action:

T cells migrate to the peripheral lymphoid tissues (lymph nodes, spleen, palatine tonsils
&Peyer’s patches in the ileum) where they come into contact with the antigens.

B cells migrate to the peripheral
lymphoid tissues where they

 Chapter 1
Communication Principles & Communication process

For Health care success, good communication ensures good working relationships, patient satisfaction,
increases patient understanding of illness & treatment, and improving patient compliance.
Good communication can also increase job satisfaction for staff and reduce work stress. Every person's
communication skills affect both personal and organizational effectiveness.
Communication Principles
Objectives







Define communication.
Describe the nature of communication.
State the benefits of good communication.
Describe the components of communication.
Outline the types of communication system.
Describe the general causes of poor communication

Definition of communication.
Communication is the process of meaningful interaction among human beings. This
definition indicates that it is a process of exchanging information and it focuses on meaningful
interactions. It shows that communication is about conveying )‫ (نقل‬information to others clearly
and receiving the information that others are sending.
Communication means that we transmit a message to a person or to a group. If this
person understands and interprets the message in the way it was intended, then one can
say that communication has been effectively carried out.
Transmission
Reception
A message transmitted is the
first half of communication

It must be received and the receiver must show
that message has been understood

Figure 1 A message is transmitted and received

2

 What do we mean by encoding and decoding?

The definition indicates that communication is a process and it is important to reach mutual
understanding. It also pointed out to two terms in the process of exchange namely encode and decode.
Encoding is how the message is conveyed to another party. The message is converted into a suitable
form of transmission. The medium of transmission will determine the form of the communication.
Decoding is the process where the message is interpreted for its content. It also means that the receiver
thinks about the message's content and internalizes the message. The receiver will compare the message
to prior experiences or external stimuli.

Figure 2 Encoding and decoding
What do we communicate?
We communicate ideas, information, norms, feelings, attitudes values and behaviors.
An attitude is a relatively constant feeling, predisposition or set of beliefs directed towards an object,
person or situation(
Value is a preference shared and transmitted within a community.
A behavior is an action that has a purpose, frequency and duration.
Why do we consider communication as a process?
Communication is moving in ingredients within a process and interacts together and each ingredient
affects all the others. In communication events and relationships are dynamic )lively and active(.
Communication is ongoing, ever changing & continuous,
does not have a beginning, and end. It is circular in nature
& not static.
Communication is a personal, social and emotional
process that occurs between people to influence, control
and motivate others, may involve changes in behavior
3

 Importance of good communication
Good communication helps people to:
 Define and understand goals.
 Receive and share information.
 Build rapport.

text: Tutorial 1, Part 2 Representation system Representation System Studying representation system helps to communicate with other people correctly. What Are The Most Used in Practicing Medicine? Language can be added to the other representative systems …how to talk to ourselves Auditory digital system (AD) What Are The Representational Systems? Preferred learning style Each of us has a preferred channel: visual, auditory or kinesthetic. It is important to know what type of learner you are to help maximize your potential learning. Select your preferred learning style : 1. I prefer to learn by showing steps of a task : I am probably a……. 2. I prefer to learn by listening or reading loudly : I am probably a……… 3. I prefer to learn by trying it or doing : I am probably a………… What are non verbal clues Non Verbal Clues Looking at The Eye Movements Visual recall : When we are seeing images from the past( recalling and remembering them from memory),your eyes will go up and to the left. You are using this type of thinking when you are answering a question like: "What did you look like when you were weighing 90 Kg?" Visual construct When you are visualizing something you have never seen before or you are making something up in your head, the eyes will go up and to the right . You use visual construct to answer a question as: "What would you look like if you lost 20 kg in weight"? Auditory recall When one remember sounds or voices that you have heard before or things that you have said to yourself before, eyes look horizontally& to the left. You use this mode to answer questions as "Do you recall hearing the systolic murmur?" or "What was the last thing I said?" Auditory construct When you are making sounds up that you have never heard before ,eyes look horizontally &to the right . You use this when you answer questions as: "What would I sound like if I were fluent in German?" Feelings (Kinesthetic) When you are assessing your feelings you tend to look down and to the right. You use this type of thinking when you answer a question like: "What does it feel like to be happy?" Auditory Dialogue When you are having internal dialogue and talking to yourself your eyes will go down and to the left . You can demonstrate this for yourself by answering: "What do you say to yourself when you diagnose a difficult case?" Histology Of MusculoSkeletal System (By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)

I- Cartilage
• Cartilage are modified type of connective tissue in which the extracellular
matrix is hardened to provide rigidity, support and attachment for soft
tissues.

Characteristic Features Of Cartilage:

1- The extra cellular matrix is firm.
2- It is avascular, no lymphatic vessels or nerves.
3- It is usually covered by perichondrium.
4- Cells are isolated in small cavities in the ground substance called
lacunae.

• Site: Cartilage is usually covered by a membrane called
perichondrium except inside joint cavities.
• Structure: It consists of two layers:
1- An outer fibrous layer: dense CT, rich in type І
collagen & few in blood vessels.
2- An inner vascular&cellular layer(chondrogenic
layer): contain chondroblasts (forming new
cartilage).
• Functions:
1- Growth of cartilage at its periphery.
2- Nourishment as it contains blood vessels.
Inside joint cavities: these functions are committed by synovial fluid

Components Of Cartilage:
1- Extracellular matrix including:
 Ground substance.
 Fibers: Collagen& elastic fibers.
2- Cartilage cells:chondroblasts &chondrocytes.

I-

Extracellular matrix:

• It is responsible for the firmness of the cartilage. It is produced by
cartilage cells.
• Structure:
1- Ground substance:
A- Water: 60-80% of cartilage weight.
Function: Diffusion of metabolites to the cartilage cells.
B- Proteoglycans: Firm gel, consists of glycosaminoglycans as:
>Bound to hyaluronic acid
 Chondroitin sulfate
 Keratan sulfate.
C- Glycoproteins: such as chondronectin (anchors chondrocytes to the matrix).

2- Fibers: mainly type II collagen fibrils, in addition to type I collagen and elastic fibers
according to type of cartilage.

IICartilage cells:
1- Chondroblasts:

• Origin: from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells.
• Site: in the inner cellular layer of perichondrium.
• Function:
1- They secrete the extracellular matrix,
2- They become imprisoned inside lacunae forming chondrocytes.
• Structure:
 Shape: Oval.
 Nucleus: Oval.
 Cytoplasm: basophilic.

2- Chondrocytes:
•
•

Origin: From the chondroblasts after secreting the matrix, trapped in
lacunae.
Site and shape:

1- Young chondrocytes:
 Site: underneath the perichondrium,
 Shape: spindle.
2- Mature chondrocytes:
 Site: deeply situated,
 Shape: rounded.
The matrix is condensed around the lacunae forming the capsule
rich in chondroitin sulphates
• Function: They maintain the extracellular matrix.

Chondrocytes can divide by mitosis

Types Of Cartilage:
•

1- Hyaline cartilage:
Fresh state:

1- Smooth & firm.
2- Bluish in color.
• Sites:
1- Skeleton of the embryo.
2- Epiphyseal plates in growing age.
3- Costal cartilages.
4- Nose, larynx, trachea and bronchi in the respiratory system.
5- Articular surfaces of synovial joints.

Musculoskeletal system Module

• Characteristic features:
 Perichondrium: It is usually covered with perichondrium
except inside joint cavity.
 Nutrition: from perichondrium, but if it is present inside
the joint cavity, it is nourished by diffusion from the
synovial fluid.
 Matrix: abundant, glassy, pale basophilic & no apparent
fibers (WHY).
 Fibers: Type II collagen fibrils.
 Chondrocytes: widely scattered, number of
chondrocytes/capsule is 1-8 forming a cell nest.
2- Elastic cartilage:
• Fresh state:
1- Flexible, can bear mechanical stress without permanent deformation.
2- Yellowish in color.
• Sites:
1- The auricle of the ear (ear pinna).
2- External auditory meatus.
3- Epiglottis.
• Characteristic features:
 Perichondrium: covered always with perichondrium.
 Nutrition: Perichondrium.
 Fibers: large number of elastic fibers (stained by VVG & orcein), in
addition to collagen type II.
 Chondrocytes: Numerous, number of chondrocytes/capsule is 1-3.

Histology Of Nervous Tissue (By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)
Nervous tissue 1
1- Types of cells in nervous tissue.
2- Nerve cells: structure, classification& sites.
3- General organization of the nervous system.
4- Definition, structure & types of the nerve fiber.
Nervous tissue
• It is one of the four primary basic tissues.
• It consists of two types of cells:
1- Neurons (nerve cells)
2- Neuroglia (supporting cells).
Neuron=Nerve
cell
• It is the structural
and functional unit of the
nervous tissue.
• It is characterized by:
1- Excitability: they respond to environmental changes by generation of action
potential or nerve impulse.
2- Conductivity: they are capable of propagation of nerve impulse to other neurons,
muscles& glands.
Histological structure of the neuron
I- Cell body (perikaryon, soma)
• It is composed of:
1- Nucleus: euchromatic.
2- Cytoplasm: contains:
 Nissl bodies
-LM: basophilic granules.
-EM: aggregates of ribosomes and rER.
-Function: protein synthesis.
- Distribution: in the cell body except in the region of axon hillock.
CNS Module

Page 1

 Histology Of Nervous Tissue (By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)
 Large perinuclear Golgi
apparatus: for packaging of
neurotransmitters into synaptic
vesicles.
 Cytoskeleton: formed of
neurofibrils that include
neurofilaments and
microtubules playing a role in
the transmission of nerve
impulses.
 Inclusions: lipofuscin
pigments and lipids.
II- Cell processes:
1- Axon:
• Origin: from the axon hillock.
• Number: always single.
• Direction of impulses: conducts nerve impulses
away from the cell body.
• Shape: long, with a regular cylindrical shape.
• Branching: no branches except at axon
termination forming terminal arborizations. It
may give off collaterals arising at right angles.
• Structure: the axoplasm contains few organelles
(neurofibrils, synaptic vesicles and mitochondria).
Nissl bodies are absent.
• Surrounding sheath: axolemma may be surrounded by sheaths according to the
type of nerve fiber.
2- Dendrite:
• Origin: from any part of the cell body.
• Number: usually multiple (in multipolar neurons).It may be single (in bipolar
neurons).
• Direction of impulses: conducts nerve impulses towards the cell body
• Shape: short, thick near its origin and tapers towards its end.
• Branching: many branches arising at acute angles, having short spines for
synapses.
• Structure: contains most of the organelles as in the perikaryon except the Golgi
apparatus. Nissl bodies are present.
• Surrounding sheath: not surrounded by sheaths.

PHYSIOLOGY OF THE NERVE
INTRODUCTION
Organization of the nervous system:
The nervous system is anatomically and functionally divided into two distinct
parts:
1.

Central nervous system (CNS ):
a. Brain
b. Spinal cord
It is an integration and command center.

2.

Peripheral nervous system (PNS) :
A complex network of nerves which resides or extends outside the
central nervous system.
They allow the brain and spinal cord to communicate with the body
tissues and organs and regulate their activity.

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 3

The anatomical unit of the nervous system : the nerve cell or neuron:
- The neuron is made up of a cell body or soma and cell processes including
dendrites and axon (nerve fiber).
- The human nervous system contains billions of neurons.
- The functional unit is formed at least of two neurons.
- The axon (nerve fiber):
- is a single elongated cytoplasmic extension,
- branches freely near its termination on:
a- the surface of the soma and dendrites of another neuron (neuroneural ) junction or synapse,
b- may end at a muscle (neuromuscular)
c- on a gland (neuro-epithelial) junctions.
- The axon ends in synaptic knobs or buttons.

Nerve and muscle are called excitable tissues because they respond to
stimuli (electrical, mechanical or chemical) when they are excited.
NERVE:
is an excitable tissue which receives stimuli, processes them, and transmits
signals to target tissues to integrate the functions of the whole body.
MUSCLE:
is an excitable tissue which contracts in response to specific stimuli. Its
function is to p roduce force and cause motion, either locomotion or
movement within internal organs.

text: Practical 1 SIMPLE MUSCLE TWITCH Department of Medical Physiology Learning objectives Investigate the physiological properties of skeletal muscle using frog gastocnemuis muscle Describe simple muscle twitch (SMT) Explain the phases of SMT Simple Muscle Twitch A single brief contraction followed by a relaxation of a skeletal muscle due to application of a single adequate stimulus. Recording apparatus Muscle So we need Electrical stimulu s As nature No permanent damage Easy for application As human Cheap Stimulus Frog 1 2 3 Preparation : Frog’s gastrocnemius muscle-sciatic nerve preparation Preparation : Gastrocnemuis muscle Sciatic nerve In the thigh Knee joint TendoAchillis To keep the vitality of the gastrocnemius muscle-sciatic nerve preparation , it is kept in Physiological saline of frog 0.69% NaCl How can we do stimulation To the frog’s gastrocnemius-sciatic nerve preparation?? Sciatic nerve In the thigh Method of Stimulation Direct stimulation Indirect stimulation Direct stimulation of the muscle Stimulation of the nerve supplying the muscle Which is better ? Direct stimulation Indirect stimulation Supply all muscle fibers equally, the same as what occurs in our body Recording apparatus : The apparatus used for laboratory experiments on the muscle and nerve consists of : 1. Stimulation set: delivers low voltage (2-15 volts) electrical stimulus for the muscle nerve preparation 2. Kymograph: For recording the response of the stimulated muscle on rotated drum 3. Myograph: For mounting muscle nerve preparation Recording apparatus : Stimulation set Kymograph Myograph Recording of Simple Muscle Twitch Simple Muscle Twitch A single brief contraction followed by a relaxation of a skeletal muscle due to application of a single adequate stimulus. Definition Phases of SMT Latent phase : the time that passes between the application of the stimulus to start of contraction Contraction phase: the period during which the muscle shorten in length Relaxation phase: the period during which the muscle restores its initial length Simple Muscle Twitch Point of stimulation Point of stimulation is drawn by doing stimulation while the drum is stopped (important to show latent period) Duration of the SMT Total twitch time = 0.1 sec Latent phase : 0.01 sec Contraction phase : 0.04 sec Relaxation phase : 0.05 sec 0.01 sec 0.04 sec 0.05 sec 0.1 sec Causes of Latent Phase 1- Action potential in the nerve 2- Chemical transmission in the neuro -muscular junction 3- Action potential in the muscle and excitation –contraction coupling 1 2 3 What could affect the force or strength of muscle contraction??? This depends on Initial length of the muscle Initial length of the muscle 1- The strength of muscle contraction is directly proportional to the initial length of muscle, within limit. ( Starling’s law) 2- If the muscle is stretched , its initial length increased with stronger contractions . 3- If the muscle is overstretched , muscle contraction becomes weaker . free (pre)loaded muscle Force of contraction varies with the starting length of the sarcomere after loaded muscle After loaded muscle If the weight attached to the muscle’s tendon is supported during relaxation and pulls the muscle only when it starts to shorten i.e the muscle carries no weight during relaxation ( unstretched ) The muscle is loaded only after start of contraction Free (preloaded) muscle When the load pulls the muscle during relaxation and increases its length (Stretched muscle) The muscle carries the weight (load) before and after contraction Preloaded muscle gives stronger contraction provided that the weight does not over stretch the muscle. After-loaded Free-loaded Over-stretched Preloaded muscle versus After loaded muscle Factors Affecting SMT Factors Affecting SMT 1- Warming 2- Cooling 3- Fatigue Learning objectives Demonstrate the effect of temperature & fatigue on muscle contraction. Give the precautions taken to study the effect of temperature Explain the effects of warm, cold exposure and fatigue on muscle contraction. Warming Warm saline (physiological saline of frog 0.69% NaCl ) 30-38°C. The effect: Duration decreases, amplitude increases. (contraction stronger and more rapid) Mechanism : - ↑ metabolic chemical reactions - ↓viscosity of the muscle warming SMT Over-heating Temperature of saline > 45ºC Effects: irreversible coagulation (denaturation) of muscle proteins. The muscle remains in a state of sustained contraction (heat rigor) Cooling Cold saline (physiological saline of frog 0.69% NaCl ) 4-5°C. Effects : Duration increases , amplitude decreases. (weaker contraction and more prolonged) Mechanism : - ↓ metabolic chemical reactions - ↑ viscosity of the muscle warming SMT SMT COOLING Over-cooling or freezing Temperature of saline < 4ºC Effects: loss of vitality & irritability These changes are reversible if the muscle is rewarmed Fatigue By Repeated successive stimulation . Duration increases , amplitude decreases (decrease strength of contraction and prolongation of all phases especially the relaxation phase) Relaxation becomes incomplete (contracture) Effects Fatigue Contracture is a state of sustained muscle contraction which occurs when the muscle becomes extremely fatigued. It is due to depletion of ATP which is important for muscle relaxation Fatigue Mechanism: Depletion of energy stores (ATP, creatine phosphate, glycogen). Acetylcholine may be depleted also from motor endplate. ↓ active transport of Ca ++ into sarcoplasmic reticulum. Accumulation of metabolites as lactic acid with ↓ pH of the muscle fibers ↓ O 2 supply SMT fatigue Fatigue The first site of fatigue is the motor end plate Factors Affecting SMT Simple Muscle Twitch Identify 1-Curve (SMT) 2-Phases a is Latent period (Define, duration and causes) b is Contraction Phase (duration) c is Relaxation Phase (duration) Simple Muscle Twitch 3- To keep vitality of the muscle, it is kept in ----------- 4- The electrodes are placed on -------- in direct stimulation & o

text: Department of Medical Physiology GENESIS OF TETANUS Practical 2 Learning objectives Observe the effects of application of several successive stimuli on skeletal muscle contraction Define the terms: - Separate twitches - Clonus - Tetanus Explain how they are normally produced. Application of multiple successive stimuli at different frequencies Gastrocnemuis -sciatic nerve preparation Genesis of Tetanus The effect of multiple stimuli depends upon the frequency of stimuli (Time interval between 2 successive stimuli) Low frequency Moderate frequency High frequency Low frequency stimulation The electrical stimulator is adjusted that Each stimulus fall after complete muscle relaxation of the first twitch caused by previous stimulus . Production of successive simple muscle twitches ( contraction then relaxation ) Separate Twitches Moderate frequency stimulation The electrical stimulator is adjusted that Each stimulus falls during the relaxation phase of the first twitch caused by the previous stimulus . Production of successive contractions, each one followed by incomplete relaxation Incomplete tetanus (Clonus) Stimulus applied Stimulus applied Clonus is a jerky tremulous sustained contraction. It consists of rapid repeated partial contractions followed by partial relaxation of the muscle. Clonus or Incomplete Tetanus High frequency stimulation The electrical stimulator is adjusted that Each stimulus falls during the contraction phase of the first twitch caused by the previous stimulus . Production of successive contractions (no relaxation) (contraction on top of contraction) Complete tetanus Rapid successive stimuli causes fusion of successive contractions, result in continuous contraction with no relaxation Complete tetanus ( sustained steady contraction ) Stimuli Complete Tetanus Effect of different frequencies application Clonus Treppe or staircase phenomenon Treppe or staircase phenomenon This phenomenon states that with successive stimulation, the force of contraction increases although the intensity is constant It occurs due to successive stimulation of the muscle whatever is the frequency of stimulation Causes of treppe phenomenon In low frequency stimuli It is due to 1- increased heat production Muscle more warm ↓ muscle viscosity which acts as resistance to contraction Causes of treppe phenomenon In moderate frequency stimuli It is due to: 1- increased heat production 2- Accumulation of Ca ++ ions As the stimulus reaches the muscle while it is in relaxation, Ca ++ is not completely pumped back to SR So each new stimulus adds more Ca ++ to the already present Ca ++ from the previous twitch and so on More Ca ++ increase force of contraction Causes of treppe phenomenon In high frequency stimuli It is due to: 1- increased heat production 2- Accumulation of Ca ++ ions As the stimulus reaches the muscle while it is in contraction, Ca ++ is still in the sarcoplasm. So each new stimulus adds more Ca ++ to the already present Ca ++ leading to stronger contraction. These factors increase force of contraction up to a certain limit where there is no further increase in contractions Relation between excitability and mechanical changes In skeletal muscle, the action potential usually preceeds muscle contraction by about 2msec (so muscle can respond to a second stimulus while it is in contraction) Tetanus never occurs in the cardiac muscle In cardiac muscle, the contraction occurs at the same time of action potential (coinciding with the refractory periods so cardiac muscle cannot respond to a second stimulus while it is in contraction) Why??? Factors Affecting TETANUS Factors Affecting CLONUS 1- Warming 2- Cooling 3- Fatigue Learning objectives Demonstrate the effect of high & low temperature on clonus. Demonstrate the effect of fatigue on clonus. Explain the effect of fatigue on muscle contraction. In this experiment, the frequency is fixed to record clonus curve Then the effect of warming , cooling and fatigue on clonus is observed and recorded Effect of warming Warming of a muscle leads to a stronger contraction than normal, together with shortening of all phases of the muscle twitch Incomplete tetanus Separate twitches Mechanism: - ↑ metabolic chemical reactions -↓ viscosity of the muscle Effect of warming Application of warm saline ( 30-38°C) accelerates the chemical reactions , thus all phases of muscle twitch are shortened The stimulus will fall at the end of relaxation instead of falling during relaxation Clonus Complete tetanus Effect of cooling Cooling of a muscle leads to a weaker contraction than normal, together with prolongation of all phases of the muscle twitch Incomplete tetanus Complete tetanus Mechanism: - ↓ metabolic chemical reactions - ↑ viscosity of the muscle Effect of cooling Application of cold saline ( 4-5°C) decelerates the chemical reactions , thus all phases of the muscle twitch are prolonged The stimulus will fall during contraction phase instead of falling during relaxation Incomplete tetanus Complete tetanus Effect of fatigue Prolonged stimulation of a muscle leads to muscle fatigue , together with prolongation of all phases of the muscle twitch Clonus Complete tetanus Fatigue Effect of fatigue Mechanism: 1- Depletion of energy stores (ATP, glycogen & creatine phosphate) 2- Accumulation of metabolites (lactic acid) and increased acidity. Effect of fatigue Fatigue usually occurs rapidly in isolated muscle But inside the body, muscle fatigue is delayed & reversible: The circulatory system supplies the muscle with O 2 and nutrients and removes the metabolites There is alteration between contracted & relaxed fibers. Anatomy of Nose
Nasal cavity:
- cavity of nose is subdivided into right and left halves by the nasal septum

and open posteriorly into nasopharynx via posterior nasal aperture (choana)

Bony skeleton of the nose:
Roof:
Floor:

- Anterior part: Nasal bone + Nasal part of the frontal bone
- Middle part: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
- Posterior part: Body of sphenoid bone
- Anteriorly: Palatine process of the maxilla
- Posteriorly: Horizontal plates of the palatine bone

1

 ARTIST OF ANATOMY

Lateral wall:

- The lateral wall of the nose is subdivided into:
(1) Vestibule.
(2) Atrium.
(3) Nasal conchae:
- bony plates covered with mucous membrane
- They are three (superior, middle and inferior)
(4) Nasal meatuses:
- depressions below and lateral to each concha
- they are three (superior, middle and inferior)

Medial wall: - Superiorly: Perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone
(Nasal septum) - Anterior-inferior: Septal cartilage
- Posterior-inferior: Vomer

2

 ARTIST OF ANATOMY

Paranasal air sinuses
- They are air-filled spaces that open into the lateral wall of the nose
- Functions: - Warming and humidifying the inspired air
- Diminishing the weight of the skull
- They add resonance to the voice

The paranasal sinuses include:
(1) Maxillary air sinus

- Inside the body of the maxilla

(2) Frontal air sinus

- Inside the frontal bone

(3) Sphenoidal air sinus

- Inside the body of the sphenoid bone

(4) Ethmoidal air sinus
(anterior – middle – posterior)

- Inside the ethmoid bone

- All the sinuses are present at birth
except frontal sinus which appears during the 2nd year

text:
Cardiac Metabolism
Respiratory Chain (ETC)

Dr. Mohamed Agha
The Genius in Biochemistry

 Contents
 Regulation of Myocardial Metabolism............... 2
 Fatty acid oxidation in the heart ......................... 3
 Carbohydrate Metabolism ................................... 3
 Randle Cycle .......................................................4
 Respiratory Chain............................................... 6
 Mechanism of Oxidative Phosphorylation .......... 8
 Inhibitors of Respiratory Chain ........................... 9

The Genius in Biochemistry

Lipid Metabolism

Dr. Mohamed Agha

 Regulation of Myocardial Metabolism
 Heart requires a high rate of energy expenditure.
 ATP is broken down to ADP and Pi.
 Mitochondria make half of volume of heart cells (Abundant Mitochondria).
 Heart doesn't store lipid or glycogen & it has small energy reserve (Creatine
Phosphate) enough for few seconds of contraction.

 In Atherosclerosis or Coronary Thrombosis → Failure of O2 to reach Heart →
region of heart will die (Heart attack = Myocardial Infarction MI).

 Energy is used to fuel :
1- Contractile work of systole of Ventricles.
2- Calcium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum → relaxation during
diastole.

 The concentration of ATP in the heart remains constant, even when the heart is
stressed by exercise.

 High rate of ATP consumption is matched with high rate of ATP
resynthesis by:
1- Oxidative Phosphorylation (ETC) in Mitochondria (Main source).
2- Glycolysis in cytoplasm.

 Oxidative Phosphorylation is fueled by reducing equivalents (NADH+H+ &
FADH2) and condenses ADP + Pi to generate ATP in Mitochondria.

 These reducing equivalents are generated by :
1. β- oxidation of fatty acid to Acetyl CoA.
2. Oxidation of Acetyl CoA in Citric Acid Cycle (CAC).

 Acetyl CoA is produced from FA and CHO oxidation.
 Glycogen → Glucose → Glycolysis → Pyruvate which is transported to
mitochondria and converted to Acetyl CoA.
 The aerobic heart takes Lactate from blood and converts it to Pyruvate.

 The rates of metabolic pathways are tightly coupled to the rate of contractile
work which is linked to:
1- Supply of Oxygen.
2- Rate of flux of Electron Transport Chain (ETC) and ATP resynthesis.
The Genius in Biochemistry

Lipid Metabolism

Dr. Mohamed Agha

  Regulation of Myocardial metabolism is complex and is linked to:
1- Arterial substrates.
2- Hormone levels.
3- Coronary flow.
4- Inotropic state.

5- Nutritional status of tissues.
 ATP resynthesis in the heart (Fed State):
 60-80% from Fatty Acids. (Aerobic)
 10-30% from Glucose. (Aerobic or Anaerobic)
 10-30% from Lactate.
 Ketone Bodies (Acetoacetate & β-Hydroxy Butyrate) levels in blood are very low
in fed state, thus they are not significant fuel. (in fasting & DM → 70% of
Energy)

 Fatty Acid Oxidation in the Heart: The rates of FA uptake and Oxidation by the heart depend on FFA
concentration in plasma → determined by the rate of Lipolysis → under tight
hormonal regulation:
 Inhibited by insulin.

 Stimulated by norepinephrine and epinephrine. (Starvation – DM).
 Once the fatty acid is transported into the cell, it is converted to fatty acyl CoA,
and either:

 Shuttled into the mitochondria by Carnitine shuttle and oxidized.
 Stored as intracellular TG.
 Heart LPL has Low Km (1/10) for TAG than Adipose LPL → redirection of FA
from TAG from Adipose to Heart.

 Carbohydrate metabolism: There are three primary sources for carbohydrate fuel for the myocardium:
a. Extracellular glucose.
b. Extracellular lactate.
c. Glycogen stores. (small amount)

 The uptake of extracellular glucose is regulated by
1- Concentration of glucose transporters in the membrane.
2- Trans-membrane glucose gradient.

PRACTICAL BIOCHEMISTRY
CARDIO-PULMONARY MODULE

DR. MOHAMED AGHA
The Genius in Biochemistry

 1

Contents
1. Lipid Profile ……………………………………………………….. 2
2. Hyperlipidemia …………………………………………………….. 3
3. Cholesterol …………………………………………………………. 3
4. Cardiac Markers …………………………………….…………...… 6

The Genius in Biochemistry

Practical Module Cardio Pulmonary

Dr. Mohamed Agha

 2

Lipid Profile
 A group of tests that are often ordered together to determine risk of CHD .
 Good indicators of whether someone is likely to have a heart attack,
hypertension or stroke caused by atherosclerosis.
 Lipid profile typically includes:1. Total cholesterol (˂ 200 mg/dL).
2. HDL-Cholesterol = good cholesterol (˃ 60 mg/dL).
3. LDL-Cholesterol = bad cholesterol (˂ 100 mg/dL).
4. Triglycerides (˂ 150 mg/dL).
5. An extended profile may also include VLDL.
 N.B. Friedewald equation: A method of calculation of LDL and VLDL concentration without
Colorimetry .
 VLDL = T.G/ 5
 LDL-Cholesterol = [Total Cholesterol] - [HDL- Cholesterol] - ([T.G]/5)
 Concentrations are given in mg/dL.
 Sampling of blood for lipid profile: 12 hours fasting (no food or drink except water).
 For the most accurate results, wait at least two months after a heart attack,
surgery, infection, injury or pregnancy.
 Thyroid or liver disease and genetic conditions can affect the level of blood
lipids.
 Drugs as corticosteroids, estrogen, androgens, oral contraceptives, diuretics,
antipsychotics (haloperidol), antibiotics and niacin can also affect the blood
lipid level.
 N.B:
 If blood sample is collected after a fatty meal,
serum will appear turbid (lipemic) due to high
content of chylomicrons.
The Genius in Biochemistry

Practical Module Cardio Pulmonary

Dr. Mohamed Agha

 3

 After a couple of hours of eating a fatty meal, plasma will be cleared by
means of lipoprotein lipase (clearing factor).
 Measuring blood cholesterol level does not need fasting as Cholesterol level is
not affected by single meal but affected by long term pattern of eating (change
from high fat diet to low fat diet for several weeks).
 Hyperlipidemia: It is the condition of abnormally elevated levels of any or all lipids and/or
lipoproteins in the blood.
 Hyperlipidemia is a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerosis and
cardiovascular disease including coronary heart disease → Both of disorders
involving hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia.
A. Primary hyperlipidemia
 Probably genetically based, but the genetic defects are known for only a
minority of patients.
B. Secondary hyperlipidemia
 Result from diseases such as
 Diabetes.
 Thyroid disease.
 Renal disorders.
 Liver disorders.
 Cushing's syndrome.
 Obesity, alcohol consumption, estrogen administration.

CHOLESTEROL
 The most abundant sterol in human tissues and fluids.
 Steroid nucleus + eight-carbon-atom hydrocarbon chain numbered 20 to 27.
 Some cholesterol is present as Cholesterol Esters having long chain F.A
attached to OH on C3 in A ring by an ester bond.

The Genius in Biochemistry

Practical Module Cardio Pulmonary

Dr. Mohamed Agha

text: Cardiac enzymes of clinical Importance ( ldh \CK-MB) BY: Dr. Marwa Ibrahim Khedr Assistant lecturer of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology 2014 Myocardial infarction Many patients with myocardial infarction have a typical history of crushing central chest pain , perhaps radiating to the arm or jaw, associated with typical ECG changes . Myocardial infarction can, however, present atypically, or even be clinically silent, particularly in the elderly. typical chest pain is not always due to myocardial infarction. Measurements of plasma enzymes are used to assist in the diagnosis of myocardial infarction. In patients with a typical history and ECG changes of myocardial infarction, enzyme measurements do not contribute to the initial management. Thrombolytic therapy is usually given unless specifically contraindicated; this should be done as soon as possible Plasma cardiac markers of post- myocardial infarction. CK (Total) and CK-MB Troponin (I) AST = aspartate transaminase LDH = lactate dehydrogenase MYOGLOBIN The first marker to increase is the MYGLOBIN , MB isoenzyme of creatine kinase ( CK-MB ) followed by total CK , AST and LDH . CK-MB is the gold standard. Myoglobin It is a low-molecular-weight haem -containing protein. Found in both skeletal and cardiac muscle. Due to its low molecular weight, it is rapidly released from the myocardium upon damage. A typical rise occurs within 2-4 hours after the onset of acute myocardial infarction. This is useful for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. Unfortunately, myoglobin is not cardiac specific , being also found in skeletal muscle, and thus is less useful in the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction unless used in conjunction with other markets. Creatine kinase and CK-MB isoenzyme Creatine kinase acts as a regulator of high-energy phosphate production and utilization within contractile tissues. Cytoplasmic CK is a dimer, composed of M and/or B subunits, which associate forming CK-MM, CK-MB and CK-BB isoenzymes . CK-MM is the main isoenzyme found in striated muscle CK-MB is found mainly in cardiac muscle Trace amounts of CK-MB are foundin skeletal muscle. CK-BB is the predominant isoenzyme found in brain, colon, ileum, stomach and urinary bladder. Serum total CK activity and CK-MB concentration rise in parallel following myocardial injury, starting to increase 4–6h after injury, reaching peak serum concentrations after 12–24h and returning to baseline after 48–72h . Serum CK-MB is more specific for myocardial damage than is serum total CK, which may be elevated in many conditions where skeletal muscle is damaged. An increase in CK-MB in the plasma may not be seen until 4-8 h after the onset of chest pain. When the diagnosis is not obvious, an elevated CK-MB or an increase in CK-MB of more than 15% over a 4-h period, even if both values are within the reference range, are suggestive of myocardial infarction. The detection of a trend by serial measurements, if feasible, may provide more information than single measurements. If CK does not increase in a patient with chest pain, myocardial infarction is unlikely; a failure of an elevated CK to fall suggests that extension of the infarct has occurred. CARDIAC TROPONIN Their function is the regulation of striated and cardiac muscle contraction. Troponin I and TnT appear in the plasma 4-8 hours after symptoms of acute myocardial infarction, and are best measured 12 hours after the start of chest pain. Troponin T may be elevated in patients with chronic renal failure and thus may not be so cardiac-specific. A new marker, ischaemia -modified albumin , is raised in the presence of myocardial ischaemia and may be used in the future in conjunction with conventional cardiac markers. text:
Cardiovascular

Circulatory system: It consists of:
1- Vascular system: heart, arteries, capillaries & veins
2- Lymphatic system.

Heart
The wall of the heart consists of
three layers:
1- Endocardium: inner layer.
2- Myocardium: middle muscular layer.
3- Epicardium: outer layer.

1-Endocardium: consists of:

-Endothelium: simple squamous epithelium.

-Subendothelial connective tissue: which is
continuous with that of the blood vessels
entering and exiting from the heart.
-The sub endocardium: a layer of
connective tissue where branches of the
conducting system are located.

2- Myocardium:
-It is the thickest coat.

-It is composed of cardiac muscle fibers bound together by
connective tissue.

3-Epicardium:

-It is the visceral layer of the pericardium.
-It consists of a simple squamous mesothelium, supported by
loose connective tissue containing the coronary vessels, nerves,
and adipose tissue.

Edited by Dr Aya Ali& R.A.A

 Cardiovascular

Cardiac muscle
•

It is striated & involuntary.

•

Its contraction is initiated by the spontaneous
depolarization of pacemaker cells.

Structure of cardiac muscle LM:
1- Connective tissue: It consists of:




Perimysium: highly vascularized, formed of collagen
and elastic fibers, which are present between the
bundles of cardiac muscle fibers.
Endomysium: a network of reticular fibers surrounds
each muscle fiber.

2- Cardiac muscle fibers:





They are long cylindrical fibers which
branch and anastomose leaving slit-like
spaces between them. Thus, in the same
section, different cuts in cardiac muscle
fibers could be seen (longitudinal,
transverse& oblique).
The fibers show fainter striations than
those seen in skeletal muscle fibers.
Each cardiac muscle fiber consists of
short columnar cells called cardiomyocytes
joined by the intercalated discs that run
transversely across the fiber.

 Each cardiomyocyte has a single,
central & oval nucleus.

Edited by Dr Aya Ali& R.A.A

 Cardiovascular

Structure of cardiac muscle EM:


Myofibrils
1- The myofibrils branch and anastomose thus
they are not perfectly in register with one
another.
2- The pattern of cross striations is identical to
that of skeletal muscle.
3- The myofibrils diverge around the nucleus
leaving the sarcoplasm at the nuclear poles
containing various organelles & inclusions
(numerous mitochondria, glycogen granules and
lipofuscin pigments).



T tubules:
Definition: inward extensions of the extracellular space at
the sarcolemma.
• Characteristic features: large & numerous.
• Site: at the Z line.
• Function:
 Excitation-contraction coupling.
 Provide additional surface area for exchange of
metabolites between cardiac muscle fibers and the
extracellular space.
•



Sarcoplasmic reticulum:
•
•



It is less organized than the skeletal muscle.
It consists of narrow anastomosing sarcotubules without
the continuous terminal cisternae that encircle the whole
myofibrils, instead, scattered small expansions of
sarcotubules are in close apposition with the T tubules
forming diads.

Intercalated discs:
•
•
•
•

Definition: specialized junctions of cell membranes
of adjacent cardiomyocytes.
Site: extend across the fiber at the level of the Z
lines.
Shape: stepwise.
Structure:

Edited by Dr Aya Ali& R.A.A

 Cardiovascular

1- Transverse portion:

Site: runs across the fibers perpendicular to the
myofilaments at the level of the Z line.
 Structure: It is formed of fascia (zonula adherens)
and macula adherens ( desmosomes attached to
desmin)
 Function: provide strong adhesion between the
adjacent cardiomyocytes.


2- Longitudinal portion:

 Site: runs parallel to the myofilaments
 Structure: many gap junctions.
 Function: allow rapid spread of excitation between the
adjacent cardiomyocytes.

Types of cardiomyocytes
1- Contractile cardiomyocytes:




Definition: They are the ordinary
cardiomyocytes that form the majority of the
myocardium of the atria and ventricles.
Function: contraction.

Edited by Dr Aya Ali& R.A.A

text:
B- Respiratory portion
1- Respiratory bronchioles:
They are lined by cuboidal ciliated epithelium with
Clara cells where the cilia gradually disappear.
The alveoli arise from their walls as outpocketings.
2- Alveolar duct: They are elongated branching
passages arising from the distal ends of the respiratory
bronchioles.
 Their walls are lined by simple squamous epithelium
and surrounded by thin lamina propria containing
elastic fibers and smooth muscle fibers.
3- Alveolar sac: They arise from the distal ends of the
alveolar ducts where a cluster of alveoli open into each
alveolar sac.

 Alveoli
• These are the structural and functional
units in which gaseous exchange
between inspired air and blood takes
place.
• They are minute air spaces which open
into the respiratory bronchiole, alveolar
ducts and alveolar sacs.
• They are responsible for the spongy
structure of the lungs.

 Anatomic consideration of blood vessels
Arteries:
• wall of the aorta and large arteries contain a relatively large amount of elastic tissues.
• transport blood under high pressure to the tissues.
stretched during systole and recoil during diastole to prevent marked increase or
decrease in the ABP.
Arterioles: (resistance vessels)
• The walls of the arterioles contain a relatively more smooth muscle fibers
• innervated by vasoconstrictor noradrenergic sympathetic nerves (the arterioles of the
skeletal muscles are innervated by vasodilator cholinergic sympathetic fibers).
• control valves (Control blood release into capillaries).
Their muscular walls can be constricted or dilated, giving them the capability of
markedly altering blood flow to the capillaries in response to changing tissue needs.
• They are the main site of resistance to blood "resistance vessels".
Capillaries: (exchange site)
The openings of the true capillaries are surrounded by minute smooth muscle
precapillary sphincter, which is not innervated but can respond to local and circulating
vasoactive Capillary bed mediators.
• Capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional and surface area.
• They are thin-walled, consisting of a single layer of endothelial cells surrounded by
basal lamina.
They are the site of exchange of nutrients, water and gases.
Venules:
• collect blood from capillaries and gradually coalesce into progressively larger veins. Veins:
The veins ("capacitance vessels".)
• as large volume of blood can be added to the venous system without a large rise in
venous pressure.
• constricted on sympathetic stimulation or by local vasoactive mediators.
• A variation in venous tone is very important in the circulatory adjustments.
• Constricting veins reduces the venous capacity and increases return of blood to heart.
• This will increase the effective circulating blood volume
• Volumes of blood in different parts of the circulation:
• 84% of the total blood volume is in systemic circulation, distributed as follow:
64% in the vein
13% in the arteries

Ra vL/r4

a-increased resistance..increases upstream pressure and decreases downstream pressure.

If in series:
RT=R1+R2+R3..
If in parallel
RT=1/R1+1/R2+1/R3
SO Total resistance is less in parallel than series
• Arterioles is the main site of resistance, not capillaries as they are in parallel.
• Doubling diameter will decrease resistance to 16 fold.
2-blood viscosity(V)
• It is a property of the fluid
• The greater the viscosity, the greater the resistance
• The prime determinant of viscosity is haematocrit (imp).
• Also affected by plasma proteins(fibrinogen and globulin)
3-vessel length(L)
• IF length doubles, the resistance doubles
• Vessel length is constat, not a physiological factor
Blood velocity
• The rate of blood flow in a vessel

Vessel compliance :
• Easy stretch not stiff

• They have 70% of blood resevoir

Cardio-Pulmonary Module

12

D efi ni tio n
The ECG is a record of the electrical changes (depolarization and repolarization)
that occur in the heart.

Principle

- As cardiac impulse passes through the heart, electrical currents spread into
tissue surrounding heart and small proportion spreads all the way to the surface
of the body.
- If electrodes are placed on the skin on opposite sides of the heart, electrical
potentials generated by these currents can be recorded. The record of these
potential fluctuations during the cardiac cycle is the Electrocardiogram (ECG).

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Gawad

 Cardio-Pulmonary Module

13

The electrocardiograph
It is the instrument which amplifies and records these electrical potentials on a moving paper
strip.

EC G e l ectr od es

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Gawad

 Cardio-Pulmonary Module

14

EC G le a d s
In order to get a complete picture about the electrical activity of the various parts of the heart, the
electrodes are placed on different positions of the body. These recording elec trodes systems which are 12
in number are referred to as leads. There are two types of leads: Bipolar leads and unipolar leads.

I- Bipolar leads (3 standard limb leads)
- two active electrodes are used (i.e. bipolar recording):
a- one connected to the negative terminal of the electrocardiograph
b- The other one connected to the positive terminal.
- Number: 3 in number
- Sites: placed on the right arm, the left arm, and the left leg.
- Function: each records the differences in potential between two limbs.

- These 3 leads form an equilateral triangle surrounding the heart. This triangle is called
Einthoven's triangle.

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Gawad

15

II- Unipolar leads
- The exploring electrode: an active electrode connected to the positive terminal of the
instrument.
- The indifferent electrode: connected to the negative terminal, that stays at zero
potential.
- Unipolar because the potential at the site of the exploring electrodes is compared to
zero, not to the potential at another site.
- Number: 9 in number
- Types:

A- 3 Unipolar limb leads

B- 6 Unipolar chest leads

- Unipolar because the potential at the site of the exploring electrodes is compared to
zero, not to the potential at another site.

A- Unipolar limb leads:
- Number: 3 leads.
- Sites: VR (right arm), VL (left arm) and VF (left foot).
- Augmented limb leads: (aVR, aVL, aVF). (The augmented limb leads increase the
size of potential by 50% without any change in configuration from non-augmented
record).
- Function: recordings between one limb and the other two limbs.

PROPERTIES OF THE CARDIAC MUSCLE
I] Cardiac Automaticity (Rhythmicity):
Definition: Automaticity is the ability of cardiac cells to spontaneously depolarize and
generate an action potential.

Origin of rhythmicity (heartbeat):
- The heart is a myogenic organ; it does not need nerve stimulation to initiate its
contraction. The heartbeat originates in the Sino-atrial node (SA node).
- SAN:
✓ Site: located at the junction of the superior vena cava with the right atrium.
✓ Frequency of discharge: It contains specialized cells, which discharge
spontaneously and rapidly at a frequency of 60-100 per minute (automaticity or
rhythmicity).
✓ Excitability:
o It is the most excitable among the myocardial cells
o Why? Because it has less negative potential than the rest.
o Therefore it is the normal cardiac pacemaker: Its rate of discharge
determines the heart rate (HR) (see later – slow action potential).
✓ Unstable RMP: It spontaneously depolarized during diastole causing what is
called pre-potential or diastolic depolarization (see later–slow action potential).

N.B.

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Gawad

 Cardio-Pulmonary Module

4

The cardiac action potentials:
The principal types of cardiac action potentials are the slow and fast types:
1- The slow type occurs in nodal system:
✓ SA node "pacemaker potential" which is responsible for cardiac automaticity.
✓ AV node.
2- The fast type occurs in:
✓ Atrial myocytes.
✓ Ventricular myocytes.
✓ Purkinje cells

1- Fast action potential (for myocardial cell) and its Ionic bases:
Fast response depends mainly on voltage gated Na channels and consists of five phases:

Na-K pump works

● Phase O: Initial Rapid depolarization & overshoot (a fast response):
✓ initial rapid depolarization: caused by opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels
leading to rapid Na influx.
✓ positive overshoot, upstroke, +20mv: it is the top of the curve where the
potential difference reverses (i.e. potential of the interior of the cell exceeded
that of the exterior)
● Phase 1: The early partial rapid repolarization:
✓ caused by activation of voltage-gated K+ channels causing outward (efflux) of K+
● Phase 2: The plateau:
✓ the flat portion of the curve persists for about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds.
✓ caused by: depolarization opens voltage gated L- type Ca++ channels causing
Ca++ influx, that is balanced by the efflux of an equal amount of positive charge
carried by K+.
✓ N.B. The influx of Ca++ triggers the release of Ca++ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum causing
muscle contraction (see later)

Principles of Human Physiology

Properties of cardiac muscle
I- Rhythmicity
• AV bundle is the only muscular connection between atria and ventricles
• Pace = speed
• Intrinsic HR = SAN
• Ectopic pacemakers (any pacemaker other than SAN):
1. AVN with rate 45-60 beat/min
2. Purkinje system with rate 25-40 beat/min (idioventricular rhythm)
• Pacemaker action potential differs from cardiac muscle action potential in the
following:
1. Depolarization phase is mainly due to Cat influx.
2. Depolarization phase is relatively slow to develop. Slow response action potential
3. Action potential is of smaller magnitude; maximum depolarization goes up to +10 mv
4. There is no plateau phase, Repolarization immediately follows depolarization.
• Factors affecting rhythmicity:
1. Factors increasing rhythmicity → increase heart rate:
a) Sympathetic nervous system
b) Temperature: every 1 degree increase in temperature will increase heart rate
by 15 beat per minute.
2. Factors decreasing rhythmicity → decrease heart rate:
a) Vagus nerve

D efi ni tio n
The ECG is a record of the electrical changes (depolarization and repolarization)
that occur in the heart.

Principle

- As cardiac impulse passes through the heart, electrical currents spread into
tissue surrounding heart and small proportion spreads all the way to the surface
of the body.
- If electrodes are placed on the skin on opposite sides of the heart, electrical
potentials generated by these currents can be recorded. The record of these
potential fluctuations during the cardiac cycle is the Electrocardiogram (ECG).

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Gawad

 Cardio-Pulmonary Module

13

The electrocardiograph
It is the instrument which amplifies and records these electrical potentials on a moving paper
strip.

EC G e l ectr od es

Dr. Gawad

 Cardio-Pulmonary Module

14

EC G le a d s
In order to get a complete picture about the electrical activity of the various parts of the heart, the
electrodes are placed on different positions of the body. These recording elec trodes systems which are 12
in number are referred to as leads. There are two types of leads: Bipolar leads and unipolar leads.

I- Bipolar leads (3 standard limb leads)
- two active electrodes are used (i.e. bipolar recording):
a- one connected to the negative terminal of the electrocardiograph
b- The other one connected to the positive terminal.
- Number: 3 in number
- Sites: placed on the right arm, the left arm, and the left leg.
- Function: each records the differences in potential between two limbs.

- These 3 leads form an equilateral triangle surrounding the heart. This triangle is called

II- Unipolar leads
- The exploring electrode: an active electrode connected to the positive terminal of the
instrument.
- The indifferent electrode: connected to the negative terminal, that stays at zero
potential.
- Unipolar because the potential at the site of the exploring electrodes is compared to

- Augmented limb leads: (aVR, aVL, aVF). (The augmented limb leads increase the
size of potential by 50% without any change in configuration from non-augmented
record).
- Function: recordings between one limb and the other two limbs.

text: PRACTICAL I Lung volumes and capacities By Prof dr. Hala Salah Ibrahim Assistant prof. Seham Zakaria Nassar Determination of lung volumes is used to : 1. Assess the efficiency of the respiratory system. 2. Diagnose respiratory diseases. The volumes of inspired and expired air can be estimated by breathing in an apparatus called spirometer . Pulmonary function tests Lung volumes and capacities VC Flow rate FVC Diffusing capacity Water sealed spirometer SPIROMETRY Lung volumes Tidal volume (V T ) is the volume of air inspired or expired in each respiratory cycle during normal quiet breathing i.e. under resting conditions. It is about 500 cc. 2. Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) It is the volume of air which can be inspired by maximal inspiration after a normal inspiration. It is about 3000 cc. IRV 3. Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the volume of air which can be expired by maximal expiration after a normal expiration. It is about 1100 cc. ERV 4. Residual volume (RV) It is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration. It is about 1200 cc. RV LUNG VOLUMES Lung capacities Capacity is a combination of more than one volume 1. Inspiratory capacity (IC) is the volume of air taken by maximal inspiration after a normal expiration. IC = VT + IRV = 500 + 3000 = about 3500 cc. IC 2. Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration. FRC = ERV + RV = 1200 + 1100 = about 2300 cc. FRC 3. Vital capacity (VC) It is the maximum volume of air that can be expelled from lung by a maximal expiration after a maximal inspiration. Slow (relaxed) VC VC Forced VC (FVC) VC = IRV + V T + ERV = 3000 + 500 + 1100 = about 4600 cc. It is a good index for pulmonary efficiency. VC 4. Total lung capacity (TLC) is the volume of air contained in the lungs at the end of maximal inspiration. TLC = IRV + V T + ERV + RV = 3000 + 500 + 1100 + 1200 = about 5800 cc TLC LUNG CAPACITIES Lung volumes and capacities are: Decreased in -The recumbent position than in standing. -Women than in men by about 20-25% . -Small and asthenic persons. -Old age. Increased in -Larger and athletic persons. All lung volumes and capacities are directly measured by the spirometer except RV, FRC & TLC . text: Sections 3 and 4 CVS By: Samah Magdy HEART SOUNDS 1- First heart sound (S1) 2- Second heart sound (S2) 1- Cause: due to sudden closure of aortic and pulmonary valves. The aortic valve (A 2 ) closes before the pulmonary 2- Character: Low pitch of 50Hz, but however, it is relatively higher than the first sound because the semilunar valves are much tight than the AV valves. its sharp like the word DUP. 3-Time: In is volumetric relaxation phase. 4-Duration: 0.11- 0.14 sec. It occurs at the onset of ventricular diastole. 5- Site of hearing: Aortic component (A 2 ): Right 2 nd .inetrcostal space near to sternum. Pulmonary component (P 2 ): Left 2 nd . Intercostal space near the sternum. 3- Third heart sound 4- Fourth heart sound Pulse examination 1- Radial pulse examination A) Getting ready: Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side ( 2 cm proximal to thenar eminence). Place the tips of the index, middle & ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: a. If regular count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. b. If irregular count for 3 min & divide by 3. How to comment on pulse? Importance of arterial pulse examination 1- Rate = Number of beats/minute. ( physiological and pathological variations) 2- Rhythm = Regular or Irregular. 3-Force: determined by ABP . 4- volume: determine pressure wave. 5-Condition of arterial wall= felt or not. 6:special character or form. Other sites for pulse examination Arterial blood pressure (ABP) 1- DEFINITIONS a-Blood pressure : It is the force exerted by the blood against the vessel wall. b-Systolic pressure(SBP): It is the max. pressure occur through out the cardiac cycle= 120 mmHg c-Diastolic pressure(DBP): It is the mini. pressure occur through out the cardiac cycle= 80 mmHg d- Pulse pressure(PP)= SBP- DBP= 40 mmHg e- Mean pressure: pressure throughout the cardiac cycle = DBP+1/3 PP = 93 mmHg which is closer to DBP However, the ’normal values’ differ from person to another High value increases the risk of heart attack and strokes. Low value increases the risk of lower oxygen perfusion e.g. in brains 2- Normal range and physiological variations a- Normal range: Systolic: 90-145 mmHg Diastolic : 60-90 mmHg b- Physiological variations: 1-Age 2- Sex 3-Body built 4- Exercice 5-Emotions 6- Meals 7- sleep c- Measurement (sphygmomanometer) Rubber bag Principle of blood pressure measurement RECOMMENDED BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT TECHNIQUE D- Methods of measurement a- Palpatory method. b- Auscultatory method 1-Palpatory method Measurement Palpatory method : 1-Feel radial artery . 2-raise the pressure in the cuff till you can not feel the pulse any more. 3-Do not move your hand from the pulse area. 4-Decrease the pressure in the cuff slowly till you can feel the pulse back . 5-At this point read the pressure = systolic pressure Determining the palpated systolic pressure and the maximum inflation level While palpating the radial pulse, inflate the cuff until you feel the radial pulse disappear. Note the pressure on the manometer at this point and deflate the cuff. When the cuff is deflated, there is a palpable pulse in the wrist. Figure 15-11. Determining the palpated systolic pressure and the maximum inflation level (MIL). The reason for estimating the palpated systolic pressure and the MIL is to assure that an auscultatory gap does not give the observer a wrong reading. After a rest period of at least 5 minutes, find the MIL. Palpate the radial artery at the wrist (A). Use this pulse to determine when the pressure in the cuff has exceeded the systolic pressure. Then determine the MIL as described in B. Palpatory Method +) The blood pressure can be measured in noisy environment too ADVANTAGES -) Only the systolic pressure can be measured (not DP) DISADVANTAGES -) The technique does not give accurate results for infants and hypotensive patients +) Technique does not require much equipment 2- Auscultatory method Auscultatory method Where to listen for blood pressure sounds From www.images.md 1- Locate the antecubital fossa of the patient’s arm and palpate the brachial artery . This location is the point over which the stethoscope is placed to listen for Korotkov . s sounds later. 2- Wrap the cuff approximately 1 inch above the antecubital fossa. Palpate the brachial artery just medial to and usually under the biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa. Place the bell of the stethoscope directly over this pulse to get the best Korotkoff (K) sounds. 4- Deflate the cuff until the sounds become muffled and then disappear. The disappearance of sound estimate the diastolic pressure ( greater importance?) . 5- Record the blood pressure reading . The Korotkoff sounds are ausculted with a stethoscope Pulse waves that propagate through the brachial artery, generate Korotkoff sounds. There are 5 distinct phases in the Korotkoff sounds, which define SP and DP Kortokov , s sounds Why we do palpatory before auscultatory ? “Auscultatory gap ”: 1- Such a gap is liable to occur in association with very high systolic pressures and aortic disease. 2- sounds appear at Systolic BP 200 mmHg, disappear from 170 to 140 mmHg and reappear at 160 to Diastolic BP. 120 mmHg where it finally disappears. The period of disappearance from 180 to 160 is called the auscultatory gap. 3-could be avoided by raising the pressure in armlet and estimating the SBP by palpatory method . 4- If one raises the pressure in the apparatus, by mistake to a level inside this gap, → NO sound is heard→ giving the belief that the cuff pressure is higher than the systolic pressure, while it is really not, and is actually below it. text:
Intradermal drug injection

INTRADERMAL DRUG INJECTION
STEP/TASK
The equipment
 Non-sterile gloves
 Prescribed medication
 Sterile appropriately sized syringe and needle
 Alcohol swab
 Dry cotton-wool ball
 Sharps box
Getting ready
1. Gather the necessary equipment.
2. Introduce yourself to the patient.
3. Discuss the procedure and obtain consent.
4. Ask the patient if he has any allergies and what happens when he
develops a reaction.
5. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water and dry with a
clean dry cloth (or air dry).
6. Wear the gloves.
Procedure
1. Attach a 21G needle to the syringe and draw up the correct volume of
the drug, making sure to tap out and expel any air.
2. Dispose of the needle and attach a new a 25G needle for ID
administration.
3. Clean the exposed site with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry.
4. Warn the patient to expect a ‘sharp scratch’
Intradermal (ID) injection technique
5. Stretch the skin taut between thumb and forefinger.
6. Hold the needle so that the bevel is uppermost.
7. Insert the needle at a 15 degree angle, almost parallel to the skin.
8. Ensure that the needle is visible beneath the surface of the epidermis.
9. Slowly inject the drug.
10.
A visible (and uncomfortable) bleb should form. If not,
immediately withdraw the needle and start again – you may have
inserted the needle too deeply.
After the procedure
1. Immediately dispose of the needle in the sharps box without
recapping.
2. Ensure that the patient is comfortable.
3. Ask him if he has any questions or concerns.
4. Thank him.
5. Sign the prescription chart and record the date, time, drug, dose, and
injection site in patient’s medical record.

AP

IP

NP

 Intradermal drug injection

AP = Adequately Performed
IP = Inadequately Performed
NP = Not Performed

Administration of Intramuscular
Injection
STEP/TASK
Equipment needed:
 Prescribed medication
 Sterile syringes and needles
 Sterile alcohol swabs.
 Dry cotton-wool ball
Getting ready
1. Gather necessary equipment.
2. Introduce yourself to the patient, tell the patient what is
going to be done.
3. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water and dry
with a clean dry cloth (or air dry).
4. Wear sterile gloves (Optional).
procedure
1. Draw up the prescribed medication for injection into the
syringe:
 By inserting the needle tip until it touches the bottom of the
bottle or vial containing the medication for injection.
 Then pull the plunger of the syringe to draw up the volume
of medication required.
 Withdraw the needle and syringe from the bottle or vial and
expel air bubbles, if present.
 Recap the needle.
2. Check that the drug and dose are correct.
3. Provide for privacy; position and cover patient.
4. Select the appropriate site for injection:
 Quadriceps muscle group of the upper outer thigh; OR
 Upper, outer quadrant of the gluteus muscle group in the
buttock; OR
 Deltoid muscle group (for immunizations).
5. Cleanse injection site with alcohol swab using a circular motion
starting at the center and moving outwards for about 5 cm.
6. Remove needle cover.
7. With your free hand, slightly stretch the skin at the site of
injection.
8. Quickly insert needle at a 90°using a smooth motion.
9. Withdraw the plunger slightly to ensure that the needle is not in
a vessel:
 If the needle is properly placed, inject the medication slowly
with steady pressure for three to five seconds.
 If blood enters needle:
– Remove the needle without injecting the medication and
apply pressure using cotton-wool
– Place a new, sterile needle on the syringe;
– Choose a new site for injection and repeat the procedure.
10. Withdraw the needle in a single smooth motion after

IP

NP

 completing the injection, and apply gentle pressure with a dry
cotton-wool ball.
Post procedure tasks
1. Dispose the needle and syringe into the proper receptacle, do
not recap the used needle.
2. Wash hands with soap and water and dry with a clean dry cloth.

text:
The Art of History Taking
Rationale: Excellent history taking remains absolutely central to best practice in medicine. The
patient must be your primary concern. As a doctor (or medical student), you have a fundamental
duty to understand your patients’ stories, including the background context. You need to learn
what your patients have experienced and what they feel. While every patient’s story is unique, in
most cases doctors can deduce a reasonable diagnosis by listening carefully and asking the right
questions. By narrowing the differential diagnosis (a list of the possible diagnoses suggested by a
set of symptoms or signs), appropriate testing and therapy can be ordered.
Good and effective history taking can:
1. Make diagnosis of some diseases, e.g. epilepsy, migraine and renal colic.
2. Help to direct the physical examination to the appropriate part of the body. For example,
in a patient presenting with a cough the respiratory and cardiovascular systems will need
to be examined.
3. Even if the possible diagnoses are not clear after the history has been taken, it will usually
be obvious which body region or system is affected. This will enable you to direct the
examination and diagnostic tests appropriately.
4. Give a better judgment of the severity and progress of the case.
History taking is a special form of the art of communication. It is the beginning of the good
doctor-patient relationship:

Make it clear that the patient has your whole attention.
Common things towards good communication is to greet the patient, by name if possible.
Don't be angered or shocked by anything he/or she says
Patients must be allowed to tell their story in their own words and in their own way.
When the patient is telling his story, always watch his body language (e.g. face
