text: Sections 3 and 4 CVS By: Samah Magdy HEART SOUNDS 1- First heart sound (S1) 2- Second heart sound (S2) 1- Cause: due to sudden closure of aortic and pulmonary valves. The aortic valve (A 2 ) closes before the pulmonary 2- Character: Low pitch of 50Hz, but however, it is relatively higher than the first sound because the semilunar valves are much tight than the AV valves. its sharp like the word DUP. 3-Time: In is volumetric relaxation phase. 4-Duration: 0.11- 0.14 sec. It occurs at the onset of ventricular diastole. 5- Site of hearing: Aortic component (A 2 ): Right 2 nd .inetrcostal space near to sternum. Pulmonary component (P 2 ): Left 2 nd . Intercostal space near the sternum. 3- Third heart sound 4- Fourth heart sound Pulse examination 1- Radial pulse examination A) Getting ready: Prepare equipment: Watch or clock with a counter for seconds Assist the patient to pronate and slightly fix the forearm. Locate the radial artery just medial to the distal radius and proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side ( 2 cm proximal to thenar eminence). Place the tips of the index, middle & ring fingers just proximal to the patient’s wrist on the thumb side, orienting them over the vessel Push lightly at first, gradually adding pressure till you feel the pulse. Check for regularity: a. If regular count the pulse rate for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. b. If irregular count for 3 min & divide by 3. How to comment on pulse? Importance of arterial pulse examination 1- Rate = Number of beats/minute. ( physiological and pathological variations) 2- Rhythm = Regular or Irregular. 3-Force: determined by ABP . 4- volume: determine pressure wave. 5-Condition of arterial wall= felt or not. 6:special character or form. Other sites for pulse examination Arterial blood pressure (ABP) 1- DEFINITIONS a-Blood pressure : It is the force exerted by the blood against the vessel wall. b-Systolic pressure(SBP): It is the max. pressure occur through out the cardiac cycle= 120 mmHg c-Diastolic pressure(DBP): It is the mini. pressure occur through out the cardiac cycle= 80 mmHg d- Pulse pressure(PP)= SBP- DBP= 40 mmHg e- Mean pressure: pressure throughout the cardiac cycle = DBP+1/3 PP = 93 mmHg which is closer to DBP However, the ’normal values’ differ from person to another High value increases the risk of heart attack and strokes. Low value increases the risk of lower oxygen perfusion e.g. in brains 2- Normal range and physiological variations a- Normal range: Systolic: 90-145 mmHg Diastolic : 60-90 mmHg b- Physiological variations: 1-Age 2- Sex 3-Body built 4- Exercice 5-Emotions 6- Meals 7- sleep c- Measurement (sphygmomanometer) Rubber bag Principle of blood pressure measurement RECOMMENDED BLOOD PRESSURE MEASUREMENT TECHNIQUE D- Methods of measurement a- Palpatory method. b- Auscultatory method 1-Palpatory method Measurement Palpatory method : 1-Feel radial artery . 2-raise the pressure in the cuff till you can not feel the pulse any more. 3-Do not move your hand from the pulse area. 4-Decrease the pressure in the cuff slowly till you can feel the pulse back . 5-At this point read the pressure = systolic pressure Determining the palpated systolic pressure and the maximum inflation level While palpating the radial pulse, inflate the cuff until you feel the radial pulse disappear. Note the pressure on the manometer at this point and deflate the cuff. When the cuff is deflated, there is a palpable pulse in the wrist. Figure 15-11. Determining the palpated systolic pressure and the maximum inflation level (MIL). The reason for estimating the palpated systolic pressure and the MIL is to assure that an auscultatory gap does not give the observer a wrong reading. After a rest period of at least 5 minutes, find the MIL. Palpate the radial artery at the wrist (A). Use this pulse to determine when the pressure in the cuff has exceeded the systolic pressure. Then determine the MIL as described in B. Palpatory Method +) The blood pressure can be measured in noisy environment too ADVANTAGES -) Only the systolic pressure can be measured (not DP) DISADVANTAGES -) The technique does not give accurate results for infants and hypotensive patients +) Technique does not require much equipment 2- Auscultatory method Auscultatory method Where to listen for blood pressure sounds From www.images.md 1- Locate the antecubital fossa of the patient’s arm and palpate the brachial artery . This location is the point over which the stethoscope is placed to listen for Korotkov . s sounds later. 2- Wrap the cuff approximately 1 inch above the antecubital fossa. Palpate the brachial artery just medial to and usually under the biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa. Place the bell of the stethoscope directly over this pulse to get the best Korotkoff (K) sounds. 4- Deflate the cuff until the sounds become muffled and then disappear. The disappearance of sound estimate the diastolic pressure ( greater importance?) . 5- Record the blood pressure reading . The Korotkoff sounds are ausculted with a stethoscope Pulse waves that propagate through the brachial artery, generate Korotkoff sounds. There are 5 distinct phases in the Korotkoff sounds, which define SP and DP Kortokov , s sounds Why we do palpatory before auscultatory ? “Auscultatory gap ”: 1- Such a gap is liable to occur in association with very high systolic pressures and aortic disease. 2- sounds appear at Systolic BP 200 mmHg, disappear from 170 to 140 mmHg and reappear at 160 to Diastolic BP. 120 mmHg where it finally disappears. The period of disappearance from 180 to 160 is called the auscultatory gap. 3-could be avoided by raising the pressure in armlet and estimating the SBP by palpatory method . 4- If one raises the pressure in the apparatus, by mistake to a level inside this gap, → NO sound is heard→ giving the belief that the cuff pressure is higher than the systolic pressure, while it is really not, and is actually below it. Thank you

1

 Chapter 1
Interviewing and Health history interview
Objectives
• Define interviewing.
• Describe the best setting to carry out an interview
• Identify types of questions.
• State use of each type.
• Describe the essentials of an interview.
• Communication skills needed for the interviewer.
Interviewing is one of the best and most common methods of obtaining information in a face to
face situation. The interview provides a situation for specific application of the techniques of
dyadic communication (i-e communication between two persons).
Definition
Interviewing is the interchange of verbal and non-verbal communication between two persons
or more in intention of exchanging information and data relevant to the topics under
consideration.
Interview settings
The setting of an interview is crucial for its success, particularly in terms of privacy and rapportbuilding. It is important to carefully consider the physical environment to ensure comfort and the
removal of any barriers. A counseling interview should be held in the most inviting area
available.

Tools used in interviews
Although questions are the most
important tool used by the interviewers, but interviews are not just a series of questions.
Interviewers often use statements to elicit opinions, feelings, beliefs, and attitudes from the
interviewees. A productive interview typically includes a mix of statements and questions at
the right moments.
Questions can make dyadic communication more accurate. They give feedback and receive
feedback. The interviewer should use an appropriate question, he has to be careful about the
wording of each question he asks and the type of question he uses at the appropriate time.
2

 The wording of the questions
The wording of the question is important, words must be chosen carefully as words can influence
how a person answers. The questions should:
Only be interpreted in one way.
Be short and have simple vocabulary suitable to the level of interviewee.
Be applicable so that the interviewee can answer them correctly.
Types of questions
1) Open- ended questions:
Usually helps you to obtain general information, they begin with phrases such as:
"How do you feel about ……………….?"
"What symptoms brought you to the hospital?"
"Can you describe your pain……?"
After the person has expressed some ideas, the interviewer might also use statements as:
"Please tell me more about your pain".
"It is interesting. Could you tell me more?"
Such statements allow people to respond freely. It is through this type of questions and
statements you can obtain more information and personal feelings and attitudes may be brought
to light.
2) Simple direct (close ended questions):
These are focused questions that are answered by: Yes or No.
Or
Eliciting single or few words as answers.
Close ended questions are used as a follow up to open ended questions to clarify or explore
more specific points.
Close ended questions do not:
• Give room to discussion.
• Show the full range of opinions, feelings, or attitudes a person has on the subject.
Examples
"Does the pain go anywhere?"
"Where did you deliver your baby?"
Remember
Use Open-to-Closed Cone
Closed direct questions interspersed with open ended questions give the interviewers much
more information.

3

 Questions that should be avoided
1) Leading questions:
Leading questions will lead the person to give only one answer. They make people give onesided answers. They are dangerous to use in interviews because interviewers will always agree
and rarely reveals their true opinions. These may suggest to the patient the desired answers.
Examples
"You do not miss any doses of your medication, do you?"
"Do not you think that …………?"
"Isn't it true …?"
"Would not it be better if …?"
"Shouldn't you have…?"
2) Double- barrel questions/ For

text: Communication step II Tutorial 1 Chapter 1 Interviewing and health history interview Objectives Define interviewing. Describe the best setting to carry out an interview Identify types of questions. State use of each type. Describe the essentials of an interview. Communication skills needed for the interviewer. Definition Interviewing is the interchange of verbal and non-verbal communication between two persons or more in intention of exchanging information and data relevant to the topics under consideration . Interviewing uses questions and statements to encourage people to supply information The Use of Open-to-Closed Cone of questions The effective strategy to get health history is: Starting with open question to give rich detailed information at the start before moving to the closed question to cover specific and important information Do not move to closed questions too early in the interview (prematurely) "What symptoms brought you to the hospital?" "Does the pain go anywhere?" Probing question is a form of closed question Questions that should be avoided 1) Leading questions : Leading questions will lead the person to give only one answer. may suggest to the patient the desired answers . E.g “are you feeling a little better since starting your antibiotic?” How you ask this question in a non- leading way? “how are you feeling since you start antibiotics” ( it is a probing question ) 2) Double- barrel questions Double-barrel questions are two questions in one E.g "Do you eat fish or meat?" Questions that should be avoided 3) Double- negative questions: are questions that use two negatives to indicate a positive statement E.g "Do not you think it is not a wise policy to have a doctor in every health center?" 4) Embarrassing or sensitive questions : E.g "Did you ever have a venereal disease?“ 5) Jargon-filled questions E.g "Has a physician ever done for you an abdominocentesis ?“ 6) Complex questions: Not simple E.g "When we collect enough data on the problems of this district and the available resources in the community, do you think that building a center is more preferable than organizing outreach activities?” 7) Inappropriate question E.g "How many cigarettes have you smoked since you have started smoking?" (Impossible to answer ) Essentials of an interview 1) Knowledge of the topic: 2) Temperament ( مزاج ) avoids bias, prejudice, and bad temper . 3) Listening and observing : Active listening to all that is being said, observes non-verbal reactions, and interprets verbal and non-verbal messages 4) Eye contact: 5 ) Good interviewer: should be on time , have an objective for the interview, aware of all the prerequisites for effective communication promote a relaxed atmosphere and make the interview comfortable, accepting the person's frame of reference , his level of knowledge , past experiences and interest. He should be direct, honest, respectful, polite, friendly and empathetic showing concern and behave according to the culture. The functions of the medical interview (3 functions) 1. Build a relation with the patient and promote it: 2. Determine and monitor the nature of the problem: 3. Educate patients on: Determine the problem Patient Education nature of the problem diagnostic procedures treatment plan compliance/adherence improved outcome 1. Build a relation with the patient and promote it: a. Non-verbal skills and behaviors: paying attention , facial expression, b . Show that you are empathetic .: Empathetic look, Using reflection statement (observed feeling in the patient ) : Dr. "You look upset to day". Using legitimation (validation ) تصديق : Dr. " I can really understand why you were upset". Indicate your personal support : Dr .: "If you need to contact me for anything please do so“ Build partnership: Dr .: "We have talked about your problem. We can now work together to find some solutions ". Be respectful to the patient and his problems : Empathetic statements versus non empathetic Patient: “I have nothing left to live for, can't you just end this now? Dr:“I'm so sorry, physician aid in dying is not legal in this country” Although this answer might be correct, it does not address the emotional content of the statement. Patient: “I have nothing left to live for, can't you just end this now? Dr:I know how hard you have worked to stay as healthy as possible. this is example of empathy statement, The components of health history interview 1. Chief complaint or reasons for attending: 2. History of present illness: further explore the chief complaint 3. Review of systems: head-to- toe- questioning of presence or absence of symptoms. 4. Past history : surgical history, childhood illness, obstetric history 5. Medication history: medications prescribed by the physician, over-the counter drugs and herbal products. 6. Health maintenance/ Immunization : screening tests as Pap smear, mammograms 7. Family history: to identify potential risk factors for a patient 8. Personal and social history: social background, housing condition, life style and behaviors ; tobacco , alcohol and substance use. The health history interview I- Opening the interview 1 . Introduce yourself. 2. Establishing aims of the interview. 3. Obtain patient consent . 4. Establish initial rapport. 5. Establish patient comfort . 6. Remove barriers to communication 1- Introducing your -self to a patient and your role 2. Establishing aims of interview 3. Obtaining patient consent Statement: -Good morning. My name is ……… I am in charge of this center . I need to take a detailed history of your condition -Well do you have few minutes to answer a couple of questions ? Good morning. My name is ……… I am a medical student. Please to meet you The Professor asked me to take a detailed medical history from you -Can we talk for a few minutes? 4. Establish initial rapport Using reflection and legitimation statement 5. Establishing patient's comfort. Statements: Before we start talking, let me raise the head of the bed. Before I ask

text: Communication step II Tutorial 2 Chapter 2& chapter 3 Instructing and Educating individuals Objectives • Describe instructing patients during physical examination and Lab investigations • Explain importance of prescribing and instructing patients skillfully. • Describe essentials in giving information and instructions related to patients concerns • Describe how to share bad news with a patient. • Describe the clinical significance of health education . • Explain how people change . • Describe how a doctor educates his patient about his illness. • Explain how patient's education can be integrated into a medical encounter. Instructing patient during physical examination Instructing the patient during a physical examination Dr.: "Ok Haj Samy , let us examine you now. I want to listen to your chest. Can you take off your shirt and sit on the bed." Patient : "Fine.“ Instruction given : Ask the nurse or your assistant or a family member to help the patient undress Ask your patient to lie down on the bed Make sure that your hands are not cold Dr.: "Now, I will listen to your chest. Just relax and breathe normally. Good. Now take a deep breath and hold….Good. Again take a deep breath and hold…. Perfect. Your chest seems ok! Instruction given: Explain each step of examination to the patient whether this is a chest, abdominal, rectal or vaginal examination Doctor pauses Dr.: "Just lie down flat on your back with your arms near your body and your head on the pillow. Good, now I need to feel your abdomen. Just relax. Do you feel any pain here?" Instruction given: Explain each step of examination Patient: "No." Dr.: "What about here or here..?" Patient: "None. I feel no pain” Dr.: "Fine, you are doing very well. Now I will do my last examination. It is a little uncomfortable but it is important for the pain you feel. Doctor pauses Dr.: "Please pull your trousers and underpants towards your knees. Good. Now, I want you to lie on your left side facing the walls and your knees towards your stomach. Good. Now I will insert a gloved finger into your back passage. Good!! You are doing very well! You can get dressed now.“ Instruction given: Explain each step of examination You can see that the doctor avoided using medical terms and showed respect and empathetic skills. Instructing the patient during a physical examination Q1 What should be communicated to the patient during any examination, as instructed by the doctor? A) "Do not worry about what's happening." B) "Do not ask any questions while I examine you." C) "I will explain each step of the examination I perform." D) "Keep quiet; this is a sensitive procedure." C Q2 How does explaining each step of the examination to the patient benefit the process? A) It lengthens the examination time unnecessarily. B) It reduces the likelihood of patient anxiety and promotes cooperation. C) It confuses the patient with too much information. D) It distracts from the examination. B Instructions related to investigations Instructions related to investigations Confirm your preliminary diagnosis . Refer your patient for laboratory investigations. Tell your patient what and why investigations are required and their importance . Indicate when they should be carried out. Give the patient a printed list of investigations needed. Give him/her the date for the next appointment . You will need to discuss the results of the investigation and the diagnosis you will make Writing Prescriptions Prescriptions Need good written communication skills. All prescriptions should be: Readable Complete Clear and specific Poor communication and poor hand writing can cause medication errors. The deadly handwritten prescription El- Ahram 9 November 2019 A 24 year old man complaining of constipation consulted a doctor who prescribed him a laxative ( Laxin ), 3 times a day for a week. The prescription was badly written , the pharmacist interpreted the drug to be (Lanoxin) a cardiac drug that is extremely toxic for the cardiac muscle if administered beyond the safe dose ( one tablet per day for 5 days , then stop for 2 days, then resume the drug ). The patient died as he took the wrong drug 3 times daily for a week. He died as a result of a careless doctor who wrote unclear prescription and a pharmacist who did not perceive the seriousness of the situation and inquired about the main complaint of the patient before giving the wrong drug. This case study indicates that: The doctor who prescribed the medication did not properly educate his patient. So, the patient did not remember the name of the medication. The pharmacist did not inquire about the indication of the medication that he could not read. He should have asked the patient: " Why did your doctor prescribe this medication ? Also, he should have revised the strength and dose of the medication he gave which did not match the dose prescribed by the physician. The pharmacist should have telephoned the doctor or asked the patient to go back to his doctor and write a clear prescription. The importance of using the computer in writing medical prescriptions to avoid bad hand writing. Also, others recommend writing the prescription in two languages Oral instruction to the patient Use clear words and expressions . Use few words . State the message in a consistent way . Be real and say what you mean. Be polite and considerate . Make sure that he/she understood your message. After giving your instructions ask your patient to repeat what you have stated . Ask your patient if he/she has any questions and then thank him/her. As a doctor you may also allow your patient to record your oral instructions on their mobile. Breaking Bad/Sad News (9 steps) 1. Prepare for the discussion. 2. Make an introductory statement. 3. State the news using clear, concise language. 4. Wait for the patient reaction . 5. Reflect the response of the patient back. 6. Legitimize the patient's reaction. 7. Explore the cause of the patient's reaction. 8. Provide realistic hope . 9. B

✓ Questions are the most important tool as they make communication more accurate.
They give and receive feedback.
✓ Interviewers use statements to elicit opinions, feelings, beliefs from the interviewees.
✓ A good interview includes a mix of statements and questions.

Wording of the questions
✓ The questions should only be interpreted in one way, short with simple vocabulary
and applicable so that the interviewee can answer them correctly.

Types of questions
1) Open-ended questions:
✓ To obtain general information.
• E.g. "How do you feel about ...?”, "What symptoms brought you to the hospital?"
2) Simple direct (close ended questions):
✓ Focused questions that are answered by: (Yes or No) Or eliciting single or few words.
✓ Used as follow up to open ended questions to explore more specific points.
✓ Close ended questions do not allow discussion nor show the full range of opinions.
• E.g. "Does the pain go anywhere?", "Where did you deliver your baby?"
Use Open-to-Closed Cone
Start with open question* to give detailed information before moving to the closed
question to cover specific and important information
1

 Step II Communication

Summary and question bank

Questions that should be avoided
1) Leading questions:* Lead the person to give only one-sided answer and rarely reveal
his true opinions.
• "You do not miss any doses of your medication, do you?"
Instead say: “how is your regularity on your medication?”
• "Don’t you think that ……?" / "Isn't it true ……?" / "Wouldn’t it be better if ……?"
2) Double-barrel questions/ Forced-choice questions: Limit the choice of answers
although the person may have different opinion. Two questions in one containing words
as “either, therefore, both & or”.
• "Would you prefer to deliver in a governmental or a private hospital?"
Instead say: “Where would you prefer to deliver?”
3) Double- negative questions: Use two negatives to indicate a positive statement.
• "Do not you think it is not a wise policy to have a doctor in every health center?"
4) Embarrassing* or sensitive questions: Blunt questions may offend or hurt the person.
• "Did you ever have a venereal disease?"
5) Jargon-filled questions: Contain words that may be unfamiliar to respondent either
technically or slang. ‫عامية‬
• "Has a physician ever done an abdominocentesis*?" Medical term is jargon*.
Instead say: "Has a physician stuck a needle in your abdomen to take water out?"
6) Complex questions: Simplify the question as much as you can.
• E.g. "When we collect enough data on the problems of this district, do you think
that building a center is more preferable than organizing outreach activities?”
7) Inappropriate question: Questions that the respondents cannot answer correctly,
because: they cannot remember/ of the language / it requests an attitude they haven’t.
• E.g. "How many cigarettes you smoked since you started?" (Impossible to answer)

Essentials of an interview)‫(محاور جيد غير متحيز يعرف عن الموضوع يستمع جيدا ويتواصل بصريا‬
1) Knowledge of the topic.
2

 Step II Communication

Summary and question bank

2) Temperament (‫)عدم التحيز أو إصدار أحكام( )مزاج‬
✓ Interviewer avoids bias, prejudice, and bad temper. He also does not make judgments.
3) Listening and observing:
✓ Active listening to all that is being said.
✓ Observing non-verbal reactions.
✓ Interpreting verbal and nonverbal messages in the context of the discussion.
4) Eye contact.
5) Good interviewer:
✓ A trained interviewer should be on time, have an objective for the interview, aware of
the prerequisit

text: Revision – endocrine glands By Prof. Dr. Abdelghany hassan Abdelghany Professor and head of department of anatomy and embryology Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University Pituitary gland It is an endocrine gland. It lies in the hypophyseal fossa of the sphenoid bone. Sella turcica It is a depression in the body of sphenoid. It is formed of : 1- hypophyseal fossa. 2- tuberculum sellae (anterior to the fossa). 3- dorsum sellae (posterior to the fossa ). tuberculum sellae dorsum sellae hypophyseal fossa Pituitary gland It is connected to the hypothalamus (tuber cinerium ) by the pituitary stalk (infundibulum). It has 2 lobes; anterior and posterior separated by the hypophyseal cleft. Pituitary gland Relations : Anteriorly : tuberculum sellae , sphenoidal air sinus. Posteriorly : dorsum sellae . tuberculum sellae dorsum sellae hypophyseal fossa Pituitary gland Relations : Superiorly : diaphragma sellae (a dural fold covering the pituitary gland and is pierced by the infundibulum), optic chiasma . Inferiorly : sphenoidal air sinus in the body of sphenoid, nasopharynx . Laterally : cavernous sinus. Test yourself Which of the following structures lies anterior to the pituitary gland? Dorsum sellae . Tuberculum sellae . Diaphragma sellae . Cavernous sinus. Test yourself Which of the following structures lies superior to the pituitary gland? Sphenoidal air sinus. Tuberculum sellae . Optic chiasma . Cavernous sinus. Development of the pituitary gland It develops from 2 ectodermal origins : 1- buccal origin : roof of the stomodium (mouth cavity) which is ectodermal. 2- cranial origin : floor of the diencephalon (ectodermal). Buccal premordium (origin) Ranthke’s pouch develops from the roof of the stomodium and elongates forming a stalk. The anterior wall of the pouch thickens to form the distalis . The posterior wall thins out to form pars intermedia . The stalk of ranthke’s pouch degenerates. Cranial premordium Pars nervosa develops from the diencephalon and its stalk is called infundibulum. Pars nervosa and pars intermedia will form the posterior lobe connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum. Pituitary gland Pars distalis gives the pars tuberalis that winds around the pars nervosa. Pars distalis and pars tuberalis form the anterior lobe. Congenital abnormalities 1- agenesis of the gland. 2- pharyngeal pituitary gland due to failure of ascent of ranthk’s pouch. Congenital abnormalities 3- cranio -pharyngeal canal due to failure of degeneration of the stalk of Ranthke’s pouch . Test yourself Which of the following will form the anterior lobe of pituitary gland? Pars nervosa and pars distalis . Pars intermedia and pars tuberalis . Pars distalis and pars tuberalis . Pars nervosa and pars intermedia . Test yourself What is the cause of craniopharyngeal canal? Failure of formation of Ranthke’s pouch. Failure of ascent of Ranthke’s pouch. Failure of formation of pars nervosa. Failure of degeneration of the stalk of Ranthke’s pouch. Test yourself What is the cause of pharyngeal pituitary gland? Failure of formation of Ranthke’s pouch. Failure of ascent of Ranthke’s pouch. Failure of formation of pars nervosa. Failure of degeneration of the stalk of Ranthke’s pouch. Thyroid gland Thyroid gland Site : lower part of the front and sides of the neck. Vertebral level : C5 to T1. It is covered by a capsule of pretracheal fascia which is attached to the cricoid cartilage (larynx). So, thyroid gland moves with deglutition. Thyroid gland Shape : butterfly having 2 lobes (right and left) connected by an isthmus. Occasionally, pyramidal lobe (excessive thyroid tissue from thyroglossal duct) extends from the upper border of the isthmus. Each lobe extends from the oblique line of thyroid cartilage to the fifth tracheal ring. Structure of thyroid gland Each lobe has : Apex. Base. 3 surfaces : superficial, medial and posterior. The isthmus has upper and lower borders, anterior and posterior surfaces. Relations of thyroid lobe Superficial surface : skin, superficial fascia with platysma muscle, sternomastoid , sternothyroid , superior belly of omohyoid muscles and pretracheal fascia. Medial surface : above : pharynx, larynx and external laryngeal nerve. below : esophagus, trachea and recurrent laryngeal nerve. Relations of thyroid lobe Posterior surface : parathyroid glands and carotid sheath (containing common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve). Relations of isthmus Anterior surface : skin, superficial fascia, pretracheal fascia, sternohyoid and sternothyroid . Posterior relations : tracheal rings (2,3,4 ). Arterial supply 1- superior thyroid artery : branch of the external carotid artery. 2- inferior thyroid artery : branch of thyrocervical trunk (of 1 st part of subclavian artery). 3- thyroidea ima artery : branch of arch of aorta or brachiocephalic artery. Test yourself Why does the thyroid gland move with deglutition? As its capsule is derived from pretracheal fascia. As it lies near the larynx. As it lies near the pharynx. As it lies deep to the infrahyoid muscles . Test yourself Where does the thyroid gland lie? Upper border of thyroid cartilage to 5 th tracheal ring. Oblique line of thyroid cartilage to 5 th tracheal ring. Oblique line of thyroid cartilage to 6 th tracheal ring. Upper border of thyroid cartilage to 6 th tracheal ring. Venous drainage 1- superior thyroid vein : drains into internal jugular vein. 2- middle thyroid vein : drains into internal jugular vein . 3- inferior thyroid vein : drains into left innominate vein. Nerve supply Sympathetic : from superior, middle and inferior cervical sympathetic ganglia. Parasympathetic : vagus nerve. Applied anatomy Superior thyroid artery runs with the external laryngeal nerve. Inferior thyroid artery runs with the recurrent laryngeal nerve . Test yourself Opposite which vertebrae does the thyroid gland lie? C 6 - T 1. C 4 to T 1. C 6 to C 7. C 5 - T 1. Test yourself What is the origin of superior thyroid artery? Common carotid art

text: Revision By Prof. Dr. Abdelghany Hassan Abdelghany Professor and head of department of Anatomy and embryology Faculty of medicine, Alexandria University Postgraduate professor, Tufts University, MA,USA Pelvic muscles Piriformis : in the posterior wall of the pelvis. Obturator internus : in the side wall of the pelvis. Levator ani and coccygeus : the pelvic floor. Piriformis Origin : pelvic surface of sacral pieces 2,3,4. Insertion : top of the greater trochanter of the femur. Nerve supply : S1,2. Action : lateral rotation of hip joint. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic notch . Pelvic muscles Origin : inner side of obturator membrane. Insertion : medial side of the greater trochanter of the femur. Nerve supply : nerve to obturator internus . Action : lateral rotation of hip joint. It leaves the pelvis through the lesser sciatic notch . MCQ Which muscle passes through the greater sciatic foramen? Obturator internus . Levator ani . Piriformis . Coccygeus . MCQ Which muscle passes through the lesser sciatic foramen? Obturator internus . Levator ani . Piriformis . Coccygeus . Pelvic floor It is formed of 2 muscles on each side : Anterior : levator ani . Posterior : coccygeus . obturator fascia : covers the inner side of obturator internus muscle. anocccygeal raphe : extends from the tip of the coccyx to the anorectal junction. Levator ani Origin : body of the pubis, tendinous line of obturator fascia and ischial spine. The muscle has 3 parts : 1- puborectalis : muscle fibers pass backwards forming with fibers of the opposite side a U-shaped sling around the anorectal junction. Levator ani 2- pubococcygeus : muscle fibers pass backwards to be attached to the perineal body, tip of the coccyx. some fibers pass across the side of the prostate ( levator prostate) or side of urethra and vagina ( pubovaginalis ). Levator ani 3- iliococcygeus : muscle fibers pass backwards to be attached to the side of the coccyx and anococcygeal raphe. It lies inferior to the pubococcygeus m uscle. Levator ani Nerve supply : S 3,4. Action : 1- support of the prostate. 2- sphincter of the vagina. 3- support of the pelvic viscera. 4- increase of intrabdominal pressure. Clinical notes - During labour , there should be support of the perineum as the pubovaginalis fibers and the perineal body may be torn with widening of the gap between the muscle fibers of both sides and prolapse of the uterus. Coccygeus Origin : pelvic surface of the ischial spine. Insertion : last piece of sacrum and first piece of coccyx. N.B. it is the pelvic side of the sacrospinous ligament. Nerve supply : S4,5. Action : support of the pelvic viscera. MCQ Which muscle lies in the posterior wall of the pelvis? Obturator internus . Levator ani . Piriformis . Coccygeus . MCQ Which muscle lies in the lateral wall of the pelvis? Obturator internus . Levator ani . Piriformis . Coccygeus . MCQ Which muscles are attached to the ischial spine? Obturator internus and piriformis . Levator ani and coccygeus . Piriformis and levator ani . Coccygeus and obturator internus . MCQ Which muscle represents the pelvic surface of the sacrospinous ligament? Iliococcygeus . Coccygeus . Levator ani . D. Pubococygeus . Internal iliac artery - Origin : one of the 2 terminal branches of the common iliac artery. - Course : - It passes downwards and backwards till the upper border of the greater sciatic foramen where it divides into anterior and posterior branches. Branches of internal iliac artery - Branches of anterior division : 1- Obturator artery. 2- Internal pudendal artery. 3- Inferior gluteal artery. 4- Umbilical artery that gives superior vesical branches. 5- Inferior vesical artery (in males) that is replaced by the vaginal artery in females. 6- uterine artery in females. 7- Middle rectal artery. Branches of internal iliac artery - Branches of posterior division : 1- Iliolumbar artery. 2- Lateral sacral arteries . 3- Superior gluteal artery. MCQ Which artery is a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? Superior gluteal. Iliolumbar . Inferior vesical . Lateral sacral. MCQ Which artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery? Inferior gluteal. Iliolumbar . Internal pudendal . Umbilical. MCQ Where does the internal iliac artery terminate? Opposite the ischial spine. 5 th lumbar vertebra. Upper border of greater sciatic foramen. Lower border of lesser sciatic foramen. Median sacral artery - Origin : at the termination of the abdominal aorta at L4 . - Course : - It passes in front of L5, sacrum and coccyx . Termination : in front of the coccyx where it forms a swelling called the glomus coccygeum . - Branches : 1- 5 th pair of lumbar arteries. 2- Sacral branches. 3- Rectal branches. Internal iliac vein - Origin : at the upper border of the greater sciatic notch . - Termination : it joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein . - Tributaries : 1- Obturator vein. 2- Internal pudendal vein. 3- Inferior gluteal vein. 4- Superior gluteal vein. 5- Lateral sacral veins. 6- Vesical vein. 7- Uterine vein. 8- Vaginal vein. 9- Middle rectal vein. MCQ Which artery terminates as the glomus cocygeum ? Internal pudendal . Internal iliac. Abdominal aorta. Median sacral. Sacral plexus - Formation : ventral rami of L4,5 and S1,2,3,4 . - L4 and L5 join to form the lumbosacral trunk that joins the sacral nerves. Site : in front of the piriformis muscle . - Branches : A- Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2,3,4) parasympathetic fibers to the pelvic viscera. B- Branches to the pelvic muscles : - Nerve to the piriformis muscle. Sacral plexus - Branches : C- Branches to the lower limb : they pass through the greater sciatic foramen to the gluteal region . 1- Sciatic nerve. 2- Superior gluteal nerve. 3- Inferior gluteal nerve. 4- Nerve to quadratus femoris muscle. 5- Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh. 6- Perforating cutaneous nerve. Sacral plexus - Branches : D- Branches to the Perineum : they pass through the greater sciat

text: Revision By Prof. Dr. Abdelghany Hassan Abdelghany Professor and head of department of Anatomy and embryology Faculty of medicine, Alexandria University Postgraduate professor, Tufts University, MA,USA Peritoneal covering of the uterus The peritoneum covers the upper surface of the urinary bladder and reflected at the isthmus on the lower surface of the uterus forming the uterovesical pouch , then covers the fundus and upper surface and continues on the upper part of the back of the vagina where it is reflected on the rectum forming the rectovaginal (Douglas) pouch . N.B. the anterior surface of the cervix is not covered by peritoneum. Peritoneal covering Ligaments of the uterus 1- broad ligament. 2- ovarian ligament. 3- round ligament. 4- lateral cervical ligament. 5- uterosacral ligament. 6- pubocervical ligament. Parts of the broad ligament 1- mesovarium : connecting the ovary to the broad ligament. 2- mesosalpinx : the part between the Fallopian tube and ovarian ligament. 3- mesometrium : the part between the pelvic floor, uterine body and ovarian ligament. 4- suspensory ligament of the ovary : connecting the ovary to the side wall of the pelvis. Other ligaments 1- ovarian ligament extends from the cornu of the uterus to the ovary. 2- round ligament extends from the cornu of the uterus to the labia majora . 3- uterosacral ligament extends from the cervix around the rectum to the sacrum. Other ligaments 4- pubocervical ligament extends from the cervix around the urethra to the pubic bones. 5- lateral cervical ( Macknrodent’s or cardinal ) ligament extending from the side of the cervix to the side wall of the pelvis. It is very important in supporting the uterus. MCQ Which structure lies in the free border of the broad ligament? Uterine artery. Round ligament. Fallopian tube. Ligament of the ovary. MCQ Which uterine ligament is connected to the labia majora ? Lateral cervical ligament. Round ligament. Pubocervical ligament. Suspensory ligament of the ovary. It has 4 triangular surfaces : superior, 2 inferolateral and posterior (base). It has an apex (anterior ), neck (inferior) and 2 postero -superior angles (where the ureters enter the bladder). Relations superior surface : in males : coils of ileum (small intestine) and pelvic colon. In females : uterovesical pouch (containing coils of small intestine) and inferior (anterior) surface of the uterus. Relations inferolateral surface : retropubic fat, obturator internus and levator ani muscles, obturator nerve and vessels. Relations Base : In males, rectovesical pouch (containing coils of ileum and pelvic colon), seminal vesicles and vas deferens. Relations Base : b. In females : cervix and vagina. Interior of the urinary bladder Trigone is bounded by the openings of the ureters and the opening of the urethra . It is smooth and mesodermal in origin . The mucosa of the urinary bladder other than the trigone is folded (endodermal in origin). Ligaments attached to the urinary bladder 1- median umbilical ligament : attached to the apex . 2- pubovesical ligaments : to the neck and adjoining part of the urethra in females . 3- puboprostatic ligaments : to the neck and base of the prostate in males . It is 3 cm in length. It receives the openings of the ejaculatory ducts and ducts of the prostate. 2- membranous urethra It is the shortest, narrowest and least dilatable part. It is 1 cm in length . It is liable to rupture during instrumentation. It lies in the deep perineal pouch and surrounded by the urethral sphincter. 3- spongy (penile) urethra It is the longest part. It is 16 cm in length . It passes through the bulb of the penis and corpus spongiosum . It ends at the external urethral meatus (narrowest point of the urethra).  ARTIST OF ANATOMY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

Bony Pelvis
- The bony pelvis consists of:
2 hip bones (anterolaterally) & sacrum & coccyx (posteriorly).
- The 2 hip bones articulate:
(a) anteriorly to from symphysis pubis (secondary cartilaginous joint)
(b) posteriorly with sacrum to form sacroiliac joint (synovial plane joint)

- The normal anatomical position of the pelvis:
- tip of coccyx & upper border of symphysis pubis
are at the same horizontal plane.
- anterior superior iliac spine & pubic tubercle
are at the same vertical plane.

1

 ARTIST OF ANATOMY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

SACRUM
- It is a triangular bone formed of 5 fused sacral vertebrae
- It has base, apex and 3 surfaces (anterior (pelvic), posterior and lateral)
Base: - formed of body of 1st sacral vertebra and ala of sacrum
- the anterior border of 1st sacral vertebra is called sacral promontory

(1) Pelvic surface:
- it shows 4 pairs of ventral sacral foramina
for passage of:
- ventral rami of sacral nerves
- Lateral sacral arteries
- Structures attached to the pelvic surface:
(a) Three muscles:
- Iliacus (origin): on the ala
- Piriformis (origin): on middle 3 pieces
- Coccygeus (insertion): on 5th sacral piece
(b) Three ligaments:
- Anterior longitudinal ligament
- Lumbosacral ligament
- Anterior sacroiliac ligament
- Structures related to the pelvic surface:
Two viscera:
- Pelvic colon & Pelvic mesocolon: to the upper 2 pieces
- Rectum: related to lower 3 sacral vertebrae
Three vessels:
- Lateral sacral arteries: enter the ventral sacral foramina (right and left)
- Median sacral artery:
- Superior rectal artery:
Four Nerves:
- Ventral rami of upper 4 sacral nerves (right and left)

text:
ARTIST OF ANATOMY

DR /IBRAHIM AMR

DEVELOPMENT OF GONADS
(A) Indifferent gonads:
- although sex of embryo is determined genetically at time of fertilization,
gonads do not acquire male or female morphological characteristics
until the 7th week of development
- Before this time, the sex gland is called "the indifferent gonad ."
- SOURCES:

(1) genital or gonadal ridge:
- from intermediate mesoderm
- the genital ridge lies on medial side
of the mesonephros.
- it gives the Leydig cells.
(2) Coelomic epithelium:
- overly the genital ridge,
proliferate and penetrate underlying
mesoderm forming primitive sex cords
- it gives the Sertoli cells.
(3) Primordial germ cells:
- they are endodermal cells which
arise from the wall of hindgut.
- they proliferate and migrate
along dorsal mesentery
to reach genital ridge.
- they induce development of gonads
into ovary or testis.
- they give oogonia or spermatogonia
27

 ARTIST OF ANATOMY

DR /IBRAHIM AMR

Development of testes
- under influence of the SRY (sex determining region on Y chromosome),
which encodes the TDF (testis determining factor),
the primitive sex cords continue to proliferate forming testis (medullary) cords
- at the hilum of the gland, the rete testis are formed
- at the periphery of the gland, the tunica albuginea is formed
- In the 4th month, testis cords become horse shoe shaped,
and their extremities are continuous with the rete testis.
- Finally, the rete testis becomes continuous with 15-20 mesonephric tubules
which become the efferent ductules of the testis.

28

 ARTIST OF ANATOMY

DR /IBRAHIM AMR

- Descent of the testis:
- Testis developed in the abdomen and descends to the scrotum
- Gubernaculum testis (fibroelastic band) has 2 ends, one end is attached to
lower pole of the testis and peritoneum of peritoneal cavity,
the other end is attached to scrotum,
- contraction of this band leads to descent of testis and part of the peritoneum
- This part of peritoneum is called processes vaginalis.
- The testis invaginates the processes vaginalis, hence the testis is covered by
visceral and parietal layers of tunica vaginalis.
- The testis descents through the inguinal canal to each the scrotum.
- After the testis reaches scrotum, connection between peritoneum
and processes vaginalis obliterates forming the vestige of processes vaginalis.

- Factors controlling the descent of the lower pole of the testis:
(1) Hormonal factor: the testis descends under effect of androgenic hormone
(2) Descent occurs due to increase in the intra-abdominal pressure
(3) Regression (contraction) of the gubernaculum testis

29

 ARTIST OF ANATOMY

DR /IBRAHIM AMR

- Abnormalities of testis:
(1) Incomplete descent of the testis:
- testis may be found in inguinal canal
for example.
(2) Ectopic testis:
- testis is found in an abnormal site
as in perineum
or in the abdominal wall.

(3) Hydrocele:
- due to failure of obliteration of
connection between peritoneum
and processes vaginalis

(4) Congenital inguinal hernia:
- due to failure of obliteration of
connection between peritoneum
and processes vaginalis

Anatomy - Endocrine System

Parathyroid gland
• Position:

- They are four small, oval, yellowish- brown bodies
- Usually lie between the posterior lobar borders of the thyroid gland and its capsule
- There are two glands on each side, superior and inferior one.
- The upper parathyroid glands are usually found adjacent to the posterior surface of the
middle part of the thyroid lobe.
- The lower parathyroid glands are found
on the lateral or posterior surface of the
lower part of the thyroid lobe (their
position is variable).

• Arterial supply:

- Inferior thyroid Artery

• Nerve supply:

- Sympathetic fibers are distributed from the superior and middle cervical ganglia of the
sympathetic trunk
- These fibers are not secretory to the gland because the parathyroid activity is controlled by
the level of the blood calcium.

Supra-Renal Gland
Adrenal Gland
• The adrenal glands lie at the superior poles of the kidneys.
• Each gland is composed of two distinct parts, the adrenal medulla and the adrenal cortex.
• The adrenal medulla is functionally related to the sympathetic nervous system, it secretes
the hormones epinephrine (Adrenal) and norepinephrine(Noradrenaline) in response to
sympathetic stimulation.
• The adrenal cortex secretes steroid hormones.

11

 Anatomy - Endocrine System
• Site:

- It lies at the upper pole and adjacent part of the medial border of the kidney.
- The right one is triangular while the left one is semilunar in shape.

• Relations:

- Posteriorly: the diaphragm.

- Postero-inferiorly: the kidney.
- Medially: the celiac ganglion.
- Anteriorly:
▪

The right one partially covered by peritoneum and related to the IVC and the liver.

▪

Left one covered by the peritoneum of lesser sac and forming part of the stomach
bed Its lower border is related to the body of pancreas and splenic vessels.

• Arterial Supply:

Each gland is supplies by three arteries:

1. Superior supra-renal artery (from inferior phrenic artery).
2. Middle supra-renal artery (from the abdominal aorta).
3. Inferior supra-renal artery (from the renal artery).
• Venous Drainage:

Each gland is drained by a single vein:

- The right supra-renal vein drains into the IVC.
- The left supra-renal vein drains into the left renal vein.

The sex of the embryo is determined genetically at the time of fertilization
• The gonads do not acquire male or female morphological characteristics until the seventh
week of development
• Gonads appear initially as a pair of longitudinal ridges, the genital or gonadal ridges
• They are formed by proliferation of the epithelium and a condensation of underlying
mesenchyme

Development of Urinary System
• Development of kidney:
Primordia: Intermediate mass of mesoderm:
- In the cervical part, it is segmented into groups of cells called nephrotomes
- In the caudal part, it gives a longitudinal ridge called nephrogenic
- Three sets of kidneys appear following each other: Pronephros, Mesonephros,
Metanephros
97

97

 1. Pronephros:
Most primitive Kidney
- The cervical nephrotomes give 5-7 pairs of pronephric tubules which open in a duct
called pronephric duct
- The pronephros are non-functioning in
mammals
- The tubules degenerate by the 4th week.
- Pronephric duct persists to become the
haic duct
mesonephric duct
2. Mesonephros
- It is formed of about 80 mesonephric tubules
- It differs from pronephros in the following:
• The mesonephric tubules are more caudal and more numerous (80).
• They have no special duct, they use the pronephric duct which is now called
mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct)
- The mesonephric duct elongates and opens into the cloaca
- Each mesonephric tubule has 2 ends; one end opens in the mesonephric duct while the
other end differentiates into a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule that is invaginated by
capillaries forming the Glomerulus
- Bowman's capsule and Glomerulus make up the Renal Corpuscle
- Mesonephric kidney functions for sometime and then degenerates.
- Some mesonephric tubules persist and give efferent ductulus in males while in female,
they give epophoron and parophoron
- The mesonephric duct forms the epididymis, vas deferens and ejaculatory duct in
males while it disappears in females leaving Gartner's duct.
3. Metanephros: It is the permanent kidney
- It begins functioning at 9 weeks
- Urine is produced and released into amniotic fluid

- It develops from two parts: secretory part and collecting part.
The collecting part:
- The ureteric bud arises as an outgrowth from the lower end of the mesonephric duct
near the cloaca
- The ureteric bud elongates forming the ureter, renal pelvis, major calyces, minor calyces
and collecting ducts and tubules.
The secretory part:
- The nephrogenic cord which is the caudal part of the intermediate mass of mesoderm is
divided into segments called meta-nephrogenic cap
- Each segment lies opposite one collecting tubule
- The meta-nephrogenic cap forms the nephron:
a. Glomerulus.
b. Bowman's capsule.
c. Proximal and distal convoluted tubules.
d. Loop of Henle

• In summer due to increased sweating, during fasting or restricted fluids.

• In acute nephritis, heart failure, shock, burns and after hemorrhage.
• During and after vomiting and diarrhea.

 -٢Metabolic function of the kidney
• The kidney tissue represents less than 1.5% of the body weight; it
receives 25% of the cardiac output and 10% of O2 consumption.
• This is required for synthesis of ATP needed for reabsorption.
• The energy reserves in the kidney (glycogen, phosphocreatine or neutral
lipids) are very low, thus the kidney must get its energy requirement from
circulating substrates.
* Substances used by kidney for energy production:I- In Fed State:
• The kidney mainly oxidizes lactate (33% of total renal O2 consumption)
and glucose.
Il-During starvation:
• There is a decrease in blood lactate and glucose concentrations and an
increase in blood ketone bodies and fatty acids.
• Renal uptake of ketone bodies and fatty acids increases, they appear to be
the major kidney fuel during starvation.
A. Carbohydrate metabolism in the kidney:• The following metabolic pathways occur in the
kidney: Glycolysis, Citric Acid Cycle, HMS,
Fructose metabolism and gluconeogenesis.
TROL PaYS
* Role of the kidney in glucose homeostasis:SIL CORTE
INSIDE THE KIDNEYS
• Kidney can be considered as 2 organs:
wwshsblebody.com
• Renal Medulla: in which glucose utilization occurs.
• Renal Cortex: in which glucose synthesis (gluconeogenesis) occurs.
• This occurs due to the differences in the distribution of enzymes in renal
medulla and renal cortex.
• In the renal medulla, the cells have glucose-phosphorylating enzymes
(hexokinase), glycolytic enzyme activity and depend on glucose as major
source energy.
The Genius in Biochemistry
Urinary System
Dr. Mohamed Agha
CamScanner ‫ب ايئوض ةحوسمملا‬

 -٣• The cells don't have glucose-6-phosphatase and other gluconeogenic
enzymes.
• Thus, cells of renal medulla can take up, phosphorylate and metabolize
glucose through glycolysis; they can form glycogen, but cannot release
free glucose into circulation.
• In the Renal Cortex, the cells have gluconeogenic enzymes, have little
phosphorylating enzymes, can't synthesize glycogen under normal
conditions.
• So, release of glucose by the normal kidney is exclusively, a result of
renal cortical gluconcogenesis.
• The most important substrates for renal gluconeogenesis are Glutamine
and lactate, followed by glycerol.
• Alanine is preferentially used by the liver.
* Renal glucose metabolism in the postprandial conditions:• After meal ingestion, glucose is mainly utilized by brain, liver & muscles.
• There is a decrease in liver gluconeogenesis.
• Renal glucose uptake is < 10% of the ingested glucose.
• Renal gluconcogenesis paradoxically increases and it accounts for 50%
of endogenous glucose release.
• This may take place due to:
• Increase in availability of gluconeogenic precursors (e.g. lactate and
amino acids)
• This increase in renal gluconeogenesis helps liver glycogen repletion
by suppression of hepatic glucose release.
•* Hormonal control of renal gluconeogenesis in Fasting:• Epinephrine has more effect on renal gluconeogenesis than hepatic
gluconeogenesis (may be due to the rich autonomic innervation of the
kidney).
• The mechanism is Hypoglycemia → Epinephrine release → 11 Lipolysis
→ iT free fatty acids.

text: Determination of blood Insulin concentration by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA ) Prepared and presented By Dr. Mohamed Agha Cases CASE I : A 50-year-old female presents to your clinic with complaints of excessive thirst , fluid intake , and urination . She denies any urinary tract infection symptoms. She reports no medical problems, but has not seen a doctor in many years. On examination she is an obese female in no acute distress. Her physical exam is otherwise normal. The urine analysis revealed high glucose level , and a serum random blood sugar level was 320 mg/dl . What is the most likely diagnosis? A case of type II DM (might be insulin resistance state ). CASE II An 82-year-old white woman presented to her primary care physician with history of episodic confusion and somnolence. The episodes occurred typically in the morning, just after waking. They lasted minutes and were relieved when she ate her breakfast or had juice . As she was waiting for check-out, she developed confusion, a capillary blood glucose test was performed, and she was noted to have a plasma glucose level of 28 mg/dl. She was given juice and her symptoms resolved after a few moments . What is the most likely diagnosis? A case of insulinomas (islet cell tumors of the pancreas ). Insulin Human insulin is a peptide hormone composed of 51 amino acids. It is produced in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. It is a hormone central to regulating carbohydrate and fat metabolism in the body. Diseases associated with insulin disturbances Elevated insulin levels are seen with: Insulinomas Insulin resistance, such as in obesity, Diabetes (Type 2) and metabolic syndrome. Decreased insulin levels are seen with: Diabetes (Type 1) Pancreatic diseases such as chronic pancreatitis (including cystic fibrosis) and pancreatic cancer Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA ) Definition: This is a sensitive and specific enzyme-based immunoassay that is used for quantification of a substance even of picograms (10 -12 g) range (ex. hormones, drugs, pathogens ). The name suggests three components : Antibody. Solid phase (sorbent ). Enzymatic amplification. Principle : Antigen: a high molecular weight (>5000) substance recognized by the immune system of an organism as foreign. The organism reacts to antigen by producing a specific antibody. Hapten: a low molecular weight (<5000) substance can´t stimulate the production of antibodies. It must be carried by a specific carrier to stimulate the production of a specific antibody. Antibody (immunoglobulin): a large Y-shaped protein used by the immune system to identify and neutralize foreign objects such as bacteria and viruses. recognizes a unique part of the foreign target, termed an antigen . ELISA: is based on an antigen-antibody (immunological) reaction Equipment: Microtiter plate Microplate sealing tape Automatic pipettes ELISA washer ELISA reader Types of ELISA : Indirect ELISA Sandwich ELISA Competitive ELISA Indirect ELISA Used to measure antibody levels. The antibody reacts with specific antigen attached to the solid phase. Enzyme activity measured is proportional to the amount of specific antibody in the original serum. Color produced is directly proportional to antibody amount. Indirect ELISA Sandwich ELISA The double antibody method. Used to measure antigen levels. The unknown antigen reacts with specific antibody attached to the solid phase. Enzyme activity measured is proportional to the amount of specific antigen in the original solution. Color produced is directly proportional to antigen amount. Sandwich ELISA Competitive ELISA Enzyme- labeled antigen and the unknown amount of the antigen in the sample react with a specific antibody attached to a solid phase. Enzyme activity measured is proportional to the proportion of labelled antigen in mixture of labelled and unlabelled antigen. Color produced is inversely proportional to unlabelled antigen amount. Principle of the insulin ELISA Based on the sandwich principle . The microtiter wells are coated with a monoclonal antibody directed towards Insulin molecule . Samples and standards are pipetted into these wells, along with the enzyme conjugate ( monoclonal antibody against human insulin, which has horseradish peroxidase ( HRP ) enzyme covalently linked to it ). The amount of bound HRP complex is proportional to the concentration of Insulin in the sample. After washing to remove unbound materials, a substrate for HRP is added. The substrate is converted to a colored compound by the action of HRP. The intensity of colour developed is proportional to the concentration of Insulin in the patient sample. Assay Procedure ELISA Specimen : Serum or Plasma (Heparin or Citrate). Sensitivity of ELISA depends on correct washing procedure . Chemiluminescence Immunoassay (CLIA): Radiation emitted by molecule or atom when it returns to the ground state from the excited state . Simplest definition: chemical reactions that emit light . Advantages: High sensitivity → Chemiluminescence . Good specificity → Immunoassay . Wide range of applications . Simple equipment . Principle of CLIA: Two components → immunoreaction technique & Chemiluminescence technique. Enzyme in the immunoreaction acts on luminescent substrate causing a chemical reaction and releasing large amount of energy to produce an excited state intermediate . When excited state intermediate returns to stable ground state → Photons are emitted at the same time → Luminescence measurement instrument can measure the amount of light quantum yield. Photon yield is directly proportional to the amount of the substance . According to reaction mode, Chemiluminescence immunoassay is divided into: Double antibody sandwich. Competition. Indirect reaction . Applications of CLIA: CLIA has gained attention in life science , clinical diagnosis , environmental monitoring , food safety and pharmaceutical analysis .

text: Presented by Dr nada soliman Milk What is the difference between a meal , a food and nutrients ? Meal a combination of multiple food items is considered a meal. Food refers to the single items in a meal we consume in solid or in liquid form such as bread, an egg , a cup of milk . Nutrients are the substances found in each food which drive biological activity, and are essential for the human body. They are categorized into two main types : Macronutrients : as proteins, fats, carbohydrates Micronutrients : as vitamins and minerals Milk composition Milk is almost a complete food because it is rich in Fat mainly triglyceride with unsaturated essential FA , small amounts of phospholipids and cholesterol Carbohydrate : lactose , non-fermentable, laxative and less sweet Proteins present in milk are of high biological value as. They include: Caseinogen 60% Lactalbumin, and Lactglobulin (simple soluble proteins) 40%. most of minerals especially calcium and phosphorus . But it is poor in some minerals such as copper and iron. it is a good source for vitamin A and most of vitamin B complex . But it is poor in vitamin D and C Composition of milk varies from one animal to another: Human's milk Cow's milk Fat 4% 4% Protein 1-2% 4% Carbohydrate 7% 4% Minerals (ash) 0.2% 0.7% Reaction Neutral Alkaline So, to humanize cow's milk, we add sugar to increase carbohydrate in cow's milk (40 g/L). Also, milk is diluted with water to decrease the percentage of proteins and ash. TYPES OF HUMAN MILK Colostrum: It is secreted in the first few days after labor (until 7-10 days). It is of high nutritive due to its high content of proteins and minerals. The proteins in colostrum are mainly gamma globulins (antibodies) which give immunity to the new born. This immunity lasts for 6 months. Mature milk: Secreted from the second week . It is fully established milk . Comparison between colostrum and mature milk Colostrum Mature Colour Yellow White (carotenes) (lipids/ Ca salts of casein) Consistency Thick Thin Reaction Alkaline Neutral Specific gravity 1040-1060 1020-1040 Composition: Protein 10-20 g% 1-2 g% Minerals 4 g% 0.2g% Lipids 3 g% 4 g% Carbohydrates 4 g% 7 g% Boiling Clotted Not clotted (due to high protein content) CASEINOGEN A phosphoprotein Precipitated at its isoelectric point, i.e. pH 4.6. Digested by Rennin enzyme (stomach of young calves) parachymosin (in infant, analogue to renin) protein in nature acts optimally at pH 6 and 37 o C . In adults this enzyme does not act because of the very low acidity of stomach (pH 1.5-2) which is not suitable for its activity. It is hydrolase enzyme (proteolase) which splits a part of caseinogen polypeptide chain to casein( soluble) , which then react with calcium giving calcium caseanate (insoluble) The function of these enzymes is to clot milk and separate it into solid (clot) and liquid (whey). Clotting of the milk is necessary if the milk is to be retained in the stomach long enough for the milk proteins to be digested properly. Young mammals would derive no benefit from the milk they drink if it passed through the stomach too quickly , which is what would happen if it was allowed to remain in its non-clotted state. Milk processing Milk clotting (cheese formation) Milk curdling (yogurt formation) Caseinogen is involved in both processes where it is transformed into a ppt but through different mechanism Milk clotting (cheese formation) Milk Clotting takes place in 2 steps: Enzymatic reaction: rennin caseinogen casein (soluble) + small polypetide Chemical reaction: Ca ++ Casein calcium caseanate (insoluble) Calcium caseinate precipitates entangling with it Calcium caseanate milk fat, fat soluble vitamins and carotenes. When the clot separates, a fluid is left, formed of H 2 O, water soluble vitamins lactalbumin, lactglobulin, lactose , Minerals, except Ca (a very small amount). Whey is greenish yellow in color due to its high content of vitamin B 2 . Milk clot whey Milk Curdling (Yogurt) Curdling is the precipitation of caseinogen of milk at its isoelectric point (4.6). it occurs by adding lactic acid bacilli in milk, these bacteria can change lactose of milk into lactic acid . The caseinogen when precipitates entangles: caseinogen the fat, fat soluble vitamins and carotenes the fluid that remains is made of water, water soluble vitamins lactic acid and small amount of lactose lactalbumin, lactglobulin, all minerals. Milk curd whey Experiments Demonstration of the action of rennin on milk clotting Role of calcium in clot formation Essential for clot formation Ca act as ppt factor and not co-enzyme for rennin Action of rennin on milk clotting Prepare a test tube containing 5 ml of milk, and then add to it 4 drops of rennin solution. Place the tube in a water bath at 37 o C Record in minutes the time taken to form a firm clot. Role of calcium in clot formation prepare 2 test tubes, each containing the following solutions: 2ml Milk + 3 drops of ammonium oxalate + 4 drops of rennin solution. Place the 2 tubes in a water bath at 37 o C. Record in minutes the time at which clotting occurs in any one of them. Observation: These 2 test tubes do not show any clotting because the Ca of milk in these 2 tubes is completely precipitated as Ca oxalate. This prove that Ca is essential for clot formation boil one of the 2 test tubes, in order to denaturate rennin Then add few drops of CaCl 2 solution A clot is formed This prove that casein is already formed in the absence of Ca, but didn’t ppt till adding calcium i.e. calcium is a ppt factor and not a co-enzyme for rennin After boiling And adding Ca Section Sheet 3 Explain: All pediatricians advise breast feeding. Milk clot is of higher biological value than milk curdle. Section Sheet 3 Explain: All pediatricians advise breast feeding. Complete food Colostrum :high in immunoglobulins Milk clot is of higher biological value than milk curdle. Because it contains Ca in the form of Ca caseinate

text: Semen Analysis Prepared and Presented By Dr. Mohamed Agha Basic Guide lines for human semen analysis: Abstinence days: W.H.O. recommended a period is between 2-7 days. Collection: In glass or plastic sterile container maintained at 20-37؛C (important to avoid rapid temperature changes) and stored in an incubator at 37؛C protected from light. Analysis of sample: between 30 and 60 minutes from the collection time. 60 minutes maximum. Semen is made up of the secretion of all the accessory glands of the male genital tract: Testes 5% Seminal vesicle 46-48% Prostate 13-33% Bulbourethral gland 2-5%. Semen is a grey opalescent fluid which is formed at ejaculation. It is composed of suspension of spermatozoa in seminal plasma. Semen analysis Physical properties Liquefaction Volume Colour pH Vicosity Specific gravity Biochemical tests Fructose Acid phosphatase Microscopic examination count Morphology Motility Viability Non sperm cells Liquefaction: It becomes more homogenous and quite watery. Occurs within 15 minutes and rarely up to 60 minutes. Delayed Liquifaction : Additional treatment with Physiological Saline, Mechanical Mixing or Enzymatic digestion. PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF SEMEN PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF SEMEN Volume: Average volume is from 2-5 ml/ejaculation. Abnormalities: Aspermia: Total absence of ejaculation (rare). Hyperspermia may be due to prolonged abstinence or due to inflammation of seminal vesicle. Hypospermia may be due to absence or decrease of seminal vesicle component of ejaculate( absence of SV, complete or partial obstruction of ejaculatory ducts) or retrograde ejaculation Volume: Hypospermia : the seminal fluid volume is less than 2 ml. Obstruction of Ejaculatory ducts. Congenital bilateral absence of Vas Deferens. Collection problem. Partial retrograde Ejaculation. Androgen deficiency. Hyperspermia : Increased volume of semen above 10 ml. Acute inflammation of accessory glands. Hyperspermia may be due to prolonged abstinence or due to inflammation of seminal vesicle. Hypospermia may be due to absence or decrease of seminal vesicle component of ejaculate( absence of SV, complete or partial obstruction of ejaculatory ducts) or retrograde ejaculation Colour Greyish white . It is opalescent due to its high content of protein. abnormalities: Urine produces pale yellow discoloration easily detected by: Consistency of the semen. urineferous odor. Jaundice : bilirubin will also cause coloration of semen in deep jaundice. The semen may be a very bright yellow . Blood ( haematospermia ) traces of fresh blood will color semen pink, while large amounts of blood give bright red color. PH: Between 7.2-8 only recorded on fresh semen by using pH paper. Inflammatory conditions of the prostate or seminal vesicle may alter the pH of semen. Causes of Acidic semen (PH less than 7) (Prostatic Secretions) Absence of Sperms Absence of Vas Deference Ejaculatory Duct obstruction. Viscosity : Normal viscosity is that which allows semen to be poured drop by drop out of the container. It is measured by the time taken by one drop to leave the standard pipette. Specific gravity: 1.028 Prostatic secretion is acidic while seminal vesicle fluid is alkaline. Acidic ejaculate (pH<7.2) may be associated with blockage of seminal vesicles. The semen is initially in liquefied state but quickly coagulate by the action of protein kinase secreted by the seminal vesicles. Proteolytic enzymes from the prostate liquefy coagulum in 20-25 minutes. Abnormal liquefaction may be cased by prostatic abnormalities, e.g. prostatitis. Increased viscosity may affect sperm motility Semen viscosity can be estimated by aspirating the sample into a wide-bore plastic disposable pipette, allowing the semen to drop by gravity and observing the length of the thread that is formed. A sA normal sample leaves the pipette in small drops with very little trailing thread. emen sample that is abnormally viscous will form a thread more than 2 cm long. MICROSCOPIC EXAMINATION: This includes: Sperm Count Motility Morphology Viability Non-sperm cells Sperm count Total sperm count is the number of sperms in an ejaculate (ejaculation). Normally, it is 20 million/ml, i.e. about 60 millions/ejaculation. It is obtained by multiplying the sperm concentration (per ml) by the volume. Count Abnormalities: Azoospermia : no spermatocytes (male sterility). Cryptozoospermia : Sperm quantity below 100,000 / ml semen. Oligozoospermia : less than 20 million/ml ( Or less than 50 millions / ejaculation ) . Polyzoospermia means : 350 million sperm /ejaculation Motility: Percentage motility (the percentage of sperms in the seminal fluid which are highly active) is performed soon after liquefaction the sample and is repeated. Normally, after one hour there must be over 60% active sperms. Grades of motility: Progressive Motility (PR): Spermatozoa moving actively, either linear or in large circle. Non-Progressive Motility (NP): All other forms of motility with absence of progression. Immotility (IM): No Movement. Viability Done for samples with less than 40% Progressive Motile Spermatozoa. Sperm Viability is assessed by Intact cell membrane. Dye Exclusion method (Eosin) Dead Sperm: take dye. Viable sperm: without dye. Hypo Osmotic Swelling (HOS) test Viable sperm: swell in hypotonic solution % of Dead cells shouldn't exceed % of Immotile sperms. % of Viable cells normally exceed % of Motile cells. Sperm Morphology Normal sperm has oval head shapes, an intact central or "mid" section an uncoiled, single tail See more at: http://dukefertilitycenter.org/tests/sperm-testing/understanding-results/#sthash.QKH5020e.dpuf Normally, sperm count contains few abnormal forms e.g. bitailed , short tailed, 2 head....etc. At least 4% of cells should be of normal shape according to the WHO (world health organization) WHO criteria: >30% normal forms At least 30% of cells should be of normal shape according to the WHO (world health organization) Non-Sperm Cells RBCs: Normally, there are no

Specific gravity : 1.028 MICROSCOPIC EXAMINATION: This includes: Sperm count motility morphology vitality Sperm count Total sperm count is the number of sperms in an ejaculate (ejaculation). Normally, it is 20 million/ml , i.e. about 60 millions/ejaculation. It is obtained by multiplying the sperm concentration (per ml) by the volume. Count Abnormalities: A zoo spermia means no spermatocytes (male sterility). Cryptozoospermia . the quantity of sperm is below 100,000 /ml semen. Oligo zoo spermia mean less than 20 million/ml ( Or less than 50 millions / ejaculation ) Poly zoo spermia means : 350 million sperm / ejaculation . Normozoospermia: 20 to 25million sperm / ml /ejaculation Oligozoospermia: < 20 million sperm / ml / ejaculation Polyzoospermia: > 250 million sperm / ml / ejaculation Morphology Normal sperm has oval head shapes, an intact central or "mid" section, and an uncoiled, single tail Sperm Morphology Normally, the sperm count contains at least 4% normal forms . Abnormal forms e.g. bitailed , short tailed, 2 heads.... etc See more at: http://dukefertilitycenter.org/tests/sperm-testing/understanding-results/#sthash.QKH5020e.dpuf Non-sperm cells RBCs : Normally, there are no RBCs . If present, this indicates haematospermia . WBCs ( Pus cells ) : Normally 0- few number of WBCs which increase in cases of inflammation. Epithelial cells : always present in semen. Spermatocytes (germinal cells) : usually present in normal semen, but few in number. Motility: Percentage motility (the percentage of sperms in the seminal fluid which are highly active) is performed soon after liquefaction of the sample. Normally, after one hour there must be over 60% active sperms . Grades of Motility I . Progressive motility (PR): spermatozoa moving actively, either linearly or in a large circle. II. Non-progressive motility (NP): all other patterns of motility with an absence of progression. swimming in small circles, the flagellar force hardly displacing the head, or when only a flagellar beat can be observed III. Immotility (IM): no movement. text: Laboratory investigations of infertility Yasmine M. Nageeb Assistant Lecturer Of Medical Biochemistry, AFM Sperm DNA fragmentation: Causes: 1-Advanced age 2-Drugs 3-Cigarette smoking 4-Exposure to pollutants 5-Varicoceles (enlarged veins of the scrotum) 6-Illnesses with fever(e.g., infection)) The degree of DNA fragmentation in sperm cells can be determined by Comet Assay. It has been associated with outcomes of in vitro fertilization(IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI). If DNA fragmentation activity is >30% indicates high risk of infertility. Principle of comet assay Comet assay, also known as )single cell gel electrophoresis(, is a sensitive technique for measuring DNA damage in single cells. Comet assay is based upon the ability of damaged DNA, to migrate under electrophoresis creating a "comet tail", while the undamaged DNA remains creating the "comet head." Types of comet assays: Alkaline Comet assay:run under alkaline conditions to detect single-and double-stranded DNA breaks Neutral Comet assay: run under neutral conditions to detect only double-stranded DNA breaks. Steps of comet assay 2- Assessment of infertility in females 2- Assessment of infertility in females 2- Assessment of infertility in females Female causes of infertility can be: anatomic (e.g., congenital abnormalities), ovulatory disorders (e.g., PCOS), and functional problems, such as abnormal cervical mucus. Steps are: 1- detailed history and physical examination, . 2- Investigations ( imaging, biopsy, postcoital testing, ovulation confirmation, endocrine evaluation, and immunological testing). Approximately 40% of female infertility is the result of ovulatory dysfunction . which manifests as abnormal menstrual cycling. The underlying causes of ovulatory dysfunction may include: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) ( most common cause) Weight extremes Thyroid dysfunction Hyperprolactinemia This Photo by Unknown author is licensed under CC BY-SA-NC . Hormonal assessment of ovulation: The most accurate assessment of ovulation is luteal phase serum progesterone measurement , where a concentration ˃ 3 ng/mL an evidence of ovulation (Progesterone is secreted in response to (LH) after ovulation) There are home testing kits for LH in urine that can detect the LH peak 1-2 days prior to ovulation;(Not accurate) TSH and prolactin may be measured as thyroid disease and hyperprolactinemia can cause infertility. Ovarian reserve: Ovarian reserve is defined by the number and quality of oocytes. Where ovarian reserve is low, the likelihood of in fertility is high. Ovarian reserve is assessed by: Direct follicle count by ultrasound Measurement of serum anti Mullerian hormone (AMH) Measurement of cycle day 3” serum (FSH) and estradiol Serum anti Mullerian hormone (AMH) AMH is secreted by granulosa cells of early ovarian follicles independent of gonadotropins. Low serum AMH concentrations can predict poor response to fertility drugs and low probability of pregnancy success with (IVF). Cycle day 3” serum FSH and estradiol. High FSH on day 3 of the menstrual cycle could indicate a low ovarian reserve (few and unresponsive follicles), as the hypothalamic pituitary axis is not suppressed by estradiol. Estradiol is measured to identify if it may be suppressing FSH; high estradiol with low FSH is thus also indicative of low reserve and lower likelihood of successful IVF.
