Endocrine cases
Pituitary cases:
1- The Neurosurgeons referred a 10-year-old boy to the Endocrine team, his mother
noticed that her son is much taller than his colleagues, and he started complaining of
a defect in his vision. • An optician reported a bitemporal field defect. • MR scan
showed a large pituitary tumor that was removed by transsphenoidal surgery. On
post-operative examination, he was found to be grossly hypothyroid and
hypogonadal and these were confirmed using biochemical tests.
• What is your diagnosis? Gigantism
• Why is the boy taller than his friends?
• before the epiphyses have fused results in excess linear bone growth.
• What is the cause of the boy’s defect in vision?
• The optic chiasm compression by tumor

2- A 41-year-old woman complains of coarse facial features with protruding lower jaw.
She also complains of amenorrhea and increased size of her hands and feet. She
sought medical advice. • Physical examination revealed that her blood pressure was
170/110. • GH and prolactin levels were elevated. • Fasting blood glucose was also
elevated. • MRI of brain revealed a pituitary adenoma.
What is your diagnosis? Acromegaly.
What is responsible for the widening in bones of the skull, hands and feet?
Growth hormone stimulates the production of insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I), or
somatomedin,
The patient did not exhibit increased linear growth of her long bones. Why?
Because excessive growth hormone secretion occurred after puberty (the epiphyseal
plates are already closed).
What was responsible for the patient’s amenorrhea?
a. Pressure atrophy of the pituitary adenoma on the gonadotrophic cells of the
anterior pituitary, which secrete FSH and LH.
b. Elevated prolactin inhibits the secretion of gonadotropinreleasing hormone
(GnRH), leading to further suppression of the secretion of FSH and LH.

 Based on your knowledge of the feedback control of growth hormone secretion,
propose a drug treatment that could lower growth hormone level ?
somatostatin analogue can be used to lower GH level.
3- A 39-year-old woman is complaining of amenorrhea and galactorrhea for 18 months.
She sought medical advice.
• Serum prolactin level was elevated. • MRI brain revealed a pituitary adenoma
(prolactinoma).
Why does the patient have galactorrhea ? Because she has hyperprolactinemia.
Prolactin stimulates milk secretion and induces the synthesis of lactose and fat in the
mammary gland.
Why does she have amenorrhea? Because prolactin inhibits the secretion of
gonadotropinreleasing hormone (GnRH) by the hypothalamus. Inhibition of GnRH
secretion leads to decreased secretion of LH and FSH.
What drug do you expect to lower her serum prolactin level? Why?
Dopamine because it inhibits prolactin secretion by the anterior pituitary.
Why is it unlikely that she could have become pregnant with elevated serum
prolactin level? Because ovulation does not occur (anovulation) and accordingly
fertilization and pregnancy are impossible.

4- A mother observed that her 15-year-old boy is much shorter than her 10-year-old
sister. His grades in school were fine, but he did not reach his puberty yet. • Physical
examination reveals proportionate growth rate with completely normal mental
functions
What is your diagnosis? Pituitary dwarfism
What are the investigations needed to establish diagnosis in this patient? Level
of GH in blood
Do you expect to find low levels of FSH and LH in all patients suffering from
dwarfism? No, In one third of the dwarfs, the deficiency is of growth H. alone.
These individuals are mature sexually.

Renal function tests are important for diagnosis, prognosis and management
Renal function is expected to reflect itself in deviation of the composition of
the blood and urine from the normal values. In view of the high renal reserve,
blood and urine may be normal in the presence of renal impairment. There
are no symptoms in kidney failure until the glomerular filtration rate falls from
125/minute to below 30 ml/minute, that is, half of one kidney is still functioning.
Renal function tests can be divided into four categories:
1. Renal clearance.
2. Measurement of substances in the blood that are normally excreted by the
kidneys.
Chemical and physical analysis of urine.

THE CONCEPT OF PLASMA

Plasma clearance:
- definition:
It is the ability of the kidney to clean or "clear" the plasma of various substances.
- measured by measuring the volume of plasma cleared from this substance / min.
- The rate of clearance of a substance from plasma = the rate of excretion of
this substance urine.
- The rate of clearance of a substance from plasma = concentration of substance
in plasma (P) x volume of plasma cleared from this substance per minute (C).
3

in urine (U) x volume of urine per minute (V).
- So: P x plasma clearance of a substance (C) (ml/min) = U x V
- So: plasma clearance of a substance (C) (ml/min) = UX V / P

text: MEDICAL PHYSIOLOGY DEAPARTMENT FACULTY OF MEDICINE, ALEXANDRIA UNIVERSITY It is a collective term for a variety of tests and procedures can be done to : Evaluate how well the kidneys are functioning It is important for diagnosis , prognosis and management of renal diseases . Renal function tests Kidney functions tests help to determine if the kidneys are performing their tasks adequately. Content Renal Clearance Tests Concept of Clearance Definition Clearance is the volume of plasma that is completely cleared of a substance each minute . Glucose Urea Inulin PAHA A B C D Different ways by which renal tubules can handle substances freely filtered at glomeruli . Principle of Clearance Some substances when filtered enter the tubules are not reabsorbed and so 100% excreted = GFR (inulin= gold standard for GFR, creatinine ). Some substances are filtered, enter tubules, and more of the substance is secreted enters the tubules by excretion. Clearance>GFR. Some substances are filtered, enter tubules, but are completely reabsorbed, so they did not reach the final urine (e.g. Glucose ) I shall review the tests in the left column today. The measurement of urine protein is important in certain conditions, e.g.diabetes. The detection of substances such as red cells or glucose could be an early indicator of renal damage. Amount of substance removed from plasma Amount of this substance excreted in urine = P x C = U x V P= The concentration of the substance in plasma C= The volume of plasma cleared per minute. U =The concentration of the substance in urine V= Volume of urine per minute. Clearance Equation Rate of Substance clearance from plasma = Rate of Substance excretion in urine Rate of Sub. clearance from plasma = Volume of plasma cleared/min ( C )x Conc. of sub in plasma ( P ) Rate of Sub. excretion in urine = Volume of urine/min ( V) x Conc. of sub in urine ( U ) Volume of plasma cleared/min C = U X V P What is the Importance of Renal Clearance? To quantify several aspects of renal functions: Rate of glomerular filtration Rate of renal blood flow Diagnose renal impairment in early stages Assess severity of renal damage 1- Measurement of GFR Glomerular filtration rate ( GFR ) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule per minute 125 ml/min . Criteria of a substance used for GFR measurement a)freely filtered b)not secreted by the tubular cells, c)not reabsorbed by the tubular cells . d)should not be toxic e)should not be metabolized f)easily measurable. Examples of Substances used for GFR Measurement Creatinine (endogenous): It is a by-product of skeletal muscle metabolism . Inulin (exogenous): It is a polysaccharide with a molecular weight of about 5200 and it fits all the above requirements. Nephron Excretion & Clearance of inulin Inulin A plant product that is filtered but not reabsorbed or secreted Used to determine clearance rate and therefore nephron function Inulin Inulin is a polysaccharide with many health benefits. Inulin is a substance used in processed foods. used to replace sugar, fat , flour It contains 25-35% of the food energy of CHO (starch & sugar) It increases calcium and magnesium absorption How the test is performed? (1) a certain amount of inulin is injected intravenously. (2) take a sample of blood and estimate the conc of Inulin (P). (3) take a sample of urine and estimate the conc of Inulin (U). (4)estimation of the volume of urine. (5) use the law to get the GFR. Inulin clearance = GFR In Inulin clearance test, if plasma inulin=0.2mg/ml, urinary inulin concentration=12mg/ml and urine flow =2ml/min. Then GFR ?? GFR=UXV/P = 12 X 2 / 0.2=120 ml/min Comparison of clearance of a substance with inulin clearance Inulin clearance: - Reference clearance method. - Not suitable for routine investigation. Exogenous material I.V. infused in such a way to maintain plasma level steady during the period of the test. (N: 125 ml / min). It measures the glomerular filtration rate =125ml/min. Endogenous creatinine clearance rate ( Ccr ): - A more convenient test and provides a reasonable estimate of the GFR. The creatinine clearance is calculated as: Ccr (ml/min)= Ucr (mg/dl) x V(volume of urine in 24 hours, ml/min) / Pcr (mg/dl). - Normal range is 80-120 ml/min. Creatinine in the plasma is filtered freely at the glomerulus and secreted by renal tubules (10 % of urinary creatinine ). Creatinine is not reabsorbed by the renal tubules. Plasma creatinine is an endogenous substance Plasma creatinine remains fairly constant throughout adult life. GFR = Ucr . V Pcr N.B: - Normal value of GFR = 125 ml/min. - Although the value of urinary creatinine is high as a result of tubular secretion the GFR still normal Because the value of plasma is also high as a result of Cr binds to plasma non-specific chromogens . Ambu bag ventilation

Bag-valve mask ventilation

and ring fingers, ensuring a tight seal (C&E)

5. Ventilate with the bag at a rate of 10 compression per minute
6. Look for a rise in the chest.

Ensure consent.

text:
Female catheterization
STEP/TASK
AP
Before starting
- Introduce yourself to the patient.
- Explain the procedure and ask for her consent to
carry it out.
- Ask her to undress from the waist down and
place a sheet over her.
The equipment
On a clean trolley, gather:
- A catheterization pack.
- Saline solution.
- Sterile gloves.
- A10 ml pre-filled syringe containing 2% lignocaine gel or K-Y
gel.
- A 12-16 French Foley catheter.
- A catheter bag.
- A 10 ml syringe containing sterile water.
- Adhesive tape.
The Procedure
- Check the expiry date of the catheter.
- Open the catheter pack aseptically
- Draw up 10 ml sterile water and' 10 ml lignocaine gel into
separate syringes.
- Wash and dry your hands.
- Put on sterile gloves
- Ask the patient to remove her sheet and lie flat on the couch,
bringing her heels to her buttocks and then letting her knees flop
out.
- Drape the patient.
- Use your non-dominant hand to separate the labia minora.
- Clean the area around the urethral meatus with saline soaked
swabs. One sweep from up down.
- Coat the end of the catheter with lignocaine gel or K-Y gel and
put small amount of the gel on the clitoris.
- Indicate that the anaesthetic needs about 5 minutes to work.
- Holding the catheter by its sleeve, gently and progressively insert
it into the urethra starting from the clitoris till reaching a dimple
(the urethral opening). Female urethra is dimple like.
- No need to insert the catheter till the bifurcation (female
, urethra is only 4cm) so insert one third or half its length.
- Once a stream of urine is obtained,' inject 10 ml of sterile water to
inflate the catheter's balloon. continually ensuring that this does
not cause the patient any pain.
- Gently retard the catheter until a resistance is felt.
- Attach the catheter bag.
- Tap the catheter to the thigh.

IP

NP

 N.B.
Never fix the catheter (i.e. inflate the balloon) unless you can find
urine coming out. if no urine comes out then do the following:
a. The gel may be obstructing the catheter opening so inject 10cc air
With Tommy syringe. if no urine
b. Suprapubic compression, still no urine
c. Fill a Tommy syringe with 20cc normal saline and inject them
then reaspirate, if this was done easily without any resistance
then the catheter is in place.
After the Procedure
- Ensure that the patient is comfortable.
- Thank the patient.
- Discard any rubbish.
- Record the date and time of catheterization, type and size of
catheter used, volume of water used to inflate the balloon, and
volume of urine in the catheter bag.
AP = Adequately Performed
IP = Inadequately Performed
NP = Not Performed

text:
LARGE INTESTINE
DR| RASHA RABEA

   It is about 150-180 cm (5 feet) in length.-It is the distal part of GIT and is formed of the caecum,
appendix, ascending colon, transverse colon, descending colon, pelvic (sigmoid) colon, rectum
and anal canal. The large intestine differs from the small intestine in three features:
1.The taeniae coli:•These are three bands of the longitudinal muscle layer of the colonThe length
of the taeniae coli is one foot shorter than the length of the large intestine.•In the ascending and
descending colons, the taeniae coli are one anterior and 2 posterior.•In the transverse colon they
are one posterior and two anterior .
2.Sacculations (or haustrations):•These sacculations are formed because the taeniae coli are
shorter than the length of the colon.•They are absent in the appendix, rectum and anal canal.
3.Appendices epiploicae:•They are small peritoneal projections filled with fat on the surface of the
large intestine.•They are absent in the appendix, caecum, rectum and anal canal.

SUPERIOR AND INFERIOR
MESENTERIC ARTERIES&
PORTOSYSTEMIC ANASTOMOSIS

DR: RASHA RABEA

 • 1. COELIAC TRUNK
• * It arises from front of aorta at level of upper border of L1, passes
forwards for 1/2 inch then it ends by dividing into 3 terminal
branches.
• * It is the artery of foregut.
• * On each side it is related to caeliac ganglion & a crus of diaphram.
• * Anterior relations: it is related to cavity of lesser sac.

 • Branches:
• a)Left gastric artery : which gives oesophageal & gastric branches.
• b) Splenic artery : Tortuous, runs above body of pancreas, gives
pancreatic branches, short gastric, Lt. gastroepiploic & splenic
branches.
• c) Hepatic artery : Passes in the free border of lesser omentum in
front of portal vein and on the left side of C.B.D. It gives right gastric
artery, gastroduodenal artery (gives sup. panceatico-duodenal & right
gastro-epiplioc arteries ) and right & left terminal branches to liver.

text:
ORAL CAVITY

 * Two Parts:

I . l of the mouth:
•

It lies between the teeth and gums internally and the cheeks and lips
externally.

•

Superiorly and inferiorly limited by the reflection of mucous membrane from
lips and cheek to the gums

•

Communicates with the exterior through the oral fissure

•

When the jaws are closed, communicates with the oral cavity proper behind
the 3rd molar tooth on each side .

•

Parotid duct opens into it opposite the upper 2nd molar tooth.

•

The cheek: Consists of: Skin, buccal pad of fat, buccopharyngeal fascia,
buccinator muscle, buccal glands (mucous glands) and mucous membrane of
the vestibule.

*Vestibule of the mouth*

 I. Oral (Mouth ) cavity proper: Boundaries:
•

In front and sides: The teeth and gums.

•

Behind: It communicates with the oro-pharynx through the oro-pharyngeal
isthmus fomed by soft palate , palate-glossal arch & dorsum of tongue.

•

Above (Roof): Consists of hard and soft palate.

•

Below (Floor): Consists of the following structures:

1- Anterior 2/3 of the tongue.
2- Lower (ventral) surface of the tongue: showing:
a- Frenulum linguae: a mucosal fold present in the midline which connects the
tongue with the floor of mouth. There are 2 structures lying lateral to it:
(1) deep vein of tongue.

(2) fimbriated ridge .

b- Sublingual papilla: small elevation on each side of the lower end of the
frenulum of the tongue, it receives the orifice of the submandibular duct.

 c- Sublingual fold: elevated mucous fold produced by sublingual gland. It lies
lateral to the sublingual papilla and it shows the orifices of the small
ducts of the sublingual glands.

text: Parotid Salivary Gland (The Largest Salivary Gland) Parts of parotid gland: 1 . A main part: Wedge-shaped, lies in the groove between the ramus of the mandible anteriorly and the mastoid process and sternomastoid muscle posteriorly. It is divided by the mandible and facial nerve into superficial and deep parts ( lobes ) . 2 . A small accessory part: Small pat lies above the parotid duct on the masseter muscle. 3. Parotid duct . *Surface Anatomy of the Gland: Upper end: Is represented by a concave line which is drawn from just in front of the tragus of the auricle (head of mandible) to the center of mastoid process, around the external auditory meatus. Anterior border: Is represented by a line drawn from just in front of the tragus , till a point in the center of masseter muscle, then to a point 1 cm below and behind the angle of mandible (lower end). Posterior border: Straight line drawn from the center of mastoid process to a point 1 cm below and behind the angle of mandible (lower end), it runs along the anterior border of sternomastoid muscle. *Relations of Parotid Gland: The main part of parotid gland has 3 surfaces, 2 ends and 2 borders. Relations of the surfaces of main part parotid gland: Superficial lateral surface: Related to skin, superficial fascia, superficial parotid lymph nodes, and great auricular nerve. Anteromedial surface: It is related to ramus of mandible, masseter muscle (laterally) and medial pterygoid muscle (medially). Posteromedial surface related to: Two processes: Mastoid and styloid processes and structures attached to it. Two muscles attached to mastoid process: Sternomastoid muscle (superficially) and posterior belly of digastric muscle (deeply). Two blood vessels: Internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein with the last 4 cranial nerves in between. Two structures enter this surface: Facial nerve and external carotid artery. Relations of borders and ends of parotid gland: Upper end: It is concave and just below the external auditory meatus. Three structures appear at this end: superficial temporal artery and vein and auriculo-temporal nerve. Lower end: It overlaps the posterior belly of digastric muscle. Three structures leave this end : cervical branch of facial nerve, anterior and posterior divisions of retromandibular vein. Anterior border: The following structures appear at the anterior border of the gland from above downwards: Temporal and zygomatic branches of facial nerve, transverse facial artery, accessory part of the parotid gland and parotid duct, buccal and mandibular branches of facial nerve . Posterior border : overlap sternomastoid muscle . Structures within the main part of parotid gland: (from superficial to deep) Facial nerve: Enters the postero-medial surface of the gland close to stylomastoid foramen. It passes forwards and divides into five branches ( T.Z.B.M.C or To Zanibar By Motor Car ) . Retromandibular vein: It is formed within the gland behind the neck of mandible by the union of superficial temporal and maxillary veins. Lleaves the lower end of the gland as two divisions (anterior and posterior). External carotid artery: It enters its posteromedial surface. It ascends vertically deep to the retromandibular vein . It divides behind the neck of the mandible into 2 terminal branches: maxillary and superficial temporal arteries. Deep parotid lymph nodes: They are embedded in the substance of the gland around the blood vessels. Auriculotemporal nerve: It has a short course within the gland. INCLUDEPICTURE "http://didier-chantier.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Anatomy-Of-Parotid-Gland-Awesome-Websites-Photo-Album-Website-With-Anatomy-Of-Parotid-Gland.jpg" \* MERGEFORMATINET Parotid duct: ( Stenson’s duct ) Thick-walled, narrow lumen, 5 cm long. It begins at the anterior border of the gland, passes horizontally , with the accessory part of the gland , on masseter muscle, one finger breadth below zygomatic arch. At the anterior border of masseter, it pierces 4 structures: buccal pad of fat, bucco-pharyngeal fascia, buccinator muscle and buccal mucous membrane ( 2 F & 2M ). It opens in the vestibule of mouth opposite the upper 2nd molar tooth. Surface anatomy of the duct: The middle 1/3 of a line extending from the tragus of auricle to a mid- point between the ala of nose and the angle of the mouth . *Nerve supply of the parotid gland: Parasympathetic: The parotid gland receives parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve. They have the following course: The preganglionic fibers arise from the inferior salivary nucleus in the medulla and pass with the glossopharyngeal nerve. Then, the fibers pass in the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve which enters the middle ear cavity to form the tympanic plexus. The tympanic plexus gives the lesser superficial petrosal nerve which passes through the foramen ovale to relay in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve which carries them to the parotid gland. Sympathetic: From the sympathetic plexus around the external carotid and middle meningeal arteries. Sensory: From the auriculotemporal nerve. *Blood vessels: Arteries: from superficial temporal artery. Veins: The retromandibular. Lymphatic drainage: The gland is drained into the superficial and deep parotid lymph nodes which finally drain into the upper deep cervical lymph nodes. *Capsules of the parotid gland : - Parotid capsule is derived from the general investing deep fascia of the neck which split at the lower end of the parotid gland into 2 layers : 1- Superficial layer : attached upwards to zygomatic arch . 2-Deep layer: attached to the styloid process forming the stylomandibular ligament which separates lower end of parotid gland from the posterior end of the subamdibular gland . *Applied Anatomy: 1.  SKIN
• Il is thin & presents the umbilicus which is inverted scar formed by
separation of umbilical stump afler birth.
• It lies in the linen alba at variable level. Usually it lies one finger below a

median umbilical ligament (obliterated urachus).
• Above the level of umbilicus the lymphatic & venous drainage pass upwards
to the axilla while below this level they pass downwards to the groin.
• Nerve supply: Skin of anterior abdominal wall is supplied by T 7.12 & Li
nerves. Skin of at level of umbilicus is supplied by To (as the nerve supply
of appendix).

and vertebral column and prevertebral muscles (posteriorly)
- Recurrent laryngeal nerve passes in the groove between trachea
and esophagus on each side
(2) Thoracic part:
- Longest
g) In superior mediastinum.
- it lies between - trachea (anteriorly)
- vertebral column and prevertebral muscles (posteriorly)
- Left recurrent laryngeal nerve lies in groove between trachea and esophagus
on left side
- azygos vein is close to right side of esophagus
while thoracic duct is close to its left side
b) In posterior mediastinum,
(3) Abdominal part:
- enters abdomen at level of T10

text:
The anterior abdominal wall of a 21-year-old woman impacts
the steering wheel during a head-on car collision. The blunt
trauma resulted in a lacerated pancreas with digestive enzyme
spilling anterior. Which of the following locations would
initially receive the contents of the lacerated pancreas?
A. Supracolic part of greater peritoneal sac
B. Infracolic part of greater peritoneal sac
C. Subhepatic space
D. Omental bursa
E. Subphrenic space
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 The answer is D: Omental bursa.
• The omental bursa (or lesser peritoneal sac) is an isolated part
of the peritoneal cavity, which lies posterior to the stomach
and anterior to the pancreas. Because of its location, the
omental bursa would receive digestive enzymes emanating
from the lacerated section of the anterior pancreas. The only
connection between the omental bursa and the remaining
aspects of the peritoneal cavity is through the epiploic
(omental) foramen.

text:
Blood
supply

 Palate
Arterial supply of the palate:
1. Greater palatine artery (branch from the maxillary artery).
2. Ascending palatine artery (branch from the facial artery).
3. Palatine branch of ascending pharyngeal artery.
Venous drainage of the palate: Through pterygoid and pharyngeal plexuses of veins.

Lymphatic drainage of the palate:
1. The hard palate drains into submandibular lymph nodes.
2. The soft palate drains into upper deep cervical and retropharyngeal lymph nodes.
Nerve supply of the palate
A-Sensory nerve supply:

Hard palate:
1. Greater palatine nerve.
2. Nasopalatine nerve
Soft palate:
3. Lesser palatine nerve.
4. Glossopharyngeal nerve.
Secretomotor fibres to the palatine glands:
The facial nerve through its greater petrosal nerve relays in the sphenopalatine
ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the palatine glands through the lesser palatine
nerves.
Taste sensation:
Taste fibers reach the inferior surface of the palate through the lesser palatine
nerves.
B-Motor nerve supply:
All the muscles are supplied by the cranial part of accessory nerve except the tensor
palati muscle which is supplied by the mandibular nerve.

 Tongue
Arterial supply of the tongue:
1. Lingual artery. ( From external carotid artery)
2. Tonsillar branch of facial artery.
3. Ascending pharyngeal artery.( External carotid artery )
Venous drainage of the tongue:

Lingual vein which drains into the internal jugular vein.
Lymphatic drainage of the tongue:
1- The tip and frenulum of the tongue drain into submental lymph nodes.
2- The peripheral lymphatics from the anterior two thirds pass to the submandibular lymph
nodes. Some pass directly to the upper and lower deep cervical lymph nodes.
3- The central lymphatics from the anterior two thirds drain mainly to the deep cervical
lymph nodes and few pass to the submandibular lymph nodes. They drain to both sides.
4- Lymphatics from the posterior third of the tongue drain into deep cervical lymph nodes
of both sides.
Nerve supply of the tongue:

1- Sensory nerve supply:
General sensation:
It is through the lingual nerve to the anterior two thirds of the tongue. The posterior
third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
Taste sensation:
It is carried by the chorda tympani to the anterior two thirds, and by the
glossopharyngeal nerve to the posterior third. General and taste sensations of the
most posterior part of the tongue are carried by internal laryngeal branch of vagus
nerve.

2- Motor innervation:
All muscles of the tongue are supplied by hypoglossal nerve, except the
palatoglossus muscle which is supplied by cranial part of accessory nerve through
the pharyngeal plexus.

 Parotid gland
Blood supply:

The external carotid artery and the terminal branches within the gland, namely,
superficial temporal and maxillary arteries, supply the gland.
The veins drain into retromandibular vein.
Lymph drainage:
The lymph vessels drain into parotid lymph nodes and the deep cervical lymph nodes.
Nerve supply:
Parasympathetic: the fibres pass through the glossopharyngeal nerve. They leave
the nerve in its tympanic branch; which reach the tympanic cavity where it breaks into
the tympanic plexus. The fibers leave the plexus through lesser superficial petrosal
nerve which leaves to the infratemporal fossa through foramen oval then relay in the otic
ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the gland through auriculotemporal nerve.
Sympathetic fibers: reach the gland as a plexus of nerves around the external carotid
artery.
Sensory:
For the capsule... Great auricular nerve.
parenchyma ...Auriculo-temporal nerve.

Protein Metabolism
 Blood amino acid level is 3 – 6 mg/dl in fasting & rises 2 - 3 mg after protein
meal.
 300 gm proteins (mainly muscle proteins) are degraded daily to amino acids.
 Amino Acids share in Anabolic & Catabolic pathways:(1) Anabolic pathways:
 Formation of tissue protein for wear and tear.
 Plasma proteins, Hb, Enzymes, Hormones.
 Non Proteins Nitrogenous compounds «NPN» as Purines,
Pyrimidines, Creatine and Thyroxine.
(2) Catabolic pathways:
 Urea → formed in the Liver → Main catabolic End product of
protein catabolism.
 Supplying Energy → 1gm protein → 4.1 Kcal, only if there is
shortage in CHO and fats.

Nitrogen Balance
 There is no storage (depot) of protein, but there is a certain percentage of
protein that undergoes breakdown & resynthesis (Turn over).
 This is a normal process and essential feature of Nitrogen Balance.

 Nitrogen Balance:
 Difference between total nitrogen intake (Dietary proteins) and total
nitrogen loss (undigested protein in stools + urea and Ammonia in urine).
 Also nitrogen output through nails, hairs, and desquamated skin.
1. Nitrogen Equilibrium:
 N2 losses (in urines & sweat) = N2 intake (Diet).
2. Positive Nitrogen Balance:
 Increased N2 intake over the output.
 Occur in growth, pregnancy or convalescence from diseases.
3. Negative Nitrogen Balance:
 N2 intake less than N2 output due to:
 Decreased N2 intake as in starvation, poverty, malnutrition,
maldigestion, malabsorption, severe vomiting and severe diarrhea.
 Increased N2 output as in hemorrhage, burns, old age or debilitating
diseases.

The Genius in Biochemistry

Protein Metabolism

Dr. Mohamed Agha

 3

General Metabolism of Proteins
 Major pathway of amino acid excess after protein synthesis is removal of
Amino group (Deamination) → α-Keto Acid + Free Ammonia →
converted to Urea in Liver → Excreted by kidney.
 Liver is the major site for the removal of amino group from amino acids.
 Amino group is removed by different Mechanisms:A. Major Process:
 Transdeamination (Transamination + Oxidative deamination by LGlutamate Dehydrogenase)
B. Minor Process:
 Oxidative Deamination by D- & L-Amino Acid Oxidase.
 Non Oxidative Deamination. (specific for individual amino acids)
I- Transamination:
 Enzymes termed Transaminases which transfer NH2 from amino acid to
α- keto Acid.
 All amino acids can participate in transamination Except Threonine,
Lysine, Proline and Hydroxy Proline. (last 2 → Imino acids)
 Vitamin B6 (PLP) is required as a coenzyme. (intermediate carrier of NH2)
 Pyridoxal Phosphate + NH2 → Pyridoxamine Phosphate.
 They are cytosolic and Mitochondrial Enzymes.
 It is a freely Reversible process.
 After protein meal → Transfer NH2 to α-Keto Glutarate.
 Deficient protein meal → Transfer NH2 to α-Keto Acid → Amino acid.
 Most transaminases require Glutamate and α-Keto Glutarate as one of the
reacting pair → all can be called Glutamate Transaminase.
 No uptake or release of free Ammonia.

Nucleotide Metabolism
 Nucleotides are essential for all cells for:
 DNA, RNA, Protein synthesis→ cell proliferation.
 Energy currency in the cell.
 Carriers of intermediates of CHO, Lipid and Protein metabolism.
 Component of essential cofactors as CoA, NAD+, NADP+ and FAD.
 Digestion and Absorption:-

 Dietary Purines and Pyrimidines are mostly catabolized and not used for the
synthesis of nucleic acids.
 Also, Pentoses (Ribose or 2-Deoxyribose) are not utilized by the body due to
absence of pentose kinase in the human body.
 Nucleotides (purine and pyrimidine bases found in them) can be:
 Synthesized de novo.
 Obtained through salvage pathways that allow the reuse of the
preformed bases resulting from normal cell turnover.

The Genius in Biochemistry

Miscellaneous GIT

A. De novo purine nucleotides biosynthesis: Sources of atoms in the purine
ring:
 Aspartic Acid (N1).
 Glycine (C4, C5, N7)
 Glutamine (N3, N9)
 CO2 (C6)
 Derivatives of tetra hydro folic
acid (C2, C8).
 Site: Liver is the major site for de novo synthesis of purine.
 Steps of Purine Biosynthesis:
 It begins with Ribose-5-P obtained from Hexose Monophosphate Shunt
(HMS) and then the ring is constructed on the sugar.
1. First step is transfer of Pyrophosphate from ATP to C1 of Ribose-5-P
forming 5-PhosphoRibosyl 1-PyroPhosphate (PRPP) by PRPP synthetase.
2. Displacement of pyrophosphate from PRPP by amide nitrogen of
glutamine forming 5-Phospho-β-D-Ribosylamine by PRPP Glutamyl
Amido Transferase (β-N-Glycosidic bond).
3. After series of reactions, Inosine Mono Phosphate (IMP) is formed.

 Conversion of IMP to AMP:

 2

Determination of toxic and nutrition elements levels
by Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy
Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS)

 Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) is a technique for determining the
concentration of a particular Metal (e.g, Fe, Cu, Al, Pb, Ca, Zn) in a sample

(water, serum, food).

 AAS applications:
1- Analyzing metals in biological fluids such as blood and urine. As trace
elements are essential to maintain the metabolism of the human body,
however, at higher concentrations they can be toxic.
2- Monitoring the environment, heavy metals enter our body via food, water and
air and cause toxicity.
3- In some pharmaceutical manufacturing processes.

 What is the principle of Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy?

 All atoms can absorb light at specific, unique wavelengths . When a sample
containing copper (Cu) and nickel (Ni), for example, is exposed to light at the
characteristic wavelength of Cu, then only the Cu atoms will absorb this
light.
 The amount of light absorbed at this wavelength is directly proportional to
the concentration of the absorbing atoms.
 A calibration curve is constructed by several solutions of known
concentration.
 This enables the calculation of the analyte concentration in the unknown
sample.

 Basic concepts to understand:
 Ground/ excited state of atoms:
 The normal and most stable orbital configuration of an atom is known as
the (ground state).
 If energy is applied to an atom, it will be absorbed, and an outer electron
will be promoted to a less stable configuration known as the (excited state)
 Since this state is unstable, the atom will immediately return to the
(ground state), releasing light energy of specific wavelength.

The Genius in Biochemistry

Practical GIT

Dr. Mohamed Agha

 3

 Since each chemical element has a unique number of electrons at its ground
state, an atom will absorb or release energy in a pattern unique to it.
 AS the name suggests, the particles must be atomized in order to perform
analysis.

 Basic steps involved in atomization of aqueous solution sample: (turning a
liquid sample into atomic gas):
1- Nebulization: Sample solution, get into fine droplets (aerosol).
2- Desolvation: the liquid solvent evaporates - convert droplets to crystals.
3- Vaporization: conversion of solid crystals into vapor.
4- Atomization: Dissociation of molecules into atoms.

 Main components of AAS and their functions:

1- Nebulizer:

 Mixes the formed fine droplets and oxidant gas and fuel thoroughly for
introduction into the atomizer as fine droplets.

2- Source of radiation: Hollow cathode lamp (HCL).

 An HCL usually consists of a glass tube containing a cathode, an anode, and
an inert gas as argon.
 The hollow cathode is coated with the element to be measured.
a. Ionization: large voltage across the anode and cathode will cause the
inert gas to ionize, creating a positive ion.
b. Sputtering: The inert gas ions (Positively charged) will then be
accelerated into the cathode, and collide with its surface. This Collision
will cause release (sputtering) off atoms from the cathode.
c. Excitation: These sputtered cathode atoms will in turn be excited by
collisions with other atoms promoting the electrons from their ground
state to higher energy levels.
d. Emission: as these excited atoms decay to lower states, they will emit
photons of the same wavelength to be absorbed by the element of
interest.

The Genius in Biochemistry

Practical GIT

Dr. Mohamed Agha

text:
GIT Practical Exam

Prepared and Presented By /
Dr. Mohamed Agha

 • Define Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy..
 AAS is a technique for determining the concentration of a Metal (Fe,
Cu) in a sample (water, serum, food).

• Mention Applications of Atomic Absorption
Spectroscopy.

1. Analyzing metals in biological fluids such as blood and
urine → Higher concentrations they can be toxic.
2. Monitoring the environment, heavy metals enter our body
via food, water and air and cause toxicity.
3.In pharmaceutical manufacturing.

 • Discuss Principle of Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy.
 All atoms can absorb light at specific, unique wavelengths..

 The amount of light absorbed at this wavelength is directly
proportional to the concentration of the absorbing atoms.

*

 A calibration curve is constructed by several solutions of known
concentration.

 This enables the calculation of the analyte concentration in the
unknown sample.

A. Fascial
B. Glossopharyngeal
C. Vagus
D. Hypoglossal

thirds of his tongue, what is the nerve affected?
A. Lingual
B. Glossopharyngeal nerve

A. Head
B. Body
C. Tail
D. Neck

 C. Guanosine - inosine- hypoxanthine - xanthine
D. Guanosine - guanine - uric acid - hypoxanthine

A. Xanthine oxidase
B.
C.
D.

A. Dairy products
B. Fresh fruits and vegetables
C. Meat and poultry

A.
B.
C. Aspartate + alpha ketoglutarate
oxaloacetate + glutamate
D.

➡️

A. Wilson's disease
B. Pellagra
C. Addison's disease
D. Rickets

weight, his blood ammonia level was found to be 400 µmol/L, which of the following
Enzymes deficiency is the most common cause for these symptoms?
A.
B.
C. Deficiency of ornithine transcarbamoylase
D.

A. Alkaptonuria
B. Albinism
C.
8.

Why is Vitamin E important for the integrity of the RBCs?
A.
B.
C. Prevent oxidation of the cell membrane by the free radicles
D.

 9. Which of the following is a complication of chemotherapy?
A. Hypernatremia
B. Hyperkalemia
C. Hyperuricemia

PHYSIOLOGY
1. What best characterizes the third phase of deglutition?
A. Is controlled only by local enteric reflexes
B. Not changed after bilateral vagotomy
C. Is antagonized by gravity
D. Mediated by peristaltic movements
2. Which of the following stimulates salivary secretion in conditioned reflex?
A. Smell of food
B. Presence of food in the mouth
C. Movement of the tongue during speech
D.
3. Which of the following abolished the Cephalic phase of the regulation of gastric
secretion?
A. Vagotomy
B.
C.
D.
4. Which of the following inhibits gastric emptying?
A. Gastric hormone
B. Enterogastric reflex
C. Somatostatin receptor blocker
D. .
5. Which of the following inhibit brunner’s gland?
A. Vagas stimulation
B. Secretin
C. Sympathetic stimulation
D. Contact of acidic chime
6.
HISTOLOGY

Histology Of GIT (By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)
Gastrointestinal tract (GIT):
1- Oral cavity: lip, tongue& salivary glands.
2- Alimentary canal:
 Esophagus.

 Stomach.

 Junctions.
3- Associated glands: liver, gall bladder& pancreas.

1- Oral Cavity
It consists of:
1- Vestibule.
2- Oral cavity proper.
Types of oral mucosa:
A- Masticatory: covers gum, hard palate & dorsum of tongue, thick, firmly
attached to underlying tissues, stratified squamous epithelium with
variable degree of keratinization.
B- Lining mucosa: elsewhere in oral cavity, non-keratinized stratified
squamous epithelium.
C- Specialized mucosa: taste buds.

Structure of the lip:
It consists of three surfaces:
1- Skin surface: thin skin.
2- Red margin:
 Transitional zone between the skin and the mucous surface.
 Rich in sensory nerve endings.
 Lined by thin keratinized stratified squamous epithelium which
is indented by long connective tissue papillae, rich in blood
capillaries.
 The red color of the lip is due to reflection of the numerous blood capillaries in the underlying
connective tissue papillae.
3- The mucous surface:
 Epithelium: non keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
 Lamina propria: contains labial salivary glands (mucous acini).
The main bulk of the lip: is formed the orbicularis oris muscle embedded in fibro elastic connective
tissue rich in fat cells.

GIT Module

Page 1

 Histology Of GIT (By Prof. Dr. Iman Nabil)

Functions:
1- Food manipulation.
2- Speech.
3- General sensory perception & the special sensation of
taste.
Anatomically:
It has 2 surfaces: dorsal & ventral.
The dorsal surface: is divided by the gustatory line (sulcus
terminalis) into anterior 2/3 & posterior 1/3.

How does the tongue adapt to its functions?

1- Dorsal surface:
 The mucosa of the anterior 2/3 is firmly attached to the
underlying tissue.
 It is modified to form lingual papillae.
2- Ventral surface:
 Covered by the lining mucosa.
 Loosely attached to the underlying tissue to permit free bending and mobility of the tongue.
3- The main bulk: of the tongue is formed of:
 Striated muscle fibers: run in three directions: longitudinal, transverse & vertical.
 They are embedded in loose areolar &adipose CT to allow maximal mobility of the tongue.

The Lingual Papillae:

 Definition: elevations on the anterior 2/3 of the dorsal surface
of the tongue.
 Function: increase the surface area of the mucosa coming in
contact with the food.
 Structure: Each papilla has a core of connective tissue covered by
stratified squamous epithelium (with variable degree of
keratinization). This core may project to indent the epithelium to
form secondary papillae.

1-Filiform Papillae:


Number: most numerous.
Distribution: arranged in rows, parallel to the gustatory line over the
anterior 2/3 of the dorsal surface of the tongue.
Shape: conical with antero posterior inclination.
Epithelium: Lightly keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Taste buds: absent.
Secondary papillae: short or absent.

text:
➢ Histology of the lip
❖ The lips are the entry point of the alimentary canal.
❖ The skin surface is formed of hairy thin skin.
❖ The oral mucosa = non keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
❖ The ducts of labial salivary glands open into the vestibule, keeping this surface moist.
❖ The orbicularis oris muscle is a striated muscle.

➢ Histology of the Tongue
❖ The tongue is a muscular organ.
❖ The main bulk of the tongue is formed of striated muscle fibers (intrinsic lingual muscles) which run in three directions:
longitudinal, transverse, and vertical (at right angles to each other).
❖ The ventral surface contains acini of mucous-secreting lingual glands.
❖ The sulcus terminalis is a V-shaped structure.
❖ The mucosa of the anterior 2/3 of the dorsum of the tongue = papillary surface.
❖ The fungiform papillae have a rounded summit and narrow base.

➢ Histology of the Taste buds
❖ Taste buds are found embedded within the epithelium of the fungiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae.
❖ Taste buds are ovoid structures oriented at a right angle to the lining epithelium.
❖ The gustatory cells have long apical microvilli which protrude out into the taste pore.
❖ Tastants = food dissolved in saliva.

➢ Histology of the Salivary glands
❖ The mouth cavity is continuously lubricated and washed out by the saliva. It is the secretory product of a group of
salivary glands that open into the oral cavity.
❖ The major salivary glands include three pairs.
❖ The major salivary glands are large compound tubuloacinar glands, which pour their products via branched system of
ducts.
1

A.S

 ❖ The minor salivary glands are small and unpaired.
❖ Regarding the stroma of the major salivary glands, the CT capsule covers the gland, separating it from the surrounding
structures and conveys its vascular and nervous supply.
❖ Regarding the stroma of the major salivary glands, the CT septa divides the gland into lobes by interlobar septa and
smaller lobules by interlobular septa.
❖ The intralobular CT is formed of network of reticular fibers that surround the secretory acini and their ducts.
❖ Regarding the parenchyma of the major salivary glands, the acinus is a group of secretory cells surrounding a lumen
and resting on a basement membrane. The cells are separated from the basement membrane by myoepithelial cells.
❖ The mucous acini secrete viscid glycoprotein.
❖ The serous acinus appears deeply stained.
❖ The intercalated ducts unite together to pour into larger secretory striated ducts.
❖ The intralobular ducts unite to form larger interlobular ducts lying in the interlobular CT septa.
❖ The interlobar ducts are large and they are found in the interlobar septa.
❖ The main duct is a large duct with wide lumen.
❖ The parotid gland has well defined lobulation.
❖ parotid glands have large numbers of fat cells within the septa and between the acini.
❖ The sublingual gland has well defined lobulation.

2

A.S

rel: y2/MED 202 - Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition & Communication and Basic Clinical Skills (4)/Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition/Histology/Dr_ Iman Nabil/زيادات/زيادات هيستو-2.pdf
text:
➢ Histology of the Pharynx
❖ The pharynx is a Musculo-membranous tube.
❖ The nasopharynx is lined by respiratory epithelium = pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
❖ The lamina propria contains sero-mucous glands and is formed of dense fibroelastic CT separating the epithelium from
the striated muscles of the pharynx.
➢

The general histological plan of the Alimentary canal

❖ Mucosa = mucous membrane.
❖ The muscularis mucosae separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
❖ Regarding the submucosa, the lymphoid tissue in the lamina propria and submucosa of the gut constitutes a part of
MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) that provides protection against bacterial invasion since most of the
digestive tract is lined by a thin epithelium (except the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal).
❖ Regarding the musculosa, the myenteric autonomic nerve plexus (Auerbach’s plexus) is situated in the thin CT found in
between the two layers of smooth muscle fibers.
❖ The serosa contains loose CT traversed by large blood and lymph vessels and nerve trunks, sometimes contains large
amount of adipose tissue.
❖ The mesothelial covering of simple squamous epithelium = visceral peritoneum.
❖ Regarding the serosa, when the peritoneum is NOT covering the viscus, this layer is called adventitia (fibrosa) which
protects the viscera and fixes them to the thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic walls.

➢ Histology of the esophagus
❖ The esophagus is a muscular organ.
❖ The terminal ½ inch passes through the diaphragm to lie in the abdominal cavity.
❖ The lamina propria is formed of loose CT rich in blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatics.
❖ Regarding the mucosal esophageal glands, they are similar to the cardiac glands of the gastric mucosa.
❖ The mucosal esophageal glands secrete neutral mucus in combination with that of the cardiac glands as this secretion
protects the esophageal mucosa against regurgitated stomach contents.

1

A.S

 ❖ The muscularis mucosae are seen as scattered bundles.
❖ The submucosa is formed of dense fibro-elastic CT.
❖ The submucosal esophageal glands are formed of groups of mucous acini with their ducts open on the luminal surface.
❖ The adventitia is formed of loose areolar CT.

2

A.S

rel: y2/MED 202 - Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition & Communication and Basic Clinical Skills (4)/Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition/Histology/Dr_ Iman Nabil/زيادات/زيادات هيستو-3.pdf
text:
➢ Histology of the Stomach
❖ The stomach is the most dilated segment of the digestive tube.
❖ The gastric pits are funnel shaped.
❖ The cardiac region contains cardiac glands.
❖ The fundic region contains the fundic glands.
❖ The pyloric region is proximal to the pyloric sphincter and contains the pyloric glands.
❖ The fundic glands secrete the main bulk of the gastric juice.
❖ The fundic glands are surrounded by little amount of highly vascular loose CT.
❖ The muscularis mucosae in all gastric regions, is formed of inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of smooth
muscle fibers.
❖ The fundic glands are perpendicular to the muscularis mucosae.
❖ The oxyntic cells are lodged between the basement membrane and the other cells lining the fundic gland.
❖ The oxyntic cells do NOT have secretory granules.
❖ The oxyntic cells have microvilli in the walls of their canaliculi which project into the lumen.
❖ The tubulovesicular system of membranes adds numerous microvilli into the walls of the canaliculi to increase the
surface area available for acid production.
❖ The intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein.
❖ The peptic cells have strongly basal basophilia due to abundant rER.
❖ The enteroendocrine cells are small cells.
❖ The enteroendocrine cells contain basal secretory granules close to the adjacent blood capillaries in the lamina
propria.
❖ The enteroendocrine cells are best visualized by immunohistochemical staining for their peptide hormones secretion
such as enterochromaffin cells (EC cells), secreting serotonin and enterochromaffin-like cells (ECL cells), secreting
histamine.
❖ The cardia is a narrow region of the stomach that surrounds the esophageal orifice.

1

A.S

 ❖ The lamina propria of the pyloric region contains some enteroendocrine cells particularly G cells secreting gastrin
hormone.
❖ The gastric musculosa is formed of spirally oriented smooth muscle fibers.

2

A.S

rel: y2/MED 202 - Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition & Communication and Basic Clinical Skills (4)/Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition/Histology/Dr_ Iman Nabil/زيادات/زيادات هيستو-4.pdf
text:
➢ Histology of the Liver
❖ The liver is the main metabolic organ of the body.
❖ Unlike the pancreas in which the mixed exocrine-endocrine function is carried out by two distinct components, the
dual function of the liver resides in the same cell, the hepatocyte.
❖ The Glisson’s capsule is thin.
❖ The capsule becomes thicker at the hilum.
❖ At the hilum, the portal vein and hepatic artery enter the liver, while the right and left hepatic ducts and lymph vessels
exit.
❖ The CT septa between the hepatic lobules aren’t apparent in human liver but evident in liver of the pig.
❖ The parenchyma of the liver consists of anastomosing cords of hepatocytes arranged in the form of plates of cells
radiating from a small central vein.
❖ The hepatocytes have euchromatic nucleus.
❖ The rER and Golgi synthesize and secrete various plasma proteins and lipoproteins.
❖ The microvilli that are found at the vascular side increases the surface area.
❖ The liver receives oxygenated blood from the general circulation via the hepatic artery.
❖ The blood from sinusoids drains into the central vein.
❖ Hepatic blood sinusoids form an anastomosing plexus between the cords of hepatocytes, presenting an enormous
surface area for exchange of metabolites between the blood and the hepatic parenchyma.
❖ Hepatic sinusoid is lined by fenestrated endothelial cells and Kupffer cells.
❖ The fenestrated endothelial cells are surrounded by thin discontinuous basal lamina which allows free passage of
plasma into the perisinusoidal space, constantly bathing the microvilli of hepatocytes at their vascular site.
❖ Kupffer cells contain many lysosomes and phagosomes.
❖ Kupffer cells can recognize and phagocytose the aged RBCs with digestion of their Hb.
❖ Ito cells are mesenchymal cells.
❖ Myofibroblasts deposit collagen type 1.
❖ The canals of hering are found at the periphery of the hepatic lobules.
1

A.S

 ❖ The central vein in the classic hepatic lobule receives blood from sinusoids.
❖ The portal canals in the classic hepatic lobule are formed of a small triangular area of CT.
❖ Regarding liver acinus, zone I is richly supplied by blood with excellent content of nutrients and oxygen.
❖ Regarding liver acinus, zone III has the poorest blood supply almost exhausted of nutrients and oxygen.
➢

Histology of the Gallbladder

❖ The lamina propria of the mucosa is vascular and rich in lymphocytes and plasma cells.
❖ The musculosa is thin.
➢

Histology of the Pancreas

❖ The pancreas contains a thin CT capsule with a thin septa that divides the pancreas into small lobules and carries with
them the vascular and nervous supply.
❖ The pancreatic acini are lined by tall pyramidal cells with peripheral deep basophilia.
❖ The lumen of the pancreatic acinus is narrow and lined by flat centroacinar cells.
❖ The interlobular ducts are present in the CT septa between the lobules.
❖ The main pancreatic duct is a large duct with a wider lumen.

2

A.S

rel: y2/MED 202 - Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition & Communication and Basic Clinical Skills (4)/Gastrointestinal System and Nutrition/Histology/Dr_ Iman Nabil/زيادات/زيادات هيستو-5.pdf
text:
➢ Histology of the Small Intestine
❖ The modification that occurs at the luminal surface increase the total surface area available for absorption of nutrients
by 400 to 600 folds.
❖ Each villus has a core of vascular lamina propria and is covered by simple columnar absorptive epithelial cells
(enterocytes) and goblet cells.
❖ The villi in the duodenum are relatively short.
❖ The microvilli are numerous and closely packed covering the intestinal villi with its characteristic glycocalyx cell coat.
❖ The muscularis mucosae in the mucosa is formed of inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of smooth muscle
fibers.
❖ The intestinal villi have a covering that Is continues with that of the intestinal glands.
❖ The intestinal villi have a central core of loose CT and a blindly-ended central lymphatic channel.
❖ The enterocytes have oval basal nuclei and these cells are present in the superficial parts of the intestinal crypts.
❖ The goblet cells are present in the superficial parts of the intestinal crypts and these cells are less abundant in the
duodenum.
❖ The enteroendocrine cells are found in the basal parts of the intestinal crypts.
❖ The stem cells are found in the basal half of the intestinal crypts and they proliferate and move superficially to
differentiate and replace the villous epithelium.
❖ Paneth cells have apical eosinophilic zymogen granules.
❖ Peyer’s patches are formed of aggregations of lymphoid nodules and loose lymphoid tissue.
❖ Regarding the serosa, the small intestine is covered by the visceral layer of peritoneum (mesothelium) continuous with

❖ The lamina propria contains a large number of tubular intestinal glands.
❖ The stem cells are located at the bases of the crypts.

located at the bases of the crypts. The muscularis mucosae underlying the bottom of the crypts and is formed of inner
circular and outer longitudinal layers of smooth muscle fibers.
❖ The serosa is formed of loose CT covered by mesothelium.

➢ Histology of the Appendix
❖ It’s called the vermiform appendix.
❖ The crypts of Lieberkühn are short tubular glands and have NO digestive or absorptive functions in humans.
❖ The crypts of Lieberkühn are lined by enteroendocrine cells particularly EC cells.
❖ The lamina propria is filled with loose (scattered lymphocytes) and dense lymphoid tissue (lymphoid nodules)
occupying the spaces between the crypts and extending around the whole circumference of the appendix.
❖ The muscularis mucosae is not well-defined.
❖ The submucosa is a narrow layer.
❖ The musculosa is formed of inner circular and complete outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers.
➢

Histology of the Junctional Sites

❖ They are studied by longitudinal sections.
❖ Regarding the mucosa of the esophago-gastric junction, the columnar epithelium of the stomach is interrupted by
gastric pits characteristic of the cardiac region.
❖ Regarding the lamina propria at the esophageal end, it shows the wider branched tubular cardiac glands.
❖ Regarding the mucosa of the pyloro-duodenal junction, the surface epithelium undergoes gradual changes, the
columnar mucous cells acquire a brush border and become absorptive cells.
❖ The submucosa of the pyloro-duodenal junction contains large numbers of mucus acini of Brunner’s glands.
❖ The musculosa of the pyloro-duodenal junction becomes as thick as the outer longitudinal muscle layers.
❖ Regarding the serosa of the pyloro-duodenal junction, both pylorus and duodenum are covered by visceral layer of
peritoneum.
❖ The rectal mucosa is typical to that of the large intestine except that the crypts of Lieberkühn become shorter and
gradually disappear.

text:
1.
Where is the primary site for absorption of nutrients?
a. Stomach
b. Small intestine
c. Ascending colon
d. Descending colon
e. Both a and b equally
Answer: b
The small intestine is the primary site for absorption of nutrients.
2.
What are the finger like projections of mucosa that are seen in the small
intestine?
a. Lacteal
b. Crypts of Lieberkuhn
c. Plicae circulares
d. Striated border
e. Villi
Answer: e
There are several features of the small intestine.
The lymphatic capillary within a villus of the small intestine is a lacteal.
Crypts of Lieberkuhn are the intestinal glands.
The plica circulares is a projection with a core of submucosa. The plica
circulares is also called the valve of Kerckring.
Microvilli that are seen on the epithelial cells in the small intestine form
the brush border or striated border.
Villi are finger like projections of mucosa seen in the small intestine.
3.
What is the outer layer of the GI tract called when it is abutting another
organ?

 a. Mucosa
b. Sub mucosa
c. Muscularis externa
d. Serosa
e. Adventitia
Answer: e
The mucosa is the innermost layer of the GI tract. It consists of epithelium,
lamina propria, and muscularis mucosa.
The submucosa is connective tissue. Within it are lymphatic vessels and
nerve plexuses. Meissner's plexus is located in the submucosa.
The muscularis externa consists of thick layers of smooth muscle. It
contains Auerbach's plexus.
The outer layer of the GI tract is either an adventitia or serosa. The serosa
consists of only a single layer of epithelial cells and underlying connective
tissue. The adventitia is the outer layer of the GI tract when it is abutting
another organ the posterior abdominal wall.
4.
Where is masticatory mucosa found
a. Tongue underside
b. Hard palate
c. Soft palate
d. Lips
e. Cheek
Answer: b
The masticatory mucosa is located on the hard palate and gingiva. Lining
mucosa is found on the underside of the tongue, lips, cheek, and soft
palate.
5.
What is the surface layer of masticatory mucosa composed of?
a. Non keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
b. Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
c. Simple squamous epithelium
d. Pseudostratified squamous epithelium
e. Both a and b
Answer: e
The masticatory mucosa is located on the hard palate and gingiva. The
surface layer of masticatory mucosa is stratified squamous epithelium.
(Remember, epithelium lines body cavities and covers body surfaces). The

 stratified squamous epithelium is keratinized. However, some regions of
the masticatory mucosa are covered with non-keratinized stratified
squamous epithelium and parakeratinized epithelium. Parakeratinized
epithelium is similar to keratinized epithelium, except that in
parakeratinized epithelium cell nuclei are present in the stratum corneum.
6.
Which layer is NOT present in masticatory epithelium?
a. Stratum basale
b. Stratum spinosum
c. Stratum granulosum
d. Stratum lucidum
e. Stratum corneum
Answer: d
The layers of the masticatory epithelium are similar to the layers of the
epidermis. The stratum lucidum is not present in the masticatory
epithelium.
The epidermis is divided into five layers: stratum basale, stratum spinosum,
stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum, and stratum corneum. The stratum
basale contains the dividing cells. This layer is also called the stratum
germinativum. The stratum spinosum consists of a layer several cells deep.
The cells have pointy or spiny processes on them. The cells in the stratum
granulosum contain keratohyaline granules. The stratum lucidum is present
only in thick skin. The stratum corneum is the outermost layer. The cells in
this layer are essentially bags of keratin. They contain no nuclei or
organelles.
Histology hint from Sarah Bellham: My favorite mnemonic for remembering
the layers of the skin: "Californian Ladies Give Superb Backrubs".
7.
Which type of papillae on the tongue is the most abundant?
a. Filiform papillae
b. Circumvallate papillae
c. Fungiform papillae
d. Foliate papillae
e. All of the a

Bile salts form cylindrical water-soluble disks called micelles.
Micelles contain FA, cholesterol, phospholipids & monoglycerides.
Micelles solubilize lipids and act as a vehicle to transport lipids to enterocytes.
Micelles move down their concentration gradient to reach brush border of
enterocytes to be absorbed.
Lipids diffuse from micelles, bile salts are reabsorbed to the portal circulation
(enterohepatic circulation of bile salts).
Micelles remove fatty acids formed by digestion from the medium and new
molecules of neutral fats are exposed to pancreatic lipase.
Bile salts facilitates absorption of fat soluble vitamins (K,E,D,A) & Carotenes.
Absorption of bile salts helps absorption of Ca & Fe by preventing their
precipitation.

text: Physiology of stomach By: Dr Eman Allam Secretory Motor Parasympathetic Sympathetic Vagus Greater splanchnic nerve (relay in celiac ganglia) Secretory to glands Pyloric alkaline mucous Motor to wall Inhibitory to wall Inhibitory to sphincters (helps emptying) Motor to sphincters (delays emptying) Gastro-ileal Gastrocolic reflexes Reduction of the blood flow Innervation of the stomach Gastric secretion 2.5- 3 liters/day It is the most acidic secretion in the body (pH 1). • Water: 99% • Enzymes: Pepsin, lipase. • Cations & Anions • HCl : 0.4% • Mucin • Intrinsic factor Proton pumb (Aerobic glycolysisi Proton Pump (Aerobic Glycolysis) Postprandial alkaline tide CA H+/K+ ATPase Stimulation of parietal cells to secrete HCl H2 receptors: stimulated by histamine ( secreted by Enterochromaffin Like (ECL) cells in the gastric mucosa) . They are blocked by H2 blocker cimetidine . 2. M1 receptors : Stimulated by Ach . They are blocked by atropine . 3. Gastrin receptors : Stimulated by gastrin hormone released from antral mucosa. Functions of HCl Activates the inactive proteolytic enzyme pepsinogen to the active form, pepsin, and gives the optimum pH needed for its action. Has an antibacterial action. Facilitates the absorption of calcium and iron. Acid chyme stimulates the release of secretin hormone from the duodenum. ( regulates the rate of gastric emptying) Pepsin Proteolytic enzyme which is active in a highly acid medium (optimum pH = 2.0). (inactivated at PH > 5) Pepsin converts proteins into proteoses , and peptones: no amino acids are formed. Pepsionogen is activated by HCl to pepsin. Any minute amounts of pepsin formed, can activate the rest of pepsinogen ( autoactivation ). Intrinsic Factor Vagus mediated 20 % of meal associated gastric secretion More Pepsin secretion Acts directly & indirectly through Gastrin. Conditioned Unconditioned Stimulus: seeing, hearing, smelling food. Food in mouth, pharynx, esophagus Receptors: any special sense organs Taste buds, pharyngeal and oesophogeal receptors. Afferent: Any nerve of special sensation such as smell, sight, hearing. chorda tympani, Glossopharyngeal, vagus. Centre: Cerebral cortex, which in turn sends impulses to dorsal motor vagal nuclei in MO. Dorsal motor vagal nuclei in the medulla oblongata. Efferent: vagus Same Effector: gastric glands Same Response: gastric secretion. Same Sham feeding can prove the role of unconditioned reflexes in gastric secretion. Gastric phase (Gastrin hormone) Stimulated by gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP) released from enteric nerve endings Gastrin secretion is inhibited by high acidity (pH<2) in the antrum (Negative feedback) Stimuli for gastrin releasing peptide Distension of the stomach by food. Certain substances called secretagogues , such as digestive products of proteins (peptides and amino acids) and caffeine . Vagal stimulation: The neurotransmitter secreted from vagal fibers at the G cells seems to be GRP and not acetylcholine. Functions of gastrin Increases gastric secretions ( HCl & pepsinogen) Increases histamine release from ECL cells Increases gastric motility and emptying Increases intestinal motility Stimulates the growth of the mucosa of the stomach and small and large intestines (trophic action) In large doses, it increases the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter Intestinal phase Secretin & CCK ------ gastric secretion Intestinal Gastrin +++++ Pacemaker of the GIT: Thin layer of interstitial cells ( interstitial cells of Cajal ) between circular and longitudinal cell layer. K out They are not followed by muscle contraction unless they reach a threshold for the spike potentials (superimposed by myenteric plexus or vagal stimulation). Pacemaker potential Their function is to provide a background of facilitation and to coordinate the motor activities Frequency of slow waves in human GIT Frequency Site 4/min Stomach 12/min Duodenum 8/min Distal ileum 2/min cecum 6/min sigmoid Gastric motility 1. Tonic contractions. 2. Hunger contractions. 3. Receptive relaxation. 4. Peristaltic movement 5. Migrating motor complex (MMC). Tonic contractions Maintained mild to moderate contractions In the fundus & to a lesser extent in the body. The severity of the tone is inversely related to the volume of the stomach contents. Their main function is to maintain a constant intragastric pressure. Hunger contractions Strong contractions that occur in body of stomach when it is empty leading to hunger pains. Hunger pains appear 12-24 hours after last meal, reach maximal intensity in 3-4 days then subside later on. During fasting, there is hypoglycemia → activation of feeding center in hypothalamus → impulses to medullary vagal nucleus → hunger contractions. Receptive Relaxation Stretchable organ Receptive Relaxation Reflex relaxation of fundus & body of stomach to receive coming bolus of food. This reflex is initiated by: Seeing, smelling, or tasting of food. Distension of the esophagus by the bolus of food. Distension of the stomach. Peristalsis Starts as a weak ring of contraction at middle of stomach that proceeds towards the pyloric antrum. At Antrum, the ring becomes very strong separating antrum from body. Continue in Pyloric antrum Peristalsis In antrum , it leads to 3 possibilities: Grinding movements: Pyloric antrum & canal remain an isolated cavity with strong contractions in their wall to press the contents. Propulsive movements: of contents through pylorus into duodenum. Mixing movements: Retropulsion of the stomach contents back into the gastric lumen. Migrating motor complex (MMC) During the inter-digestive period any food left in the stomach is removed by the MMC. The parasympathetic

 Main physiological functions of GIT:
1-digestion: breakdown of food into small particles,ready for absorption and
utilization by cells
Site:mainly in proximal part of small intestine
2-absorption:transfer of contents of the gut from lumen into mucosa then blood
3-secretion:transfer of fluid,electrolytes,peptides from mucosa to lumen of GIT
Amount:7500 ml daily

• Function:against micro.organisms in lumen of gut

a) Three main pairs of salivary glands:
1- Parotid 2- Submandibular
3- Sublingual.
b) Buccal mucosa contains a large number of small glands secreting mucus.
Type:exocrine glands
• Salivary secretion is an active process
• Primary secretions from acini is identical to plasma
- Modification of saliva occurs during its passage in duct system under effects of
aldosterone which causes reabsorption of Na+ in exchange with K+ and H+.
• Cl is reabsorbed and Hco3 is secreted
Thus saliva is hypotonic solution.

text:
GIT
PHYSIOLOGY 2
DR.ALIAA

 GASTRIC MOTILITY
Basic electrical rhythm(slow wave)
 Spotaneous rhythmic fluctuations in membrane potential between -65:-45mv in all
GIT Smooth muscle except in oesophagus and proximal part of stomach
Initiated by :interstial cells of cajal,stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells (smooth
muscle like) send long branched processes into intestinal SM
Rarely cause muscle contraction but spike potential superimposed on depolarizing
portion of slow wave increase muscle tension
Factors make SM more excitable: ( BER and spike potentials)
 1-streching of the muscle
 2- by acetylcholine from parasympathetic endings
 3-some GIT hormones
The depolarizing portion of each spike is due to ca influx
Repolarizing portion is due to k efflux
Rate of BER
 4/min in stomach…12/min in duodenum…8/min in distal ileum
 In colon rise from 2/min in cecum to 6/min in sigmoid
The function of BER is to coordinate peristalisis and segmentation

 1. Tonic contractions
 strength: maintained mild to moderate contractions.
 site: a- mainly in the fundus and to a lesser extent in the body.
 severity of the tone: inversely related to volume of stomach contents.
 main function: maintain a constant intragastric pressure.
2. Hunger contractions:
 strength: strong contractions, exacerbated peristaltic waves.
 site: the body
 stimulus: when stomach is empty
 mechanism: - when stomach is empty (fasting) → hypoglycemia → activation
of feeding center in the hypothalamus → impulses to the medullary vagal
nucleus → strong vagal stimulation → hunger contractions
- Bilateral Vagotomy:
a- abolishes hunger contractions,
b- but the sense of hunger still occurs due to stimulation of the feeding center.
 sequence: They may fuse together → tetanic contractions for 1-3 min →
hunger pains.
 Time:
o appear 12-24 hours after the last meal,
o reach maximal intensity in 3-4 days
o then subside later on.
● They play a little or no role in the control of appetite.
3. Receptive relaxation:
● stimulus:
a- Seeing, smelling, or tasting of food.
b- Distension of the esophagus by the bolus of food.
c- Distension of the stomach.
● mechanism: stimulus → reflex relaxation of the fundus and body → receive
bolus of food.

 4. Peristaltic movement:
● stimulus and timing: Shortly after the intake of food.
● mechanism: starts at the middle of the stomach as a weak ring of contraction
→ proceeds towards the pyloric antrum and becomes very strong ring of
contraction → may obliterate the gastric lumen → isolating pyloric antrum and
canal from the rest of lumen.
● main function: strong peristaltic in the pyloric antrum and canal leading to
three possibilities:
a) Mixing movements: Squirt the stomach contents back into the gastric
lumen (retropulsion).
b) Propulsive movements: Squirt the contents through the pylorus into the
duodenum. The pyloric aperture acts as a sieve that allows only small
particles to pass through.
c) Grinding movements: The pyloric antrum and canal remain an isolated
cavity with strong contractions in their wall to press the contents.
5. Migrating motor complex (MMC):
● time: every 60-90 min during the inter digestive period
● main function: any food left in the stomach is removed by the MMC
● mechanism: - peristaltic wave that begins within the esophagus → travel
through the entire gastrointestinal tract.
- The hormone motilin:
i- released from endocrine cells within the epithelium of the small intestine.
ii- increase the strength of MMC.

SYSTEM

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 Gastrointestinal System

3

Intrinsic innervation of the gut
The enteric nerve plexus comprises:

1- The myenteric (Aurbach's plexus):
- lies in the musculosa between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
- function: controlling the motor activity of the alimentary canal. It is mainly
excitatory to the tonic and rhythmic contractions, but it also contains some
inhibitory neurons.

2- The submucosal (Meissner's plexus):
- lies in the submucous layer.
- function: controlling the local secretory function of the GIT by stimulating the
local exocrine and endocrine secretory cells. It contains the neurons of the sensory
afferent nerves which arise from the mucosal layer.
Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 Gastrointestinal System

4

Extrinsic innervation of the gut
- The intrinsic neural plexuses of the enteric nervous system are connected together
and

are

modulated

by

extrinsic

autonomic

nerves

(sympathetic

and

parasympathetic).
- The parasympathetic supply:
- is generally excitatory to the enteric nervous system, it stimulates the
motility and secretion.
- However, it contains also some inhibitory vagal fibers to the stomach and
the gastrointestinal sphincters.
- The sympathetic nerve supply:
- generally inhibits secretion and motility.
- However, it contains also some excitatory fibers.
- Sensory fibers arise from the luminal epithelium and wall of the gut to the enteric
plexuses and from there to the prevertebral ganglia, spinal cord and brain stem.

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

Artist Of Physiology

New Look

DR/Ibrahim

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/IBRAHIM AMR

Physiology of GIT
- Parts of the digestive system:
(1) The alimentary canal:
- it extends from mouth to anus.
(2) The associated glands:
- include salivary glands, liver and
pancreas which empty their secretion
into alimentary canal.
(3) Accessory organs:
- include tongue, teeth
and muscles of mastication.

- Physiological functions of the GIT:
(1) Digestion: - it is the breakdown of food materials into small particles
(2) Absorption: - transfer of the contents of the gut from lumen into the mucosa.
(3) Secretion:
- it is the transport of fluid, electrolytes, etc.…… from blood to lumen of GIT
- about 7500 ml of secretions are added daily to the lumen of the GIT.
- Secretions are usually isotonic, except for saliva which is hypotonic
(4) Immune function:
- lymphocytes in Peyer's patches protect the body against micro-organisms
in the lumen of the gut.
(5) Endocrine function:
- e.g. release of somatostatin, intestinal glucagon, gastrin, secretin and CCK

1

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/IBRAHIM AMR

INNERVATION OF THE GIT
- Musculature of digestive tract is composed of smooth muscle fibers except
striated muscles of mouth, upper part of esophagus and external anal sphincter
- All smooth muscles are involuntary, and controlled by 2 types of nerves:
(1) Intrinsic (enteric nerve plexus)
(2) Extrinsic (sympathetic and parasympathetic)

Intrinsic innervation of the gut:
- The enteric nerve plexus consists of:
(1) Myenteric (Aurbach's plexus):
- lies in the musculosa between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers.
- It controls motility of the alimentary canal.
- It is mainly excitatory, but it also contains some inhibitory neurons.
(2) The submucosal (Meissner's plexus):
- lies in the submucous layer.
- It controls secretion of the GIT

Extrinsic innervation of the gut:
- The intrinsic neural plexuses are
connected together and are modulated
by extrinsic autonomic nerves
(sympathetic and parasympathetic)
(1) The parasympathetic supply:
- it stimulates the motility and secretion.
- is generally excitatory to the enteric nervous system
- However, it contains also some inhibitory vagal fibers to GIT sphincters.
(2) The sympathetic nerve supply:
- it inhibits the motility and secretion.
- However, it contains also some excitatory fibers.
- Sensory fibers arise from luminal epithelium and wall of gut to enteric plexuses
and from there to the prevertebral ganglia, spinal cord and brain stem .
2

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/IBRAHIM AMR

SALIVARY SECRETION
- There are 3 pairs of salivary glands, which are the parotid, submandibular
and sublingual salivary glands.
- Buccal mucosa also contains large number
of small glands secreting mucus.
- Salivary glands are exocrine glands,
with ducts opening into the oral cavity.

- Types of salivary secretion:
(1) Serous (watery) secretion:
- containing the enzyme ptyalin (α-amylase) which is used for starch digestion.
(2) Mucous secretion:
- containing mucin that makes the saliva viscous for protection and lubrication

- salivary secretion is almost entirely controlled by nervous system
- the parasympathetic nerve plays the most prominent role
- the sympathetic nerves slightly modify the composition of the saliva

Artist Of Physiology

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

Pancreas
- Pancreatic secretion contains:
- digestive enzymes: for digesting proteins, carbohydrates and fats.
- sodium bicarbonate: for neutralization of acidic chyme
- exocrine portion of pancreas consists of alveolar glands (acini) containing
digestive enzymes in the form of (zymogen granules) which are discharged from
the cells into the lumen of the pancreatic ducts
- The small ducts unite together forming
a single duct, the main pancreatic duct,
which usually joins common bile duct
to form the ampulla of Vater.
- The ampulla opens into duodenum,
this opening is encircled by
sphincter of Oddi
- there may be accessory pancreatic duct
which opens in duodenum proximally

Composition of pancreatic secretion:
- About 1500 ml of pancreatic juice is secreted per day.
- pancreatic secretion is the most alkaline juice in the human body.
- Its pH is 8.3.
- It contains sodium bicarbonate in a concentration about 5 folds that of plasma.
- flow of gastric acid chyme into the duodenum is the main stimulus for
bicarbonate secretion.
- Bile and intestinal juices are also neutral or alkaline, and these three secretions
neutralize the gastric acid, raising the pH of the duodenal contents to 6 - 7

1

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

- the main enzymes present in pancreatic secretion are:

(1) Proteolytic enzymes:
(a) Trypsinogen:
- it is secreted in an inactive form and then activated to trypsin by an enzyme
present in intestinal secretion called enterokinase (enteropeptidase)
- Any amount of trypsin formed auto-activates the rest of trypsinogen present,
and also activates other proteolytic enzymes
- The optimum pH for its action is between 8 and 9.
- It converts proteins into peptides of various sizes
but does not cause release of individual amino acids, it is an endopeptidase.
(b) Chymo-trypsinogen:
- it is secreted in an inactive form, activated into chymotrypsin by trypsin
- it is also an endopeptidase,
it acts specifically on peptide linkages, which contain aromatic amino acids.
(c) Pro-carboxypeptidase:
- This enzyme is activated by trypsin into carboxy-polypeptidase
- it is an exopeptidase,
because it hydrolyses polypeptides separating the amino acid
with a free carboxylic group.
(d) Pro-elastase:
- This enzyme is activated by trypsin to the active form elastase.
- It attacks the elastic fibers.
- It cleaves peptide bonds of aliphatic amino acids.
(e) Ribonucleases and deoxyribonucleases:
- nucleases split 2 types of nucleic acid, ribonucleic and deoxyribonucleic acids
into nucleotides.

2

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

- Secretion of trypsin inhibitor:
- once trypsin is activated, there is an autocatalytic chain reaction.
- release of any minute amount of trypsin into the pancreas is very dangerous
because it gives many active enzymes which might digest the pancreas itself.
- However, activation of proteolytic enzymes occurs only in the intestine.
- This is because pancreatic acini secreting the enzymes secrete at the same time
a trypsin inhibitor, this substance is stored in cytoplasm of the glandular cells
surrounding the zymogen granules, and prevents activation of trypsinogen
in the pancreas, thus protecting it from autodigestion.

(2) Pancreatic amylase:
- This enzyme hydrolyses starches, glycogen, and most other carbohydrates
except cellulose to form oligosaccharides (maltose, malto-triose and α-dextrins).
- It has a more powerful action than salivary amylase, it can split uncooked starch.
- Chloride ions serve as a coenzyme for it.

(3) Lipolytic enzymes:
(a) Pancreatic lipase:
- This enzyme hydrolyzes triglycerides (triacylglycerols)
to free fatty acids and 2-monoglycerides (2-monoacylglycerols).
- Colipase:
- is also secreted in pancreatic juice, and when it binds to pancreatic lipase,
it facilitates its action.
(b) Cholesterol esterase:
- catalyzes hydrolysis of cholesterol esters.
(c) Phospholipase:
- splits fatty
