Esophageal peristalsis In upright position, food bolus usually travels along esophagus faster than the primary peristaltic wave & reaches lower esophageal end in about 7 seconds. Fluids reach stomach very rapidly. Semisolids take a longer time than fluids and solid materials are slower than semisolids . The cardiac sphincter dose not open until a peristaltic wave opens this sphincter. Esophageal peristalsis The movements in upper third esophagus are rapid while those in lower third are slow. M uscles of the upper third are striated and supplied by the vagus nerve while in its lower third are plain and depend on local plexus of Auerbach . This phase is helped by mucin and gravity in erect position. Esophageal peristalsis Bilateral vagotomy abolishes primary and secondary waves in upper half of esophagus, but peristaltic wave in lower half of esophagus can occur as they could be conducted by the local myenteric plexus. So , with bilateral vagotomy , there is difficulty in swallowing until the bolus passes through the upper part by the effect of gravity. Lower esophageal sphincter It is the lowest 3-5 cm of the esophagus. This sphincter is tonically contracted between meals to prevent reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. text: Gastric motility By: Dr Eman Allam 1 . Tonic contractions. 2 . Hunger contractions. 3 . Receptive relaxation. 4 . Peristaltic movement 5. Migrating motor complex (MMC). Tonic contractions M aintained mild to moderate contractions I n the fundus & to a lesser extent in the body . The severity of the tone is inversely related to the volume of the stomach contents. Their main function is to maintain a constant intragastric pressure. Hunger contractions S trong contractions that occur in body of stomach when it is empty leading to hunger pains. Hunger pains appear 12-24 hours after last meal, reach maximal intensity in 3-4 days then subside later on. During fasting, there is hypoglycemia → activation of feeding center in hypothalamus → impulses to medullary vagal nucleus → hunger contractions . Receptive Relaxation Stretchable organ Receptive Relaxation R eflex relaxation of fundus & body of stomach to receive coming bolus of food. This reflex is initiated by: Seeing , smelling, or tasting of food. Distension of the esophagus by the bolus of food. Distension of the stomach. Peristalsis Starts weak at m iddle of stomach At Antrum ….. v ery strong s eparating antrum f rom body. Continue in Pyloric antrum Peristalsis In antrum , it leads to 3 possibilities: Grinding movements: P yloric antrum & canal remain an isolated cavity with strong contractions in their wall to press the contents. Propulsive movements: Squirt contents through pylorus into duodenum. ----- P yloric aperture acts as a sieve that allows only small particles to pass through. Mixing movements: Squirt the stomach contents back into the gastric lumen ( retropulsion ). Migrating motor complex (MMC) During the inter-digestive period any food left in the stomach is removed by the MMC. P eristaltic wave that begins within esophagus and travels through entire GIT. It occurs every 60-90 min during inter-digestive period. Stimulated by motilin hormone Gastric emptying Normally, force of tonic contraction of pyloric sphincter is weak, leading to its incomplete closure and easy passage of fluids through it . This force is sufficient to prevent passage of semisolid chyme into duodenum except in presence of strong antral peristaltic waves which drives food toward the duodenum. Antral peristalsis (Pyloric pumb ) Contraction of pyloric sphincter Regulation of stomach emptying Gastric factors Duodenal factors Other factors Gastric Factors Nervous stimulation ( myentric & vagal): stimulated by gastric distension. Hormonal (Gastrin): stimulates both gastric secretion and motility . I ncreases activity of pyloric pump R elaxes pyloric sphincter Duodenal factors Nervous ( Enterogastric reflex) Reflex inhibition of antral peristalsis with contraction of pyloric spincter . L ocal myenteric reflex & vago -vagal reflex . Stimulated by: Duodenal distension Irritants Acidic chyme Duodenal factors Cholecystokinin (CCK) Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) Secretin Somatostatin Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) Gastrin Gastrin Secretin GIP Somatostatin VIP Other factors Chemical agents Stimulants: Cholinergic drugs, sodium bicarbonate, coffee, alcohol, and vitamin B. Inhibitors: Adrenergic drugs, cholinergic blockers (as atropine), smoking, and bacterial toxins depress stomach emptying. Other factors Emotions A nxiety and anger +++ gastric motility Fear , pain, depression, sadness, and muscular exercise --- gastric emptying. Consistency of food Fluids Semisolids Solids Other factors Type of food Proteins faster emptying as they stimulate gastrin. Fat (heavy meal) inhibits motility & emptying . E ntry of fats and fatty acids in duodenum releases some duodenal hormones that delay gastric emptying. Autonomic stimulation THANK YOU

text: Small intestine The small intestine performs both endocrine and exocrine functions In the small intestine the chemical digestion of food is completed and most of the absorption of nutrients takes place. Intestinal secretion ( succus entericus ) Intestinal juice mucus About 1 liter of isotonic intestinal secretion is secreted daily by the glands of the small intestine (crypts of Lieberkuhn ). Pure intestinal juice is similar to extracellular fluid The pH of intestinal juice is usually between 7-7.5. It contains no digestive enzymes . text: INTESTINAL MOTILITY The movements of the small intestine mix the intestinal contents & propel them toward the large intestine. INTESTINAL MOTILITY Intestinal motility is coordinated by: 1- Basic electrical rhythm 2- Enteric nervous system 3- Autonomic nervous system 4- GIT hormones Pacemaker of the GIT: Thin layer of interstitial cells ( interstitial cells of Cajal ) between circular and longitudinal cell layer. Insert fig. 18.16 Pacemaker potential 1- distension 2- myenteric plexus 3- nervous stimulation 4- hormones They are not followed by muscle contraction unless they reach a threshold for the spike potentials (superimposed by myenteric plexus or vagal stimulation). Pacemaker potential Their function is to provide a background of facilitation and to coordinate the motor activities Frequency of slow waves in human GIT Frequency Site 3/min Stomach 12/min Duodenum 8/min Distal ileum 2/min cecum 6/min sigmoid INTESTINAL MOTILITY Ingestion of a meal During fasting Migrating motor complex along the intestine at regular intervals Other types of contractions replaced INTESTINAL MOVEMENTS 1- Segmenting movements (mixing contractions) Segmentation: occurs In response to distension with chyme . 1- Segmenting movements (mixing contractions) Ring like contractions dividing a loop of the intestine into equal portions, giving the appearance of a chain of sausages. Then, the contractions relax and a new set of contractions begin in previously relaxed points Segmentation Mixing Chyme with Digestive Juice Exposing Chyme to absorption Surface Digestion Absorption Slowly propel chyme Digestion &Absorption 1- Segmenting movements (mixing contractions) Little forward movement Frequency of segmentating contractions 12/min 8/min Segmenting movements (mixing contractions) Although slow waves in the smooth muscle cause the segmentating contractions, these contractions are ineffective without background excitation mainly from the myenteric nerve plexus . These movements occur independent of extrinsic innervation. 1- Segmenting movements (mixing contractions) The segmenting movements are myogenic in nature 1- nervous stimulation 2- distension 3- hormones 4- myenteric plexus 2- Peristaltic movements (propulsive movements) Peristalsis is a reflex response , initiated by stretch of the gut wall by the contents of the lumen. It occurs in all parts of GIT from esophagus to rectum. Circular muscle contraction behind the stimulus area of receptive relaxation in front of the stimulus 2- Peristaltic movements (propulsive movements) The wave of contraction moves in an oral-to-caudal direction propelling the contents of the lumen forward. 2- Peristaltic movements (propulsive movements) 2- Peristaltic movements (propulsive movements) The movement of food along the small intestine normally averages 1 cm/min. So, 3 to 5 hours are required for passage of chyme from the pylorus to the ileocecal valve. Peristalsis – law of the gut 1- Entry of food into duedenum stretch of the wall release of serotonin 2. relaxation of circular smooth muscle distal to the bolus via NO, VIP, and ATP Propulsion of food from oral to caudal direction 1. contraction of circular smooth muscle proximal to the bolus via substance P and acetylcholine initiates local enteric reflex (Myenteric reflex) + serotonin Peristalsis 2- Gastroenteric reflex: Distention of the stomach excites some receptors and this reflex is carried out by the myenteric plexus from the stomach down along the wall of the small intestine to initiate peristaltic activity of the small intestine initiates peristalsis Intestinal Motility Segmentation movement Peristaltic movement Ring like contractions dividing a loop of the intestine into equal portions. Then, these contractions relax and a new set of contractions begin in the previously relaxed points. Description Circular muscle contraction proximal to the bolus and receptive relaxation distal to it The wave then moves in an oral-to-caudal direction Segmentation movement Peristaltic movement Distension with chyme in the small intestine Stimulus 1- stretch of the deudenal wall 2- gastroenteric reflex frequency= 12 in the duodenum and 8 in the terminal ileum Frequency or velocity 1 cm/ min slower distally Myogenic: (BER + spike potential by distension + myenteric plexus stimulation) Control Local myenteric reflex (low of the gut), but increase or decrease by autonomic nerves. Intestinal Motility Segmentation movement Peristaltic movement 1- Mixing the contents with intestinal secretion 2- Increase its exposure to the brush border 3- It slows transit in the small intestine. 4- Segmenting movements have some propulsive effect. Functions 1- Forward movement of food towards the ileocecal valve 2- Spread out of the chyme along the intestinal mucosa. 3- Peristaltic movements have some mixing effect. Intestinal Motility 4. Antiperistalsis This is peristalsis in opposite direction 1. Between duodenum and stomach. 2. Between ileum and coecum . Description Function 1- Between duodenum and stomach: to allow time for neutralization. 2. Between ileum and coecum: to allow time for absorption. Between duodenum & stomach Between coecum & ileum 4. Antiperistalsis 4. Migrating motor complex (MMC) Description In the period between meals , the intestine is relatively quiescent. Every 90 min, it is swept through by a large peristaltic wave triggered by motilin hormone. Start at Stomach Terminal Ileum Migrating Motility Complex Clean Remnants of Food / Mucosal Debris / Bacteria to Colon Prepare GIT for the next meal Function: Control of Migrating Motility Complex Motilin A hormone secreted by endocrine cells in small intestinal mucosa, regulates migrating motor complex. Peristaltic rush Description It is a powerful series of peristaltic waves that travel along the small intestine in a few minutes. It occurs in some infectious diseases. it is not present in normal conditions. Function Peristaltic rush takes the intestinal contents toward the colon to get rid

text: Liver & biliary system By: Dr Eman Allam LIVER functions Bile secretion Detoxification Blood reservoir Filtration of portal blood Production of RBCs Blood clotting Destruction of aged RBCs Excretion of bile pigments Storage of iron, vitamins Metabolic Endocrine Synthesis of plasma proteins The functional unit of liver is the Hepatic lobule Pathway of Bile Secretion Bile Secretion By hepatocytes In between meals, secreted bile is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder Liver Hepatic portal vein Gallbladder Ileum Jejunum Duodenum Bile Bile Bile Bile Bile Bile Bile Figure 2.16 Enterohepatic circulation of bile. Bile Composition Water Organic constituents: bile salts bile pigments cholesterol fatty acids lecithin mucin -like substances phosphatidyl choline alkaline phosphatase Inorganic constituents: cations and anoins Bile Composition 500 ml/day, golden yellow color Acidified in the gall bladder by reabsorption of its NaHCO 3 content . WHY? Enterohepatic circulation Specific gravity : hepatic bile= 1008 gall bladder bile= 1050 Enterohepatic circulation Differences between human hepatic duct bile and gall bladder bile Hepatic Duct Bile Gall bladder Bile Percentage of solids 2–4 10–12 Bile acids (mmol/L) 10–20 50–200 pH 7.8–8.6 7.0–7.4 Specific gravity 1008 1050 Bile acids ( cholic acid & chenodeoxy cholic acid) are formed from of cholesterol. The liver cells synthesize about minute amounts (0.2-0.4 g bile salts/day). T hen bile slats are conjucated with either glycine or taurine . Bile salts Bile salts are sodium and potassium salts of bile acids. Bile salts Deoxy cholic lithocholic Bile salts functions Digestion Choleretic (best) Absorption Solvents to cholesterol and fatty acids Slimulants of peristalsis Anti-putrifactive by helping fat absorption Functions of bile salts Dietary Fat (large TG droplet ) Bile Salts Lipid emulsion Lipase 2-Monoglyceride + 2 FFA 1- Emulsification of fat: reduces surface tension increases surface area 2- bile salts activates pancreatic lipase enzyme Digestive function of bile salts Is it essential for fat digestion???? 2- Absorptive function of bile salts Is it essential??? K E D A Figure 2.14 A micelle. Bile salts functions Digestion Choleretic (best) Absorption Solvents to cholesterol and fatty acids Slimulants of peristalsis Anti- putrifactive by helping fat absorption (Indirect) Functions of bile salts Choleretics Nervous Vagus +++ Sympathetic --- Secretin ( hydrocholeretic ) Regulation of Bile secretion ( Choleretics ) blood flow Bile salts (best) Functions of gall bladder Storage of bile Concentration & acidification of bile Secretion of white bile Buffering of biliary pressure Evacuation of bile when needed Cholecystokinin (main) Nervous (minor) Parasymp +++ Sympathetic ---- Gall bladder evacuation Cholagogues Effects of cholecystectomy The periodic discharge of bile from the gallbladder aids digestion but is not essential for it. Cholecystectomized patients maintain good health and nutrition with a constant slow discharge of bile into the duodenum The bile duct becomes somewhat dilated, and more bile is secreted by the liver after meals. Bilirubin and biliverdin They have no digestive function Normal concentration 0.2-0.8 mg/dl plasma Major end products of hemoglobin and myoglobin metabolism Bile pigments Normal plasma, urine and stool Stercobilinogen (normal color of stool) Urobilinogen (colorless) Free of both types of bile pigments Both forms of bile pigments JAUNDICE Yellow discoloration of sclera, skin, mucous membranes and deep tissues due to increased serum bilirubin above normal value (normal value: 0.2- 0.8 mg/dl). Clinically detected with serum bilirubin 2mg/ dL or  causing deposition of bile pigments in tissues. JAUNDICE Causes and types: 1- prehepatic ( hameolytic jaundice) 2- hepatocellular (hepatic jaundice) 3- posthepatic (obstructive jaundice) JAUNDICE Cause Blood Urine Stool Hemolytic Hepatic Obstructive Excessive hemolysis Haembilirubin (indirect) Normal ( acholuric ) Dark( stercobilin ) Damage to hepatic cells Haembilirubin Cholebilirubin Dark brown Pale grayish Obst . of bile ducts by stones or cancer head of pancreas Cholebilirubin (direct), bile salts Dark brown ( Liquorice ) Clay MCQS The most powerful cholagouge is: Secretin hormone. Cholecystokinin hormone. Gastrin hormone. Bile salts. Bile salts: act as a route for excretion of haemoglobin metabolic products. Increase intestinal motility. Activate pancreatic amylase enzyme. Inhibit the release of stomach enzymes and HCl . Urobilinogen is : a) A mixture of colorless compounds also known as Stercobilinogen . b) Formed in the reticuloendothelial system from Bilirubin. c) It is the dark pigment in urine. d) It is increased in case of obstructive jaundice. The cause of jaundice is likely to be a) Bile duct obstruction, if the urine is paler than normal. b) A post hepatic cause, if the hemobilirubin level in the blood is high. c) Haemolysis , if the urine is darker than normal. d) Bile duct obstruction, if the stool is paler than normal. About bile salts, all the following is true EXCEPT: They are the only constituents of bile essential for digestion. About 90% is reabsorbed from the intestine and re-secreted by the liver. They promote lipid digestion and absorption. They cause jaundice when their blood level increases. All the following stimulate bile secretion from the liver except : Secretin CCK Increased hepatic blood flow Stimulation of parasympathetic nerves that supply the liver. The enterohepatic circulation of bile salts Bile salts: Are secreted by the liver at the time of meals only. Secreted in the duodenum will be lost in feces. Stimulates formation of new bile salts by liver cells. Cause contraction of gallbladder. The functions of gall bladder include: a) Increasing pH of bile through secretion of HCO3. b) Absorption of bile salts. c) Formation of bile pigments. d) Helps continuous flow of liver bile. In a normal gall bladder: a. The pH of stored bile is decreased.

text: Physiology of Pancreas By: Dr Eman Allam Exocrine Pancreas The most important source of digestive enzymes for the three major types of food Volume = 1500ml & pH=8.3 (alkaline) Composition of pancreatic juice Water Organic: enzyme Inorganic : Cations & Anions Pancreatic secretion The most alkaline juice in the human body. The flow of gastric acid chyme into the duodenum is the main stimulus for bicarbonate secretion . Bile and intestinal juices are also neutral or alkaline. These three secretions neutralize the gastric acid, raising the pH of the duodenal contents to 6.0- 7.0. Pancreatic amylase Starch Glycogen CHO Except cellulose Lipolytic enzymes Pancreatic Lipase Cholesterol esterase Phospholipase Proteolytic enzymes Why Pancreas is not autodigested by its proteolytic enzymes? Activation of enzymes occur only in intestine as the pancreatic acini secrete at the same time trypsin inhibitor. Regulation of pancreatic secretions Nervous Vagus +++++ secretion (small in amount, rich in enzymes, poor in water & NaHco3. Hormonal Secretin, Cholecystokinin, VIP Secretin Site of secretion: S cells in upper portion of SI. small intestine. Stimulus: entry of acid chyme to duodenum. Actions C opious secretion of a very alkaline pancreatic juice poor in enzymes by acting on duct cells which probably secrete water and bicar-bonate . N egative feedback control. What is the importance of this large volume of alkaline pancreatic secretion? a- It neutralizes the acidity since the intestinal mucosa cannot withstand the digestive properties of the acidic gastric juice .(protect against duodenal mucosa) b- P rovides suitable pH for action of pancreatic enzymes which act optimally at pH about 8 . c- It augments CCK actions on the pancreas . Extra-pancreatic action of secretin It stimulates bile secretion i.e. hydrocholeretic b. It decreases the intestinal movements. c . It decreases gastric acid secretion and may cause contraction of the pyloric sphincter. Cholecystokinin (CCK) Site : I cells at the mucosa of the upper small intestine ------- Also by: nerves in distal ileum and colon & cerebral cortex. Stimulus: presence of digestive products or proteins, and fats. Effect: pancreatic secretion rich in enzymes and poor in water and bicarbonates Positive feedback Augment action of secretin on pancreas Extra-pancreatic action of CCK C holagogue . Increases intestinal movements. It inhibits gastric motility, emptying and secretion. It augments the contraction of the pyloric sphincter. R egulation of food intake. I t appears to be related to anxiety & analgesia . VIP Site: neurohormone found in neurons & endocrine cells throughout the intestine. It stimulates secretion of water & bicarbonate from pancreas, but it i s weaker than secretin . Relax LES ++++ intestinal secretions Relax GIT smooth muscles MCQs The major anion present in the pancreatic secretion obtained through the stimulatory effect of secretin . a-Chloride. b-Bicarbonate. c-Protein. d-Bromide. The pancreatic secretion rich in enzymes and poor in water is believed to be induced by:- a-Cholecystokinin . b-A chyme with low PH. c-Secretin. d-A very large gastric distension. About exocrine pancreatic secretion :- a-Its volume is about 3 liters daily. b-It is under hormonal control only. c-70 % of it occurs while the chyme is still in the stomach. d-Its bicarbonate contents is secreted by ductal cells. Which of the following are C orrectly paired :- a-Cholecystokinin-gall bladder relaxation. b-Secretin- relaxation of sphincter of Oddi . c-Secretin – stimulation of enzymatic release from the pancreatic acinar cells. d-Cholecystokinin-relaxation of sphincter of Oddi . Which of the following statements is true :- a-Trypsin inhibitor inhibits activation of proteolytic pancreatic enzymes in the small intestine. b-Trypsin activates the precursor of enterokinase . c- Proelastase is activated to elastase by the effect of trypsin. d-exocrine pancreatic secretion is rich in bicarbonate on vagal stimulation. Inhibition of which of the following enzymes has the greatest effect on digestion: a-chymotrypsin. b- enterokinase . c-pancreatic amylase. d-ptyalin. Pancreatic secretion evoked by CCK is: poor in enzymes rich in water rich in bicarbonate Similar to effect of vagal stimulation. Which of the following would not be produced by total pancreatectomy :- a- hyperglycemia. b-weight gain . c-metabolic acidosis. d-decreased absorption of amino acids. VIP: Causes contraction of LES. Stimulates intestinal cells to secrete electrolytes and water. Stimulates gastric secretion. Stimulates intestinal cells to secrete enzymes. THANK YOU

• The wall of the primitive pharynx is formed of three layers; ectoderm
(outermost), endoderm (innermost) and mesoderm (in between).
• The mesoderm is segmented into six horse-shoe (U-shaped) arches in a
successive manner from above downwards (i.e. the first arch will appear first,
followed by the second, third and so on).
• The branchial arches are originally six arches (first arch is called "mandibular
arch" while the second arch is called "hyoid arch").

DURAL VENOUS SINUSES
Superior sagittal sinus (SSS):
- it begins at the apex of falx cerebri
- it continues as the right transverse sinus at internal occipital protuberance.
Inferior sagittal sinus (ISS):
- it runs along the posterior half or two-thirds of the free margin of falx cerebri
- and ends at the free margin of tentorium cerebelli
by uniting with the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus
Straight sinus (SS):
- it is found at the junction of the falx cerebri with tentorium cerebelli.
- it is formed by union of the inferior sagittal sinus and the great cerebral vein.
- it terminates at the internal occipital protuberance
by forming the left transverse sinus.

rel: y2/MED 203 - Nervous System & Professionalism, Medical Law and Ethics/Nervous System/Anatomy and Embryology/Faculty PPT & Tutorial/Blood supply of the brain.pptx
text: BLOOD SUPPLY OF BRAIN Rasha Ibrahim Amer The brain is supplied by: 1.Vertebro-basilar system. 2.Internal carotid system. Vertebro -basilar system consists of: 1. 4th part of vertebral artery (two). 2. Basilar artery (single). 3. Posterior cerebral artery (two). Origin: arises from first part of subclavian artery. Course: 1st part: from its origin to foramen transversorium of 6th cervical vertebra. 2nd part: ascends from foramen transversorium of C6 to C1 vertebra. 3rd part: lies in suboccipital triangle. 4th part: enters skull through foramen magnum to ascend on each side of medulla oblongata. Termination: right and left arteries unite together at lower border of pons to form basilar artery. Vertebral artery Vertebral artery The intracranial part gives branches: 1. Anterior spinal artery; Two arteries unite together to form a single trunk run in anterior median fissure of spinal cord. 2. Posterior spinal artery; Two arteries. Each artery divides into two longitudinal branches. 3. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) is a tortuous artery and is largest branch of vertebral artery. 4. Medullary branches; to supply medulla oblongata. Basilar artery Origin: at lower border of pons by union of 2 vertebral arteries. Course: it passes on front of pons in the midline ( pontine sulcus, basilar groove). Termination: at upper border of pons by bifurcation into 2 posterior cerebral arteries Basilar artery Branches: 1. Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA); supplies anterior part of inferior surface of cerebellum. 2. Superior cerebellar artery; supplies superior surface of cerebellum 3. Pontine branches; supply pons. 4. Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery; supplies inner ear. 5. Posterior cerebral arteries (terminal branches). Posterior cerebral artery Origin: 2 posterior cerebral arteries begin at upper border of pons as 2 terminal branches of basilar artery. Course & relations: it passes round midbrain to reach occipital pole of cerebrum. It sinks inside calcarine sulcus. Termination: it terminates by dividing into its terminal cortical branches. Internal carotid artery (intracranial part) ICA enters middle cranial fossa by passing through carotid canal then through upper part of foramen lacerum . It passes inside cavernous sinus; lastly it pierces its roof & passes backward above it. Abducent nerve lies infero -lateral to ICA inside cavernous sinus. At base of brain below anterior perforated substance, it terminates into anterior & middle cerebral arteries. Anterior cerebral artery It is the smaller of the 2 terminal branches of ICA. It passes on medial surface of the brain below rostrum then in front of genu then backward above corpus callosum through callosal sulcus. It gives: cortical branches and central branches . Middle cerebral artery - It is the larger of the two terminal braches of the ICA. - It passes through stem of the lateral sulcus then in posterior ramus of lateral sulcus. - It gives: central branches & cortical branches. Cortical branches of cerebral arteries The superolateral surface: It is supplied by middle cerebral artery except: one finger breadth at upper border supplied by the anterior cerebral and occipital lobe supplied by posterior cerebral artery. The medial surface: It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery except occipital lobe, (behind the parieto -occipital sulcus) supplied by posterior cerebral artery. The inferior surface: The medial part of orbital surface is supplied by anterior cerebral artery. The temporal pole and lateral part of orbital surface are supplied the middle cerebral artery. Remaining tentorial surface is supplied by posterior cerebral artery. Circulus arteriosus (circle of Willis) Is formed at the base of the brain by the interconnecting vertebrobasilar and internal carotid systems of vessels. 1- An anterior communicating artery connecting left and right anterior cerebral arteries to each other. 2-Two posterior communicating arteries, one on each side, connecting internal carotid artery with posterior cerebral artery. The primary purpose of this vascular circle is to provide anastomotic channels if one vessel is occluded.

text: T he last 4 cranial nerves Dr. Basma Mady Lecturer of Anatomy & Embryology Alexandria faculty of medicine Cranial nerves on the base of the brain Cranial nerves on the base of the brain Cranial nerves exiting the cranial cavity Names of cranial nerves Last 4 cranial nerves Glossopharyngeal N Hypoglossal N Accessory N Vagus N Glossopharyngeal nerve IX The glossopharyngeal nerve is a mixed (motor and sensory) nerve, It emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata , It passes laterally in the posterior cranial fossa  jugular foramen, The superior and inferior sensory ganglia are located on the nerve  through the foramen. Glossopharyngeal nerve IX it curves forward lateral to stylopharyngeus on reaching it, the nerve and the muscle pass between the internal and external carotid arteries, Then the nerve and the muscle pass between the superior and the middle constrictors of the pharynx, It passes deep to the hyoglossus muscle  posterior 1/3 tongue . Branches of Glossopharyngeal N T ympanic br  tympanic plexus in middle ear  lesser petrosal N  otic ganglion, T onsillar br  palatine tonsil & soft palate, P haryngeal br  pharyngeal plexus, L ingual br  taste and sensation from post 1/3 tongue, Carotid  carotid sinus & carotid body. Motor  stylopharyngeus muscle. Carotid branch Tympanic branch Summary The glossopharyngeal nerve thus assists swallowing , It also conducts sensation from the pharynx and the back of the tongue , It carries impulses, which influence the arterial blood pressure and respiration , from the carotid sinus and carotid body. Vagus nerve X The glossopharyngeal nerve is a mixed (motor and sensory) nerve, It emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata , It passes laterally in the posterior cranial fossa  jugular foramen, It has superior and inferior sensory ganglia. At the inferior ganglion  the cranial root of the accessory nerve joins  pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches. Vagus nerve X Vagus nerve descends in the neck  carotid sheath between IJV & ICA. At the level of upper border of thyroid cartilage , it lies between IJV & CCA  carotid sheath . Vagus nerve X It passes through mediastinum of the thorax  behind the root of the lung, It enters the abdomen through the esophageal opening in the diaphragm as anterior and posterior gastric nerves . Branches of the vagus nerve in the neck: Meningeal & auricular branches, Pharyngeal branch contains nerve fibers from the cranial part of the accessory nerve: This branch joins the pharyngeal plexus and supplies all the muscles of the pharynx ( except for stylopharyngeus) & all muscles of soft palate ( except for tensor veli palatini). Branches of the vagus nerve in the neck: 3. Superior laryngeal nerve divides into the internal and the external laryngeal nerves. The internal laryngeal N  sensory to mucous membrane of piriform fossa and larynx above vocal cords. The external laryngeal nerve  motor and is located close to the superior thyroid artery ; it supplies the cricothyroid muscle Branches of the vagus nerve in the neck: 4. Recurrent laryngeal nerve  c losely related to the inferior thyroid artery, it supplies all muscles of the larynx , except for cricothyroid muscle, the mucous membrane of the larynx below the vocal cords , and the mucous membrane of the upper part of the trachea . Left recurrent laryngeal nerves The left recurrent laryngeal nerve arises in the thorax; it hooks around the arch of the aorta and then ascends into the neck between the trachea and the esophagus . Right recurrent laryngeal nerves The right recurrent laryngeal nerve arises in the neck; The nerve hooks around the first part of the subclavian artery and Then ascends in the groove between the trachea and the esophagus . Branches of the vagus nerve in the neck: 5. Cardiac branches (two or three) arise in the neck, descend into the thorax, and end in the cardiac plexus. Branches of the vagus nerve in the neck: 6. Branch to the carotid body . Summary The vagus nerve thus innervates: Heart & great vessels in the thorax, The larynx , trachea, bronchi & lungs Much of the alimentary tract from the pharynx  splenic flexure . Glands associated with the alimentary tract, such as the liver and pancreas. Accessory nerve XI It is a motor nerve. It consists of cranial & spinal roots: Cranial root  emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata, running laterally in the posterior cranial fossa. Spinal root  C1: C5-6. This root ascends alongside spinal cord and enters the skull through the foramen magnum . It then turns laterally to join the cranial root. The two roots unite and leave the skull through the jugular foramen . The roots then separate : Accessory nerve XI The cranial root joins the inferior ganglion of vagus nerves and is distributed in its branches to the muscles of the soft palate and pharynx (via the pharyngeal plexus) and the muscles of the larynx . B ranches of the cranial accessory nerve XI The cranial root, together with the vagus gives nerve supply the following: Muscles of the palate except for tensor palati . 2. Muscles of the pharynx except for stylopharyngeus . 3. All intrinsic muscles of the larynx . B ranches of the spinal accessory nerve XI The spinal root runs downward and laterally and enters the deep surface of sternomastoid muscle, which it supplies  crosses the posterior triangle of the neck  supply the trapezius muscle. Hypoglossal nerve XII It is a motor nerve. It emerges on the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata , crosses the posterior cranial fossa, and leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal . The nerve then passes downward and forward in the neck and crosses the internal carotid artery and the first part of lingual artery to reach the tongue. In the upper part of its course, it is joined by C1 fibers from the cervical plexus. text: Development of CNS Dr Melad Naim Bushra Kelada Assistant professor Anatomy and Embryology department Faculty of medicine, Alexandria university CNS development Dr Melad Naim Origin : Ectoderm Development: At the 3 rd week an ectodermal thickness (neural plate) appeared in the mid dorsal region cranial to the primitive node. The lateral edges of this plate called the neural folds. These folds elevate and approach each other in the mid line. They fuse together to form the neural tube The neural tube is separated from the surface ectoderm. The fusion occurs at the 4 th week; it starts in the cervical region and extends cranial and caudal. CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim The cranial portion of the neural tube shows 3 dilatations:- (future brain) Prosencephalon (fore brain vesicle). At the 5 th week it differentiates into central portion called diencephalon having the optic vesicle, and 2 lateral extensions called telencephalon Mesencephalon (mid brain vesicle). Rhombencephalon (hind brain vesicle). Differentiates into metencephalon (future pons and cerebellum) and mylencephalon (future medulla oblongata CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim 2 flexures appear: Cephalic flexure: In the mid brain region 2. Cervical flexure: at the junction between the hind brain and spinal cord Later on another flexure called pontine flexure appears between the pons and myelenencephalon . CNS development Dr Melad Naim The neural canal (cavity of the neural tube): Cavity in the telencephalon forms the lateral ventricle Cavity in the diencephalon forms the 3rd ventricle Cavity of the hind brain forms the 4 th ventricle Cavity in the spinal cord forms the central canal CNS development Dr Melad Naim Neural crest cells: This is group of cells on either side of the neural plate. They are originated from ectoderm. They are found along the whole length of the neural tube. The cells of the neural crest migrate to form neural crest derivatives: Melanocytes Meninges ( pia & arachniod matter) Mesenchyme of the pharyngeal arches Suprarenal medulla Schwann cells ( neurolemmal sheath of peripheral nerves) Ganglia (spinal & autonomic) Ganglion cell layer of the retina Odontoblasts Carotid body CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim Development of the spinal cord Origin: From the caudal part of the neural tube Development: The neuroepithelial cells lined the caudal part of the neural tube proliferates to form neuroblastic cells. These cells accumulate superficial to the neuroepithelial lining of the tube. They form the mantle layer (future gray matter). Proliferation of the mantle cells leads to the formation of the marginal layer; this layer lies superficial to the mantle layer. Mylination of the nerve fibers of the marginal layer leads to the formation of the white matter of the spinal cord . CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim Additional thickness of the neuroblasts of the mantle layer leads to the formation of dorsal & ventral thickness in the mantle layer. The dorsal thickness is a sensory area ( alar plate or lamina =future dorsal sensory horn ). (future posterior horn) The ventral thickness is a motor area and called basal plate or lamina ( future motor horn ). The 2 plates are separated on the surface by sulcus limitans . CNS development Dr Melad Naim The 2 alar plates are separated by the roof plate that lies in the dorsal mid line. the 2 basal plates are seperated by the floor plate that lies in the ventral mid line . The roof & floor plates are devoted of neuroblasts ; they are pathways for the crossing of nerve fiber from side to the other. CNS development Dr Melad Naim Abnormalities of the spinal cord: Neural tube defect ( spina bifida) This anomaly is due to abnormal closure of the neural folds which is normally occurred at the 3 rd or 4 th week. Usually there is a splitting of vertebral arches, which may be accompanied by splitting of the underlying neural tissue. CNS development Dr Melad Naim There are 2 types of spina bifida: A. Spina bifida occulta : there is defect of the vertebral arch covered with a patch of hair overlying the lesion. The neural tissue is normal. It occurrs in the lumbosacral region B. Spina bifida cystica : there are defect of the vertebral arch & neural tube defect affecting the meninges & or neural tissue . The meninges & or neural tissue protrude through the defect in the the vertebral arch. It occurs in the lumbosaccral region. CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim Spina bifida cystica This condition is not associated with mental retardation. There are 3 types: 3 ascending grades 1 . Meningocele Defect in the vertebral arch and protrusion and swelling of meninges ( Meningeal sac containing CSF) 2. Meningomyocele Meningocele + meningeal sac containing herniated spinal cord 3. Syringomyelocele : Meningomyelocele +dilatation of the neural canal Rachischisis (failure of neural folds formation) CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim Development of medulla oblongata (brain stem) It develops from Myelencephalon The roof plate extends and expands . The roof plate is formed by a single layer of ependymal cells. As a result of the extension (expansion) of the roof plate , the alar lamina becomes lateral to the basal lamina. Both laminae are separated by the sulcus limitans CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim CNS development Dr Melad Naim Both laminae contain nuclei arranged in columns The basal lamina (motor) contains 3 different columns These columns are arranged from medial to lateral GSE column : contains cranial nerve nuclei motor to skeletal muscles (derived from somite ) (3.4.6.12) SVE column: contains cranial nerve nuclei motor to striated muscles derived from branchial arches. Boundaries and content of suboccipital triangle Dr: Azza Zaki Triangles Of The Neck Dr: Azza Zaki The side of the neck is divided by the sternomastoid muscle into: Anterior triangle in front of the muscle. Posterior triangle behind the muscle. Dr: Azza Zaki Origin: by 2 heads: Sternal (medial)head: rounded &tendinous from the anterior surface of the manubrium sterni Clavicular (lateral)head: flat fleshy head from the medial ⅓ of the upper surface of the clavicle. Insertion: Into the lateral surface of the mastoid process and the lateral ½ of the superior nuchal line . Nerve supply: Motor: Spinal part of accessory nerve (XI) Sensory: C 2 and C 3 for (proprioceptive) Sternocleidomastoid Muscle Dr: Azza Zaki Action: Acting on one side , it tilts the head to the same side and rotates the face to the opposite side. Acting together , the muscles of the two sides flexes the neck forwards If the head is fixed, they act as muscles of inspiration. Superficial Relations to Sternocleidomastoid External jugular vein Superficial cervical L.N Great auricular nerve Transverse cervical nerve Supraclavicular nerves Structures Deep To Sternomastoid Muscle: Carotid sheath and its contents ( common and internal carotid arteries, vagus nerve and internal jugular vein) Deep cervical lymph nodes. Dr: Azza Zaki Torticollis (Wry neck) Is a spasmodic contraction of the sternomastoid muscle, producing twisting of the neck with the chin pointing upward to the opposite side . 1- Congenital: it result from excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. The mastoid process is pulled down toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side. 2-Spasmodic, which results from repeated chronic contractions of the sternocleidomastoid. It is psychogenic in origin. Dr: Azza Zaki Digastric Muscle Origin : arises by two bellies: Anterior belly : digastric fossa of mandible Posterior belly : mastoid notch on the inner ( medial)surface of mastoid process of the temporal bone. Insertion: the two bellies meet in an intermediate tendon which perforates the stylohyoid muscle and runs in a fibrous sling attached to the body of hyoid bone. Nerve supply: The anterior belly is supplied by mylohyoid nerve, because it is a muscular derivative of the first pharyngeal arch. The posterior belly is supplied by facial nerve (VII) because it is a muscular derivative of the second pharyngeal arch. Action : Elevates the hyoid bone; depresses the mandible . Dr.: Azza Zaki Omohyoid Muscle Origin : by two bellies Inferior belly: from upper border of scapula and suprascapular ligament. Superior belly: from lower border of body of hyoid bone. Insertion : By an intermediate tendon which lies on internal jugular vein and held in position by a fascial sling connecting it to clavicle. Nerve supply : Ansa cervicalis Action : depression of hyoid bone Dr.: Azza Zaki Dr: Azza Zaki The posterior triangle divided into occipital and supraclavicular (subclavian ) triangles by inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle. The anterior triangle divided into : digastric (submandibular), submental, carotid and muscular triangles. Subdivisions of the Triangles Of The Neck Dr: Azza Zaki Boundaries: Anteriorly: by the posterior border of the sternomastoid. Posteriorly: by the anterior border of the trapezius. Inferiorly: by the middle third of the clavicle – Apex: at the superior nuchal line. - Roof: The investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Posterior Triangle Of The Neck Roof is formed by: The skin Superficial fascia Platysma External Jugular vein. Cutaneous branches of cervical plexus Investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Subclavian artery (3rd part). b. Suprascapular artery. c. Transverse cervical artery. d. Occipital artery. Roots and trunks of the brachial plexus & their branches : From the roots: N. to rhomboids & N. to serratus anterior muscle. From the upper trunk: Suprascapular n. & N. to subclavius muscle. b. Supraclavicular nerve. 4. Muscles: Inferior belly of omohyiod muscle. 5. Lymph node: Occipital and supraclavicular lymph nodes. Course: Descends obliquely Superficial to the sternocleidomastoid and just above the clavicle it pierces the deep fascia. Termination: drains into the subclavian vein . Surface marking: From angle of mandible till midpoint of clavicle Tributaries: Posterior auricular. Posterior division of the retromandibular . Posterior external jugular. Transverse cervical. text: CEREBRAL CORTEX (1) By Prof. Dr. Maha Safwat Head (Prev.) of Human Anatomy & Embryology department Lecture ILOS: Anatomy of cerebrum-1(supero-lateral surface) The cerebral hemisphere presents: A. Three surfaces: 1. Supero -lateral surface. 2. Medial surface. 3. Inferior surface. Corpus callosum The cerebral hemisphere presents: B. Three borders: Supero -medial border. Infero -lateral border presents the pre-occipital notch which is about 5 cm in front of the occipital pole. The anterior part of this border is called superciliary border. Medial border: which is divided into: a) Medial orbital border. b) Medial occipital border. Medial orbtal border Medial occiptall border Superciliary border Inferolateral border B. Three borders: Supero -medial border. Infero -lateral border presents the pre-occipital notch which is about 5 cm in front of the occipital pole. The anterior part of this border is called superciliary border. Medial border: which is divided into: a) Medial orbital border. b) Medial occipital border. The cerebral hemisphere presents: C. Three poles: Frontal pole. Occipital pole. Temporal pole. Each cerebral hemisphere is divided into 4 lobes : 1. Frontal lobe. 2. Parietal lobe. 3. Temporal lobe. 4. Occipital lobe. Superolateral Surface Central sulcus: The upper end of this sulcus lies approximately midway between the frontal and occipital poles. It descends downwards and forwards on the superolateral surface where it ends slightly above the posterior ramus of lateral sulcus. The central sulcus also extends on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere. Superolateral Surface Lateral sulcus: This sulcus consists of a stem and 3 rami. The stem is present on the inferior surface of the cerebral hemisphere. This stem ends on the superolateral surface by dividing into 3 rami. Anterior ramus. Ascending ramus. Posterior ramus. The main sulci and gyri of the frontal lobe are : Precentral sulcus: This sulcus runs parallel to and in front of the central sulcus. - Precentral gyrus: This gyrus lies between the central and the precentral sulci. This gyrus corresponds to area 4 of Brodmann . Functionally, this gyrus is considered as first or primary motor area . Here, the body is represented upside down. Cerebral cortex: functional localization Motor Homunculus The main sulci and gyri of the frontal lobe are : Superior and inferior frontal sulci: The superior frontal sulcus runs forwards from about the middle of the upper part of the precentral sulcus. The inferior frontal sulcus runs below and parallel to the previous one. These two sulci divide this area of the frontal lobe into 3 gyri: The main sulci and gyri of the frontal lobe are : Superior frontal gyrus: Above the superior frontal sulcus. Middle frontal gyrus: Between the superior and inferior frontal sulci. The posterior part of this gyrus presents area 8 which is the main part of the frontal eye field. Inferior frontal gyrus: Below the inferior frontal sulcus. This gyrus receives the anterior and ascending rami of the lateral sulcus. The motor speech area (= Broca's Area) lies on both sides of the ascending ramus, a region concerned with the motor mechanisms of speech formulation. Its lesion produces expressive aphasia i.e. the patient can understand written and spoken words but cannot speak. Cerebral cortex: functional localization The main sulci and gyri of the frontal lobe are : Prefrontal area: It includes much of the 3 frontal gyri, the orbital gyri (orbitofrontal area), most of the medial frontal gyrus and the anterior half of the cingulate gyrus. The prefrontal area (frontal association area) is responsible for initiative, judgment, reasoning, creativity and socially appropriate behavior. Thus, it is concerned with the makeup of the individual's personality. The main sulci and gyri of the parietal lobe are : Post central sulcus: It runs parallel to and behind the central sulcus. Post central gyrus: This gyrus lies between the central and the post central sulci. It also extends on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere to form part of the paracentral lobule. Functionally it lodges the first or primary somatosensory area . Here also the body is represented upside down. The taste area is situated at the lower end of the postcentral gyrus in the superior wall of the lateral sulcus and in the adjoining area of the insula ( Brodmann area 43). Cerebral cortex: functional localization The main sulci and gyri of the parietal lobe are : Intra-parietal sulcus: It runs from before backwards behind the post central gyrus dividing that area into superior (somatosensory association area) and inferior parietal lobule. The inferior parietal lobule receives the posterior parts of 3 sulci: The posterior end of the posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus which is surrounded by the supramarginal gyrus (area 40). The posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus which is surrounded by the angular gyrus (area 39). The posterior end of the inferior temporal sulcus The main sulci and gyri of the parietal lobe are : Function of area 39 and 40: Areas 39 and 40 are termed Wernicke’s area; it is responsible for understanding of the written and spoken language. This area enables a person to read a sentence, understand it, and say it out loud (i.e. vision, reading, perception & speech). Its destruction leads to word blindness i.e., the person can see words but unable to interpret their meanings. The main sulci and gyri on the temporal lobe are : Superior temporal sulcus: It runs from before backwards parallel to and below the posterior ramus of lateral sulcus. Inferior temporal sulcus: It also parallel to and below the superior temporal sulcus. Superior temporal gyrus: The auditory area is present mostly in the floor of the lateral sulcus. It extends into the superior temporal gyrus below the sulcus , and is here surrounded by the auditory association area. Middle temporal gyrus: It lies below and parallel to the superior temporal sulcus. Inferior t

text: Dural folds professor of anatomy and embryology Master Degree of Tropical medicine Nutrition diploma HIph By : professor Dr. EL-Sayed Metwally The meninges The brain and spinal cord are surrounded by three layers of meninges which are: Dura mater. Arachnoid mater. Pia mater. Dura matter - The dura mater lines the inner aspect of the skull cap and the cranial cavity. - It protects the brain from shocks and friction with the hard skull. - The dura is composed of 2 layers: 1. Outer (endosteal) layer , lines the brain box. 2. Inner (meningeal) layer , covers the brain. The two layers are closely adherent to each other. They are only separated to form dural venous sinuses . Dural venous sinuses Valveless veins. Receive venous blood from the orbit, brain and adjacent skull bones. Present between the two layers of the dura. Their walls are devoid of muscular tissue. The inner layer of the dura forms 4 folds inside the cranial cavity. Falx cerebri . Tentorium cerebelli . Falx cerebelli . Diaphragma sellae . Dural folds 1. Falx cerebri: Shape: A sickle-shaped fold, lies between the 2 cerebral hemispheres. Attachments: Anterior: crista galli& frontal crest. Posterior: upper surface of tentorium cerebelli . Superior: to the lips of the sagittal sulcus on the inner aspect of the skull cap. Inferior: lower concave free border Venous sinuses related to it: Superior sagittal sinus in its upper attached border. Inferior sagittal sinus in its free concave lower border. Straight sinus in the attachment of the falx cerebri with the tentorium cerebelli . 2. Tentorium cerebelli: Shape: A tent-like fold covers the cerebellum. Attachments: The attached margin (peripheral) : posterior clinoid process - upper border of petrous temporal bone - margin of the transverse sulcus on each side. The free margin: anterior clinoid process & forms tentorial notch around the midbrain . The trochlear nerve pierces the dura at the point of crossing. The occulomotor nerve pierces the dura in front of the crossing point. The upper surface gives attachment to the falx cerebri. Venous sinuses related: Straight sinus. Superior petrosal sinus. Transverse sinus 3. Falx cerebelli Shape: A small crescentic fold between the two cerebellar hemispheres. Attachments: To the internal occipital crest. Venous sinuses related to it: Occipital sinus. 4. Diaphragma sellae: Shape: It is a dural fold covering the pituitary gland in the hypophyseal fossa. It is pierced by the pituitary stalk. Attachments: It is attached to the anterior and posterior clinoid processes. Venous sinuses related to it: anterior intercavernous sinus. posterior intercavernous sinus . The outer layer of meninges: Pia Archnoid Endosteal Dura Meningeal dura Dural venous sinuses are the following except Receive venous blood from the orbit Present between the two layers of the dura . Drain into diploic veins Valveless veins. Dural fold which separates cerebrum from cerebellum is falx cerebri . Diaphragma sellae . Tentorium cerebelli . Falx cerebelli Dural fold which separates the 2 cerebral hemispheres is falx cerebri . Diaphragma sellae . Tentorium cerebelli . Falx cerebelli Dural fold which separates the 2 cerebellar hemispheres is falx cerebri . Diaphragma sellae . Tentorium cerebelli . Falx cerebelli Dural venous sinuses related to falx cerbri are the following except Superior sagittal sinus Straght sinus Sigmoid sinus Inferior sagittal sinus Dural venous sinuses related to tentorium cerebelli are the following except Superior petrosal sinus Straght sinus Sigmoid sinus Transverse sinus Dural venous sinus related to falx cerebelli is Superior petrosal sinus Straght sinus occipital sinus Transverse sinus Dural venous sinus related to diaphragma sellae is Superior petrosal sinus Straght sinus Intercavernus sinus Transverse sinus Cranial nerve that peirce the dura at the point of crossing of attached and free border of tentorium cerebelli is Occlumotor Abducent Troclear Trigeminal Cranial nerve that peirce the dura just in front of crossing of attached and free border of tentorium cerebelli is Occlumotor Abducent Troclear Trigeminal Practical exam SHIFT Identify the pointed structure mention dural venous sinuses related to it Falx cerebri SSS, ISS, SS SHIFT Identify the pointed structure mention dural venous sinuses related to it Tentorium cerebelli SPS, TS, SS SHIFT Identify the pointed structure mention dural venous sinuses related to it Tentorium cerebelli SPS , TS , SS Your feedback about this lecture is Not interesting Not interesting boring boring

text: Anatomy of the face By: Dr/ Amira Gaber Objectives: Venous drainage Introduction: The skin of the face possesses numerous sweat and sebaceous glands. No deep fascia is present in the face. Muscles: Orbicularis occuli: It is the sphincter of the eye. It has three parts; orbital, palpebral and lacrimal . Orbital part closes the eye firmly. Palpebral part closes the eye lightly. Lacrimal part helps to drain the tears by dilating the lacrimal sac. Buccinator: It is the muscle of cheeck. It is an accessory muscle of mastication. It empties the vestibule of the mouth. Orbicularis oris : It is the sphincter of the mouth. Important in articulation. Motor nerve supply (Facial nerve): Facial nerve palsy: Sensory innervation: The skin of the face is supplied by branches of the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve , except for the small area over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland , which is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) . Arterial supply: The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery . Passing upward and over the submandibular salivary gland, it curves around the inferior margin of the body of the mandible at the anterior border of the masseter muscle. It is here that the pulse can be easily felt . It runs upward in a tortuous course toward the angle of the mouth. It then ascends along the side of the nose to the medial angle of the eye, where it anastomoses with the terminal branches of the ophthalmic artery and ends as angular artery . Branches of Facial artery: Arterial Supply: Superficial temporal artery, the smaller terminal branch of the external carotid artery , arises in the parotid gland. It ascends in front of the auricle to supply the scalp. Arterial Supply: The transverse facial artery, a branch of the superficial temporal artery , arises within the parotid gland. It runs forward across the cheek just above the parotid duct. Arterial Supply: The infraorbital artery, the continuation of the maxillary artery , pass through the infraorbital foramen. Arterial Supply: The supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries, branches of the ophthalmic artery, supply the skin of the forehead. text: Development of the face IBRAHIM ELSAID Professor of Anatomy and Embryology Alexandria Faculty of Medicine Development of Face (weeks 4-8) Five processes appear around the stomodeum . Single frontonasal process Paired maxillary processes Paired mandibular processes Origin: The face is developed from five processes: Two maxillary processe s (one on each side, originated from the first branchial arch ). These processes are found lateral to the primitive mouth ( stomodium ). Two mandibular processes (one on each side, originated from the first branchial arch ). These processes are found caudal to the primitive mouth ( stomodium ). One frontonasal process formed by proliferation of the mesoderm ventral to the brain . This process forms the cranial border of the primitive mouth . Development: The ectoderm on both sides of the frontonasal process will form local thickening. This thickening is called nasal placode . The nasal placode invaginates the underlying structures, and hence this placode will transform into nasal pit . The nasal pits divide the frontonasal process into lateral nasal process (lies lateral to the nasal pit) and medial nasal process (lies medial to the nasal pit). The frontonasal process will form the bridge of the nose ; the medial nasal processes will form the tip of nose , while the lateral nasal processes will form the alae of the nose . The nasal pits excavated to form the nasal cavities. The maxillary processes increase in size and grow medially. They meet the medial nasal processes; compress them towards the mid line forming the so called inter-maxillary segment . Finally the maxillary process fuses with the medial nasal process. The maxillary process continues to grow so they meet at the mid line and fuses with each other and burry part of the medial nasal process deep to them. The maxillary process will form : 1- the upper lip and 2- the philtrum . The buried deep part will form 3- the primitive palate. The lateral nasal process and the maxillary process are separated by deep groove called ( naso lacrimal groove). Canalization of this groove leads to formation of nasolacrimal duct . This duct extends from the medial angle of the eye to the nose. The ectoderm of the maxillary processes and the lateral nasal processes will fuse together burring the nasolacrimal duct. This fusion leads to the formation of the upper part of the cheek and the maxilla . Fusion of the maxillary and mandibular processes leads to formation of the lower part of the cheek. The two mandibular processes grow medially meet and fuse to form the 1- lower lip and 2- lower jaw . The nerve supply of the processes: 1- Frontonasal process is supplied by the ophthalmic nerves . 2- The maxillary processes are supplied by the maxillary nerves . 3- The mandibular processes are supplied by the mandibular nerves . Fate of the processes forming the face Frontonasal Forehead , bridge of nose, medial and lateral nasal processes *. Medial nasal process - Primitive palate and tip of nose *. Lateral nasal process - Alae of nose 2. Maxillary - Upper part of cheeks, maxilla, philtrum and upper lip 3. Mandibular - Lower lip and lower part of the cheeks Abnormalities: 1) Cleft upper lip (hare lip): Most common congenital anomaly, more common in male, it is due to failure of fusion of the maxillary process and the medial nasal process (defect between the philtrum and the lateral part of upper lip ). 2) Oblique facial cleft: Defect in the face extends from the medial angle of eye to upper lip. It is due to failure of fusion of maxillary process and medial nasal process and lateral nasal process . The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface. 3) Median cleft lower lip It is a rare anomaly. It is due to failure of fusion of the two mandibular processes . 4) Macrostomia : Due to arrest of fusion of the maxillary and mandibular processes . 5) Microstomia : Due to excessive fusion between the maxillary and mandibular processes. A. Lateral cleft lip. B. Bilateral cleft lip. C. Cleft lip, cleft jaw & cleft palate. D. Midline cleft lip. A A B B C D Development of the palate Origin: It has double origins: The primitive palate is derived from the intermaxillary process of the frontonasal process. Definitive (secondary) palate is derived from the maxillary process of the first branchial arch. Development: Two shelves like processes arise from the inner aspect of the maxillary processes. These processes termed the palatine processes. They grow medially trying to meet and fuse with each other; they meet the tongue in their way, so they change the direction of growth. They grow backward . Then they grow medially above the tongue . They meet in the mid line and the 2 palatine processes fuse with each other, and with the primitive palate . At the same time the nasal septum grows down and joins the newly formed palate. The primary palate is represented by the incisive fossa . The anterior three fifth of the palate will ossify forming the hard palate , while the posterior two fifth gives the soft palate . Incisive Fossa When the two maxillæ are articulated, a funnel-shaped opening, the incisive fossa , is seen in the middle line, immediately behind the incisor teeth. Abnormalities: 1) Cleft palate: This is due to failure of fusion between the two palatine processes with each other, or with the primitive palate. This includes three types: 1- Bifid uvula 2- Cleft soft palate 3- Cleft soft and hard palate. This anomaly may be associated with cleft upper lip. 2) Perforated palate: It is due to failure of fusion between the two palatine processes at certain point at the mid line. Development of the tongue Origin of the muscles of the tongue : They are derived from occipital myotomes . They migrate from the occipital region to the tongue, carrying with them their nerve supply (hypoglossal nerve). text: Tutorial 3 Last 4 cranial nerves & Development of Head & Neck Anatomy & Embryology Department Glossopharyngeal Nerve How it leaves the skull? It leaves the skull by passing through the jugular foramen. Course. It passes superficia l to internal carotid artery and deep to external carotid artery . It passes between the superior and middle constrictors of the pharynx. It lies on the medial (deep) surface of hyoglossus muscle. It runs with the stylopharyngeus muscle. It ends in the posterior third of the tongue. Branches: Tympanic branch Carotid branch Nerve to the stylopharyngeus muscle Pharyngeal branches Lingual branch: sentory to the posterior third of tongue. Tonsillar branch: supplies the palatine tonsil and the inferior surface of the soft palate Which branch of glossopharyngeal nerve carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland? Tympanic branch Carotid branch Nerve to the stylopharyngeus muscle Pharyngeal branches Which branch of glossopharyngeal nerve carries parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland? Tympanic branch Carotid branch Nerve to the stylopharyngeus muscle Pharyngeal branches Which branch of glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensory fibers from the inferior surface of soft palate? Carotid branch Pharyngeal branches Lingual branch Tonsillar branch Which branch of glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensory fibers from the inferior surface of soft palate? Carotid branch Pharyngeal branches Lingual branch Tonsillar branch Vagus nerve How it leaves the skull? It leaves the posterior cranial fossa through the jugular foramen. Course in the neck. Vagus nerve descends in the neck within the carotid sheath between the internal jugular vein and the internal carotid artery. At the level of upper border of thyroid cartilage , it lies between the internal jugular vein and the common carotid artery in the carotid sheath. text: Tutorial 4 Cerebrum & blood supply Anatomy & Embryology Department Cerebral hemisphere The cerebral hemisphere presents: A. Three surfaces: 1. Superolateral surface. 2. Medial surface. 3. Inferior surface. . Medial orbtal border Medial occiptall border Superciliary border Inferolateral border B. Three borders: Supero -medial border. Infero -lateral border presents the pre-occipital notch which is about 5 cm in front of the occipital pole. The anterior part of this border is called superciliary border. Medial border: which is divided into: a) Medial orbital border. b) Medial occipital border. C. Three poles: 1. Frontal pole. 2. Occipital pole. 3. Temporal pole. Each cerebral hemisphere is divided into 4 lobes : 1. Frontal lobe. 2. Parietal lobe. 3. Temporal lobe. 4. Occipital lobe. Superolateral Surface The main sulci & gyri of the frontal lobe Precentral sulcus: This sulcus runs parallel to and in front of the central sulcus. This sulcus may be divided. Precentral gyrus: This gyrus lies between the central sulcus and the precentral sulcus. It also extends on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere to from part of the paracentral lobule. This gyrus corresponds to area 4 of Brodmann. Functionally, this gyrus is considered as primary motor area. Its function is to carry out the individual movements of different parts of the body. Here, the body is represented upside down. The area of cortex controlling a particular movement is proportional to the skill involved in performing the movement and is unrelated to the mass of muscle participating in the movement. Superior and inferior frontal sulci: The superior frontal sulcus runs forwards from about the middle of the upper part of the precentral sulcus. The inferior frontal sulcus runs below and parallel to the previous one. These two sulci divide this area of the frontal lobe into 3 gyri: 1. Superior frontal gyrus: Above the superior frontal sulcus. 2. Middle frontal gyrus: Between the superior and inferior frontal sulci. The posterior part of this gyrus presents area 8 according to Brodmann which is the main part of the frontal eye field concerned with voluntary conjugate eye movement. This gyrus may present a middle frontal sulcus. 3- Inferior frontal gyrus: Below the inferior frontal sulcus. This gyrus receives the anterior and ascending rami of the lateral sulcus. The motor speech area (= Broca's Area ) lies on both sides of the ascending ramus, a region concerned with the motor mechanisms of speech formulation. Its lesion produces expressive aphasia i.e. the patient can understand written and spoken words but cannot speak. Subdivisions of the frontal lobe A. Precentral area: This area is designated as the first or leading somatomotor area, it is divided into: Precentral gyrus : Primary motor area or area 4. Premotor area: Includes area 6, 8, 44 and 45. The function of area 6 (**premotor area) is to store programs of motor activity assembled as the result of past experience. Thus, the premotor area programs the activity of the primary motor area. B-Prefrontal area: It includes much of the 3 frontal gyri, the orbital gyri (orbitofrontal area), most of the medial frontal gyrus and the anterior half of the cingulate gyrus. The prefrontal area (frontal association area) is responsible for initiative, judgment, reasoning, creativity and socially appropriate behavior. Thus, it is concerned with the makeup of the individual's personality. The Parietal lobe Post central sulcus: It runs parallel to and behind the central sulcus. Post central gyrus: This gyrus lies between the central sulcus and the post central sulcus. It also extends on the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere to from part of the paracentral lobule. This gyrus corresponds to areas 3, 1, 2 of Brodmann. Functionally it lodges the primary sensory area. The taste area is situated at the lower end of the postcentral gyrus in the superior wall of the lateral sulcus and in the adjoining area of the insula (Brodmann area 43). Here also the body is represented upside down. The apportioning of the cortex for a particular part of the body is related to its functional importance rather than to its size. The face, lips, thumb, and index finger have particularly large areas assigned to them. In fact, the size of the cortical area allocated to each part of the body is directly proportional to the number of sensory receptors present in that part of the body. Intraparietal sulcus: It runs from before backwards behind the post central gyrus dividing that area into superior and inferior parietal lobule. Superior parietal lobule: It lies above the intra-parietal sulcus. Functionally, it is considered as sensory association area . It plays important roles in deciphering deeper meanings of the sensory information in the somatosensory areas. It is believed that its main function is to receive and integrate different sensory modalities. For example, it enables one to recognize objects placed in the hand without the help of vision. In other words, it does not only receive information concerning the size and shape of an object but also relates this to past sensory experiences; thus, the information may be interpreted, and recognition may occur. Inferior parietal lobule: It lies below the intra-parietal sulcus, and receives the posterior parts of 3 sulci: The posterior ramus of the lateral sulcus which is surrounded by the supramarginal gyrus (area 40 according to Brodmann ). Superior temporal sulcus which is surrounded by the angular gyrus (area 39 according to Brodmann ). Inferior temporal sulcus which is surrounded by an arcus tempro-occipitalis . Function of area 39 and 40: Areas 39 and 40 are termed Wernicke’s area ; it is responsible for understanding of the written and spoken speech. This area enables a person to read a sentence, understand it, and say it out loud (i.e. vision, reading, perception & speech). Cavernous sinus

Site and Size
.It is one on each side of the body of the
sphenoid bone.
.Two cm long and one cm wide.

Diaphragma sellae

Falx cerebri
Relations
- Anterior: Superior orbital fissure.
- Posterior: Apex of the petrous part of the
temporal bone.
- Medial: Pituitary gland and body of sphenoid
containing sphenoid air sinus.
- Lateral: Temporal lobe of the cerebral
hemisphere (uncus).
Superior: Internal carotid artery.
- Inferior: Body of the sphenoid and the
sphenoidal air sinus.

contents
A. Structures lying within the cavity of the
cavernous sinus:
1. Internal carotid artery (on the floor)
2. Abducent nerve (inferolateral to the
internal carotid Artery.
B. Structures embedded within the lateral
wall of cavernous sinus:
-Oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, and
maxillary nerves.
Tributaries
1.Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins.
2. Superficial middle cerebral vein.
3.Central retinal vein.
4.Sphenoparietal sinus.
5. The anterior (frontal) tributary of the middle
meningeal vein.
6. Intercavernous sinuses and veins from the
pituitary gland.
7. Some inferior cerebral veins.
Communications

1. With the cavernous sinus on the other side
through the intercavernous sinuses.
2.With the anterior facial vein through
superior and inferior ophthalmic veins.
3.With the pterygoid plexus of veins through
emissary veins passing through the
foramen ovale, foramen spinosum, and
emissary sphenoidal foramen.

Drainage
- It is drained by two sinuses:
1. Superior petrosal sinus: Drains into anterior
end of the transverse sinus.
2. Inferior petrosal sinus: Drains into internal
jugular vein just below skull base

Applied Anatomy
Cavernous sinus thrombosis:
- Infection of the dangerous area of the face
may be transmitted to
the cavernous sinus through superior + inferior
ophthalmic veins or deep facial vein connects
anterior facial vein to the pterygoid
plexus of vein.
Mmanifestation :
a.It leads to thrombosis of the cavernous sinus
(pulsating
exophthalmous due to the presence of the
internal carotid artery
inside the sinus).
b.The abducent nerve may be affected

Cranial cavity

Site:- In the midline between
the two cerebral
hemispheres.
Shape:- Sickle-shaped fold.
Attachments:- Anterior-- Crista galli.
- Posterior --- Upper surface
of the tentorium cerebelli in
the midline.
Venous dural sinuses
related:1. Superior sagittal sinus: In
the upper attached border
2. Inferior sagittal sinus: In
the lower free border.
3. Straight sinus: At the
base of the falx cerebri (at
the junction of the
falx cerebri with the
tentorium cerebelli).

Tentorium Cerebelli

Site:- Between the occipital
lobes of both cerebral
hemispheres and the
cerebellum in the posterior
cranial fossa.
Shape:- Tent shaped fold.
Attachments:It has two margins:
a.Attached margin:- It is attached on either side
to the posterior clinoid
process, petrosphenoidal
ligament, upper border of
the petrous part of the
temporal bone and the
margins of the transverse
sulcus.
b. Free margin:
- It is U-shaped band called
"tentorial notch" which
surrounds the midbrain.
- It is attached anteriorly to
the anterlor clinold process
on each side.
.The free margin crosses
over the attached margin at
the apex of the petrous
part of the temporal bone.
Surfaces:a. Upper surface: Gives
attachment to the base of
the falx cerebri.
b. Lower surface: Gives
attachment to the base of
falx cerebelli.
Venous dural sinuses
related:1. Superior petrosal sinus
(right and left): At the
attached margin on each
side.

contents

CNS
Brain Metabolism & Neurosecretion
Telegram: @Nutshell_AFM_28

 Nutshell - Biochemistry of CNS Module

Brain Metabolism
Key Features
Extracts: ~50% oxygen, ~10% glucose from arterial blood
Fuel: Glucose (main); Ketone bodies (starvation)
Needs: ~120g glucose/day (~60% of body usage at rest)
Energy Use: 60–70% for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (maintain membrane potential)

Glucose Transport & Hypoglycemia
Transporter: GLUT3
Low Km → High affinity → Saturated under normal conditions
Severe Hypoglycemia:
Below 40 mg/dL → danger (lethargy, coma, death)
Triggers release of: Glucagon, Epinephrine, Cortisol

Alternative Fuels
Fatty acids: Not used (bound to albumin, can't cross BBB)
Ketone bodies (e.g., β-hydroxybutyrate):
Used in starvation (converted to Acetyl-CoA)
Spare glucose and muscle protein

Glutamate Metabolism in Brain
Glutamate → Glutamine (in astrocytes) for ammonia detox
Enzymes: Glutamate dehydrogenase, Glutamine synthetase
High NH₃ → Glutamine accumulation → Astrocyte swelling
Depletion → Affects neurotransmitters (Glutamate, GABA)

Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)
Characteristics
Appearance: Clear, colorless
Volume: ~150 mL; Secreted: ~750 mL/day
Formation: Mostly by choroid plexus; 30% elsewhere
Functions: Shock absorption, support, nourishment, waste removal, brain weight reduction

Bloody: Hemorrhage or traumatic tap

Glucose ↓: Encephalitis, tumors; ↑ in hyperglycemia

Receptor Types
Ionotropic: Ligand-gated ion channels (fast)
Example: Na⁺ → depolarization (Ach, Glutamate)

 Receptors are integral membrane proteins.
 Each neuron usually releases one type of Neurotransmitters as:

 Acetyl Choline → Cholinergic Neurons.
