text: BRAIN METABOLISM What percentage of oxygen does the brain extract from arterial blood? A) 20% B) 30% C) 50% D) 70% Answer: C) 50% What is the primary fuel source for the brain under normal conditions? A) Fatty acids B) Ketone bodies C) Glucose D) Amino acids Answer: C) Glucose During prolonged starvation, what alternative fuel does the brain use? A) Fatty acids B) Lactate C) Ketone bodies D) Glycogen Answer: C) Ketone bodies BRAIN METABOLISM The metabolic pattern of the brain differs from other tissues. The brain extracts from the arterial blood: 50% of oxygen 10% of glucose (120 gram/day) Brain uses fuels to meet its energy needs from : Glucose Ketone bodies Glucose As a Fuel To The Brain Glucose is virtually the sole fuel for the human brain, except during prolonged starvation . Low fuel stores in Brain Needs a continuous supply of glucose Consumes 120 g daily , = 60% of the utilization of glucose by the whole body in the resting state. So Which glucose transporter is mainly responsible for glucose uptake in neurons? A) GLUT1 B) GLUT2 C) GLUT3 D) GLUT4 Answer: C) GLUT3 What is the primary function of GLUT4 transporters? A) Basal glucose uptake B) High-affinity glucose transport in neurons C) Insulin-regulated glucose uptake D) Glucose export in hepatocytes Answer: C) Insulin-regulated glucose uptake Glucose transport into brain by GLUT3 Low value of K m for glucose  saturated under most conditions Constant supply of glucose. Name Distribution Notes GLUT1 Is widely distributed in fetal tissues. In the adult, it is expressed at highest levels in erythrocytes and also in the endothelial cells of barrier tissues such as the blood –brain barrier. However, it is responsible for the low-level of basal glucose uptake required to sustain respiration in all cells Levels in cell membranes are increased by reduced glucose levels and decreased by increased glucose levels. GLUT2 Is expressed by renal tubular cells and small intestinal epithelial cells that transport glucose, liver cells and pancreatic beta cells. All three monosaccharides are transported from the intestinal mucosal cell into the portal circulation by GLUT2 Is a high capacity and low affinity isoform GLUT3 Expressed mostly in neurons (where it is believed to be the main glucose transporter isoform), and in the placenta. Is a high-affinity isoform GLUT4 Found in adipose tissues and striated muscle (skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle Is the insulin-regulated glucose transporter. Responsible for insulin-regulated glucose storage. What happens when blood glucose falls below 39.6 mg/dL? A) Glycolysis slows down B) GLUT3 transporters increase C) Neurons switch to amino acid metabolism D) Brain activity increases Answer: A) Glycolysis slows down Glucose transport into brain Glycolysis slows down when the blood glucose is below 39.6 mg/dl (approaches the Km value of GLUT3 and Hexokinase ). Blood glucose levels of 40 mg/ dL and below constitute severe hypoglycemia Case Study 1: Hypoglycemia & Brain Function A 65-year-old diabetic patient is brought to the emergency room with confusion, sweating, and tremors. His blood glucose is found to be 35 mg/dL. What is the most immediate concern for this patient? A) Brain glucose deficiency leading to neuronal dysfunction B) Increased fatty acid oxidation in the brain C) Elevated levels of ketone bodies D) Excessive neurotransmitter synthesis Answer: A) Brain glucose deficiency leading to neuronal dysfunction What hormone is primarily responsible for raising blood glucose levels in this situation? A) Insulin B) Glucagon C) Epinephrine D) Growth hormone Answer: B) Glucagon Physiological effects of low blood glucose in humans. What percentage of the brain’s energy is used for maintaining the Na+/K+ membrane potential? A) 30-40% B) 50-60% C) 60-70% D) 80-90% Answer: C) 60-70% Energy of the brain (60% to 70%) is used to : 1- Power transport mechanisms that maintain the Na+-K+ membrane potential required for the transmission of the nerve impulses. 2- Synthesis of neurotransmitters and their receptors to propagate nerve impulses. Why can’t the brain use fatty acids directly for energy? A) They are not metabolized in neurons B) They cannot cross the blood-brain barrier C) They require insulin to be used as fuel D) The brain lacks fatty acid oxidation enzymes Answer: B) They cannot cross the blood-brain barrier Case Study 2: Starvation & Ketone Body Utilization A 30-year-old individual is stranded without food for several days. His blood glucose drops, and ketone bodies begin to rise. Which ketone bodies are primarily used by the brain in starvation? A) Acetone and lactate B) Acetoacetate and β- hydroxybutyrate C) Pyruvate and alanine D) Glucose and free fatty acids Answer: B) Acetoacetate and β- hydroxybutyrate Why does the brain shift to ketone body metabolism? A) To spare muscle proteins from being broken down B) To reduce the use of oxygen in metabolism C) To increase insulin sensitivity D) To improve neurotransmitter production Answer: A) To spare muscle proteins from being broken down Ketone bodies As Fuel To The Brain Neurons of the brain cannot directly use free fatty acids or lipids from the blood as fuels because FAs are bound to albumin in plasma and so do not traverse BBB (the blood-brain barrier) In starvation ,  ketone bodies generated by the Liver partly replace glucose as fuel for the brain. (β- hydroxybutyrate & acetoacetate ) Oxidation of ketone bodies to acetyl- CoA during prolonged fasting or starvation, after liver glycogen has been depleted, allows the brain to use body fat as an energy source. This spares muscle proteins until they become the brain’s ultimate source of glucose (via liver gluconeogenesis ) during severe starvation .  1) Which of the following muscles is supplied by the trochlear nerve?

d. Inferior oblique

C

2) The tectum is formed of:
a. 4 geniculate bodies.

d. 4 colliculi.

D

a. Floor of middle ear.

b. Roof of middle ear.

c. Posterior wall of middle ear

d. Anterior wall of middle ear.

A

4) In the stretch reflex, relaxation of antagonist muscles is due to:
a. Presynaptic inhibition.

b. Antidromic conduction.

c. la fiber stimulation.

d. Reciprocal innervation

D

5) Chloride level in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is decreased in:
a. Meningitis

b. Neurosyphilis

c. Encephalitis

d. Brain tumors

A

might be affected?
a. Mandibular.

b. olfactory.

c. Abducent.

d. Optic.

C
2|P ag e

emotions and memory:
a. The ventral anterior nucleus

b. The intralaminar nuclei

c. The pulvinar

d. The anterior nucleus

D

layer of proteoglycans?
a. The cupula.

b. Tectorial membrane.

c. The phalangeal cells.

d. Stereocilia of the hair cells.

A

9) Superior cerebellar artery arises from:
a. Basilar artery

b. vertebral artery.

c. Circle of willis.

d. Pontine artery.

A

a. it is due to change in the receptors by the same degree of stimulation.
b. It is a decline in the rate of firing in spite of constant stimulation.
c. it occurs due to fatigue of the receptors.
d. The cold receptors adapt more rapidly than the warmth receptors.
B

a. caudate and putamen nuclear

b. mammillary bodies

c. gracile and cuneate nuclei

d. inferior olive nucleus

A

a. The central sulcus

b. The lunate sulcus

c. The cingulated sulcus

d. The transverse sulcus

A

the resting eye?
a. Anterior surface of the cornea

b. Posterior surface of the lens

C. Posterior surface of the cornea.

d. Anterior surface of the lens.

A

15) Which component of the scala media is formed of gelatinous mass
with collagen fibrils?
a. Stereocilia of the hair cells.

b. The tectorial membrane.

c. Kinocilium of outer hair cells.

d. The pillar cells.

B

a. Located in the upper part of the pre central gyrus.
b. Located in medial frontal gyrus
c. Located in the upper part of the post central gyrus.
d. Located in paracentral lobule
A

attached margin of Tentorium cerebelli is:
a. Occulomotor

b. Abducent

c. Trigeminal

d. Trochlear

D

• During the intrauterine life up to the third month intrauterine: the spinal

consisting of the second through fifth lumbar
nerve pairs, the first through fifth sacral
nerve pairs, and the coccygeal nerve.
• Cauda equina syndrome: is a condition that occurs
when the cauda equina is compressed. This results
in low back pain, pain that radiates down the leg,
numbness, and loss of bowel or bladder control.
• The cause is usually a disc herniation in the lower
region of the back, cancer, trauma, epidural
abscess and epidural hematoma.

text:
➢ Histology of ganglia & receptors
❖ The craniospinal ganglia is found in the sensory root of some cranial nerves like the trigeminal nerves.
❖ The craniospinal ganglia is larger than the autonomic ganglia.
❖ Regarding the craniospinal ganglia, the ganglion cells are separated by CT septa.
❖ Satellite cells = neuroglia
❖ The nerve fibers of the craniospinal ganglia run within the CT septa.
❖ Autonomic ganglia synapses occur between the preganglionic fibers and the ganglion cells.
❖ Nerve endings are biological transducers which are classified as follows:
-

Motor nerve endings (effectors): they are terminals of axons which transmit impulses from the CNS to the muscle
fibers to contract (motor end plate) or to glandular cells to secrete.

-

Sensory nerve endings (receptors): they detect various forms of physical and chemical stimuli. Following their
stimulation, the resulting receptor potentials are transmitted as sensory input to the CNS.

❖ The non-encapsulated receptors are NOT covered by a CT capsule.
❖ Free nerve endings are unmyelinated & without neurilemma.
❖ Nociceptors are found in the granular layer of the epidermis.
❖ Thermoreceptors are parallel to the skin surface.
❖ Encapsulated receptors are more specialized and exhibit a characteristic CT capsule.
❖ Sensory nerve fibers lose their myelin and neurilemmal sheaths in Meissner’s corpuscles.
❖ Pacinian corpuscles = Corpuscle of Pacini.
❖ Pacinian corpuscles appear like a sliced onion in histological sections.
❖ Ruffini’s corpuscles are surrounded by CT capsule.
❖ Ruffini’s corpuscles are stimulated by displacement of collagen fibers.
❖ Muscle spindles are fusiform in shape, and they are stimulated by when the muscle is stretched.
❖ To distinguish the intrafusal muscle fibers from the ordinary extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers, the intrafusal fibers are
present in the interior of the spindle’s cavity that is filled with gelatinous fluid.
❖ The principal role of motor innervation is to maintain the sensitivity of the muscle spindle.
1

A.S

 ❖ Golgi tendon organs = Tendon spindles
❖ Tendon spindles are fusiform and are found parallel to the muscle tendon fibers.
❖ Tendon spindles lacks intrafusal muscle fibers.
❖ Tendon spindles don’t contain motor nerve endings.
❖ Tendon spindles are stimulated by straightening of the collagen fibers of muscle tendon.
❖ Golgi tendon organs are specialized for monitoring the degree of muscle tension produced by muscle contraction
(Golgi tendon reflex).

text:
➢ Histology of the spinal cord
❖ Nerve cells in grey matter are aggregated into large and small nuclei.
❖ Myelinated nerve fibers in white matter is longitudinally arranged into ascending and descending tracts.
❖ The spinal cord is an elongated cylindrical cord about 45 cm long and occupies the upper 2/3 of the vertebral canal.
❖ As age advances, the vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord (differential growth).
❖ A transverse section shows that the spinal cord is a bilateral structure, consisting of central grey matter and peripheral
white matter. The two halves are separated posteriorly by the posterior median septum and anteriorly by the anterior
median fissure. They are continuous in the intermediate zone through the and the white commissures. The central
canal is always present in the middle of the grey commissure.
❖ Unlike the cerebrum and cerebellum the grey matter, the grey matter in the spinal cord is central in position.
❖ The grey matter is divided into three horns also called grey columns and their shapes and sizes differ in different
regions of the spinal cord.
❖ The laminar architecture of the spinal cord is based upon the cytological features of the neurons in different regions of
grey matter.
❖ Anterior horn = motor nuclei.
❖ The lateral group are like the central group in position but absent the thoracic region.
❖ Dorsal horn = sensory nuclei.
❖ Cells of the dorsal horn are small stellate neurons (afferent neurons) that belong to the sensory system (they receive
and process sensory input).
❖ Nucleus thoracicus = Clarkes column.
❖ Lateral horn is found between the dorsal and ventral horns.
❖ Cells of the lateral horn are small stellate neurons belonging to the ANS.
❖ Associative nuclei are found in all the grey matter (anterior and posterior horns).
❖ The axons of commissural neurons cross to the opposite side.
❖ The axons of intersegmental neurons ascend and descend for few segments on the same side.

1

A.S

 ❖ The white matter is subdivided by the two horns of grey matter in each half into three columns these are; dorsal white
column, ventral white column and lateral white column.
❖ The ventral (anterior) white column lies between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn at the exit of the
ventral root of spinal nerves.
❖ The dorsal (posterior) white column lies between the posterior median septum and the posterior horn. In the cervical
and upper thoracic regions, this column is further divided by the posterior intermediate septum into gracile tract
medially and cuneate tract laterally.
❖ The lateral white column lies lateral to both posterior and anterior horns.
❖ Ascending (sensory) tracts arise from the nerve cells in the spinal ganglia or from the nerve cells of the posterior horns
and end in higher sensory centers. They are of two types:
•

•

Tracts carrying sensations that will finally reach the cerebral cortex. They include:
-

Gracile and cuneate tracts (dorsal column pathway).

-

The ventrolateral pathway (spinothalamic, spinoreticular and spinomesencephalic tracts)

Tracts carrying impulses which won’t reach the cerebral cortex but end in subcortical levels. They include:
-

Dorsal, ventral spinocerebellar & cuneocerebellar tracts.

-

Spino-olivary tract.

-

Spino-tectal tract.

❖ Descending (motor) tracts begin in higher motor centers in the cerebral cortex and brainstem and end in the anterior
and lateral horns of the spinal cord. They include:
•

Pyramidal tracts:
-

The ventral corticospinal tract (uncrossed pyramidal tract) and the lateral corticospinal tract (crossed
pyramidal tract).

•

Extra-pyramidal tracts:
-

Rubrospinal tract.
Tectospinal tract.
Lateral and medial (ventral) reticulospinal tracts.
Lateral and medial (ventral) vstibulospinal tracts.

❖ The cerebral hemispheres consist of a convoluted cortex of grey matter overlying the central medullary mass of white
matter.

text:
➢ Histology of the Ear
❖ The inner ear is one of the special sense organs concerned mainly with hearing and maintaining the body equilibrium.
❖ The osseous labyrinth = bony labyrinth consists of a series of connected irregular spaces within the petrous portion of
the temporal bone.
❖ The cochlea and semicircular canals arise from the vestibule.
❖ The membranous labyrinth is formed of a continuous series of sacs and channels that are suspended inside the bony
labyrinth.
❖ The endolymph inside the membranous labyrinth is surrounded by the perilymph lying between the membranous and
bony labyrinths.
❖ The utricle and saccule are joined by a Y-shaped endolymphatic duct.
❖ Macula sacculi and macula utriculi = otolith organ.
❖ The stereocilia and kinocilium are found at the free surface of hair cells.
❖ The kinocilium is long and found at one side of the cell.
❖ The afferent fibers in type l hair cells arise from the vestibular ganglion cells and penetrate between the supporting
cells.
❖ The otolithic membrane is a thick gelatinous layer of proteoglycans.
❖ Lateral semicircular canal = horizontal semicircular canal.
❖ Anterior semicircular canal = superior semicircular canal.
❖ Each SSC has a dilatation at its base called the ampulla.

➢ Histology of the Eye
❖ The eye is a highly developed photosensitive organ that provides the sense of sight.
❖ The eyeball is located within the bony orbit.
❖ Outer fibrous coat = corneo-scleral coat.
❖ Corneal epithelium has a high regenerative capacity.
❖ Tear film = pre-corneal tear film = a protective layer of lipid and glycoprotein.
❖ Cells of the corneal endothelium are involved in metabolic exchange between aqueous humor of the anterior chamber
and cornea.
❖ The dense irregular CT of sclera contains type l collagen fibers and elastic fibers.
❖ The choroid is found adjacent to the inner surface of the sclera.
❖ The two layers of ciliary epithelium are covering the ciliary processes.
❖ The non-pigmented layer of ciliary epithelium lies towards the posterior chamber.
❖ The pigmented layer of ciliary epithelium lies towards the ciliary stroma.
❖ The ciliary muscles the bulk of the ciliary body.
❖ The iris is responsible for the color of the eye.
❖ The aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary epithelium.
❖ The aqueous humor passes through the pupil between the iris and the lens in order to reach the anterior chamber.
❖ Iridocorneal angle = angle of the limbus.
❖ Canal of Schlemm is a scleral venous sinus.
❖ Canal of Schlemm runs circularly around the limbus, it collects the aqueous fluid from the anterior chamber for its
drainage into the episcleral veins.
❖ The lens is flexible and is formed of tightly packed elongated lens fibers.
❖ The lens is enveloped by the lens capsule.
❖ Retinal pigmented epithelium = RPE.
❖ The apex of RPE faces the rods and cones.
❖ The melanin is stored in the apical portion of cytoplasm in RPE.
1

A.S

 ❖ The blood retinal barrier isolates the neural retinal cells from the blood-borne toxic substances.
❖ The numerous lysosomes in the apical cytoplasm are involved with the renewal of the photoreceptors by phagocytosis
of the tips of their outer segments.
❖ The ratio of rods to cones is 20 : 1
❖ Rods and cones are thin elongated modified neurons oriented parallel to one another but perpendicular to the retina.
❖ The tips of cones are invaginated by the microvilli of RPE.
❖ The outer segments of rods and cones are formed of numerous flat membranous discs that contain specific light
sensitive compounds which initiate the visual impulses (rhodopsin).
❖ The pyriform neurons in ganglion cell layer are few and large.
❖ Optic nerve fibers are myelinated by oligodendrocytes (without neurilemma).
❖ The inner limiting membrane limits the retina from inside separating it from the vitreous.
❖ The conjunctiva contains vascular loose CT in lamina propria.
❖ The eyelids are two movable folds of tissues that protect the eye.
❖ Eyelashes project from the lid margin.
❖ The skin surface contains fine hairs.
❖ The secretion of lacrimal gland is continuous.

INTRODUCTION
2 control systems coordinate the functions of various systems to maintain hemostasis:
(1) The endocrine glands:
Exert a relatively slow control, through secreting hormones which regulate growth and metabolic
processes within the cells.
(2) The nervous system:
- Exerts rapid control by serving three broad functions: sensory, integrative and motor.
- First, it senses changes within the body and in the outside environment; this is its sensory
function.
- Second, it interprets the changes; this is its integrative function.
- Third, it responds to the interpretation by initiating action in the form of muscular contractions
or glandular secretions, this is its motor function.

FUCTIONAL ORGANIZATION OF THE NERVOUS SYSTEM
The nervous system is divided into: the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral
nervous system (PNS) .

Principles of Human Physiology

SYSTEM

Receptors are specialized structures that act as both:
(1) Detectors: detect changes in the external or internal environment.
(2) Transducers: convert energy of the stimulus into electrical changes (nerve
impulses).

Types & classification of receptors:

Motor Cortical Areas
I- Primary motor area (area 4)
Site:
• This area occupies the precentral gyrus in the frontal lobe
• It contains large pyramidal cells called Betz cells
It is characterized by:
1. The body is represented in an inverted manner (the head is down while the legs

are upward). However, the upper part of the face, respiratory muscles and
abdominal wall muscles are bilaterally represented.
2. Cortical representation of any part of the body in area 4 is directly proportional
to the complexity of its function not to its size so, the areas representing the hands
and muscles of speech are larger than the areas of the trunk and legs.
Functions of area (4)
1.

It initiates the delicate isolated voluntary movements of the distal parts of

the body (hands and fingers) on opposite side of the body
2.

It facilitates the spinal reflexes as stretch reflex

II- Premotor area 6
Site: lies anterior to the primary motor area; anterior to the precentral gyrus, on the
lateral and medial cortical surface. It also contains a somatotopic map of the body.
It is characterized by:
It also contains a somatotopic map of the body. The body representation is roughly
the same as that of the primary motor area.
Functions of premotor area 6
1. Initiates gross movements on the contralateral limbs
2. Shares together with the basal ganglia in initiation of automatic associated
involuntary movements like, swinging of the arms during walking
3. Involved in planning of voluntary movements.

Site: It is a small area that lies anterior and superior to area 6 on the medial surface
of the frontal lobe
It is characterized by:
1.

The body representation is bilateral and horizontal

2.

It is less excitable than area 4

Functions:
1. Primarily involved in planning of voluntary movements
2. Involved in bilateral movements and coordinates contraction of many muscles
to provide background for performanceof fine movements together with
premotor area.

(Cortical Areas for Integrative Functions)
- They are areas which receive and analyze signals from both motor and sensory

- They aren’t involved directly with sensory perception or execution of motor
actions.

PRINCIPLES OF HUMAN

PLASTICITY, MEMORY, SPINAL REFLEXES,

By

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 Central nervous System

80

SYNAPSES AND SYNAPTIC
TRANSMISSION
Definition:
the site of contact between the axon terminals of one neuron (presynaptic
neuron) and another neuron (postsynaptic neuron) across which transmission
of nerve impulses occur.
A synapse is a specialized functional junction between two neurons.

Types:
In the nervous system, there are two types of synapses: electrical and chemical
synapses.
Electrical synapse:
- they are extremely rare in the nervous system.
- At an electrical synapse, the membranes of the presynaptic and postsynaptic
neurons come close together forming areas of fusion called gap junction or tight
junction,
- In these junctions the opposing membranes are held in position by connectin g
protein channels called connexon, which contain pores that permit ions to pass
directly from one cell to the other.
- This allows rapid direct conduction of electrical potential from one neuron to the
next as if no membrane barrier exists.
Chemical synapse:
- Almost all synapses in the human central nervous system are chemical synapses.
- In these synapse, the impulses in the presynaptic axon causes secretion of a
chemical transmitter at the synapse, and this transmitter act on receptors located in
the membrane of the postsynaptic neuron to modify its activity either exciting or
inhibiting it depending upon the nature of the postsynaptic receptors.

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 Central nervous System

81

Mechanism of neurotransmitter release from a synapse:
● Exocytosis:
- When an action potential arrives at the synaptic knob → opening of voltagegated Ca + channels → increase permeability to Ca → influx of Ca ions →
release of the neurotransmitter by exocytosis (proportional to the Ca ++ influx).
- The neurotransmitter diffuses through the synaptic cleft → binds to receptor
on the postsynaptic membrane → opening of chemical-gated channels for
specific ions → a small local change in the membrane potential of the post
synapse.

● Nature of the postsynaptic change:
1- During rest, the polarized state:
a- resting membrane potential (RMP) = -70mv.
b- The threshold for its excitation = -59 mv.
2- The neurotransmitter released at the synapse (i.e. during activity) will
lead to either:
a. Excitation of the postsynaptic neuron:
if the transmitter is excitatory e.g. Acetylcholine, noradrenaline and
serotonin.
b. Inhibition of the postsynaptic neuron:
if the transmitter in inhibitory e.g GABA and glycine.

● Electrical events in excitatory synapses (excitatory postsynaptic
potential - EPSP):
- Binding of the excitatory transmitter to postsynaptic receptors → increases the
permeability to all ions, but Na + predominates (due to its large electrochemical
gradient across the membrane) → slight depolarization of the postsynaptic
neurone → increase its excitability and bring it closer to threshold.
This change in voltage above RMP is called excitatory postsynaptic potential.
Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 Central nervous System

82

- The EPSP:
a- localised
b- lasts for about 15 milliseconds.
c- A single EPSP is not enough to increase the neuronal potential to
threshold value (-70 mv → -59 mv), but several EPSP must add up or
summate to trigger an action potential.

● Electrical events in inhibitory synapses
1- Inhibitory postsynaptic potential - IPSP:
Binding of the inhibitory transmitter to postsynaptic receptors → increases the
permeability of the postsynaptic membrane to K + and Cl- → increases the
degree of intracellular negativity → hyperpolarisation at the postsy naptic
neurone → inhibition.

2- Presynaptic inhibition

RETICULAR FORMATION (RF)
- The Reticular formation is an anatomic area in the brainstem made up of various
neurons and fibers with discrete and multiple functions.
- It is associated with the regulation of various sensorimotor, cortical arousal and
autonomic functions.
- It also contains neurons that utilize specific amines that function as
neuromodulators.

Function of the Reticular Formation:
1 - Modulation of muscle tone reflexes and posture: the nuclei of the reticular
formation, give rise to the reticulospinal tracts of the spinal cord. These tracts
function in maintaining muscle tone, and posture.
2 - Control of gaze:

3 - Regulation of autonomic functions: The reticular formation includes the
cardiac and vasomotor centers, as well as the respiratory centers.
It also contains neurons regulate complex behaviors as chewing and swallowing.
4 - Pain modulation:
- Ascending: The reticular formation is one means by which pain signals from
the lower body reach the cerebral cortex.
- It is also the origin of the descending analgesic pathways. The raphe
nucei and locus coeruleus nuclei contain neurons whose axons synapse
onto interneuorns in the spinal cord to block the transmission of pain.
5 - Consciousness:
The reticular formation has projections to the thalamus and cerebral cortex
through fibers known as the reticular activating system which regulate the
sleep wake cycles, and the level of consciousness and alertness.

SLEEP
Definition:
a state of physiological loss of consciousness from which a subject can be aroused by
appropriate stimuli.

Phases of sleep:
During sleep a subject passes periodically through several stages in an orderly
fashion. These stages are defined by appearance of certain wave patterns in the EEG:

1. Slow wave sleep (non-REM sleep):
- characterized by:
a- drop of blood pressure (10-30%)
b- decrease in heart rate
c- decrease in peripheral vascular tone
d- decrease in respiratory rate
e- decrease in basal metabolic rate.
f- Increased growth hormone secretion during stage 3 & 4
g- dreams do occur but they are not consolidated therefore not remembered.
- Stages of slow wave sleep and EEG pattern, 4 stages:
- During wakefulness with closed eyes and relaxed mind the alpha waves of EEG
appear.
- Passage from wakefulness to non-REM sleep is characterized by progressively slower
frequencies and higher voltage activities in the EEG. Non-REM sleep comprises four
stages:
a- Stage I: Theta waves start to appear
b- Stage II: sleep spindles superimposed on the theta waves
c- Stage III: EEG starts to show slower delta waves
d- Stage IV: stage of deep sleep: delta waves

EQU I LI B R I U M
Labyrinth (inner ear):
- is a small sense organ present within temporal bone of skull
- concerned with equilibrium and hearing.
- It is formed of:
1- system of bones called bony labyrinth
2- the labyrinth is lined by a membrane called membranous labyrinth.
3- Between both is the perilymph, while within membranous labyrinth is the
endolymph.
- The membranous labyrinth is composed of 2 main divisions:
1- Auditory part: (cochlea).
2- Non auditory part: (vestibular apparatus): formed of 3 semicircular canals,
utricle and saccule.

Principles of Human Physiology

Dr. Mohammed Abdel Gawad

 128

Utricle and saccule:
Inside the utricle and sacule is located a receptor called macula (otolith organ)

Sense organ (receptor): macula (otolith organ):
● Mechanisms of action of macula: The hair cells of macula:
- act as stretch receptors
- stimulated by stretch when their cilia become bent secondary to displacement of
otoconia secondary to changes in head position → depolarized and discharge
impulses along vestibular nerve endings.

● Functions of utricle and saccule:
1. Orientation of head position in space:
a. If the head is in the central position → hair cells in both maculae are
exposed to a uniform stretch → equal discharge from maculae on both sides
→ reach cerebral cortex → give the sense of erect position of the head.
b. if the head is tilted to the right side → displacement of otoconia to the

leaning forward.

EQUILIBRIUM
- The inner ear is one of the special sense organs
which is concerned mainly with hearing and maintaining the body equilibrium.
- The inner ear is a fluid-filled cavity
that consists of bony and membranous labyrinths, with perilymph between them
(A) The osseous (Bony) labyrinth:
- it consists of the following structures:
(1) Cochlea, which Iies anteriorly.
(2) Vestibule, which lies centrally.
(3) Three bony semicircular canals, which lie posteriorly.

(B) The membranous labyrinth:
- it consists of the following structures:
(1) Cochlear duct: in the bony cochlea and containing organ of Corti.
(2) Utricle and saccule: in the bony vestibule and containing maculae.
(3) Three membranous semicircular ducts:
-in the three bony semicircular canals and containing cristae ampullaris.

1

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

- Mechanism of action of the macula:
- The hair cells of macula act as stretch receptors that are stimulated by stretch.
- changes in head position
causes displacement of the otoliths (otoconia).
so the kinocilia become bent
the hair cells of macula become stretched, they become depolarized
and discharge impulses along vestibular nerve endings.

- Functions of the utricle and saccule:
(1) Orientation of the head position relative to gravity:
- If the head is in a central position,
the hair cells in both maculae are exposed to uniform stretch
resulting in equal discharge from maculae on both sides.
- This discharge on reaching the cerebral cortex,
will give the sense of erect position of the head.
- If the head is tilted to the right side,
there will be displacement of the otoconia to the right side
with bending of the cilia of both maculae towards the right.
- However, the bending in the right macula is more than in the left,
resulting in unequal discharge from both maculae
that when reaching the cortex will give the sense of right tilt of the head.

2

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

(2) Perception of linear acceleration:
- Sudden forward horizontal movement leads to a sense of back fall.
- This can be explained by that the otoconia become displaced backward
due to their inertia stretching all the hair cells of both maculae,
leading to increase discharge of vestibular nerve that reaches the cortex
giving the sense of back fall.
- Corrective movements are initiated by the cortex to support the body
by leaning forward.

- The macula of the utricle:
- helps to orient the head position in the erect posture
and responds to horizontal linear acceleration.
- The macula of the saccule:
- is important in equilibrium when the person is lying down or swimming.
- it also responds to vertical linear acceleration.

PHYSIOLOGY OF SENSORY RECEPTORS
- Sensory receptors are specialized structures that act as both:
- Detectors: they detect changes in external or internal environment of the body.
- Transducers: convert energy of change they detected to electrical impulses.

- According to the type of stimulus, receptors can be classified into:
(1) Mechanoreceptors:
- they respond to mechanical stimuli and include:
- Touch, Pressure and Vibration receptors: located in the skin.
- Proprioceptors: located in muscles, tendons and joints.
- Baroreceptors: located in the aortic arch and carotid sinus.
- Stretch receptors: located in the alveoli of the lungs and right atrium.
- Vestibular and auditory receptors
(2) Thermoreceptors:
- stimulated by thermal form of energy and detect changes in temperature
and include:
(a) Cold receptors.
(b) Warmth receptors.
(3) Chemoreceptors:
- stimulated by chemical forms of energy; include:
- Taste receptors.
- Olfactory receptors.
- Gluco-receptors and osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus.
(4) Nociceptors:
- stimulated by any form of energy potent enough to cause tissue damage.
(5) Electromagnetic receptors:
- respond to electromagnetic waves of light
and include the rods and cones in the retina
1

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

Properties of receptors:
(A) Differential sensitivity (specificity):
- Differential sensitivity of receptors is illustrated by:
Muller's law of specific nerve energies which states that:

"each receptor is most sensitive to one specific type of stimulus called
its adequate stimulus giving rise to one type of sensation
regardless of method of stimulation because the sensation perceived
depends on the area in the brain ultimately activated”
- The sensory fiber from the receptor terminates in an area of brain that gives
the sensation perceived by the receptor.

- The sensation perceived after stimulation of a receptor is called
modality of sensation
- the pathway of certain receptor to the brain is called specific projection
- Some receptors can be stimulated by stimuli other than their adequate stimulus
provided that the intensity of stimulation is sufficiently high,
but will still be giving its own specific modality of sensation.

2

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

(B) Excitability:
- it is the ability of the receptor to respond to stimuli.
- In the resting condition, the receptor is in a polarized state
(its outer surface is positively charged while its inner surface is negatively charged
with a resting membrane potential of about -70 mV)
- On stimulation, inflow of Na+ ions occurs as a result of opening of Na channels
in receptor membrane producing a local graded potential called
the receptor or generator potential.
- when the receptor potential reaches the threshold value, action potentials are
generated in the first node of Ranvier of the afferent sensory fiber.
- increased stimulus intensity increases
the amplitude of receptor potential
which causes an increase in the
action potential frequency
in afferent sensory fiber.
- Properties of the receptor potential:
(1) It is a local, unpropagated potential
whereas action potentials are propagated.
(2) It is a graded potential
(it does not obey the all or none rule)
(3) It can be summated,
as it has no refractory period.
(4) Receptor potential is caused by activation of mechanically gated channels
whereas action potentials are caused by activation of voltage gated channels.
(5) It is not blocked by local anesthetics,
whereas action potentials are blocked by these drugs

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION
- Communications between neurons in the central nervous system occurs
through synapses
- A synapse: is a specialized functional junction between two neurons.
- In nervous system, there are 2 types of synapses: electrical & chemical synapses
(A) Electrical synapse:
- They are extremely rare in the nervous system.
- At electrical synapse, the membranes of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons
come close together forming areas of fusion called gap junction.
- In these junctions, the opposing membranes are held by connecting protein
channels called connexon,
which contain pores that permit ions to pass directly from one cell to the other.
- This allows rapid direct conduction of electrical potential from one neuron
to the next as if no membrane barrier exists.
(B) Chemical synapse:
- Almost all synapses in human central nervous system are chemical synapses.
- In these synapses, impulses in presynaptic axon causes secretion of
a chemical transmitter at the synapse.
- this transmitter act on receptors located in membrane of post-synaptic neuron
to modify its activity either exciting or inhibiting it depending upon the nature
of the postsynaptic receptors.

1

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

Mechanism of neurotransmitter release from a synapse:
- When an action potential arrives at the synaptic knob, depolarization occurs,
which increases permeability of the knob to Ca+2 through opening of
voltage-gated ca+2 channels leading to influx of Ca+2 ions into the synapse.
- This causes release of neurotransmitter by exocytosis proportional to Ca+2 influx.
- The neurotransmitter diffuses through the synaptic cleft
and binds to receptor molecules on the postsynaptic membrane
leading to opening of chemical-gated channels for specific ions,
which are allowed to pass the membrane
causing small local change in the membrane potential of the post synaptic neuron

2

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

Nature of the postsynaptic change:
- During rest, the postsynaptic neuron is in the polarized state,
showing resting membrane potential (RMP) of about -70 mv.
- The threshold for its excitation is about -59 mv.
- The neurotransmitter released at the synapse will lead to either:
(A) Excitation of the postsynaptic neuron:
if the released transmitter is excitatory
(as acetylcholine, noradrenaline and serotonin)
(B) Inhibition of the postsynaptic neuron:
if the released transmitter is inhibitory
(as gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), and glycin)

Electrical events in excitatory synapses:
- Binding of the excitatory transmitter to postsynaptic receptors increases
the permeability of postsynaptic membrane to all ions,
but movement of Na+ predominates due to its large electrochemical gradient
across the membrane.
- The Na+ influx results in slight depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron,
which will increase the excitability and bring it closer to threshold.
- This change in voltage above rest membrane potential (RMP)
is called excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)

3

Artist Of Physiology

Amr

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

The Reticular Formation
- Functions of the reticular formation:
(1) Modulation of muscle tone, reflexes and posture:
- through the reticulospinal tracts of the spinal cord.
(2) Pain modulation:
- it receives pain and temperature information from the ascending tracts
and projects to the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus.
- it is also the origin of the descending analgesic pathways where raphe nuclei
and locus coeruleus nuclei contain neurons whose axons synapse onto
interneurons in the spinal cord to block the transmission of pain.
(3) Control of gaze:
- its pontine nuclei help in generating conjugate eye movements.
- they receive input from superior colliculus and discharge to
the ocular motor nuclei.
(4) Regulation of autonomic functions:
- it includes cardiac, vasomotor centers,
as well as the respiratory centers.
- it also contains neurons that
regulate chewing and swallowing.
(5) Consciousness:
- it has projections to the thalamus
and cerebral cortex through fibers
known as reticular activating system
which control level of consciousness by regulating arousal and sleep

1

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

Areas of Arousal and Sleep
(A) Brain areas involved in arousal: (brainstem and hypothalamus)
(1) The brainstem:
(a) The reticular activating system (RAS):
- it is a set of connected nuclei in the upper pons and midbrain that form
several pathways originating in the upper brainstem and project to
the intralaminar thalamic nuclei and to the cerebral cortex.
- Function of the RAS:
- The main function of the RAS is to discharge to the thalamus and cortex
to stimulate thalamic and cortical activity and promote arousal.
- Injury to the reticular activating system can result in irreversible coma.
- Factors increasing RAS activity:
• Impulses from sensory pathways.
• Impulses from motor cortex.
• Stress.
• Sympathomimetic drugs.
• Caffeine.
• Thyroid hormone.
- Factors decreasing RAS activity:
• Impulses from medullary and pontine sleep centers.
• Anesthetic drugs.
• Damage to the fibers of RF in midbrain or thalamus can lead to coma.
(b) Other arousal areas and neurotransmitters in the brainstem
that promotes wakefulness:
- Cholinergic neurons in the pontine reticular formation:
- secrete acetylcholine
- Locus coeruleus: - secretes noradrenaline
- Raphe nuclei: - secrete serotonin

2

 ARTIST OF PHYSIOLOGY

DR/ IBRAHIM AMR

(2) The hypothalamus:
(a) Posterior hypothalamus:
- histaminergic neurons in the posterior hypothalamus maintain wakefulness
(This is why antihistaminic drugs induce sleep).
(b) Lateral hypothalamus:
- its neurons stimulate other wakefulness areas in the brain
by releasing the neuropeptide orexin.
- Orexin promotes wakefulness and its deficiency causes narcolepsy
(a condition characterized by tendency to fall asleep).

(B) Brain areas and neurotransmitters involved in sleep:
(1) The anterior hypothalamus:
- preoptic nucleus contains neurons that are particularly active during sleep
and release the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA, and galanin
to inhibit neurotransmitters of arousal.
(2) The pineal gland:
- melatonin is secreted from the pineal gland at night
and it is a sleep promoting factor.
(3) ADP accumulation in the brain:
- during prolonged wakefulness, energy producing brain systems run down
and ATP levels are depleted.
- ADP levels accumulate and extracellular adenosine levels rise with time
and it induces sleep (Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors).
(4) Interleukin-1:
- it is one of the cytokines which has a role in the body immune system,
and was found to promote sleep.
- CSF levels of interleukin-1 increase during infection,
possibly explaining why we sleep more when we are sick.

3

text: MOTOR DESCENDING TRACTS By: Dr Eman Allam DESCENDING TRACTS They are tracts that deliver efferent impulses from the brain to the spinal cord. Pyramidal tracts Extrapyramidal tracts Pyramidal Extrapyramidal Origin: cerebral cortex End: spinal c or brain stem O: different nuclei in brain stem End: spinal C Voluntary control Automatic subconscious support muscle tone, posture,balance & equilibrium Develop later Develop earlier Mainly crossed Crossed & uncrossed Control fine movements in distal muscles Gross movement Axial & proximal muscles Corticospinal pathway Origin : 1-60% In area 4 & premotor area . 2-40% Somatosensory Areas of parietal lobe Course 1- Pyramidal cells 2- Corona radiata 3- Internal capsule 4- in upper medulla: Medullary pyramid 5- in lower medulla: 80% Decussation 6- lateral corticospinal tract 7- 20% uncrossed 8- 14% cross at segmental level (proximal & axial contralateral) 9- 6% proximal & axial ipsilateral 10- Ventral sypplies proximal muscles bilaterally. (Contralateral) Axons of corticospinal tract synapse either with interneurons or with the anterior horn cells (AHC). Arise from various nuclei in the brain stem and descend in the spinal cord to terminate at the AHCs. They are controlled by several areas particularly premotor cortex and basal ganglia. text: Cerebral Cortex The cerebral Cortex Composed of 2 cerebral hemispheres The surface of each hemisphere is formed of elevations (gyri) separated by depression (sulci) Each gyrus is divided into areas identified by numbers called Brodmann’s areas Each hemisphere contains 4 lobes: Frontal , Parietal , Temporal, and Occipital Functional areas in more details ( Brodmann areas) Somatosensory cortical areas Site : Parietal lobe Include: Primary somatosensory areas I and II.  SOMATIC SENSATIONS
The somatosensory system tells us what's going on in the "environment" by providing information about bodily sensations.
such as touch, temperature, pain, position in space, and movement of the joints. It is distributed throughout the entire body.
Sensory receptors
are the specialized structures that carry
information about external and internal environment to different
levels of the nervous system
8/27/2010

 WHAT DISTINGUISH THE SENSORY RECEPTORS
Properties of the receptors
1- Specificity
2- Excitability
3- Adaptation
8/27 2010

 ADEQUATE STIMULUS
> Each type of receptor is specialized to respond to one type of stimulus, (ADEQUATE STIMULUS).
But can respond to another form of energy provided the intensity of stimulation is sufficiently high but will
still be giving its own specific modality of sensation.
Muller's law: Each receptor is most sensitive to one specific type of
stimulus called its adequate stimulus giving rise to one type of sensation
regardless of the method of stimulation because the sensation perceived
depends on the area in the brain ultimately activated. (specific
projection).

time as two separate points of touch provided that the distance between the two points is
more than a certain threshold variable in different areas of the body.
Tract:dorsal column leminscus

Compass test for tactile discrimination
Procedure
1.Compass or an opened paper clip(calipars) with
two parallel ends.
2.Demonstrate to the patient ,with eyes open, by
applying either one or two points of stimuli to finger
pad.
3.Ask the patient to close their eyes.
4.Ask the patient to report whether they feel one or
two points
5.Alternate irregularly with one point touch.
6.Find the minimal distance at which the patient can discriminate.
7.Compare between dermatomes, distal versus proximal and right versus left for the upper and
lower extremities.

important Notice
The two point discrimination threshold is a measure of tactile acuity.
The magnitude of two-point discrimination thresholds varies from place to place on the body
and is smallest where touch receptors are most abundant.
• on the back at least 65 mm
• on the fingertips 2 mm.

It is the ability to discriminate different weights

PHYSIOLOGY

 Motor system examination
1. Muscle status
2. Muscle tone
3. muscle power
4. Examination of deep reflexes (tendon jerks)
5. Examination of superficial reflexes
a. Plantar reflex
b. Abdominal reflex
6. Involuntary movements

a. Rapid Alternating Movements
b. Finger to nose test
c. Heel Knee shin test

 1. Muscle status
- Observe any atrophy or hypertrophy

Observe muscle
atrophy

Cause: Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL)

 2. Muscle tone
Flex and extend the patient's fingers, wrist, elbow, ankle and knee
and observe the response

-

N.B. There is normally a small, continuous resistance to passive movement,
this is known as muscle tone. (static stretch reflex)
- Causes of decreased tone (flaccidity – hypotonia):
- Lower motor neuron lesion (LMNL)
- Neo-cerebellar syndrome

- Causes of increased tone (spasticity or rigidity – hypertonia):
- Upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL) – (clasp knife)
- Parkinsonism (cog wheel – lead pipe)

In UMNL, the phenomenon of clasp knife spasticity is felt.
This means that passive flexion of the elbow joint
will show initial resistance,
but with more flexion (overstretch of triceps muscle),
triceps muscle will relax and initial resistance disappear
(inverse stretch reflex).

 RECORDING BRAIN WAVES
USING BIOPAC SYSTEM

 The electroencephalogram
(EEG)
• EEG: is a recording of the electrical
activity of the brain through electrodes
placed on the surface of the scalp.

• The main four waves are alpha, Beta,
theta and delta wave.

 The usefulness of EEG:
- Diagnose different diseases as epilepsy, Brain tumors, or Stroke.
- Confirm brain death for patient in a coma.
- Diagnose sleep disorders or brain injuries,
- Monitor brain activity during brain surgery

text: Sensory system examination 2020-2021 By the end of this practical class students should be able to: 1. Define sensations and their types. 2. Identify the equipment used for sensory examination. 3. Conduct different tests of sensory examination. 4. Differentiate between different types of sensory loss 5. Identify different causes of sensory loss. OBJECTIVES Examination of the sensory system Superficial sensations Deep sensations Cortical sensation Pain Touch Temperature Pressure Sense of joint movement and position. Vibration sense . Stereognosis Pain Touch Temperature Pain Temperature Touch Light touch Tactile discrimination Romberg’s test Tracts: Dermatomes Figure 13–8 A dermatome is an area of skin that is mainly supplied by a single spinal nerve. Each of these spinal nerves relay sensation from a particular region of the skin to the brain . D amage to a spinal nerve can trigger symptoms in the corresponding dermatome. Dermatomes Figure 13–8 Dermatomal Map Importance: Determine the level of spinal cord injury . Test Ponits : Upper limb: C3 - Supraclavicular Fossa C4 - Acromioclavicular Joint C5 - Lateral Antecubital Fossa C6 - Thumb C7 - Middle Finger C8 - Little Finger T1 - Medial Antecubital Fossa T2 - Apex of Axilla Rules Explain the test to the patient 1 st at the center of for head to know the type of sensation Closed eyes Start distally then proceed proximal Dermatomal Rt versus Lt Record and Map Pain sensation Procedure (pin prick) Use a sharp end Ask the patient to close their eyes and report whether they feel sharp or dull. be sure to apply the sharp stimulus to all sites. Select areas from different dermatomes and peripheral nerves in both upper and lower extremities. Compare between dermatomes, distal versus proximal and right versus left for the upper and lower extremities. Observe and record the response. Pain sensation Temperature sensation Procedure Use a tuning fork heated or cooled by water or test tube filled with warm or cold water . Ask the patient to identify "hot" or "cold." different dermatomes and peripheral nerves Compare between dermatomes, distal versus proximal and right versus left for the upper and lower extremities. Observe and record the response. Often examination of temperature is omitted if pain sensation is normal Temperature sensation Tactile mechano-receptive sensations Light touch Tactile discrimination Vibration Itch and tickle Stereognosis (requires integrity of the cortical association area) Light touch sensation It is the ability to localize a touched cutaneous spot while the eyes are closed. Procedure: A blunt object. Ask the patient to localize the touched skin point Apply a gentle touch to the skin at one point Compare between dermatomes, distal versus proximal and right versus left for the upper and lower extremities. Tactile/two-point discrimination : It is the ability to perceive, with closed eyes, two touch stimuli applied to the skin at the same time as two separate points of touch provided that the distance between the two points is more than a threshold variable in different areas of the body. The magnitude of two-point discrimination thresholds varies from place to place on the body and is smallest where touch receptors are most abundant . on the back at least 65 mm on the fingertips 2 mm. Tactile Acuity If the distance is very small, each caliper point is touching the receptive field of only one sensory neuron. If the distance between stimulation points is less than this threshold only one point of stimulation can be felt. Compass test for tactile discrimination Procedure Compass or an opened paper clip with two parallel ends . Demonstrate Ask the patient to close their eyes. Ask the patient to report whether they feel one or two points Alternate irregularly with one point touch. Find the minimal distance at which the patient can discriminate. Compare between dermatomes, distal versus proximal and right versus left for the upper and lower extremities. This test is dependent on touch and position sense, so it cannot be performed when the touch and position sense are clearly abnormal. The two point discrimination threshold is a measure of tactile acuity . Pressure sense It is the ability to discriminate different weights The procedure 1. Use different metal rings . 2. Explain the test to the patient . 3. With the patient’s eyes closed, place a known number of rings on the patient’s palm. 4. Remove them and place a different number of rings in the patient’s palm a second time still with the eyes closed. 3. Ask the patient to identify whether the first or the second time feels heavier. 4. Compare between both sides. 5. Report your response Procedure: Demonstrate Ask the patient to close their eyes. Stabilize the distal interphalangeal of the digit. Ask the patient to report after each movement the direction of movement If the patient can't accurately detect the distal movement, then progressively test a more proximal joint Compare Joint movement and position (Conscious proprioception) (kinesthetic sensation) N.B. The patient should be able to detect 1 degree of movement of a finger and 2-3 degrees of movement of a toe Vibration sense Results from rapidly repetitive sensory signals from tactile receptors . Procedure: Use a 128 hertz vibration fork Test with a non-vibrating tuning fork first Place the stem of the fork over bony prominence Ask the patient to tell you if they feel the vibration If vibration sense is impaired proceed proximally Compare distal versus proximal and right versus left. Bony prominences Interphalangeal Metacapophalangeal (knuckles) Wrists Elbows Humerus (shoulder) Clavicle Head of 1st metatarsal Medial malleoli Patellas Anterior superior iliac spines Spinous processes Stereognosis Procedure: Ask the patient to close his eye Give to the patient any common and familiar object. Ask the patient to identify the object Record the response Inability to identify familiar objects by touch is known as (astereognosis) N.B.

text: Sense of Hearing Tutorial 2021 Sound is the sensation produced by longitudinal vibrations of the molecules in the external environment.(gas –Fluid-Solid) Alternate phases of condensation and rarefaction of air molecules , strike the tympanic membrane in form of pressure waves per unit time ..such movements are called Sound waves. Speed of sound through different media: It is the distance travelled by a sound wave per unit of time. The sound waves travel in air at a speed of 344 m/s . The speed of sound in fresh water is 1450 m/s. It is greater in salt water.( the whistle of the blue whale is as loud as 188 decibels and is audible for 500 miles ) In Solids like bone ,the velocity is greater than water ( it is known as bone conduction). Hearing is a mechano -receptive Sense Sound waves that spread in air pass through the external auditory canal to strike the tympanic membrane as pressure energy causing its vibration . Vibrations lead to movement of the bony ossicular chain :( ossicular conduction) , this mechanical device has : Special arrangement and special dimensions (acts as lever system that increase the force of movement and magnifies sound. Strong magnified movement of the stapes can overcomes the inertia of the cochlear fluid . sound waves displaces the basilar membrane leading to Kinking of the stereocilia of hair cells, it is the mechanical stimulus that leads to generation of electric signals that ascend via auditory nerves to the auditory centers . MCQS a Increases the movement distance of the stapes b-allows utilization of 75% of energy in the incoming sound waves. c- Matches between sound frequencies below 300 Hz. d-Its arrangement directs 100% of total sound force on the cochlear fluid. 2- The ossicular system: b 3- What is the greatest factor for sound magnification ? a-resonance of external auditory canal . b- lever system of the ossicular chain . c- areal ratio of tympanic membrane / stapes foot-plate . d- outer hair cell′s amplification. c 4-What happens if the round window does not dissipate sound pressure energy? a- increased pressure inside the middle ear. b- loss of pitch discrimination due to overlap of consecutive waves. c- increased displacement of basilar membrane . d- loss of excitation of outer hair cells of organ of Corti . b 5-Which one is the first site of Intensity analysis ? a-Cochlear nuclei. b- middle ear ossicles . c-basilar membrane of the inner ear. d-tympanic membrane . C 6-At which site could be a lesion in a patient suffering from unilateral loss of hearing ? a- superior olivary nuclei. b- inferior colliculus of the same side. c- cochlear nucleus of the same side. d- lateral geniculate body. C 7- Where is the high pitches are discriminated ? a- The helicotrma . b- The long basilar fibers at the top of the cochlea. c- The short basilar fibers at the base of the cochlea. d- The tectotial membrane. C 9-Sounds can evoke emotional responses due to : a-connection between olivary nucleus and reticular formation. b-analysis of sound pitch in the primary auditory cortex. c- information projection from subcortical structures to amygdale. d- connection between auditory psychic area and Wernicke′s area. C 8- What is the function of the inner hair cells of organ of Corti ? a- masking of high intensity sounds. b-Protection of the cochlea against outer noise. c- transduction of sound mechanical energy into nerve signals. d-amplification of low frequency sounds C 10- The function of medial geniculate body is : a-processing of information of audiospinal reflexes. b-processing of complex vocal communications as human speech. c-localization of sound direction in space. d-pitch discrimination by its tonotopic maps. b 11-Potential difference across hair cell border: a-Is high to increase their ability to respond to slightest sound . b-Is low to increase their stability. c-Its value is about – 40mv. d-Is due to high concentration of sodium ions. a 12 -Which is the best discriminated pitch range by human ear? a- 5000Hz to 8000Hz. b-3000Hz up to 10000Hz. c-1000 Hz to 4000Hz. d- 20000 Hz to 60000Hz . C 13- Which is true about functions of auditory centers: a-Primary auditory cortex for understanding the meaning of wards. b-Brain arousal via connection of olivary nucleus with reticular formation. c- Cocholear nuclei are centers of auditory reflexes. d-Inferior colliculus is a center for pitch analysis. b 14- impedance matching : a-Prevents loss of about 5 decibels at the cochlear base. b-Allows reflection of 90% of sound energy at the cochlear fluid. c-Is mediated by the ossicular chain. d-Amplifies movements at the tympanic membrane. C 15- Which is true about the attenuation reflex ? a-Is an absolute bilateral protective reflex. b-Its higher center is the thalamus. c-Its latent period is 40 seconds. d-It is partial bilateral protective reflex. d Put True or False : 1-Time lag neurons of the superior olivary nucleus can detect the sound direction in space . 2- the amplitude of action potential of hair cells is inversely proportionate to sound intensity . 3-The great displacement of basilar membrane leads to excitation of a great number of hair cells of organ of Corti . 4-The myelinated auditory nerve fibers transmit information from outer hair cells. 5- Tonotopic organization present in the organ of Corti is reversed within the cochlear nuclei and the primary auditory cortex. text: Tutorial class special senses 2021 ( Vision ) An introduction about the visual system The mammalian visual system begins with the eye. Refractive media of the eye are the structures that focus external light on retinal receptors At the back of the eye is the retina which contains photoreceptors specialized to convert light energy into neural activity that travel along visual pathway to the visual areas in the brain Downloaded from: StudentConsult (on 5 January 2008 06:15 AM) © 2005 Elsevier refractive media of the eye have a total power of 60 diopters at rest . The cornea and the lens are the two main refractive media of the eye At rest,the cornea provides 42 diopters of the total 60 doipters of the resting eye (2/3) and the lens provides 18 diopters of this total(1/3). However, the lens can increase its power during accommodation for near vision. This occurs by ciliary muscle contraction What happens when the ciliary muscle contracts? When the ciliary muscle contracts→ ↑lens convexity and diopteric power Lens shape Suspensory ligaments Ciliary muscle Light rays Object Thin flat less convex Under tension Relaxed Parallel Distant (resting Eye) Thick globular more convex Slacken or becomes loose Contracted Diverging Near (accommodated eye) - Phototransduction ; is to convert light to receptor potential then to action potential in ganglion cells that give optic nerve axons strarting visual pathway Visual pathway ends at primary visual cortex that project to secondary association visual cortical areas. Perception of the image occurs in primary occipital cortex ( V1or area 17) then interpretation of different aspects of image takes place along many secondary areas along ventral and dorsal streams. Function of neurons in primary visual cortex: orientation columns/ color blobs 1-Simple and complex neurons Arranged in vertical orientation Columns detect lines ,borders At specific orientation to identify Object form or shape. 2- Blob neurons present as Color blob areas detect object Color. Secondary visual (association) areas 18 and 19 and more distal areas along dorsal and ventral streams Secondary visual areas 1- Dorsal stream areas ( occipito –parietal pathway) ( third dimensional position 3D , object location in space-gross form-motion pathway also called (Where pathway )or pathway of Spatial vision 2- Ventral stream areas ( occipito –temporal )for analysis of visual details and colors) also called (What pathway ) or Object recognition pathway Visual field . The visual field is how wide of an area your eyes can see in front of you when you focus on a central point Normal limits of the visual field The central parts of both visual fields overlap in a common binocular field Binocular field ( Area shown in pink color ) Lateralization: objects in the left binocular field are seen by right occipital cortex and vise versa Light rays from objects in left common binocular field project to nasal side of the retina of the left eye and temporal side of the retina of the right eye forming right optic tract that project to right occipital cortex . Types of field defects - Lesion (A) at the optic nerve of right eye leads to anopia - lesion at (B ) the optic chiasma (crossing nasal fibers of both sides) leads to loss of temporal field from both eyes called Bitemporal hemianopia - Lesion at (C) right optic tract gives left homonymous hemianopia (Inability to see objects in left binocular field) What is the importance of visual field examination ? We have many causes for visual field losses such as: 1- Glaucoma 2- Macular degeneration 3- Neurological causes 4- lesions along the visual pathway So, visual field exam . Is highly diagnostic and is important also in follow up of the course of the disease. Pupillary pathways What are the components of near reflex and their significance? Components of the near reflex The near reflex starts where eyes are directed from a distant to a near object The reflex is initiated by blurring of retinal image. The reflex has three components : 1- Accommodation : is caused by contraction of the ciliary muscle to increase diopteric power of the lens to focus image on the retina 2- Convrgence : due to contraction of medial recti muscles to bring the image in both eyes on two correspnding retinal points (fovea of each eye) 3- Miosis : help to sharpen the retinal image by certain mechanisms Convergence as a component of accommodation reflex Light reflex When beam of light is shone on the eye, reflex constriction of the pupil occurs. Two components occur; 1- Direct reflex; Constriction of the pupil of the eye in which light is shown II- Indirect reflex (Consensual reflex): Constriction of the pupil of the other eye which is not directly stimulated by light Pathway of light reflex Consensual light reflex is due to : 1- Crossing of nasal fibers in optic chiasma 2- Bilateral innervation of both edinger westphal nuclei from each pretectal nucleus Rods versus cones receptors provide us with two types of vision : Photopic and scotopic Photopic (central vision) The main receptors are cones at fovea centralis High threshold needs bright light High visual acuity : detect details Color is discriminated Scotopic (Peripheral vision) Rods are the main receptors High sensitivity so can work in dim light/low light threshold Low acuity Colors appear as shades of grey What is the fovea centralis ? The fovea is a small indentation at the center of the retina. Only cones are present. Light falls directly on photoreceptors. It is specialized for high acuity vision i.e it can resolve small details The fovea is the part with the highest visual acuity across the retina due to : 1- Less convergence along the pathway from foveal cones to bipolar and ganglion cells. 2024/2025

Preface
As a collective whole, doctors are regarded as “professionals” both by the
public and by their peers. They remain the most trusted profession among the
public, which has been the case for many years. Professional competence is the
habitual and judicious use of multiple skills. Communication, knowledge,
1

 technical skills, clinical reasoning, emotions, values, and reflection in daily
practice must be considered for the benefit of the individual and community
being served.

Sharing Departments
The board of professionalism
Department of forensic medicine and clinical toxicology
Department of medical education

Course Rationale
The core competency of the medical graduate is to be able to
provide appropriate and satisfactory management tailored to the patient’s
particular medical problem. This is the essence of clinical practice.
Unquestionably a successful clinical practice requires competence in many
important areas besides medical knowledge; such as communication,
2

 technical, and mental skills. It also requires the acquisition of specific
behaviors, attitudes, and ethics particular to medical practice.
The course on professionalism aims to introduce and develop the
skills, attitudes, and competencies essential to modern healthcare
professional training. This encompasses the ability to work according to
the legal and ethical responsibilities of the medical practitioner, to
collaborate within a health care team framework, to communicate
effectively in a professional environment, to understand and respect the
doctor-patient relationship, to appreciate the duty of the doctor in his
community, and to understand the role of a medical practitioner as a
lifelong learner.
Course Description
This course includes all the knowledge and skills required by the
professional physician to help him to be competent in all aspects of the
profession. The course clarifies the difference between medicine as a
science and the medical profession as a work.

Preface
As a collective whole, doctors are regarded as “professionals” both by the
public and by their peers. They remain the most trusted profession among the
public, which has been the case for many years. Professional competence is the
habitual and judicious use of multiple skills. Communication, knowledge,
1

 technical skills, clinical reasoning, emotions, values, and reflection in daily
practice must be considered for the benefit of the individual and community
being served.

Sharing Departments
The board of professionalism
Department of forensic medicine and clinical toxicology
Department of medical education

Course Rationale
The core competency of the medical graduate is to be able to
provide appropriate and satisfactory management tailored to the patient’s
particular medical problem. This is the essence of clinical practice.
Unquestionably a successful clinical practice requires competence in many
important areas besides medical knowledge; such as communication,
2

 technical, and mental skills. It also requires the acquisition of specific
behaviors, attitudes, and ethics particular to medical practice.
The course on professionalism aims to introduce and develop the
skills, attitudes, and competencies essential to modern healthcare
professional training. This encompasses the ability to work according to
the legal and ethical responsibilities of the medical practitioner, to
collaborate within a health care team framework, to communicate
effectively in a professional environment, to understand and respect the
doctor-patient relationship, to appreciate the duty of the doctor in his
community, and to understand the role of a medical practitioner as a
lifelong learner.
Course Description
This course includes all the knowledge and skills required by the
professional physician to help him to be competent in all aspects of the
profession. The course clarifies the difference between medicine as a
science and the medical profession as a work.

Chapter 1: Attributes of the Doctor
Doctors must embody values, behaviors, and skills that make them fit to handle the sanctity of human
life. These include:

I. Concepts and Values
Sanctity of life: Respect and maintenance of human life.

●

Desire to serve: Helping patients beyond medical needs.

Value of self: self appreciation + realize
your own strengths/weaknesses

Devotion to welfare: Patient satisfaction and partnership.
Self-improvement: Continuous learning and recognizing personal strengths/weaknesses.

II. Personal Qualities
Essential personality traits include:
Patience, friendliness, affection, smile, cheerfulness
Hopefulness, politeness, consideration, humility, honesty
Respectability, self-confidence, accuracy, deliberation, soberness (mentally-balanced)

III. Virtues in Behavior Virtues are desirable character traits that shape the behavior of the individual.
Empathy: Feeling and acting to reduce others’ pain.

Beyond Empathy (feeling that you care):
●
Compassion: which is empathy with a
strong desire to alleviate someone else's
trouble or pain.
●
Pettiness: which is sympathy
associated with a feeling of sadness
for someone, is not a desirable
character trait for doctors. The reason
is that it would lead to a cumulative
emotional burden on them.

●

Integrity: Fair, honest behavior in all circumstances.
Firmness: Stability and dependability.
Wisdom: Practical, informed decision-making.
Trustworthiness: Deserving of trust.
Faithfulness: Loyalty to duties.
Respectfulness: Consideration for patients' needs.

Emotional stability: Managing emotions professionally, being able to guard against his negative feelings
towards his patients, especially in the case of misunderstanding and dissent.
Imperturbability: Calmness in crisis, coolness and presence of mind under all circumstances.
Described by William Osler.

IV. Professional Qualities qualities related to clinical practice.
Calm demeanor, effective listening, attention to detail
Quick and efficient responses in emergencies
Diplomatic communication and observation skills

●
●

●

V. Life Skills

Be able to put the patient at ease.
Act calmly with agitated patients or
relatives.
Notice subtle changes and reactions;
minor deviations from normal may indicate
serious disease.

Communication: Includes body language and interacting with special groups.
Time management: Reduces stress, organizes tasks.
Problem-solving: Defining and resolving clinical problems.
Decision-making: Evaluating treatment options, weighing the advantages and disadvantages of each.
Emotional intelligence: Managing one’s own and others' emotions.
Teamwork: Effective collaboration in healthcare settings.

 VI. Appearance
General: Traditional, clean, professional attire preferred.
Healthiness: Healthy lifestyle and image.
Clothes: Well-ironed, white coat or scrubs, no casual dress.

Accessories: Modest and minimal, female doctors should avoid strong make up, strong perfumes…
Male doctors need not to wear more than two accessories
Name badge: Should be visible and fixed.
Avoid putting earphones, ear plugs...
Posture: Must show respect, confidence, and empathy.

VII. Rights of Doctors
Choose patients and type of service, can put limit on the type/type of the patient.
Refuse patients (except in emergencies)
Be paid fairly and take time off
Abandon a patient ethically when needed

VIII. Professional Style
Influenced by personality, culture, and age.
Skeptic: Overly cautious. (better to worry than to be sorry)
Right-brain thinker: Emotion-driven decisions, more likely to be permissive and tolerant and to comply
with the patient's or family desires.
Obsessive: Rigid and over-detailed, exaggerated carefulness.
Culture: Affects treatment choices and ethics.
Age:
Seniors: Formal, experienced, culturally sensitive (can adapt to different patient cultures).
Juniors: Casual, open to new id

text: CONSENT IN MEDICAL PRACTICE What is the medical consent? It is the patient's agreement to receive any type of medical care whether diagnostic or therapeutic . Based on the ethical principle of patient autonomy and basic human rights The patient has all the freedom to decide what should or should not happen to his body and to receive necessary information before undergoing a test/procedure/surgery . Treating a patient without informed consent constitutes medical malpractice Obtaining valid consent is an ethical obligation and legal compulsion Consent in medical practice is needed in the following situations: 1-Examination of a patient for the purpose of diagnosis and subsequent treatment. 2- Examination of a patient for medico-legal purposes. 3- Involving patients in medical research studies . To protect the patient from unauthorized procedures. To protect the physician from claims of malpractice. If the consent is not obtained, the patient has the right to sue for medical malpractice Why is consent important? Types of medical consent 1 ) Implied consent. Known by the behavior of the patient 2) Express (informed) consent. patient expressly asks the doctor to provide care and consents by direct words, oral or written The patient or his/her representative has the right to be provided with sufficient information by the physician to allow him/her to make an informed decision to decide whether or not to consent to a certain procedure. 1- The act of a patient entering a doctor's chamber and expressing his problem is taken as an implied consent for general physical examination and routine investigations such as x-rays , etc … 2- The action of extending the arm for giving a blood sample . 3- The act of the patient standing in line to receive a vaccination. Implied consent: Express(informed) consent a- Oral consent : For intimate examinations e.g. vaginal and rectal. Simple procedures e.g. insertion of an intravenous cannula. Procedures performed under local anesthesia e.g. suture of minor lacerations. b- Written consent: For more invasive tests or for major procedures with significant risks e.g. - blood transfusion - breast biopsy - all operations requiring general or spinal anesthesia. Written consent is needed to prove patient’s agreement 1- "Disclosure " المصارحه providing relevant information by the clinician and its comprehension by the patient. The information should include: The patient's diagnosis. Nature and purpose of a proposed treatment or procedure. Risks and benefits of a proposed treatment or procedure. Alternatives. The risks of not receiving or undergoing a treatment or procedure. Prognosis (expected outcome). Components of a valid Informed Consent 2- "Competency" : الكفاءة ( adult, sane and conscious) The patient's ability to understand the relevant information and to appreciate the consequences of his decision. 3- Voluntariness" : طواعية ( No force or pressure, No fear, No fraud) The patient's right to come to a decision freely, without force or fraud . A valid Consent is not given for illegal act as criminal abortion and euthanasia. A valid Informed Consent should be obtained by a health care provider who is involved with the patient's care Exceptions to requirement of consent 1- Mentally incapacitated patient: - If patient is insane, mentally ill. - Close family members or legal guardians can give consent for him. 2- Minor (child): - At age of 18 years a patient can be presumed to have the capacity to decide on treatment. - Under this age, the parents (mother or father) can give consent for him. 3- Comatose patient: A close family member can give consent for him. 4- Certain occupations involving public risk: e.g. food dealers and drivers cannot refuse to have checkup tests. 5-In emergency requiring immediate action, only to save the patient’s life or avoid major deterioration of the patient's health. 6- Imprisoned patient: The legal authority can give consent for him. Documentation: It is important to document the process of obtaining consent : It should be dated and signed by the patient or guardian. It should be prepared in duplicate and a copy given to the patient. The original form should be kept, like all other medical records, as a legal document that the patient agreed to the treatment. The Right to Refuse Treatment Although the term "consent" usually means acceptance of treatment, the principle of consent applies equally to refusal of treatment. Competent patients have the right to refuse treatment regardless of the reason. The reasons may include: ** Religious beliefs ** Cultural beliefs ** W orrying about risks and chances of success of a certain procedure. Informed refusal If the patient has decided to refuse treatment or diagnostic tests, the health care provider should inform him of the risks his refusal . The doctor may ask the patient to sign a form that states he received this information, and that he still chooses not to be treated. This refusal form (Against Medical Advice (AMA) form) is obtained from the patient to protect the health care provider from legal claims for not providing the needed treatment. Overall, it is helpful to keep in mind that physicians can try to convince patients against refusing treatment, but the decision ultimately lies in the hands of the patient. Case 1 A 66-year-old man recently diagnosed as having prostate cancer is scheduled for a meeting to discuss his treatment options. The attending physician asks a resident to meet the patient and obtain informed consent before starting treatment. The resident meets the patient and returns with a signed informed consent form, indicating that the patient has chosen radiation therapy to treat his cancer. On reviewing the conversation with the resident, the attending physician discovers that the resident did not mention a relatively new surgical procedure as a possible treatment option.
