text: MEDICAL CONFIDENTIALITY Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Department Medical Confidentiality It is the right of a patient to have his medical and personal information kept private. Such information should be available only to the treating physician and other medical personnel involved in the patient's care, Information should not be disclosed to others unless the individual has given a specific permission for such a release ( release form) Children, elderly, mentally disabled and the dead all have the same right to confidentiality. Breach of confidentiality is not only unethical , it is also illegal . Hippocratic oath "What I may see or hear in the course of the treatment or even outside of the treatment in regard to the life of men, which on no account one must spread abroad, I will keep to myself, holding such things shameful to be spoken about". “ قسم أ بقراط : " أقسم بالله العظيم أن أكون أمينا ًعلى الشرف والبر والصلاح فى مزاولة صناعة الطب وأن أسعف الفقراء مجانا ً ولا أطلب أجرا ًيزيد على أجر عملى ، وأنى ﺇذا دخلت بيتا ً لا أتعرض لما لا يعنينى من أموره ولا أفشى سرا ً ، ولا أستعمل صناعتى فى ﺇفساد الخصال الحميدة و ﺇرتكاب الآثام ، ولا أعطى سما ً البته ولا أدل عليه ولا أشير به ولا أعطى دواء يضر الحوامل أو يسقط أجنتهن ، وأن أكون موقرا ً للذين علمونى معترفا ً بفضلهم مسديا ً لأولادهم ما فى ﺇستطاعتى من معروف وﺇحسان ". قسم الطبيب : مادة (1) من لائحة مزاولة المهنة: " أقسم بالله العظيم أن أراقب الله في مهنتي ، وأن أصون حياة الإنسان في كافة أدوارها في كل الظروف والأحوال باذلاً وس ا عي ا في استنقاذها من الهلاك والمرض والألم والقلق، وأن أحفظ للناس كرامتهم ، وأستر عورتهم ، وأكتم سرهم ، وأن أكون على الدوام من وسائل رحمة الله باذلاً رعايتي الطبية للقريب والبعيد ، للصالح والخاطئ ، والصديق والعدو وأن أثابر على طلب العلم أسخره لنفع الإنسان لا لأذاه ، وأن أوقر من علمني ، وأعلم من يصغرني ، وأكون أخاً لكل زميل في المهنة الطبية متعاونين على البر والتقوى ، وأن تكون حياتي مصداق إيماني في سري وعلانيتي ، نقيةً مما يشينها تجاه الله ورسوله والمؤمنين، والله على ما أقول شهيد". مادة (310 ( من قانون العقوبات: " كل من كان من الأطباء أو الجراحين أو الصيادلة أو القوابل أو غيرهم مودعاً إليه بمقتضى صناعته أو وظيفته سر خصوصي ائتمن عليه فأفشاه في غير الأحوال التي يلزمها القانون فيها بتبليغ ذلك يعاقب بالحبس مدة لا تزيد على ستة أشهر وبغرامة لا تتجاوز خمسمائة جنيه مصري ﺇلا ﺇذا طلبت المحكمة ذلك ". Patient`s information covers: identifiable material in the medical records e.g. written records, photographs, video films. oral information obtained from the patient or his relatives. Medical confidentiality includes: Information about the disease: (type, cause, diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, complications). Information not related to the disease: (personal, social, economic). Importance of medical confidentiality 1- Respects patient's autonomy. autonomy is the right of the competent individual to choose actions regarding his health and future. these actions are consistent with his values, goals, and life plan. 2- Respects natural human desire for privacy. Importance of medical confidentiality 3- Protects from social embarrassment, discrimination, disapproval, or stigmatization . 4- Prevents misuse of information against patient. 5- Builds confidence and trust between doctor and patient. Breach of confidentiality It means that a physician discloses patient data that he has learned within the physician-patient relationship to other parties without patient consent or court order . Breach of confidentiality Breach of medical confidentiality results in physical , psychological or financial harm to the patient and subjects' physicians to punishment by law. When can confidentiality be breached? Confidentiality is not an absolute obligation. situations arise where the harm in maintaining confidentiality is greater than that brought by disclosing information. A- For the sake of the community ( required by law) to the proper authority 1-Notification of births and deaths, abortion, accidents, poisoning. 2- Notification of infectious diseases (HIV, hepatitis). A-For the sake of the community 3- In case of accidents: (e.g. where a doctor has concerns over a patient’s fitness to drive, RTAs involving drugs/alcohol). A-For the sake of the community 4- in criminal cases: to prevent occurrence of crimes e.g. murder. threats of serious harm to others . 5- order of court . in case of medical malpractice and compensation: For the sake of the community 6-Psychotic patients with violent tendency. 7-To safeguard national security e.g. terrorist activity . B- For the sake of the patient 1-Victims of neglect or abuse e.g. child abuse. (the doctor should report the case to the authorities to prevent further harm to the child). 2- In times of emergency: (which may require an attending doctor to provide the identity of patients he/she has treated following a road traffic accident). B-For the sake of the patient 3-To prevent harm to patient ( patient requiring special care) e.g epilepsy, psychotic patients. 4- If the patient is incompetent or minor , information is normally delivered to parents or guardians. 5- In case of poisoning: (e.g. when a doctor has a patient attempting suicide by taking a poison to end his life. the doctor has to disclose this information to the patient’ family to take care if the patient tries to commit suicide another time). Principles that should be followed on allowing breach of confidentiality It must be to proper authorities. Not beyond what is required or relevant. text:
Chapter 17: Ethical Aspects of Organ
Transplantation
MCQs
1. A 27-year-old man suffers severe facial burns after an industrial accident. The
plastic surgery team decides to perform a skin graft using healthy skin from his thigh.
Which of the following statements is MOST accurate regarding this procedure?
A) The procedure requires approval from an ethics committee because it involves tissue
transfer.
B) This is considered an example of allotransplantation.
C) This is considered autotransplantation and has no legal or ethical restrictions.
D) The donor must be matched immunologically before the graft is applied.

2. A 35-year-old woman wants to donate one of her kidneys to her husband who is
experiencing end-stage renal disease. She insists on proceeding despite being
unrelated to him. What type of donor is she?
A) Living Non-Directed Donor (LNDD)
B) Living Related Donor (LRD)
C) Living Non-Related Donor (LNRD)
D) Cadaveric Donor

3. During a medical ethics class, a student argues that anyone should be allowed to
sell their kidney to help others. Which of the following is the MOST ethical response?
A) Selling organs should be legalized under strict regulations.
B) Paid donation is ethically acceptable as long as informed consent is given.
C) Selling human organs is unethical and constitutes medical malpractice.
D) Payment for organs should only be allowed for unrelated donors.

 4. A 40-year-old man dies after a traumatic brain injury. He had signed an organ
donation card before death. The transplant team is ready to retrieve his organs. What
is the MOST appropriate next step?
A) Proceed with organ retrieval immediately.
B) Request written consent from the family.
C) Confirm brain death by the transplant surgeon.
D) Ensure declaration of death by an independent medical team before retrieval.

5. A young woman develops acute liver failure. Her father offers to donate part of his
liver. What is the MOST important prerequisite before proceeding?
A) The father must sign a legal contract.
B) The father must undergo hypnosis therapy.
C) There must be voluntary informed consent and no harm to the donor.
D) The donor must have a matching blood group only.

6. A patient in a vegetative state is considered for organ donation. However, brain
stem reflexes are still present. Which of the following is TRUE?
A) The patient is legally brain dead and can donate organs.
B) The patient must be taken off the ventilator to confirm death.
C) Brain death is not confirmed until brain stem reflexes are absent.
D) The family can decide whether to proceed with donation regardless of brain death.

7. After a patient is declared brain dead, the transplant team directly speaks to the
family to ask for organ donation. Which ethical guideline has been violated?

A) The transplant team must not approach the family due to conflict of interest.
B) The transplant team is not qualified to discuss brain death.
C) Family consent is not necessary if the patient is brain dead.

 D) The transplant team must request permission before declaring brain death.

8. A woman is declared brain dead after a stroke. Which of the following criteria is
NOT essential for confirming brain death?
A) Deep coma without pain response.
B) Absence of brain stem reflexes.
C) Lack of spontaneous respiration.
D) Family consent for organ retrieval.

9. A 45-year-old man with a terminal lung disease is waiting for a transplant. He
expresses concern that organs might be removed before a donor is officially declared
dead. What can the medical team say to reassure him?
A) Organs can be retrieved when the heart stops.
B) Organs are removed only after official declaration of death by a separate team.
C) The transplant team always confirms death.
D) Brain death is not a real legal death.

10. A 16-year-old boy wants to donate part of his liver to his sister. Which of the
following is MOST accurate?
A) He can donate with parental consent.
B) His consent is valid because he understands the procedure.
C

Chapter 18: Medical/Medico-Legal
Reports
MCQs
1. Q1. A 45-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with multiple
facial fractures following a car accident. The treating physician is later asked to
write a medico-legal report by the prosecution. What is the MOST appropriate
initial step before writing the report?
•
•
•
•

A. Review the patient's medical records and clarify the purpose of the report.
B. Provide the report without patient consent.
C. Write the report from memory since it was a serious case.
D. Contact the insurance company directly.

2. Q2. A lawyer contacts a physician requesting a report about his client’s injury that
occurred at work. What should the doctor do FIRST before preparing the report?
•
•
•
•

A. Immediately begin writing based on the lawyer’s description.
B. Ask the lawyer to send the diagnosis.
C. Get written consent from the patient.
D. Decline to write the report.

3. Q3. Which of the following statements about writing a medico-legal report is
CORRECT?
•
•
•
•

A. The report should be written as a narrative story.
B. Avoid dividing the report into sections to save space.
C. It is acceptable to accuse another colleague if you are sure they are wrong.
D. Medical facts should be presented in chronological order.

4. Q4. A patient with a known history of epilepsy had a seizure at work and
sustained a head injury. His employer requested a report about the incident. The
treating doctor is unsure whether to include personal information. What should
the doctor do?
•
•
•
•

A. Include everything, including unrelated history.
B. Exclude the epilepsy because it is private.
C. Only include relevant facts supported by medical records.
D. Use dramatic language to explain the seizure.

5. Q5. In the format of a medico-legal report, which of the following is NOT one of the
essential components?

 •
•
•
•

A. Patient’s clinical presentation.
B. Doctor’s professional background.
C. Emotions and sympathy for the patient.
D. Response to requested questions.

6. Q6. A physician receives a court order requesting a report on a criminal assault
victim. What is TRUE regarding patient consent in this case?
•
•
•
•

A. Consent is still required from the patient.
B. Consent is not needed if the request is from the court.
C. The doctor must refuse the request.
D. Only verbal consent is needed.

7. Q7. A doctor is writing a medico-legal report. Which of the following is considered
UNPROFESSIONAL?
•
•
•
•

A. Referring to medical records.
B. Avoiding legal terms.
C. Explaining medical concepts simply.
D. Providing opinion based on limited experience.

8. Q8. Which party is NOT typically authorized to request a medico-legal report from
a treating doctor?
•
•
•
•

A. The patient
B. The patient’s employer
C. The patient’s neighbor
D. The prosecution

9. Q9. Which of the following is a professional obligation when writing a medical
report?
•
•
•
•

A. Verify all contents before signing the report.
B. Use technical abbreviations without explanation.
C. Include predictions about future complications.
D. Omit less relevant facts to keep the report short.

10. Q10. A young woman was injured in a domestic violence case. Her physician wrote
a report and later realized he forgot to include the informed consent document.
What should he do?
•
•
•
•

A. Do nothing; it’s not important.
B. Add it secretly without documentation.
C. Provide a supplementary report including the consent.
D. Blame the nurse for misplacing it.

 11. Q11. Why is it discouraged to use emotive language in a medico-legal report?
•
•
•
•

A. It makes the report longer.
B. It may bias the legal process.
C. It shows the doctor cares too much.
D. It is only used in academic articles.

12. Q12. A doctor was asked to testify in court about a report he wrote. What’s the
BEST advice?
•
•
•
•

A. Say what you think the judge wants to hear.
B. Only defend what is clearly stated in your report.
C. Avoid reviewing the patient’s records before court.
D. Change your test

condition, treatment options, and possible complications, and allows the patient to ask
questions. Which patient right is this an example of?
A) Consultation
B) Confidentiality
C) Information disclosure
D) Participation in treatment decisions

2. A patient refuses a recommended surgery after being informed of all the consequences.
According to ethical principles, what should the physician do?
A) Force the patient to undergo the surgery
B) Ask the patient’s family to convince him
C) Respect the patient’s decision
D) Cancel all treatment options

investigations. Later, the patient is diagnosed with prostate cancer and dies. What was the
main ethical violation?
A) Performing surgery without consent
B) Breach of confidentiality
C) Failure to consult a specialist and use proper diagnostic tools
D) Discrimination against the patient

4. A physician refuses to treat a patient in an emergency because he cannot pay fees. This
is a violation of which ethical principle?
A) Avoiding discrimination
B) Respect for autonomy
C) Informed consent
D) Duty to treat emergency cases

reflects:
A) Ethical behavior and professional responsibility
B) Violation of confidentiality
C) Conflict of interest
D) Disrespect to the patient

6. A physician prescribes medications with unclear handwriting and without specifying
dosage. What is the ethical issue here?
A) Overprescription
B) Failure to communicate clearly in prescriptions
C) Disrespect for autonomy
D) Using patients for experiments

7. In case of an upcoming vacation, a doctor should:
A) Leave without informing patients
B) Cancel all appointments
C) Inform patients in advance and arrange for a replacement doctor
D) Continue to treat patients remotely

8. Which of the following is a duty of the patient?
A) To provide accurate information about their health condition
B) To demand treatment regardless of physician judgment
C) To choose their own medication
D) To refuse all hospital regulations

him. What ethical principle was likely violated?
A) Confidentiality
B) Respect and nondiscrimination
C) Informed consent
D) Emergency treatment

right was violated?
A) Right to consultation
B) Right to information disclosure
C) Right to respectful care
D) Right to confidentiality

11. A physician begins a treatment plan without recording the patient’s history or current
condition. This violates the responsibility of:
A) Equal treatment
B) Proper patient examination
C) Insurance cooperation
D) Hospital regulation compliance

12. During a surgery, the surgeon leaves the procedure midway and allows a resident to
complete it without patient consent. What ethical principle is violated?
A) Confidentiality
B) Patient responsibility
C) Duty to perform the operation personally
D) Insurance fraud

13. A patient says: “Doctor, I want to ask another consultant about my case.” What is the
doctor’s best response?
A) "You don’t need a second opinion."
B) "Other doctors may confuse you."
C) "I will not continue treating you if you do that."
D) "Sure, you have the right to seek a second consultation."

What does the doctor's behavior reflect?

 A) Concealment of diagnosis

C) Patient disrespect
D) Experimental treatment

A) Respecting patient’s decision
B) Explaining the illness i

text:
Cancer genetics
By: Clinical Medical Genetics Staff
Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University

 ILOs
1. Define carcinogenesis
2. Understand the mechanism of carcinogenesis.
3. Identify the causative genes underlying carcinogenesis.
4. Recognize the group of inherited cancer syndromes and their
underlying genetic causes.
5. Discuss some examples of inherited cancer syndromes and
modes of inheritance through presenting clinical problems of
familial breast and colonic cancer.
6. Analyze the role of genetic counseling and preventive measures
for some inherited cancer syndromes.

 Definition of cancer
• Cancer is a genetic disease of somatic cells.
• A genetic defect: the primary genetic mutation happening in a
cell (progenitor cell) and is not repaired (Stage of Initiation).
• The initiated cell is promoted by exposure to some agents such as
hormones to stimulate uncontrolled proliferation (Stage of
promotion & clonal expansion).
• Multistep of carcinogenesis and tumour progression: during
uncontrolled proliferation, there is accumulation of extra
secondary genetic changes which results in tumour progression.

Structural chromosomal alterations
Pathogenesis: results from misrepair of chromosome breaks or defect in recombination events that occur
between homologous chromosomes during crossing over in meiosis or between non-homologous
chromosomes in case of abnormal rejoining of broken chromosomes.
Types of structural chromosomal abnormalities:
The resulting chromosomal defect will depend on whether
single or two chromosomes
1. Deletions: loss of chromatin from a chromosome
a) Terminal deletions: arise from one break at one of the
chromosome, the resulting acentric part is lost in the subsequent
cell division. The chromosome misses a terminal part from the p or q arm.
b) Interstitial deletions: two breaks in the same chromosome. Fusion at the break
sites with loss of the interstitial part.
c) Ring chromosome: arises from breaks at either side of the centromere and
fusion occurs at the breakpoints.
Some cases of Turner Syndrome result from any of the types of deletion in X
chromosome. For example terminal deletion: 46, XX, del Xp21; or ring
chromosome of one X chromosome 46, X r(X).
2. Duplications (Dup): a gain of chromosomal material, this results from two breaks and
unequal sister chromatid exchange (within one chromosome) or unequal recombination
(between two chromosomes). This will result in partial trisomy of duplicated chromosome
region
3. Isochromosomes: from abnormal centromeric division that is at a right angle to the
normal separation (horizontal division instead of vertical) due to abnormal attachment to
the mitotic spindle. The result is that both arms on either side of the centromere are similar
in daughter cells, either 2 p or 2 q arms, causing duplication of one of the chromosome
arms (p or q) and deletion of the other arm in the daughter cells.
Some cases of Turner syndrome may result from isochromosome of X chromosome for example 46, X
i(Xp) or 46, Xi(Xq).

 4. Inversion (inv) is a reversal of the order of
chromatin between two breaks on the same
chromosome.
a) Pericentric inversion results from breaks and
rearrangements on both sides of the centromere.
b) Paracentric inversion results from breakage and
rearrangement on thesame side of the centromere.
The individual with an inversion may have a normal
phenotype but problems occur during gametogenesis
due to defective meiotic pairing of bivalents involving
inverted chromosome and usually result in deletion
and/or duplication of chromatin segments and causing
abnormal gametes with chromosomal imbalances
5. Translocations (t): is the exchange of chromosomal segments between mis-repaired broken nonhomologous chromosomes.
a) Reciprocal translolcation: resulls from breakage and exchange of segments between chromosomes of
metacentric and submetacentric types.
b) Robertsonian Translocation results from fusions of whole q ams of acrocentric chromosomes. It is a
balanced translocation because the short arms of the acrocentric chromosomes carry only genes for rRNA,
which are present on other acrocentric chromosomes, and therefore caries are phenotypically normal and
have a balanced karyotype, for example, described as 45, XX, t (13;14(q10, q10)
The carriers of the translocation have balanced karyotypes, and usualy are nomal.However, presence of
translocation results in offspring with unbalanced karyotypes and a high risk of miscarriages and stilbirth.

6. Chromosome fragile site is a morphologic feature
affecting a particular site of a chromosome with tendency to
break resulting in gaps or breaks in chromosomes. It can be
visualised in a karyotype if the cell culture of a patient is
provided with specific conditions. They are genetically
transmitted traits being inherited from affected parents to
their offspring.
Clinical example :Fragile X Mental Retardation.

chromosomal breaks at different sites appear in multiple visible structural lesions in a metaphase
chromosome preparation . It r

IV. X-linked dominant inheritance
1. Affects either sex, but within a family there are more females
affected thanmales.
2. Females are often more mildly affected than males.
3. The child of an affected female, regardless of the sex have 50%
chance of beingaffected.
4. In case of an affected male, all daughters, but non of the sons will
be affected.
Example isVitamin D resistant rickets.
Differentiation between X-linked recessive and dominant inheritance
is difficult becauseof X-inactivation, "Lyonization" (dosage effect to
compensate for the single copy of X-chromosome in males), which blurs distinction of both types
V. Y-linked inheritance
1. Affects only males.
2. All affected males have an affected father unless it resulted from a
newmutation.
3. Genetic risk: Transmitted to all sons of an affected male.
Examples:hairy ears, azospermia (one of the causes of infertility due to SRY
genemutation, males may have offspring by assisted reproduction).

Some Unusual features in single gene patterns of inheritance
a. Pleiotropy:
Two or more unrelated effects resulting from single gene
disorder, e.g. neurofibromatosiswhich involves skin
hyperpigmented patches, CNS tumours and
neurofibromas,Lischnodules of the iris).
b. Variable expressivity
The disease shows variation in the clinical phenotype
amonggenerations within the same
family. For exampleAdult polycystic kidney disease

c. Reduced / Incomplete Penetrance
Carry the gene of an AD disorder → but NO clinical disorder
Example :retinoblastomadespite being AD genetically inherited cancer yet its penetrance is less than 100%.

 d. Anticipation
More severe phenotype in successive and recent generations.
Cause: mutation causing the disorderresults in more-unstable DNA (Dynamic mutation resulting from
unstable expansion oftriplet DNA repeats).
Example, Huntington disease, Myotonic dystrophy, Fragile X Syndrome.
e. New mutation
An affected person with an AD disorder without affection of the parents or there is anegative family history
of the disorder (e.g. Achondroplasia; a form of short-limb dwarfism)
f. Mosaicism
Is the presence of more than one cell line within an individual.

g. Locus/Genetic Heterogeneity (Genocopy)
A disorder inherited due to mutations in more than one gene(at different loci) and yet shows the same
phenotype,
Examplehearingloss (congenital hearing loss) most commonly are AR and could result from 20 different
genes. If both parents have hearing loss (heterozygous)→ their offspringwill not be affected.

 B. Non-Mendelian Inheritance
1. Genomic imprinting:
During gameteformation →inactivation of some genes (by methylation) → persist permanentlyand passes
on to offspring and it will be expressed according to the parent of origin
Prader Willi Syndrome (Mental handicap with obesity)
Occurs if the mutant geneon chromosome 15 (15q11-q13) was inherited fromthe father OR maternal
uniparental disomy
Angelman Syndrome (mental disability and convulsions)
occurs if the defective geneon chromosome 15 (15q11-q13) is inherited from the mother OR paternal
uniparental disomy

2. Mitochondrial inheritance:
The disorder is transmitted to both sex, but is only transmitted through females due toexclusive maternal
contribution of mitochondrial DNA to offspring.
The proportion ofaffected offspring is variable and the clinical picture within a family is variable, this is due
to HETEROPLASM (the proportion of normal and mutant copies of mitochondrial DNA)
Examples include:
1. Leber's optic atrophy
2. Deafness
3. Diabetes mellitus
4. Mitochondrial variant of cardiomyopathy.

 This mutation results from expanding the number of trinucleotide repeats within particulargenes. Clinical

1. Fragile X Syndrome:X-linked disorder which present more in males.
Syndrome results from expansion of CGG repeats within the Fragile X gene

premutation →50-200

 Important Terms:
Chromosome: The unit of genetic information which transmitted from one generation to the next.
Allele: alternative forms of a gene at a given locus, in homologous chromosome.
▪ If similar  homozygous.

▪ If different  heterozygous.

Locus: position occupied by a gene on a chromosome.
Homozygous: person has both alleles are similar either normal or mutant.
Heterozygous: person has both alleles are different one normal & one mutant.
Hemizygous: a ♂ having one gene on each locus on X & Y chromosome.
Genotype: the genetic constitution of an individual, i.e. the particular genes at a given locus.
Phenotype: the observed expression of a particular gene or genes.
Polymorphism: two or more alternatives genotypes, found in normal individual,
present at a frequency of > 1% in a certain population & not
associated with a diseased phenotype regardless of the frequency.

Co-dominance: the term used if both alleles are expressed equally in a heterozygote.
e.g. AB blood group.
Mutation: permanent heritable change in the DNA sequence.

Dominant trait: those characters, which are phenotypically expressed in heterozygote
(i.e. individuals with one normal and one mutant allele of a gene).
♦ One mutant gene is enough to express the disease.

Recessive trait: those conditions which are expressed only in homozygote
(i.e. individuals have both mutant alleles of a particular gene locus).
♦ The 2 alleles must be mutant to express the disease.

Carrier: An individual heterozygous for a mutant allele that generally
causes disease only in the homozygous state (recessive) and is
phenotypically normal, & can transmit the mutant allele to the offspring.

Proband: an affected family member goes to the doctor "who brings the family to
clinical attention", from him the family pedigree is drawn.

text: Practical class of pedigree analysis By: Clinical Medical Genetics Staff Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University ILOs: Recognize and interpret different symbols used in pedigree construction. Define a proband and a consultand . Use pedigree symbols to construct a 3 generation pedigree. Interpret pedigrees of different modes of inheritance of genetic disorders. Practice pedigree construction based on clinical scenarios. Calculate the genetic risk of different modes of inheritance. Symbols used in pedigree construction: Important terms: A proband : the family member who brings the family to clinical attention. A consultand : an unaffected person seeking genetic counseling. Case 1 A 33-year-old woman presented with a history of multiple café-au- lait spots and skin neurofibromas . She had a family history of NF1; her maternal grandfather, mother, maternal aunt, and younger sister had been diagnosed with NF1. Construct a pedigree for this family. What is the mode of inheritance of such a disease (explain your answer)? What is the genetic risk of offspring of this woman if she got married to a healthy individual? I II III III ? The genetic risk of her children Case 2 Hind is pregnant for the second time. Her first child Hany has cystic fibrosis. Hind has 2 brothers Ahmed and Said and a sister Hoda . Ahmed is married to unrelated woman, Amal and has 2 years old daughter called Hadir . Hind parents are Ismail and Amina . Amina’s sister Adeela is the mother of Hind’s husband, Aly . There is no previous family history of CF. Sketch the pedigree What is the pattern of transmission of CF and what is the risk of CF for Hind’s next child Which people in this pedigree are obligate carriers Ahmed Said Hoda Hind Aly Amal Amina Adeela Ismail Hadir Hany I II III IV Case 3 Mohamed is a proband with hemophilia A seeking medical counseling to determine the genetic risk of his offspring. His parents are free of the disease. He has an affected maternal uncle who has a healthy son and a daughter. He also has a healthy aunt who has an affected son and a healthy daughter. And his grandparents are healthy. 1) Draw a pedigree for this family 2) What is the mode of inheritance of this disease? 3) What is the genetic risk of his offspring if he got married to a woman who has no family history of such a disease? Punnet square of an affected male and healthy female of X-linked recessive disorder X X XX XX X XY XY Y Case 4 This pedigree shows multiple affected family members with a genetic disease and 2 deceased males. 1) Deduce the type of inheritance met in this family (explain your answer) 2)What is the genetic risk of children of an affected male? Case 5 1) What is the mode of inheritance of this disorder? 2) Explain why individual IV-3 is affected? 2) Explain why individual IV-3 is affected? Affected male Carrier female Case 6 A pedigree demonstrating recurrence of the autosomal dominant disorder achondroplasia . Both affected children have the same point mutation. Their father (arrow II-2) is unaffected and has no such mutation in DNA from examined somatic tissues (blood sample). Explain the normal phenotype of the father in spite of 100% penetrance of achondroplasia ? Mosiac for his germ cells Reduced penterance Case 7 What is the mode of inheritance of the disease running in this family? Give an example of a condition inherited by this mode? A pedigree of Leber’s hereditary optic atrophy, a form of spontaneous blindness caused by a defect in mitochondrial DNA. Inheritance is only through maternal lineage, in agreement with the known maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA. No affected male transmits the disease. Case 8 1) Explain why individual II-6 didn’t demonstrate this autosomal dominant disorder? Pedigree of split-hand deformity demonstrating failure of penetrance in the mother of the consultand (individual II-6). Reduced penetrance must be taken into account in genetic counseling. Quiz 1-What is the mode of inheritance of disorders illustrated in the following pedigrees? 2-Give an example for each? 1 X-linked dominant 2 Autosomal recessive 3 X-linked recessive 4 Autosomal dominant 5 mitochondrial 6 Autosomal dominant- reduced penetrance 7 Mitochondrial 8 X-linked dominant 9 Autosomal dominant -reduced penetrance Flow Chart for interpretation of disease transmission within a family to determine mode of inheritance. Thank you

Neoplasia

82

 INTRODUCTION
• the term 'neoplasia' means new growth; the new growth produced is called 'neoplasm' or 'tumour'.
• Scientific Definition of a neoplasm or tumour :
» mass of tissue formed as result of abnormal, excessive, uncoordinated, autonomous and purposeless
proliferation of cells even after cessation of stimulus for growth which caused it'.
- Uncoordinated :badly organized
- Purposeless : have no value or use
- Autonomous : act independently, loss of control and regulation of replication
- Neoplasms may be :
• benign: when they are slow-growing and localized without causing much difficulty to the host.
@ malignant: when they are rapidly-growing, spread throughout body and may eventually cause death of host.
• Oncology (oncos=tumour, logos=study) :branch of science dealing with the study of neoplasms or tumors
• Basic components of any tumors benign | malignant:
1- Parenchyma; comprised by proliferating tumor cells, parenchyma determines the nature and evolution of
the tumor.
2- Supportive stroma: composed of fibrous CT and blood vessels; it provides the framework on which the
parenchymal tumor cells grow.
• Origin of cancer cells :
- Cancer cells originate by clonal proliferation of a single progeny of a cell (monoclonality).
- Cancer cells arise from stem cells , characterized by : prolonged self-renewal and asymmetric replication
and trans-differentiation.
• Nomenclature of benign tumors:
› The suffix '-oma' is added to denote benign tumors.
» Add Sarcoma : (sarcos = fleshy) Malignant tumors originating from mesenchymal origin .
» Add Carcinoma : (carcin = hard) Malignant tumors originating from epithelial origin.
> Exceptions :
- Melanoma | carcinoma of the melanocytes.
- Hepatoma | carcinoma of the hepatocytes,
- Lymphoma | malignant tumor of the lymphoid tissue,
- Seminoma | malignant tumor of the testis.
- Leukaemia \ malignant tumor of blood forming cells.
• Classification of tumors is based on :
Histogenesis (cell of origin)
Biologic behaviour
- Epithelial,
- Benign, malignant, borderline ‚or locally malignant
- Mesenchymal,
- Primary or secondary
- Hematopoietic,
- Clinical features,
- Germ cell tumors.
- Morphological characteristics
SPECIAL CATEGORIES OF TUMOURS
1. Mixed tumors: When two types of tumors are combined in the same tumor. e.g.
- Adenosquamous carcinoma, Adenoacanthoma, Carcinosarcoma
- Mixed tumour of the salivary gland (or pleomorphic adenoma) benign tumour having combination of both
epithelial and mesenchymal tissue elements.
2- Teratomas: tumors arising from totipotent cells derived from the three germ cell layers; ectoderm,
mesoderm and endoderm.
- Most common sites for teratomas are ovaries and testis (gonadal teratomas).
3. Hamartoma:
- benign tumor which is made of mature but disorganized cells of tissues indigenous to particular organ
e.g. hamartoma of the lung consists of mature cartilage, mature smooth muscle and epithelium.
4. Choristoma: heterotopia but is not a true tumor, composed of ectopic islands of normal tissue.

 ARTERIOSCLEROSIS (Hardening of arteries)
Definition: A group of non-inflammatory diseases characterized by thickening and loss
of elasticity of the arterial wall.
Three main forms: differ in microscopic appearance and in distribution.
1. Atherosclerosis: commonest and most important, affects large and
medium sized (muscular) arteries
-Characterized by internal thickening of the vessel wal and lipid deposition.
2. Monckeberg's medial sclerosis /calcification: characterized by
calcification of the tunica media of medium-sized (muscular arteries) arteries.
3. Arteriolosclerosis: characterized by hyperplastic or hyaline thickening of
the walls of small arteries and arterioles.

 ATHEROSCLEROSIS (AS)
• Definition: Non-inflammatory vessel disease characterized by
thickening and loss of elasticity of the arterial wall with lipid
deposition.
• Vessels: large and medium sized muscular arteries, the aorta,
coronary, cerebral, carotid and mesenteric or any artery can be
affected.
• Incidence:
-A disease of western countries
-Gradual onset and progressive course.
-Begins in childhood, becomes manifest at middle age or later
(when arterial lesions precipitate clinical manifestations by organ

 Rheumatic fever
Definition:

occurs as a complication of streptococcal pharyngitis (Group A
beta-hemolytic streptococci)

Age incidence:
-Common in children between 5-15 years
-More common in low socioeconomic class who live in
overcrowded conditions that favour streptococcal pharyngitis

 Rheumatic fever
Pathogenesis:
The relationship between streptococcal pharyngitis and
rheumatic fever is evidenced by:
1) Acute rheumatic fever usually occurs 2-3 weeks after an
episode of pharyngitis caused by group A beta-hemolytic
streptococci
2) Early treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis by penicillin
deceases the incidence and severity of acute rheumatic fever
and its recurrences

 Pathology: Patho = Suffering
Scientific study of diseases, that deals with disease process.
It's the study of abnormal form, function & relationship between them.
"Causes, mechanisms, manifestations, progress, sequels".
♦ General: study of common changes in all tissues (principals, basic patterns)
of the diseases (regardless the organ or the cause).
♦ Systemic "special": study of specific pathological changes in individual organ
or organ systems (with well defined causes).

Health:

State of harmony between body & the surrounding environments.

WHO:

A condition of complete physical, mental and social well being
& not just the absence of overt illness.

Disease:

Any disturbance or deviation from normal structure & / or function of the
body or any of its constituent parts (tissues) outside the normal range
i.e.: discomfort dt structural or functional abnormalities

Manifestations of disease: the summation of the damage done by a harmful agent
& the body’s response to it.

Goal of study: to identify the cause  diagnose  treat  prevent diseases.
Pathological study of disease: is study of
1- Definition.
2- Epidemiology.
3- Classification (types): according to particulate basis. *
4- Cause = Etiology.
5- Mechanisms of its development = Pathogenesis
6- Structural alterations (cells & organs) = Morphologic changes.
7- Functional consequences = Clinical significance.

Definition of Diseases:
A certain no. of events or items in a certain order describing the disease

*

Epidemiology of Diseases: = How common??
● Incidence.
● Common or rare.
● Population distribution. (age, sex).
● Endemic, sporadic, epidemic or pandemic.
-1-

1- Genetically:

(Inherited)

Abnormalities of chromosomes & component genes.
Mutations: genetic / chromosomal changes.
dt radiation, chemicals, infective agent or unknown cause in majorities.
e.g.: Hemophilia.
Some diseases have genetic susceptibility as:
* Lack of melanin pigment (blonds)  skin damage by UVR of the sun.
* Blood gp A.  pernicious anemia & gastric cancer.
* Blood gp B.  duodenal peptic ulcer.
* Autoimmune diseases associated with some HLA.

2- Acquired: "Environmental agents"
a- Physical "trauma, radiation, extremes temp, electric shock".
b- Chemical "toxins, poisons, drugs, acids, caustics, phosphorous".
c- Nutritional: ▪ Excess as ↑cholesterol (VLDL)  Atherosclerosis.
↑ calories intake  obesity  Metabolic syndromes.
▪ Deficiency as ↓vit.  rickets or ↓ proteins  PCM.
d- Infections & infestations: "B, V, F, P".
e- Psychological stress  ▪ Mental illness.
▪ Psychosomatic with organic lesion, anixity  peptic ulcer.
f- Abnormal immunologic reactions "hypersensitivity & autoimmunity".

3- Multifactorial:
Diseases have more than one risk factor as DM, cancer, hypertension, …………..

4- Unknown:
Idiopathic, 1ry, essential or cryptogenic.
N.B.1:
Congenital Dis.: Dis. Present at birth & it may by genetically or acquired (How?)
Metabolic diseases: may be genetically inherited with very important role
to environmental factors e.g. DM
N.B.2: In some diseases there is Predisposing factor beside the Precipitating factor.

Pathogenesis of the Disease:
► The mechanism of its development.
► The sequence of events of response of the cells & tissues to an etiological agent
from the start ( initial stimulus) to the end ( ultimate expression )
without any treatment.
► Explain How ?? Etiology  morphological & Functional changes.

the disease & diagnostic to its causes.

1- Gross = naked eye appearance.
2- Microscopic

(Light, Electron & Fluorescent).

Lesion:- Structural changes or alterations which are recognized by gross
& microscopic examinations. i.e: Anything abnormal.
Examples of structural changes: Mass - Ulcer - Atrophy ……………..

 Inflammation: is a (local) reaction of vascularized, living tissue to an injurious agent
provided that the injury is not so strong to cause immediate cell
de-vitalization (death - necrosis) of the tissue.

Aims: Protective & Defensive Mechanism
1- Elimination of causative agent & dead tissues.
2- Dilution of toxins.
3- Prepare tissues for repair.

Nomenclature: Add ''itis'' to the name of organ, with some exceptions.
Causes: 1- Non living agents (irritants): physical or chemicals.
2- Inert materials such as undigestible foreign bodies.
3- Living agents: bacteria and its toxins, viruses, fungi & parasites.
4- Immunologic reactions.
5- Metabolic error as gout - Chemical injury as ↑ Hcl

Types:
1- Acute inflammation: (More sever)
- Onset: sudden (min  hours).
- Duration: short, (hours  few days).
- Course: rapid.
- Characterized by:
a- Fluid rich by plasma protein "exudation".
b- Accumulation of PNL "neutrophiles".

2- Chronic inflammation:

(Less sever)
- Onset: gradual (days  weeks).
- Duration: long, (months  years).
- Course: gradual decline.
- Characterized by:
a- Influx of lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages.
b- Tissue destruction & repair. (Vascular proliferation & fibrosis).

3- Subacute inflammation:
Clinical term
- Type of inflammation between acute & chronic. - E.g.: bacterial endocarditis.
4- Hyperacute inflammation: Clinical term (rare)
- Immediate reaction develops within minutes.

Def: Replacement of damaged tissues by new viable ones.

Types:

Replacement of the lost parenchymal cells by surviving parenchymal cells
of the same type by proliferation of adjacent surviving parenchymal cells.
"Injured tissue restored to its normal pre-injury state"
"Replacement of specialized tissue"

II- Organization "Scar Formation":
Replacement of damaged tissue by connective tissue with fibrosis.

♦ No capacity for regeneration in postnatal life.

is a Genetic disease at somatic cell level affecting single progenitor

1- Stage of Initiation: 1ry genetic mutation or defect in a single progenitor cell

3- Stage of tumour progression: accumulation of 2ry genetic mutations

1. Which of the following statements does not describe
cell injury?

injury?

B. Hyperplasia
C. Calcification
D. Necrosis

3. Which of the following is the most important cause of
cell injury?
A. Alcohol
B. Biological agents
C. Aging
D. Deficiency of oxygen

due to hypoxia?

5. Regarding cellular response to injurious agents, which
of the following statements is correct?
A. Partial ischemia leads to irreversible cell damage.
B. Cells in the brain can withstand hypoxia for 5 minutes
C. Cellular response does not depend on nutritional status.
D. Prolonged deficiency of oxygen causes reversible damage.

6. Which of the following is an irreversible effect of ATP
depletion?
A. Initial Pyknosis
B. Increase in intracellular fat
C. Release of lysosomal enzymes
D. Loss of microvilli

7. Which of the following is not a chemical cause of cell
injury?
A. Hypertonic Solutions
B. Electric trauma
C. Cyanide
D. Alcohol

8. Which of the following is the first manifestation of
cell injury?

B. Clumping of chromatin

membrane injury?
A. Ca-modulated activation of endonucleases
B. Hydrogen peroxide
C. Bacterial toxins
D. Activated complement system

10. Which of the following is not an effect of altered
DNA?
A. Abnormal cell division
B. Unregulated growth
C. Failure of synthesis of structural proteins
D. Increased synthesis of enzymes

11. The major mechanism of cellular swelling in
ischemia is:
A. Reduced intracellular pH
B. Increased intracellular accumulation of sodium.
C. Increased fat accumulation in the cytoplasm
D. Reduced aerobic respiration

12. Which of the following is the most reactive free
radical?
A. Hydroxyl radical
B. Superoxide
C. Hydrogen peroxide
D. Vitamin C

Problem Solving
1- A 4Y ♂child coming to Emergency department complaining of skin burn on his both
legs caused by boiled water. The area inflamed & contain large amount of
inflammatory exudates. The type of exudate is:
a- Purulent exudate.
b- Fibrinous exudate.
c- Serous exudate.
d- Hemorrhagic exudate.
2- A 15 years old ♂ patient complaining with sudden sever abdominal pain
in Rt iliac fossa & vomiting. On examination  high fever, chills, malaise.
The doctor ask for some blood investigations which reveals  leukocytosis,
↑ CRP & ESR. On doing ultra-sound on abdomen showing  swelling of
appendicular wall which containing turbid fluid denoting inflammation.
Q: Type of appendicular inflammation.
a- Phelegmonous inflammation.
b- Non suppurative inflammation.
c- Appendicular abscess.
d- Appendicular curbuncle.

floor. After 3 days the site of injury become red, hot, swollen with sever pain.
On the next 2 days there is a cavity containing pus start to appear.
Q: Name of the condition & the lesion.
a- Cellulitis.
b- Curbuncle.
c- Boil.
d- Abcess

On regular shake-up, she developed gradual splenomegaly & neuropathy. More
investigations was done showing proteinurea in urine analysis. Biopsy was done
using Congo red stain revealed red amorphous homogenous extra cellular deposits.
Possible diagnosis: ………………………………………….

On Examination an abnormal heart sounds & congested neck veins are founded
denoting a case of heart failure. ECHO was done reveals enlarged heart specially the
Rt ventricle. Biopsy was taken shows yellow streaks extending between the
myocardial fibers.
Possible diagnosis: ………………………………………….

examination she has diffuse tenderness in all abdominal quadrants,
↑↑ levels of serum lipase & amylase. An abdominal CT reveals peritoneal
fluid collection & swelling of the pancreas.
Which of the following cellular changes is most likely to associate these findings?
a- Coagulative necrosis.
b- Dry gangrene.
c- Fat necrosis.
d- Apoptosis.
e- Liqufactive necrosis.

Biopsy was done & revealed fat vacuoles in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes.
a- Fatty change of the liver
b- Cloudy swelling of the liver
c- Liver amyloidosis.
d- Coagulative necrosis of hepatocytes.

contusions. On routine barest examination the doctor noticed a tumour

b- Enzymatic fat necrosis.
c- Metastatic calcification.
d- Traumatic fat necrosis.
e- Liqufactive necrosis

after one month the infected area become black swollen & foul odor.
a- Wet gangrene
b- Dry gangrene
c- Dry gangrene on top of wet gangrene
d- Wet gangrene on top of dry gangrene

mother noticed gradual bronze colorization of skin resulting from pigment deposition
what is the type of pigment?
a- Bilirubin
b- Lipofucine
c- Melanin
d- Hemosiderin

after ingestion of a Mango

text:
IA- Drugs decreasing intraocular pressure & can be used in treatment of glaucoma:
1. Direct cholinergic agonists (pilocarpine) & cholinesterase inhibitors by increasing
drainage (outflow) of aquous humor.
2. Alpha 2 agonists (Brimonidine) by decreasing formation of aquous humor
3. Beta blockers ( timolol) by decreasing formation of aquous humor
B- Drugs increasing intraocular pressure: parasympathetic antagonists (e.g.
tropicamide).
IIA- Drugs causing bronchospasm:
1- Non-selective beta blockers
2- Direct cholinergic agonists (pilocarpine) & cholinesterase inhibitors
B- Drugs causing bronchodilation:
1- Beta 2 agonists (Salbutamol)
2- Parasympathetic antagonists
IIIA- Drugs causing dilatation of pupil (mydriasis)
1. Active mydriatics: Alpha 1 adrenergic agonists ( e.g. phenylephrine): due to contraction
of iris dilator muscle ; light reflex is present
2. Passive mydriatics (parasympathetic antagonists e.g. tropicamide): due to paralysis of
constrictor pupillae muscle ; Light reflex is absent
B- Drugs causing meiosis (constriction of eye pupil): Direct cholinergic agonists
(pilocarpine) & cholinesterase inhibitors
IVA- Drugs contraindicated in Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Parasympathetic
antagonists ( Contraction of sphincter)
B- Drugs used in treatment of Benign prostatic hyperplasia: Selective Alpha 1
blockers (tamsulosin)
VA- Drugs causing dry mouth: Parasympathetic antagonists
B- Drugs causing increased salivation ( used in treatment of dry mouth): Direct
cholinergic agonists (pilocarpine) & cholinesterase inhibitors.
VIA- Drugs causing urine retention : Parasympathetic antagonists
B- Drugs causing increased micturition: Direct cholinergic agonists (pilocarpine) &
cholinesterase inhibitors.
VII-

A- Drugs increasing skeletal muscle strength (used in treatment of myasthenia gravis
& reverse action of competitive neuromuscular blockers): cholinesterase inhibitors
(neostigmine)

 B- Drugs causing skeletal muscle weakness & paralysis: irreversible cholinesterase
inhibitors (organophosphorous poisoning).
C- Drugs causing skeletal muscle tremors: adrenaline (stimulation of beta 2)
VIII- A-Drugs used in treatment of hypertension:
1- Selective Alpha 1 blockers (Prazosin)
2- Beta blockers
3- Alpha 2 agonists (agonist on central alpha 2 receptors): methyldopa
4- Fenoldepam ( emergency hypertension and given intravenous).
B- Drugs used in treatment of shock (severe hypotension with decreased blood flow
to vital organs):
1- adrenaline ( used in anaphylactic shock),
2- noradrenaline( used in acute hypotension; postoperative),
3- dopamine ( used in some types of shock and has an advantage of increasing renal
blood flow.
C-Drugs causing hypertension as a side effect : Oral adrenergic nasal decongestants
e.g. pseudoephedrine.
IX-

A- Drugs used in treatment of heart failure: Beta blockers
B- Drugs causing heart failure: combination of calcium channel blockers with beta
blockers

X-

Beta blockers effect on blood sugar: interfere with recovery from hypoglycemia
because of blocking of beta 2 receptor-induced glycogenolysis & mask symptoms of
hypoglycemia( mask tachycardia).
A- Therapeutic uses that need lipophilic beta blockers e.g. propranolol (beta blockers
that reach CNS): prophylaxis of migraine.
B- Lipophilic beta blockers also decrease central sympathetic nervous system
activity.

XI-

X- Diseases in CNS:
A- Alzheimer’s : treatment by drugs increasing acetylcholine in the brain ( cholinesterase
inhibitor rivastigmine)
B- Parkinsonism: treatment by drugs antagonizing acetylcholine in brain: benztropine
C- Prophylaxis against migraine: lipophilic beta blockers.
AZZA BARAKA
PROFESSOR OF CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY

text:
Pharmacology of ANS, Analgesia, Antihistamines,
Diuretics, Iron, and Dyslipidemia
1. ANS Pharmacology
1.1 Important Mechanisms
Cholinergic Agonists
Direct agonists stimulate cholinoceptors (e.g., pilocarpine).
Indirect agonists (anticholinesterases) inhibit cholinesterase → ↑ ACh (e.g., neostigmine,
donepezil).
Reversible anticholinesterases form temporary enzyme binding (e.g., edrophonium).
Irreversible anticholinesterases bind irreversibly (e.g., organophosphates).

Cholinergic Antagonists (Antimuscarinics)
Compete with ACh at muscarinic receptors (e.g., atropine, scopolamine).
↓ Parasympathetic tone → mydriasis, dry mouth, urinary retention, bronchodilation.

Neuromuscular Blockers (NMBs)
Non-depolarizing (e.g., pancuronium): Compete with ACh at NMJ → flaccid paralysis.
Depolarizing (succinylcholine): Persistent depolarization → paralysis.

Spasmolytics
Central: Enhance GABA (e.g., baclofen, diazepam, tizanidine).
Peripheral: Block Ca²⁺ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum (e.g., dantrolene).

Adrenergic Agonists
Direct: Bind receptors (e.g., epinephrine).
Indirect: Release NE or block reuptake (e.g., amphetamine, cocaine).
Mixed: Both (e.g., pseudoephedrine, dopamine).
Selectivity: α1 (phenylephrine), α2 (methyldopa), β1 (dobutamine), β2 (salbutamol).

Adrenergic Antagonists

 α-blockers: Prazosin (α1), phenoxybenzamine (non-selective).
β-blockers: Atenolol (β1), propranolol (non-selective), carvedilol (α & β blocker).
Ergotamine: Used to treat acute attacks of migraine, but causes peripheral ischemia and
ischemic abortion (vasopressor action)

1.2 Important Pharmaceutical Uses
Cholinergic Agonists
Neostigmine: Post-op ileus, urinary retention, myasthenia gravis.
Pilocarpine: Dry mouth.
Edrophonium: Diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.
Donepezil/Rivastigmine: Alzheimer’s.

Cholinergic Antagonists
Atropine: Pre-anesthesia, bradycardia, organophosphate poisoning.
Scopolamine: Motion sickness (transdermal patch).
Benztropine: Parkinson’s.
Tropicamide/cyclopentolate: Eye exams.
Oxybutynin: Overactive bladder, post-surgical spasms.

Neuromuscular Blockers
Surgery (muscle relaxation).
Succinylcholine: Rapid intubation, ECT.

Spasmolytics
Baclofen: Spasticity in MS, CP, spinal injury.
Dantrolene: Malignant hyperthermia.
Botulinum toxin: Focal spasms, cosmetic use.

Adrenergic Agonists
Phenylephrine: Nasal congestion, hypotension.
Methyldopa: Hypertension in pregnancy.
Dobutamine: Heart failure, cardiogenic shock.
Salbutamol: Asthma, COPD.

 Ritodrine: Premature labor (tocolysis).
Epinephrine: Anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest.
Norepinephrine: Septic shock.
Dopamine: Shock (renal/cardiac doses).
Pseudoephedrine: Nasal/sinus congestion.
Amphetamines: ADHD, narcolepsy.

Adrenergic Antagonists
Prazosin: BPH, resistant hypertension.
Tamsulosin: BPH, ureteric stones.
Propranolol: Hypertension, migraine, anxiety, thyrotoxicosis.
Metoprolol/Atenolol: Hypertension, angina, heart failure.
Timolol: Glaucoma (topical).
Carvedilol: Chronic heart failure (with antioxidant & vasodilator effect).

1.3 Important Adverse Effects
Cholinergic Agonists
Muscarinic excess: Salivation, sweating, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia.
CNS effects (with anticholinesterases): Confusion, seizures, coma.
Nicotinic effects: Fasciculations, muscle weakness → flaccid paralysis.
Organophosphate toxicity: Requires atropine + oximes + supportive care.

Cholinergic Antagonists
Dry mouth, mydriasis, blurred vision, ↑ IOP (glaucoma risk).
Atropine fever: Especially in children.
Hallucinations/coma (scopolamine in high dose).
Contraindications: Glaucoma, BPH.

Neuromuscular Blockers
Pancuronium: Tachycardia.
Succinylcholine:
Malignant hyperthermia (Tx: IV dantrolene).
Succinylcholine apnea: In patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency.

 Hyperkalemia: Especially in trauma/burns.

Spasmolytics
Sedation (common in all).
Baclofen: Seizure risk in epilepsy.
Dantrolene: Muscle weakness (dose-dependent).

Adrenergic Agonists
α-agonists: Hypertension, headache, nasal dryness, rebound co

text:
OPIOID ANALGESICS
Dr./Gehad Salama
Lecturer of clinical pharmacology
Faculty of medicine
University of Alexandria
2024-2025

 Opioids
Opium
• Opium is derived from the dried milky juice exuded by incised seed
capsules of a species of poppy, Papaver somniferum.
• Opium is a complex mixture of alkaloids, the principal components
being morphine, codeine, and papaverine.
• The main analgesic action of opium is due to morphine.

 Opioids
• Several endogenous peptides with analgesic properties are widely distributed
throughout the nervous system.
• They can be divided into encephalins, dynorphins and, endorphins. These peptides
act as neurotransmitters or neuromodulators.
• They act on three types of opioid receptors, named u (mu), 6 (delta), and k (Kappa).
All belong to the G-protein coupled receptor family, and u is the most important.
• Opioid receptors are distributed within the CNS as well as throughout the peripheral
tissues.

 Opioids
• Mu (4) receptors are responsible for supraspinal analgesia, respiratory depression,
euphoria, sedation, decreased gastrointestinal motility, and physical dependence.
• Delta (8) receptors may be responsible for psychomimetic and dysphoric effects.
• Kappa (k) receptors are responsible for spinal analgesia, sedation, dyspnea, dependence,
dysphoria, and respiratory depression.

text:
Drugs for treatment of
dislipidemia

Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine-Alexandria University

 Overview
Most of the cholesterol in plasma is transported on 3 major lipoprotein
classes: VLDL cholesterol (VLDL-C), LDL cholesterol (LDL-C), and
HDL cholesterol (HDL-C).
Total cholesterol is the sum of all the cholesterol carried by these 3
lipoproteins.
Both VLDL-C and LDL-C are associated with atherogenic processes,
whereas HDL-C prevents atherogenesis.

  Overview
The atherogenic apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins, LDL and β-VLDL
(remnants of VLDL), can activate a dysfunctional vascular endothelium.
When the apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins enter the vessel wall,
they can be oxidized and taken up by macrophages which can be transformed
into foam cells, which secrete growth factors that stimulate the proliferation
and migration of smooth-muscle cells, resulting in the formation of an
atherosclerotic lesion.
Conversely, HDL appear to have an antiatherogenic effect; first, HDL can
remove cholesterol from the macrophage for transport back to the liver;
secondly, HDL may retard the oxidation of LDL.

whereas HDL-C prevents atherogenesis.

 Overview
The atherogenic apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins, LDL and β-VLDL
(remnants of VLDL), can activate a dysfunctional vascular endothelium.
When the apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins enter the vessel wall,
they can be oxidized and taken up by macrophages which can be transformed
into foam cells, which secrete growth factors that stimulate the proliferation
and migration of smooth-muscle cells, resulting in the formation of an
atherosclerotic lesion.
Conversely, HDL appear to have an antiatherogenic effect; first, HDL can
remove cholesterol from the macrophage for transport back to the liver;
secondly, HDL may retard the oxidation of LDL.

(Part 2)

Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine-Alexandria University

 Cholesterol Absorption Inhibitors: Ezetimibe

Pharmacokinetics:
• Ezetimibe is rapidly metabolized to an active
glucuronide metabolite.
• Both the drug and its metabolite have antidyslipidemic effects which permits once-daily
dosing.

 Mechanism of action of ezetemibe

It inhibits selective cholesterol transporter at enterocyte brush
border leading to inhibition of dietary and biliary cholesterol
absorption.
This will reduce the pool of cholesterol available in the liver,
which will trigger up-regulation of LDL receptor, to trap more
LDL particles from the circulation.

 Clinical Indications of ezetemibe
Adding ezetimibe to ongoing statin therapy leads
to additional reduction in LDL-C levels,
facilitating attainment of goals.

Ezetemibe is used as monotherapy in patients
with contraindication to statins.

text:
Drugs for treatment of
dislipidemia

Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine-Alexandria University

 Overview
Most of the cholesterol in plasma is transported on 3 major lipoprotein
classes: VLDL cholesterol (VLDL-C), LDL cholesterol (LDL-C), and
HDL cholesterol (HDL-C).
Total cholesterol is the sum of all the cholesterol carried by these 3
lipoproteins.
Both VLDL-C and LDL-C are associated with atherogenic processes,
whereas HDL-C prevents atherogenesis.

  Overview
The atherogenic apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins, LDL and β-VLDL
(remnants of VLDL), can activate a dysfunctional vascular endothelium.
When the apolipoprotein-B–containing lipoproteins enter the vessel wall,
they can be oxidized and taken up by macrophages which can be transformed
into foam cells, which secrete growth factors that stimulate the proliferation
and migration of smooth-muscle cells, resulting in the formation of an
atherosclerotic lesion.
Conversely, HDL appear to have an antiatherogenic effect; first, HDL can
remove cholesterol from the macrophage for transport back to the liver;
secondly, HDL may retard the oxidation of LDL.

text:
Drugs for treatment of dyslipidemia
(Part 2)

Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine-Alexandria University

 Cholesterol Absorption Inhibitors: Ezetimibe

Pharmacokinetics:
• Ezetimibe is rapidly metabolized to an active
glucuronide metabolite.
• Both the drug and its metabolite have antidyslipidemic effects which permits once-daily
dosing.

 Mechanism of action of ezetemibe

It inhibits selective cholesterol transporter at enterocyte brush
border leading to inhibition of dietary and biliary cholesterol
absorption.
This will reduce the pool of cholesterol available in the liver,
which will trigger up-regulation of LDL receptor, to trap more
LDL particles from the circulation.

 Clinical Indications of ezetemibe
Adding ezetimibe to ongoing statin therapy leads
to additional reduction in LDL-C levels,
facilitating attainment of goals.

Ezetemibe is used as monotherapy in patients
with contraindication to statins.

 General Pharmacology
-Pharmacology cames from the greek wards:
…Pharmacon = drug or medicine

-Pharmacology is the science that deals with the study of drugs and their interaction
with living systems.

-Drugs:
...any substances {other than Food & Water} that affect living cell , tissue , organ or
organisms and used in diagnosis , prevention and treatment of diseases.

*Aim of study pharmacology:
...Pathology "abnormal" = Disease ---------→Physiology "Normal"
-Ex: Hypertensive patient --------------------→ Normotensive.
...by drugs "pharmacology"

*Subdivisions of Pharmacology: "Aspects covered by pharmacology"
1-Pharmacokinetics.
2-Pharmacodynamics.
3-Pharmacotherapeutics.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 2

 1-Pharmacokinetics.
…is the study of Absorption , Distribution , Metabolism ''biotransformation'' and
Excretion of drugs = study of ADME
= The study of what the body does to the drugs. ‫هو الجسم بيعمل ايه ف الدواء‬
= The effect of the body on the drug.
= change in drug after it's administration

2-Pharmacodynamics:
…is the study of physiological effects of drugs and their mechanism of action.
= The study of what drugs do to the body. ‫هو الدواء بيعمل ايه ف الجسم‬
= The effect of the drug on the body
= start when drug interact with target.

3-Pharmacotherapeutics:
...is the study of clinical uses of drugs and drug selection in different medical
problems.
...how to choose a certain drug for treatment of a certain disease in a certain patien.
= combination of pharmacokinetic + Pharmacodynamic.

-Ex: Asthmatic Patient with hypertension.

-N.B:
-Pharmacogenetics = .................................................................................................

 Pharmacodynamics
*Def:
…is the study of physiological & biochemical effects of drugs and their mechanism of
action. = The study of what drugs do to the body.

-To initiate an effect the drug need Target:
a-Protein in nature

b-Present on cell surface or within cell.

joint in gout"

Page 20

 II-Pharmacokinetics
…is the study of Absorption , Distribution , Metabolism ''biotransformation'' and
Excretion of drugs = study of ADME
= The study of what the body does to the drugs.

-Oral Drug → Absorption → Blood → distribution → Target organ "receptor /
enzyme / Carrier" → Liver "metabolism" → Kidney "excretion".

-IV drug → Blood "no absorption"

1-Absorption
*Def:
…Transferring of the drug from site of administration to systemic circulation ''blood''.
N.B:
-Oral drugs must pass through several barriers:
…Wall of GIT → Wall of cappiliers supplying GIT → Wall of cappiliers supplying
the target organ.

*Passage of drugs across cell membrane ''cell barriers'':
-Cell membrane consists of:
...two lipid layers (phospholipid bilayer) attached on both sides to protein layer.
-Cell membrane is highly permeable to lipid soluble substances.
-Cell membrane contains pores or channels whish allow passage of water & small
sized water soluble drugs.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 21

 *Types of movements ''passage of drugs across cell membrane :
I-Passive diffusion: "main mechanism"
1-Along concentration gradient → from high Concentration to low concentration.
2-No need for energy or carrier
-Types of Passive diffusion:
a-Lipid diffusion:
→ via Continous , fenestrated , discontinuous capillaries "sinusoids ".
b-Aqueous diffusion "pores or fenestra":
→ via fenestrated & discontinous.

II-Active transport:
...transport against concentration gradient + Need energy & carrier.
-Ex: L-dopa "parkinsonism".

III-Facilitated diffusion:
...diffusion along concentration gradient + carrier + no energy.
-Ex: passage of Glucose via BBB

IV-Pinocytosis:
...invagination of cell membrane + engulfment of large Molecular weight molecules as
VitB12 , IF , VIT KEDA.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 22

 *Factors affecting passage of drugs across cell membrane 'Absorption':

A-Drug Factors:
1-Lipid solubility & Polarity: "lipid water partition coefficient"
...more lipid soluble = non polar = Lipophylic / Hydrophobic → more easy to pass.
...↑ Polarity of the drug "Polar = Hydrophylic'' → less pass.
2-Molecular weight & Size: Smaller molecular size → more easy to pass.
3-Concentration Gradient: ↑ concentration gradient → ↑ absorption.

4-Degree of ionization:
-Most of drugs are weak electrolytes present as ionized & unionized forms.
-Unionized form of the drug is lipid soluble:
...more unionization → more easy to pass → more absorption.
...more ionization → less easy to pass.

B-Host Factors: "GIT factors"
1-Ph of the medium: "Stomach is acidic"
a-Protein drugs → denaturation & destruction.
-Ex: Penicillin G → unstable in gastric acidity → given as enteric coated tablets.
2-Food:
...may interfefere with some drug absorption.
-Ex: Food contain Ca as milk + Tetracycline = insoluble complex.
3-GIT Motility: "Peristalsis":
... ↑ motility "in diarrhea" → decrease contact time between the drug and absorbing
surface → ↓ absorption.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 23

-May necessitate withdrawal of drug.

*Pharmacopeia:

-Drugs are listed & categorized in an official publication called Pharmacopeia.

Pharmacology

Page 38

 ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS
-Def:
...Adverse drug reaction (ADR) is an unwanted undesirable effect of a medication
that occurs during or after usual clinical use.

-CLASSIFICATION OF ADRs

*Type A (Augmented) :
-Exaggerated + Predictable pharmacological response due to High dose of the drug
{Dose Related}
-Common & Related to the pharmacologic action of the drug
-Low mortality
-Examples : bleeding from the anticoagulant warfarin , Bradycardia , Hypotension.
-Management : Reduce Dose or withhold drug according to the severity Consider the
effects of concomitant drug therapy.

*Type B (Bizarre) :
- Abnormal , Unpredictable , Non-Dose Related
- Uncommon & Not related to the pharmacologic action of the drug
- High mortality
- Examples:

 Skeletal Muscle Relaxants
-Mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction:
...Ach → +Nm in NMJ {MEP} → open Na channels → Na influx → depolarization
→ Muscle contraction.

*Difference between:
1-Skeletal muscle spasm "Strain" → due to acute injury to muscle or tendon
"Peripheral" → spasm + pain.
2-Spasticity:
-Def: ↑ basal muscle tone + ↑ Stretch reflex → stiffness or tightness of the muscle → affect
normal movement, speech , gait → due to spinal injury / Stroke / Cerebral palsy "Central".
*Skeletal Muscle Relaxants:
a-Peripherally acting {at NMJ OR inside the muscle}: Neuromuscular blockers
b-Centrally acting {↓muscle tone}.
*Classification according the use:
I-Spasmolytic agents

II-Neuromuscular blockers

I-Spasmolytic drugs:
…drugs reduce abnormal elevated muscle tone due to pathological condition.
-Classification:

1-Drugs for treating Acute muscle spasm: Local spasm

-Ex: Cyclobenzaprine
-MOA: → inhibit spinal reflexes → relax muscles.
-Use:
1-Relieve signs & symptoms of acute local muscle spasm & strain.
2-Adjunctive treatment with physiotherapy in muscle spasm in musculoskeletal disorders.
-Many are combined with non-opioid analgesics

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 2

 2-Drugs for treating Chronic spasticity: Central cause
-Cause of chronic spasticity:
…Neurological disorder as multiple sclerosis , stroke , cerebral palsy , spinal injury.
-Treatment:
a-Centrally acting spasmolytic drugs:
1-Benzodiazepines "diazepam" → enhance binding of GABA to GABAA receptors → Open
Cl- channe l → Cl influx → hyperpolarization → post synaptic inhibition → CNS inhibition.
2-Baclofen "oral " → agonist on GABAB receptors → ↓Ca influx in granules
→ cause presynaptic inhibition → ↓↓ release of excitatory neurotransmitters in brain &
spinal cord.
-SE: may ↑ seizure in patient with epilepsy.
3-Tizanidine: central α2 receptor agonist → presynaptic inhibition of motor neurons
→ ↓↓ release of excitatory neurotransmitters
4-Gabapentin: bind to α2-delta subunit of Ca channels in CNS →↓↓ Ca influx in neurons
→ ↓↓ release of excitatory neurotransmitters in as glutamate, substance P , NE → Analgesic
+ anticonvulsant action.

b-Peripheral acting spasmolytic drugs:
1-Dantrolene sodium: "must be oral // but IV in malignant hyperthermia"
-Act directly on skeletal muscle → block Ryanodine Ca++ channels "RyR" in sarcoplasmic
reticulum → prevent Ca++ release from SR → relax muscle.
-SE: dose dependent Muscle weakness.

2-Botulinum toxin:
-MOA: inhibit synaptic proteins responsible for release of Ach from cholinergic vesicles
→ prevent Ach release → flaccid paralysis.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 3

 -Uses:

…local motor nerve blocker → injected local → effect last for 3-4 months.
a-Focal muscle spasm & spasticity as writer's syndrome
b-Decrease facial Wrinkles "local injection in affected muscle" {cosmetically}

-Side effect of antispaticity drugs: …Sedation: major SE "CI in driver or operating machinery"

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------II-Neuromuscular blockers: "Peripheral Muscle Relaxant → act on NMJ''
...block cholinergic transmission between somatic nerve ending & Nm receptors → muscle
paralysis required for surgical procedures.

*Classification:
1-Competitive NM Blockers: "non-depolarizing NMB"
-Ex: 1-d-Tubocurarine ''DTC = curare {hunt animals}
2-Pancuronium , Vecuronium , Rocuronium.
3-Mivacurium , Cisatracurium
-MOA
…Compete with Ach for NM-receptor of skeletal ms at NMJ {MEP}
→ block action of Ach "can't open Na channels" = transmission failure → prevent
depolarization → no ms contraction → muscle relaxation or paralysis ''Flaccid paralysis''

2-Depolarizing NM Blockers:
-Ex: Succinylcholine ''Suxamethonium'': only depolarizing agent in clinical use.
-MOA:
-Succinylcholine has {Biphasic}:
a-Initially: Succinylcholine bind to and activate Nm rec as Ach → Depola

ADVANTAGES DISADVANTAGES Oral administration is unsuitable in an emergency because of the delayed onset of action. It is not suitable for comatose patients. Some drugs may cause gastric irritation (e.g., aspirin). It is not applicable for drugs destroyed by gastric acidity (e.g., penicillin G) or gastric enzymes (e.g., insulin and oxytocin). It is not used for drugs with extensive first-pass effects (e.g., testosterone). It is not suitable for drugs with very poor absorption (e.g., gentamycin). The absorption of some drugs may be affected, delayed, or enhanced by the presence or absence of food in the stomach and whether they are given before or after meals. For example, most antibiotics are better given on an empty stomach to prevent interference with their absorption by food. Sometimes tablets are taken without or with a small quantity of water, and while the patient is in the supine position, they may lodge in the oesophagus, and its absorption is delayed, and even may cause ulceration, especially in the elderly (e.g., sustained release KCl). Essential investigations for such a case. Iron preparations, routes of administration, dose calculation. BACKGROUND The objective of therapy in iron deficiency anemia, is to normalize hemoglobin levels and replenish iron stores with correction of the underlying cause. Iron Supplementation (Iron replacement therapy) is available as oral or parenteral supplements. ORAL IRON THERAPY ORAL IRON THERAPY 1. Ferrous iron formulations 2.Ferric iron formulations 3. Modified-release iron formulations 1. Ferrous iron formulations =65mg =35mg =60mg 2.Ferric iron formulations Such as ferric maltol , Iron bioavailability from ferric iron preparations, is lower than that of ferrous sulfate. 3. Modified-release iron formulations They decrease gastrointestinal upsets and reduce the dosing schedule. However, most of the iron is released beyond the duodenum where iron absorption and hematologic responses are poor. They should not be used for initial treatment. Treatment regimen prerequisites Dose Duration Monitoring Daily Oral dose for treatment of iron deficiency in adults: As an example, a single 325 mg ferrous fumarate (65 mg elemental iron) tablet taken orally three times daily between meals provides an oral dose of 195 mg of elemental iron per day. 100 -200 mg/day of elemental iron A D uration of treatment Treatment should be continued for 3-6 months after correction of anemia for replenishment of iron stores. B Monitoring Monitoring the therapeutic response to iron supplementation is required. For oral iron, the adequate response is evaluated by the reticulocytotic , which starts on the fourth day and lasts for 12 days, A s well as by the progressive rise in hemoglobin level of about 0.15 gm/dl/day, usually starting one week after the initiation of therapy. C PARENTRAL IRON FORMULATIONS When would parenteral iron therapy be indicated? In case of : 1) Failure to respond to oral iron therapy: malabsorption (e.g. GIT disease), 2) Continuing blood loss 3) Intolerance to oral therapy PARENTRAL IRON FORMULATION S Iron sorbitol citrate complex. Reactive thrombocytosis happens with anemia The exact pathway of how IDA can lead to thrombocytosis is not fully mapped, but research studies suggest the following:⁶ The mother cells of platelets are called megakaryocytes, and the mother cells of red blood cells are called erythroid. N M This slide to discuss with them neuromuscular transmission Drugs affecting neuromuscular transmission Cholinesterase inhibitors Neuromuscular blockers We can ask them about any other competitive blocker they should know the other names that are mentioned in their book (Competitive NMBs include pancuronium, rocuronium, vecuronium, and cisatracurium.) Mechanism of action of competitive NMBs and reversal of their action Specific agents include pancuronium, rocuronium, vecuronium, and cisatracurium. They are competitive antagonists at nicotinic receptors, i.e. they compete with acetylcholine for the NM receptors at the MEP and thus decrease the ability of acetylcholine to open the ligand-gated channels in skeletal muscle, producing a transmission failure and flaccid paralysis. This blockade can be reversed by increasing the concentration of acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) by cholinesterase inhibitors, such as neostigmine. Mechanism of action of non-competitive NMB Reversal of its action? Breakdown of succinylcholine by pseudo choline esterase enzyme is needed for the reversal of the action invivo It is the only depolarizing agent currently in clinical use. Initially, Succinylcholine binds to and activates NM receptors in the same manner as acetylcholine. It produces initial stimulation (depolarization) of NM receptors manifested as muscle fasciculations. However, succinylcholine is not metabolized by the acetylcholinesterase enzyme, resulting in receptor occupation for a relatively prolonged period leading to persistent depolarization, and muscle paralysis. The duration of action of succinylcholine is extremely short and depends on diffusion from the MEP and hydrolysis by plasma cholinesterase. text: PRESCRIPTION WRITING Clinical Pharmacology Department By the end of this session, you will be able to : Distinguish OTC from prescription medications. Write prescriptions according to the guidelines for prescription writing and local practice. Differentiate between simple prescription and prescription for controlled drugs. ILO s What is a prescription? A prescription is an instruction from a prescriber to a dispenser to supply certain quantity of a specific substance(s) or drug(s) to a specific patient . Few drugs and most of nutritional supplements can be available to consumers without prescription. Such drugs are termed non-prescription drugs or Over the counter (OTC) drugs . OTC drugs/Prescription drugs/ Controlled drugs A drug can be approved to be an OTC if: Its benefits outweigh its risks. The potential for misuse and abuse is low. The consumer can use it for self-diagnosed conditions. It can be adequately labelled. Health practitioners are not needed for the safe and effective use of the product. With the exception of OTC products, all other medications are termed prescription drugs (Non-controlled drugs) , whose dispensing requires a prescription. Pharmacokinetics
• Pharmacokinetics refers to what the body does to a drug from the time of
administration and absorption, along its distribution, till its elimination.
• Thus, it involves Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion

DRUG ABSORPTION
Absorption is the transfer of a drug from the site of its drug administration to its
passage to the bloodstream.

❖ FACTORS AFFECTING DRUG ABSORPTION:
➢ Drug Factors:
 Size and Molecular weight

 Polarity
 Lipophilicity

Transport of drug
through Cell
membrane

1. Passive diffusion: Neither energy nor a carrier
2. Facilitated: Needs no energy but needs a carrier
3. Active transport: Energy-dependent and needs a specific transporter
4. Pinocytosis: Transfer of drugs with large sizes “Vit.”

1. Passive diffusion: “Neither energy nor a carrier”
• Most of the drugs pass the cell membrane by passive diffusion.
• The driving force is the concentration gradient of the drug across a
membrane, i.e., the drug moves from a region of higher concentration to
region with a lower concentration.
✓ Thus, a water-soluble drug penetrates the cell membrane through aqueous pores
✓ Whereas a lipid-soluble drug moves across membranes due to its solubility in
membrane lipid bilayers.
•

Therefore, lipophilic, non-polar, and small molecular weight drug in highconcentration passes easily through the cell membrane.

2. Facilitated Transport or Diffusion: “Needs no energy but needs a carrier”
•

It is a type of passive transport that allows substances to cross membranes
with special transporter proteins embedded in the cell membrane.

•

It is used to transport some drugs such as norepinephrine which cannot pass
through the lipid bilayer of cell membranes.

• Transfer of drugs through the blood-brain barrier (BBB) occurs mainly with
this process.
