text:
Karyotyping
By: Clinical Genetics Staff
Faculty of Medicine, Alexandria University

 ILOs:
• Realize the speciality of cytogenetics as part of medical genetics.
• Recognize the different steps involved in the methodology adopted in the
cytogenetic lab.
• Identify the practical steps involved in a karyotype preparation.
• Classify the chromosomes according to size and centromere position.
• Distinguish the various abnormalities met in a karyotype.
• Recognize the indications of karyotype analysis.
• Interpret normal and some clinical examples of abnormal karyotypes.
• Describe a karyotype using the symbols according to the International System
for Cytogenetic Nomenclature (ISCN)

 • Cytogenetics:
the branch of medicine that deals with study of the genetic makeup
of a cell (represented by chromosomes analysed during
metaphase of dividing cells examined by the light microscope.

 Chromosomal analysis Indications:
❖Premarital genetic counselling for couples before marriage
especially if there is a family history of repeated abortions or
abnormal livebirths.
❖History of repeated abortions or intrauterine foetal deaths.
❖Child born with multiple congenital malformations.
❖Unexplained mental retardation.

Definition: Bone disease characterized by
increased porosity of the skeleton due to
reduction in bone mass leading to increased bone
fragility and susceptibility to fractures.
Types:
1. Localized osteoporosis: e.g. disuse
osteoporosis in a limb
2. Generalized osteoporosis: primary or
secondary.

 A) Secondary Generalized
Osteoporosis
May be due to:
-Endocrine disorders: Hyperparathyroidism,
Cushing's syndrome.
-Neoplastic: Multiple myeloma, metastatic
carcinoma.
-Gastrointestinal: malnutrition, vit C and D
deficiencies.
-Rheumatologic disease: e.g. Rheumatoid
arthritis
-Drugs: e.g. corticosteroids and chemotherapy.

Diseases of URT
Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
Incidence:
- Endemic in some areas in Asia & Africa as Southern China.
- Sporadic in the rest of the world.

Risk factors: - Strong correlation with EBV "its genome in all cases".
- Age, hereditary & environmental.

Gross: Mass: ulcerating > or fungating.
Histological variants:
(1) Keratinizing Sq.C.C., least radiosensitive.
(2) Non-keratinizing Sq.C.C.
(3) Undifferentiated Sq.C.C.: commonest, most radiosensitive.

Spread: Occult carcinoma
Grow silently, at diagnosis  un-resectable + 70% metastasis in LN
1- Local invasion
2- Cervical LN “early” 3- Blood distant metastasis.

Prognosis: Radiosensitive, 3Y survival rate is 50-70 %

Laryngeal Mass
I- Non- Neoplastic:
Vocal cord nodules - polyps
Causes: chronic irritation or abuse of voice as in heavy smokers or singers, teachers
"Singer's nodule"

Incidence: mainly adults, ♂
Gross: Multiple, smooth, hemispheric, < 0.5cm diameter, sessile or pedunculated
on true vocal cords may ulcerate, usually bilateral.

Micro: ► Cover: st.sq.epi. The mucosa may ulcerate.
► Core: fibrous connective tissue.

Fate: Never turn to malignant.

II- Neoplastic Masses:
Papilloma of vocal cords
Def: Benign tumour.
Risk factors / Causes: Human papilloma virus (HPV 6 & 11)
Incidence:
* Single in adults.
* Multiple in children "juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis"  regress at puberty.
-1-

 Dr. Hassan Abdelrahman Soliman

Gross: - On true vocal cords
- Soft, raspberry like, >1cm diameter.

Microscopic: Multiple slender fingers like projection
► Cover: stratified squamous epithelium.
► Core: central fibro-vascular.

Fate: * No malignant transformation.
* Tend to recur in children.

Carcinoma of the larynx
Incidence:

* 2% of all cancers.
* ♂: ♀ 7: 1
* > 40 Ys.

Risk factors: 1- Smoking "proportionate to level of exposure".
2- Alcohol.
3- Others: asbestos, irradiation, nutritional factors & HPV in 5%.

* In aryepiglottic folds
* In pyriform sinuses “occult”.

C/P: 1- Hoarseness of voice.
2- Pain, dysphagia, haemoptysis or dyspnea.
3- Infection (2ry).

Prognosis: depends on the stage of tumor.
♠ with surgical removal or radiotherapy or combination the patient may cure.
33% death dt distal respiratory infections or metastasis or cachexia.

Osteoporosis
Def: increased porosity of the skeleton dt decreased the total bone mass,
of normally mineralized bone.
♣ Associated with structural changes leading to ↑ bone fragility
& susceptibility to fractures.

Types:
I- Localized e.g. disused limb.
II- Generalized: affecting all skeleton "primary - secondary".

1- Secondary Generalized Osteoporosis
- Endocrinal: Hyperparathyroidism, cushing's syndrome.
- Neoplastic: Multiple myloma, metastatic carcinoma.
- Nutritional: ↓ vitamins C, D, protein malnutrition.
- Gastro-intestinal: mal-absorption.
- Drugs: Anti coagulants, chemotherapy, corticosteroid, ………….
- Rheumatologic diseases: Rheumatoid arthritis.

2- Primary Generalized Osteoporosis
"Commonest"

Types:
 Senile  old people of both sexes.
 Post menopausal ♀.

Pathogenesis:
BONE is a dynamic tissue with continuous remodeling cycles
characterized by alternative periods of bone resorption & new bone formation.
So, any imbalance ↑↑ bone loss &/or ↓↓ bone formation
 Decrease in total bone mass & density = Osteoprosis.

Factor affecting total bone mass:
Personal factors (Age & Genetic factors) OR
Constitutional external factors (Physical, diet, hormonal)
Age:
♦ 1st 2 decades: Bone formation > Bone resorption.
♦ After 3rd decade: Bone formation < Bone resorption.
The maximum bone density at 3rd decade (20-25Y)
then it decrease gradually with each remodeling cycle
by rate of about 0.7 % per year.
(Normal phenomenon)
-1-

 Dr. Hassan Abdelrahman Soliman

Physical activity:
↓  ↑ Bone loss  ↓ bone mass and density.
e.g. paralyzed limb.
↑  ↑ Bone formation  ↑ bone mass & density. e.g. Athletes.
dt mechanical forces  + bone formation & remodeling.

Diet:
Ca++ deficiency "at periods of active bone growth" ↓ maximum bone mass.

Hormones:
♦ ↓ Estrogen  + osteoclastic activity  ↑ bone resorption & ↓ formation
 imp role in post-menopausal osteoporosis.
♦ ↓ Androgens "testosterone"  role in 30% of senile osteoporosis in ♂.

Sites: whole skeleton is affected.
♠ Mostly weight bearing bones:
1- Vertebral bodies. (++ in post menopausal ♀)
2- Neck of femur.
3- Metacarpals.
♠ Then: distal radius, proximal humerus, proximal tibia.

Morphology:
 Cortex & Trabeculae  thin, attenuated + pores.
 Medullary cavity  widened.
 Normal bone composition (minerals to proteins matrix ratio).

C/P:
1- Asymptomatic till advanced skeletal fragility.
2- Bone pains especially back dt compression micro fractures of vertebrae
Especially thoracic & lumber vertebrae.
3- Loss of height.
4- Instability & deformity of spine  lordosis, kyphosis, kyphoscoliosis.
5- Fractures e.g. neck of femur, distal radius, wrist & vertebrae.

Diagnosis:
1- Measurement of bone density:
* Dual- photon absorptiometry.
* Dexa Scan.
2- X-ray: if loss of > 30-40 % of bone mass.
3- Quantitative CT scan.
4- Normal serum levels of Ca+, P, Alkaline phosphatase.
Q: Osteoporosis is difficult in diagnosis?
1- The disease is remain asymptomatic until advanced stages.
2- X-ray changes not detected until 30-40% of bone mass is lost.
3- Blood levels of ions are normal in uncomplicated cases.
-2-

CNS Infections
Routes of Infection:
1- Blood most common
2- Penetrating trauma.
3- Iatrogenic as in lumbar puncture.
4- Ascending through peripheral nerves: rabies, herpes simplex.
5- Adjacent infected structures: sinuses, middle ear & mastoid.

Meningitis - Leptomeningitis
Def: It is the inflammation of: Leptomeninges (PIA & arachnoid).
+ Sub-arachnoid space (C.S.F)

Types:
1- Acute pyogenic / purulent meningitis (bacterial)
2- Acute lymphocytic meningitis (viral)
3- Chronic meningitis (TB, fungal)

1- Acute Purulent Meningitis
* Important cause of death at all ages caused by bacteria.

Causative Organisms:
♦ Neisseria meningitidis: Most common cause of acute meningitis
* In adolescence & young adults.
* Organisms are oral commensal transmitted by air.
♦ E-coli in neonates.
♦ Haemophilus Influenzae in infants & children.
♦ Pneumococci in all age groups.

Morphology:
Gross:
● Meninges: edematous, congested, dull opaque & covered by purulent exudate.
● Brain sulci: filled with pus.
● Brain gyri: odematous  flattening.

Microscopic: Leptomeninges are congested and infiltrate with neutrophiles & fibrin.
♣ Infection of underlying parenchyma is rare.

Clinical Picture:
● General signs of infection & fever: = Septicemia
As Heamorrhagic peticheal rashes on skin & MM.
● Signs & symptoms of meningeal irritation:
Headache - Photophobia - Neck stiffness - Irritability & disturb consciousness.
● C.S.F examination:
• Turbid fluid under ↑↑ pressure
• ↑↑proteins level dt pus formation.
• Infectious agents + on the smear.

• ↑ cells mainly polymorphes.
• ↓ sugar content dt utilized by bacteria.
-1-

 Dr. Hassan Abdelrahman Soliman

2- Acute Lymphocytic Meningitis:
(Viral) (Aseptic) (Atypical)
Causative Organisms: Viruses as mumps, herpes simplex, EBV.
Clinical Picture:
* Less severe than pyogenic meningitis.
* Self limited (no fatal complications).
* C.S.F: • Clear fluid under ↑↑ pressure
• ↑ cells mainly lymphocytes
• Moderate ↑ proteins
• Normal glucose.

3- Chronic Meningitis:
Causative agents:
♦ Mycobacterium tuberculosis (mostly).

♦ Fungi (sometimes).

Morphology:
Grossly:
► Meninges: opaque, thickened.

In late cases  dense fibrous adhesions.

Microscopically:
► Exudates formed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, histiocytes & fibroblasts.
► Granulomas & caseation for (TB).

C.S.F. Examination:

• Moderate ↑ cells mainly lymphocytes.
• Moderate ↑ proteins.
• Moderate ↓ sugar.
• ↓↓ chloride (TB).

Complications of Meningitis:
I- Spread of infection:
1- Brian ventricles  ventriculitis.
2- Veins & sinuses  thrombo-phlebitis  vascular occlusion  brain infarct.
3- Sub and extra-dural spaces.
4- Blood:
♦ Septicemia of meningococcal meningitis  Waterhouse Friderichsen syndrome
* Extensive bleeding.
* Bilat adrenal hemorrhage.
* Hypercoagulability.
* Shock.
♦ Localize tissues infection  arthritis, endocarditis, pericarditis, ………..
II- Healing process:
a- Arachnoid fibrosis  hydrocephalus = impaired CSF drainage.
b- Cranial nerve compression  nerve palsy. E.g.: 3rd, 4th, 6th  squint.
c- Vessels obliteration  ischemia or brain infarct.

5.1.ANTICOAGULANTS
Anticoagulants inhibit thrombus formation or progression by
inhibiting production or action of coagulation factors.
Classification According to Mechanism of Action (Figure 5-1)
·Indirect Anticoagulants act by inhibiting coagulation factors via
binding to antithrombin III. Examples are unfractionated heparin
, low molecular weight (LMWH), and fondaparinux.
·Direct Anticoagulants act by directly binding and inhibiting
coagulation factors such as with
- Direct Thrombin Inhibitors such as bivalirudn, and dabigatran.
- Direct Factor Xa Inhibitors such as rivaroxaban.
·Vitamin K Antagonist (VKA) such as warfarin acts by
preventing hepatic synthesis of coagulation factors.
Classification According to the Route of administration
·Parenteral Anticoagulants such as unfractionated heparin, LMW
Hs, bivalirudin, and fondaparinux.

3

 Principles of Pharmacology for Medical Students. PART II

· Oral Anticoagulants such as warfarin, dabigatran, and rivaroxaban.
In acute insults, treatment is usually initiated by parenteral drugs (IV or
subcutaneous). Intramuscular administration is avoided for fear of
hematoma formation.
- On shifting to oral VKAs such as warfarin, the parenteral drug is with
drawn after 4-5 days of warfarin administration because of its latency
in action. However, on shifting to direct oral anticoagulants, the
parenteral drug can be immediately withdrawn.

General Therapeutic Uses of Anticoagulants
1. Prophylaxis and treatment of deep vein thrombosis and thrombosis
on prosthetic valves.
2. Prophylaxis and treatment of pulmonary embolism, peripheral
arterial embolism, and thromboembolic complications of atrial
fibrillation (AF).
3. Prophylaxis in medical and surgical procedures in patients at risk
of thromboembolic complications, such as in orthopedic or cardiac
surgery, intervention for myocardial infarction, during blood
transfusion, or dialysis.
5.1.1.Unfractionated Heparin (UFH)
Heparin is a glycosaminoglycan, naturally present in the body.
Pharmacokinetics
·Heparin is given parenterally, usually in hospital settings.
·It is highly bound to plasma protein, with a low bioavailability and
a variable anticoagulant response.
·It acts rapidly and for a short time, with a half-life of 90 minutes.

Concept II
Blood, CVS, Endocrine

 Nutshell - Pharmacology of Concept II

1. Blood
1.1 Pharmacology of Anticoagulants
Important Mechanisms
Indirect anticoagulants: Bind to antithrombin III (e.g. UFH, LMWH, fondaparinux).
Direct anticoagulants:
Thrombin inhibitors: bivalirudin, dabigatran.
Factor Xa inhibitors: rivaroxaban.
Vitamin K antagonists (VKA): Warfarin → Inhibits hepatic synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X.
UFH: Enhances antithrombin III, inhibits thrombin > Xa, XI, XII, XIII.
LMWH: Inhibits factor Xa more than thrombin (4:1 ratio).
Fondaparinux: Indirect Xa inhibitor via ATIII.
Rivaroxaban: Direct Xa inhibitor, oral.
Bivalirudin: Direct thrombin inhibitor, parenteral.
Dabigatran: Direct thrombin inhibitor, oral prodrug.
Warfarin: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → ↓ activation of clotting factors.

Important Actions and Therapeutic Uses
Prophylaxis/treatment of:
DVT, PE, AFib complications, thrombosis on prosthetic valves.
Thromboembolism in surgeries (e.g. orthopedic, cardiac).
Myocardial infarction intervention, dialysis.
LMWH: Can be used at home, long-term.
Fondaparinux: Once daily dosing.
Dabigatran & Bivalirudin: Alternative in HIT.
Bivalirudin: Used in cardiac intervention.
Warfarin: Long-term anticoagulation, overlap with UFH 4–5 days.
NOACs (e.g. rivaroxaban, dabigatran):
Rapid onset, predictable, no food interactions.
Can be initial treatment without bridging.

Important Adverse Effects
UFH:
Bleeding (minor: adjust dose; major: give protamine sulfate).
Re-thrombosis due to fibrin-bound thrombin.
HIT/HITT (immune-mediated).
Long-term: osteoporosis, cutaneous necrosis, hyperkalemia.
LMWH:
Less bleeding/HIT than UFH.
Fondaparinux: Safe in HIT.

2

 Rivaroxaban:
Bleeding (antidote: andexanet alfa).
CYP3A4 & P-glycoprotein interactions.
Dabigatran:
Bleeding (antidote: idarucizumab).
Warfarin:
Bleeding (treat with FFP or vitamin K).
Teratogenic (crosses placenta).
Rare skin necrosis.
Narrow therapeutic window.
Drug/food interactions:
↑ Bleeding: antibiotics, CYP inhibitors, aspirin.
↓ Efficacy: vitamin K foods, cholestyramine, CYP inducers, estrogens/contraceptives.

Important Contraindications
General: Active bleeding, bleeding disorders, recent surgery, hypersensitivity.
UFH: HIT/HITT history, severe HTN.
LMWH: Same as UFH. + Must be monitored with renal insufficiency and obese patients.
Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran: Avoid in pregnancy, severe renal impairment.
Warfarin: Pregnancy, bleeding disorders, drug interactions.

1.2 Pharmacology of Anti-platelets
Important Mechanisms
TXA2 inhibitors: Aspirin → Irreversible COX-1 inhibition in platelets.
ADP receptor antagonists:
Clopidogrel: Irreversible P2Y12 inhibitor, prodrug.
Ticagrelor: Reversible, active drug, also vasodilator.
GPIIb/IIIa receptor antagonists: Tirofiban → Final pathway blockade of platelet aggregation.
PAR-1 antagonists: Vorapaxar → Inhibits thrombin receptor on platelets.

Important Actions and Therapeutic Uses
Prophylaxis and treatment of:
ACS, TIA, stroke, peripheral vascular disease.
Post-PCI or coronary angioplasty.
Aspirin:
Chewable in acute events (onset: 5 min).
DAPT with ADP antagonists after stroke/ACS.
Clopidogrel: Loading dose in acute events, maintenance for 6–12 months.
Ticagrelor: Rapid action, used in ACS.
Tirofiban: IV during/after PCI.
Vorapaxar: Oral, used in MI and cardiac intervention.

 Important Adverse Effects
Bleeding (all).
Ticagrelor: Dyspnea (↓ compliance).
Aspirin: Peptic ulcers (↓ gastric PGs) — use enteric-coated form.
Tirofiban: Requires renal dose adjustment.

Important Contraindications
Active bleeding.
Severe bleeding risk conditions.
Drug-specific interactions:
Aspirin: NSAIDs like ibuprofen reduce efficacy.
Clopidogrel: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs), statins, CCBs ↓ activation.

1.3 Pharmacology of Fibrinolytics/Thrombolytics
Important Mechanisms
Convert plasminogen → plasmin → fibrin lysis.
Fibrin-specific (tPA): Alteplase → Targets fibrin-bound plasminogen.

text:
Overview
• Diabetes mellitus (DM) describes a group of chronic metabolic
disorders.
• DM is characterized by hyperglycemia which may result in long-term
microvascular complications such as retinopathy, neuropathy, and
nephropathy and macrovascular complications such as stroke, cardiac
diseases, and peripheral vascular diseases.
• Type 1 DM is usually diagnosed before age 30 years but can develop at
any age. It is associated with autoimmune destruction of the
pancreatic β-cells resulting in insulin deﬁciency.
• Type 2 DM accounts for approximately 90% to 95% of all diagnosed
cases of DM. A combination of insulin def ic iency, insulin resistance,
and other hormonal irregularities, are the key problems in type 2 DM.
Majority of people with type 2 DM are overweight, and an increasing

 Treatment goals in DM
• Reduce, control, and manage microvascular and macrovascular
complications.
• Preserve β-cells function.
• Prevent acute complications from high blood glucose levels and
minimize the risk of hypoglycemic episodes.
• Improve the patient’s health related quality of life.

 Treatment goals in DM
• To achieve most of these goals, near-normal blood glucose levels are
fundamental.
• Patients with type 1 diabetes are insulin-dependent and must be
treated with exogenous insulin.
• Patients with type 2 diabetes need lifestyle modif ic ation (weight
reduction, exercise, and dietary modif ications), which may be suf ifcient
for mild cases. Most patients also require oral or injectable antidiabetic
drugs. Initially, they are not insulin-dependent; however, insulin therapy
is often needed as the disease progresses.

text:
Pharmacology of drugs used
for heart failure

+

Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine
Alexandria University

 Overview
 Heart failure (HF) is the inability of the heart to pump enough blood to

maintain cardiac output (COP) to meet the metabolic demands of the
body.
 Chronic heart failure (CHF) is a clinical syndrome characterized by

specific signs and symptoms related to congestion and hypoperfusion.
 The term acute heart failure (AHF) is used to signify either an acute

decompensation of a patient with a history of chronic HF or to refer to a
patient presenting with new-onset HF symptoms.

 Compensatory neurohormonal
activation in chronic heart failure
The failing heart evokes compensatory mechanisms to enhance cardiac output (COP)
including:
• Increased sympathetic activity: Baroreceptors sense a decrease in blood pressure and
activate the sympathetic nervous system
• Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS): A fall in cardiac output
decreases blood flow to the kidney, prompting the release of renin, and resulting in
increased formation of angiotensin II and the release of aldosterone
Both mechanisms lead to increased preload (through sodium and water retention), increased
afterload through arterioconstriction, and ventricular hypertrophy and remodeling. Although
initially beneficial, these alterations ultimately result in further deterioration of cardiac
function.

 Pharmacotherapy of Chronic Heart Failure

Types of heart failure according to the left ventricular ejection
fraction (LVEF) of the patient:
• Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) (previously
diastolic dysfunction) due to restricted ventricular filling.
• Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) (previously
systolic dysfunction): due to decreased myocardial contractility.

Drugs
Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine
Alexandria University
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 Classification of Oral Anti-diabetic Agents
Several categories of oral anti-diabetic agents are now available for
treatment of patients with type 2 diabetes.
• Sulfonylureas
• Meglitinides
• Biguanides
• Thiazolidinediones
• Alpha-Glucosidase Inhibitors
• Incretin Enhancers: Glycopeptide-1 Receptor Agonists - Dipeptidyl
Peptidase 4 Inhibitors
• Sodium-glucose Co-Transporter 2 Inhibitors.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 I- Sulfonylureas
These agents are classified as insulin secretagogues, because
they promote insulin release
Ve from the beta cells of the
pancreas.
The sulfonylureas (SUs) mostly used in clinical practice are
the second-generation drugs; glibenclamide and glipizide,
and the 3rd generation drug glimepiride.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 Pharmacokinetics of sulfonylureas
All sulfonylureas are well absorbed from the intestine after oral intake. The rate of
absorption is reduced when taken with food. For this reason, sulfonylureas should be taken
30 min before meals to optimize their absorption. In circulation, sulfonylureas bind almost
completely to plasma proteins, especially albumin (average 95%).
The biological effect of sulfonylureas often lasts much longer than their plasma half-life,
because of the receptor interaction and formation of active metabolites. Due to their
prolonged effect, sulfonylureas are given once or twice daily. Their dosage should be
increased every 2 weeks if glycaemic control has not been reached.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

(Part 2)
Azza Baraka
Professor of Clinical Pharmacology
Faculty of Medicine
Alexandria University
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 IV-Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors
• They include acarbose.
• Pharmacokinetics: Acarbose is not absorbed systemically, and it is eliminated
in the feces.
• Mechanism of Action: Acarbose competitively inhibits alpha-glucosidase
enzyme and delays the conversion of starch and disaccharides to glucose and
other monosaccharides. This action decreases the rate of glucose absorption
and reduces postprandial hyperglycemia.
• Adverse Reactions: Malabsorption, flatulence, and diarrhea.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 V-THIAZOLIDINDIONES (GLITAZONES)
• They are insulin sensitizers.
• They are considered euglycemic, when used as monotherapy.
• The only available agent now is pioglitazone.
• Pharmacokinetics: -- It is well absorbed from the GIT. It is metabolized
through the hepatic cytochrome P450 system.
• Mechanism of Action: It improves insulin sensitivity at the level of the
peripheral tissues; muscles, adipose tissues, and liver through stimulation of a
nuclear receptor "Peroxisome Proliferator Activated Receptor gamma" (PPAR
gamma).
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 V-THIAZOLIDINDIONES (GLITAZONES)
Pharmacological Actions:
• It increases glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissues.
It also inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis and has effects on
distribution of body fat.
• It decreases triglycerides and increases HDL cholesterol.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

of Insulin
AZZA BARAKA
PROFESSOR OF CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY
FACULTY OF MEDICINE -ALEXANDRIA UNIVERSITY
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 Insulin and insulin analogs
Insulin is a polypeptide hormone secreted by the ß cells of the pancreas. It
consists of two peptide chains that are connected by disulfide bonds.
In type 1 diabetes mellitus, the ideal goal of insulin therapy is to mimic
the pattern of physiologic insulin secretion to control fasting and
postprandial blood glucose level. This was achieved by combining the
long-acting basal component that cover basal body needs and a shorteracting component to address disposition of nutrients after meals.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 Classification of Insulin Preparations
Once absorbed into the circulation, all insulins have the same mechanism of
action on target tissues. Therefore, the different time-action profiles of
various insulins result from differences in their behavior in the
subcutaneous space, which then affects the rate of absorption into the
circulation.
Human insulin used in therapy is manufactured by bacterial recombinant
DNA technology.
CS CamScanner

CamScanner

 Classification of Insulin Preparations
According to their onset and duration of action, insulin preparations are
classified into:
Short-Acting Insulin Preparations (Prandial insulins, bolus insulins).
Long-Acting Insulin Preparations (Basal insulins)

..Drugs that can inhibit thrombus formation and/or progression by decreasing platelet activation and

…of choice in prophylaxis and treatment of acute arterial thrombosis {rich in platelets}: as in case

-Acute coronary syndrome & stroke → Chewable aspirin is preferred ? → fast acting

→ inadequate secretion of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland.

-In adult: myxedema: fatigue / Wt gain

a-1ry hypothyroidism = primary gland failure.

1-Replace the missing hormones
2-Relieve signs and symptoms

…These goals are achieved by hormonal replacement therapy.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 2

 THYROID HORMONES (T4 & T3)
-Pharmacokinetics:
-Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) in the plasma are reversibly bound to
protein called thyroxine-binding globulin.
-Only about 0.04% of total T4 and 0.4% of T3 exist in the free form.
-Inactivation of the thyroid hormones occurs mainly in the liver.
-The half-life of T4 is 7 days → reach steady state after 6 weeks.
-The half-life of T3 is only one day.
-In patients with hyperthyroidism → the metabolic clearances of T4 and T3 are increased
and their half-lives decreased → the opposite is true in patients with hypothyroidism.

-Mechanism of Action:
-Free forms of thyroid hormones enter the target body cells by diffusion or by active
transport.

-

Within the cell, T4 is converted to T3 → T3 enters the nucleus → binds to a specific T3
receptor protein causing DNA-directed mRNA transcription and protein synthesis →
mediating a response.

.

-This explains the time lag of hours or days for the hormone to give maximal response
after administration {delayed action}.

-Thyroid Hormones Preparations:
1-LevoThyroxin = L-thyroxine (T4): Synthetic T4 is the preparation of choice for
thyroid replacement because of:
a- low cost + easy laboratory measurement of serum levels
b-once-daily administration due to long half-life.
c-T4 is converted to T3 intracellular: administration of T4 produces both hormones and T3
administration is unnecessary.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 3

 2-Liothyronine sodium (T3):
-It has a quicker onset of action + shorter duration.
-Although liothyronine (T3) is three to four times more potent than levothyroxine
→ it is not recommended for routine replacement therapy because of: Not 1st choice
a-The need for multiple daily doses due to shorter half-life.
b-Difficulty in monitoring its adequacy of replacement by laboratory tests.
c-Many patients have symptoms of thyrotoxicosis after each dose administrations.
d-It should also be avoided in patients with cardiac disease {cardiotoxic}.
3-Liotrix: a mix of T4 and T3 in the ratio of 4:1.

-Therapeutic Uses:
-L-Thyroxin is used as an oral replacement therapy in hypothyroidism as cretinism,
and myxedema coma {acute rapid drop in thyroxine} .
-Liothyronine may be given intravenously in emergency as in Myxoedema coma .

-Adverse Reactions:
…Thyroxine toxicity is directly related to the hormone level.
1-In children: restlessness, insomnia , accelerated bone maturation and growth.
2-In adults: nervousness, heat intolerance, episodes of tachycardia, unexplained
weight loss.
…To confirm that these symptoms are due to excess thyroxine blood levels → it is
important to monitor serum TSH and free T4 levels.

text:
Insulin delivery methods

Activity (1)
Search online about other methods for insulin delivery and
mention the advantages and disadvantages of each one
Answer:
Insulin Inhalers
Inhaled insulin (e.g., Afrezza) is a fast-acting insulin that is delivered through the lungs
via an inhaler.
Advantages:
• Fast-acting: Quick onset of action, ideal for managing postprandial (mealtime)
blood sugar levels.
• Non-invasive: No injections required, which can be less intimidating for people
who are afraid of needles.
• Convenience: Easy to use and discreet.
Disadvantages:
• Limited coverage: Primarily used for mealtime insulin, not suitable for longacting insulin needs.
• Potential lung issues: Not recommended for people with lung diseases (e.g.,
asthma, COPD) due to potential pulmonary side effects.
• Regulatory concerns: Not universally covered by insurance, and may be less
widely available.
Oral Insulin (Experimental)
Oral insulin is an emerging delivery method where insulin is taken by mouth in a pill
form (currently in experimental stages for some products).
Advantages:
• Convenient: No injections or devices needed, simply take a pill.
• Patient preference: For patients who are reluctant to inject insulin, this could be a
desirable option.
Disadvantages:
• Absorption issues: Insulin is a large molecule, and it is difficult for the body to
absorb it effectively through the digestive system.
• Still in development: Oral insulin products are not yet widely available or
approved for regular use in most countries.

 Activity (1)
Go online and search for food with a high and low glycaemic
index and instruct the patient about the condition in which each
one would be preferred
Answer:
The glycaemic index is a scale that ranks carbohydrate-containing foods based on how
quickly they raise blood glucose levels after consumption.
High GI foods cause a rapid spike in blood glucose.
Low GI foods lead to a gradual and steady rise in blood glucose.

Examples of High GI Foods
High GI foods include items like white bread, white rice, potatoes (especially baked),
cornflakes, watermelon, and sugary snacks such as candies and jaggery. These foods
are quickly digested and absorbed, which can rapidly increase blood sugar levels.

Examples of Low GI Foods
Low GI foods include barley, lentils, beans, oats (especially steel-cut), apples, oranges,
carrots, leafy vegetables like spinach, nuts like almonds, and plain yogurt. These are
absorbed more slowly and help in maintaining stable blood glucose levels.



High glycemic index to maintain blood glucose within normal without shouting in
insulin secretion.
High glycemic as juices are better during early attacks of hypoglycemia

 When to Prefer High GI Foods
High GI foods are beneficial in certain clinical situations, such as:


During hypoglycemia: For a patient with low blood sugar (below 70 mg/dL), high
GI foods provide a quick energy source to rapidly elevate glucose levels. For
example, a diabetic patient experiencing dizziness and sweating due to
hypoglycemia should consume glucose tablets or fruit juice.



Post-exercise recovery: After intense physical activity, consuming high GI foods
helps to rapidly replenish glycogen stores in muscles.

When to Prefer Low GI Foods
Low GI foods are ideal for:


Diabetic patients: These foods help maintain stable blood sugar levels
throughout the day, reducing the risk of both hyper- and hypoglycemia.



Weight management: Low GI foods promote satiety, reduce cravings, and help in
maintaining a healthy weight.
Heart health: Because they reduce insulin spikes and lower cholesterol levels.

• Fast-acting: Quick onset of action, ideal for managing postprandial (mealtime)
blood sugar levels.
• Non-invasive: No injections required, which can be less intimidating for people
who are afraid of needles.
• Convenience: Easy to use and discreet.
Disadvantages:
• Limited coverage: Primarily used for mealtime insulin, not suitable for longacting insulin needs.
• Potential lung issues: Not recommended for people with lung diseases (e.g.,
asthma, COPD) due to potential pulmonary side effects.
• Regulatory concerns: Not universally covered by insurance, and may be less
widely available.
Oral Insulin (Experimental)
Oral insulin is an emerging delivery method where insulin is taken by mouth in a pill
form (currently in experimental stages for some products).
Advantages:
• Convenient: No injections or devices needed, simply take a pill.
• Patient preference: For patients who are reluctant to inject insulin, this could be a
desirable option.
Disadvantages:
• Absorption issues: Insulin is a large molecule, and it is difficult for the body to
absorb it effectively through the digestive system.
• Still in development: Oral insulin products are not yet widely available or
approved for regular use in most countries.

 Activity (1)
Go online and search for food with a high and low glycaemic
index and instruct the patient about the condition in which each
one would be preferred
Answer:
The glycaemic index is a scale that ranks carbohydrate-containing foods based on how
quickly they raise blood glucose levels after consumption.
High GI foods cause a rapid spike in blood glucose.
Low GI foods lead to a gradual and steady rise in blood glucose.

Examples of High GI Foods
High GI foods include items like white bread, white rice, potatoes (especially baked),
cornflakes, watermelon, and sugary snacks such as candies and jaggery. These foods
are quickly digested and absorbed, which can rapidly increase blood sugar levels.

Examples of Low GI Foods
Low GI foods include barley, lentils, beans, oats (especially steel-cut), apples, oranges,
carrots, leafy vegetables like spinach, nuts like almonds, and plain yogurt. These are
absorbed more slowly and help in maintaining stable blood glucose levels.



High glycemic index to maintain blood glucose within normal without shouting in
insulin secretion.
High glycemic as juices are better during early attacks of hypoglycemia

 When to Prefer High GI Foods
High GI foods are beneficial in certain clinical situations, such as:


During hypoglycemia: For a patient with low blood sugar (below 70 mg/dL), high
GI foods provide a quick energy source to rapidly elevate glucose levels. For
example, a diabetic patient experiencing dizziness and sweating due to
hypoglycemia should consume glucose tablets or fruit juice.



Post-exercise recovery: After intense physical activity, consuming high GI foods
helps to rapidly replenish glycogen stores in muscles.

When to Prefer Low GI Foods
Low GI foods are ideal for:


Diabetic patients: These foods help maintain stable blood sugar levels
throughout the day, reducing the risk of both hyper- and hypoglycemia.



Weight management: Low GI foods promote satiety, reduce cravings, and help in
maintaining a healthy weight.
Heart health: Because they reduce insulin spikes and lower cholesterol levels.



Infection I module
Introduction to infectious diseases
Community medicine department

1

 Lecture 1: Cycle of infection
Learning Objectives:
1. Identify the elements of the cycle of infection of a communicable disease
2. List different types of infectious agents of communicable diseases
3. Indicate how to measure of pathogenicity, infectivity and virulence an infectious
agent
4. Explain the difference between the second attack frequency and secondary attack rate
5. List the types of reservoirs of infection
6. Classify carriers and explain their public health importance in disease transmission
7. Explain different modes of transmission of communicable diseases
8. Discuss the factors that affect the susceptibility of the host to communicable diseases
9. Describe the key strategies to control infectious diseases at different points
in the cycle of infection
Definitions of some terminology relevant to infectious diseases and their transmission:
Infection: It is the entry, development and/or multiplication of an infectious agent in the body of
man or animal.
Infectious diseases: Disease caused by entry, development and/or multiplication of an
infectious agent in the body of man or animal. This might be in the form of unapparent (without
relevant symptoms or signs) or apparent (with relevant symptoms and signs) infection.
Communicable disease: A subset of infectious diseases that are transmissible from one person
(or animal) to another, either directly or indirectly.
Sporadic disease: It is the occurrence of few cases of the disease that are separated widely in
terms of geographic location and time of occurrence and showing no connection to each other.
Endemic disease: It is the constant presence of a disease or an infectious agent within a given
geographic area or population group E.g. bilharziasis in Egypt, malaria in the tropics and
typhoid, hepatitis in many developing countries.
Epidemic: The occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness, clearly in excess of
its normal expectancy for the same time of the year.
Outbreak: An occurrence of more cases of a particular disease than expected in a given area or
among a specific group of people over a particular period.
Pandemic: An epidemic occurring over a very wide geographical area, crossing international
boundaries, and usually affecting many people (e.g. influenza A H1N1 in 2009, COVID -19
starting December 2019).

2

 Herd immunity: It is the immunity of a group of people or a community. The resistance of a
group of people or a community to a particular disease depends on the immunity acquired by a
high
proportion
of
individual
members
of
this
group
or
community.
Herd immunity threshold: It is the level of immunity of a population, indicated by the
proportion of immune persons, above which the incidence of the disease decreases. The
threshold of herd immunity is variable from one disease to another; it is nearly 80% for smallpox
while it is estimated to be 60% of COVID-19.
The concept of Herd immunity is important in planning public health interventions for
prevention and control of communicable diseases. For example, the target of vaccination
programs is to raise the vaccination coverage above the level of herd immunity threshold that
provides protection to un-vaccinated individuals. As herd immunity becomes diluted by new
individuals born susceptible, vaccination programs are targeting newborns and children to
maintain herd immunity level above the critical level.
Cycle of Infection:
Cycle of infection is a process that begins when an agent leaves its reservoir or an infected
person through a portal of exit and is transmitted by some mode of transmission then enters
through an appropriate portal of entry to infect a susceptible host.

text:
Viral vaccines
•
•
•

Immune response in immunized individual are faster stronger than for unimmunized ones.
Immunization of a population can stop the spread the infectious agent by reducing the number of
susceptible hosts (herd immunity) .
The main property to make a virus candidate for vaccine development, is to be the cause of a
significant illness.

Immunization programs have achieved:
•
•
•
•

Protection of population from the symptoms eg: rabies
Protection and control of spread of measles, mumps, rubella, varicella zoster, influenza and
rotavirus
Elimination of wild type poliomyelitis in most of the world and smallpox worldwide
Reduction in cancer risk caused by human papilloma virus and HBV.

Vaccine preventable diseases still occur, and outbreaks take place wherever immunization is unavailable
due to high expenses (developing countries).

Inactivated Vaccines
Produced by inactivating viral infectivity to prepare large amounts of structural viral proteins and use
them to elicit protective antibody immune response without the risk of infection can be attained.

Preparation
- exposure of a wild type (virulent) virus to
Chemical agent eg formalin, or physical agent as
irradiation or heat inactivation, Use of various
purification and concentration techniques
-

Adjuvant that boosts the immunogenicity by
enhancing uptake by presenting cells
e.g. aluminium hydroxide or aluminium phosphate (the most approved adjuvant) are used
* Inactivated viral vaccine: Polio (salk), rabies, influenza , Hepatitis A.
* Inactivated bacterila vaccine: cholera and Q-fever.

Advantages of Inactivated Virus Vaccines:
1- No risk of reversion to virulence
2- Can be given safely in immunocompromised patients and during pregnancy

 Disadvantages of Inactivated Virus Vaccines:
1- Immunity is usually brief and not usually lifelong
2- Immunity may be only humoral with satisfactory levels of circulating IgG and IgM while cell
mediated immunity is generally poor
3- Vaccine does not elicit a local ig A response at portal of entry
4- Booster shots are required to maintain effectiveness
5- Larger doses must be used
6- Some inactivated vaccines can induce hypersensitivity to subsequent infection

Live attenuated Vaccines
Vaccines that resembles natural infection in that the immune response progresses through the natural
innate and antigen specific immune responses so that humoral, cellular and memory immune responses
are developed.

Preparation:
Live vaccines are prepared with avirulent or attenuated vaccines limited in their ability to cause
pathology, this may consist of any of the following:
•

Attenuated viral vaccines Less virulent mutants of the wild type virus.

1- Wild type viruses are attenuated by growth in animals or tissue culture cells at non-physiologic
conditions, attenuation occurs due to Conditions that select or allow the growth of viral strains that are
less virulent e.g: viruses that grow poorly at 37°c eg. measles, cold adapted strains of influenza virus
2- Serial passage in tissue cell lines to induce ability of the virus to replicate at the benign site without
disease development e.g, polio vaccine replicate in GIT but do not reach neurons
•

Recombinant techniques by insertion of gene coding for the protein of interest into genome of
an avirulent vector virus from other species that share antigenic determinants e.g. vaccinia virus
for smallpox vaccination or rotavirus

•

Genetically engineered viruses lacking virulence properties (by deletion of virulent genes)

Live attenuated are mainly for protection of enveloped viruses as they require T cell
Advantages:
1-immunity more efficient and last longer
2-immune response to live vaccines stimulate that produced by natural infection
3-production of IgA at the portal of entry
4-induce a good cell mediated response

Disadvantages:
1-risk of revision of the virus to virulence

 2-Care for storage temperature and limited shelf life(mg cl in poloi overcome this problem)
3-can not be given to imm

text:
Cytokines
➢ a large group of proteins involved in signaling between cells during the immune response.
➢ secreted by specific cells of the immune system, which carry signals locally between cells, and
thus have an effect on other cells.
➢ They are a category of signaling molecules that are used extensively in cellular communication.
➢ They are proteins, peptides, or glycoproteins.
➢ produced widely throughout the body by cells of diverse embryological origin

Mode of action: Cytokines are secreted by certain cells in response to specific stimuli and they bind
to specific receptors on target cells exerting their effect on these cells.
Cytokines include the followings: Interleukins (ILs), Interferons (IFN)), Colony stimulatingfactors (CSFS),
Tumour necrosis factors a and B (TNF-a& B), Transforming growth factors (TGF B), Chemokines as (IL-8).

Interleukins: This is a large group of cytokines which are produced mainly by T-cells, but also by
mononuclear phagocytes or by tissue cells.
➢ Most are involved in directing other cells to divide and differentiate.
➢ Each interleukin acts on a specific limited group of cells with correct receptors for that IL.

IL-2: The most powerful activator and growth factor for T-cells,
3. Proinflammatory cytokines of innate immunity (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-a): Secreted mainly
by macrophages.
* local and systemic inflammatory effects on the tissues (fever, increased production of leukocytes by
the bone marrow and production of acute phase proteins by the liver).
* At higher temperatures (during fever), bacterial and viral replication is less efficient, whereas the
adaptive immune response is more efficiently.
* Acute phase proteins include C reactive protein (CRP), mannose binding lectin and complement
components. C-reactive protein acts as an opsonin.

PATHOGENESIS OF BACTERIAL INFECTION
Infection is the invasion of the host by microorganisms and multiplying within host's tissues.
Colonization occurs when microorganisms live on or in a host organism but do not invade tissues or
cause damage.
Bacterial infectivity results from a disturbance in the balance between bacterial virulence and
host resistance.
The "objective" of bacteria is to multiply rather than to cause disease,only 50/103 of bacterial species
we carry cause disease.
Types of Microorganisms
1. Commensal or normal microbial flora found on skin and mucous membranes.
2. Opportunistic microorganisms (potential pathogens).
3. Pathogenic microorganisms (true pathogens).

1. Commensal flora
•
•
•

present on body surfaces covered by epithelial cells and are exposed to the external
environment (gastrointestinal and respiratory tract,vagina, skin, etc.). skin and mucous membrane
The number of bacteria colonizing mucosal and skin surfaces exceeds the number of cells(10:1).
Commensal bacteria co-evolved with their hosts,but become pathogenic under specific
conditions

2. Opportunistic microorganisms
These potential pathogens can cause diseases under certain conditions;
a. When host defense mechanism is lowered as in case of diabetics, immunosuppressed or
leukemic patients.
b. When the natural habitat of the microorganism is changed.
eg. E.coli leaves the intestine causing urinary tract infection.
c. When alteration in the host tissue occurs.
eg. viridans streptococci (one of the normal oral flora) may produce subacute bacterial endocarditis in a
previously damaged heart valve, if the organism reaches the blood stream after tooth extraction or
tonsillectomy.

 eg. Clostridium perfringens (one of the normal intestinal flora) may produce gas gangrene in damaged
tissue.

3. Pathogenic microorganisms (True Pathogens):
•
•

Pathogens capable of infecting the tissues of normal healthy subjects,as Yersinia pestis causing
plague.
The true pathogens have their ways of overcoming the body defenses.

Properties of True Pathogens:
a. Infectivity:
-The pathogen must have a portal of entry to the host in order to initiate infection
- The capacity to initiate infection is related to:
-Dose of the pathogen (the infective dose); the number of bacteria required to cause
disease.
-Its growth phase (bacteria are more infective in the log phase than the lag phase).
- Its virulence.
b. Virulence:

Degree of pathogenicity of the organism
e.g. Some strains of Corynebacterium diphtheria are highly virulent, others are moderately virulent
while many are avirulent.
This depends the ability to produce the toxin and its potency.
Virulence factors:
These are certain structures or products that help the microorganisms to:
(1) invade the host, (2) cause disease, and (3) evade host defenses.
The following are types of virulence factors:
i. Adherence factors: Certain bacteria have specialized structures eg. pili, or substances e.g. slime that
help their adherence to the host cell mucous membranes thus allowing them to start the disease
process. If they did not adhere they will be swept away e.g. Neisseria gonorrohoea and E.coli have pili to
mediate the attachment to urinary tract epithelium.

 ii. Invasiveness: Is the ability to invade the tissue and multiply and spread rapidy
Highly invasive bacteria include those causing anthrax and plague.
iii. Antiphagocytic Factors: Some pathogens have surface factors that impede phagocytosis e.g.
•
•
•

Str.pneumoniae has a polysaccharide capsule,
Str. Pyogenes have M protein.
Other bacteria as Bordetella, produce soluble factors that inibit chemotaxis, thus evade
phagocytosis by a different mechanism.

iv. Toxin production: Toxins are bacterial products that have a direct harmful action on tissue cells. They
fall into two groups: Exotoxins and Endotoxins .
Extracellular enzymes: These are produced by pathogens to help the establishmet of infection. As
coagulase, hyaluronidase,.

Genetic Engineering
•
•

direct manipulation of an organism's genome using biotechnology
by the use of two important tools: restriction enzymes and cloning vectors.

Restriction Enzymes (RES): These are different types of bacterial enzymes that cut DNA from different
sources into pieces, at specific recognition sequence site(s).
A cloning vector (also called expression vector) is a plasmid, or a bacteriophage that can be stably
maintained in an organism for cloning purposes.
It is easy for pieces from different sources cut with the same enzyme to recombine forming a new DNA
(recombinant DNA).
Gene cloning and production of recombinant vaccines (2 strategies)

A-Cloning into a plasmid
1.Identify the genes coding for an antigenic protein (genes of interest) e.g. HBSA9& cut them by RE.
2.Cut the expression vector (a plasmid) by the same RE (to create sticky ends).
3. Insert HBSA9 gene into the expression vector to create a new recombinant DNA.
4.Insert the vector into bacteria or yeast & allow to grow.
5.HBs genes will be expressed & HBs protein will be produced.
6. HBs protein will be purified then used as a vaccine.

B- Cloning into an avirulent virus
1. Insert the genes of interest into an avirulent virus e.g. Vaccinia virus.
2. Inject the modified virus (recombinant) directly into a human as a vaccine.
3. The human body will produce Abs to both HBSAG & Vaccinia virus.

BACTERIAL RESISTANCE TO CHEMOTHERAPEUTIC AGENTS
mechanisms by which microorganisms might exhibit resistance to drugs:
1. Microorganisms produce enzymes that destroy the active drug, e.g,
➢ staphylococci resistant to penicillin G produce a B-lactamase that destroys the drug.
➢ Bacteria resistant to aminoglycosides produce adenylating, phosphorylating or acetylating
enzymes that destroy the drug.

 ➢ Bacteria may be resistant to chloramphenicol if they produce a chloramphenicol
acetyltransferase.
2. Microorganisms reduce their permeability to the drug.
➢ In resistant cells the drug is either not actively transported into the cell or leaves it so rapidly (by
efflux pump) that inhibitory concentrations are not maintained.
As: tetracyclines, aminoglycosides and polymyxins.
3. Microorganisms develop an altered structural target for the drug, e.g,
➢ Chromosomal resistance to aminoglycosides is associated with the loss or alteration of a specific
protein on the 30 S subunit of the bacterial ribosome.
➢ Erythromycin resistant organisms have an altered receptor on the 50S subunit of the ribosome.
➢ Resistance to some penicillins may be a function of the loss or alteration of PBPS.
4. Microorganisms develop an altered metabolic pathway that bypasses the reaction inhibited
by the drug, e.g. some sulphonamide resistant bacteria do not require extracellular PABA
but, like mammalian cells, can utilize preformed folic acid.

Origin of Drug Resistance
1. Non genetic origin (natural or inherent): This is an innate property of the bacterium, so it is
predictable.
• It is often due to absence of a target structure for drug action (e.g. absence of cell wall in
Mycoplasma).
• It may also be due to the presence of a permeability barrier in the cell envelope (e.g.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa has a complex cell wall that limits penetration of many antibacterial
agents).
• Also, micro-organisms that are metabolically inactive (non-multiplying) may be resistant to
drugs
e.g. mycobacteria often survive in tissues for many years after infection and do not multiply.

2. Genetic origin (acquired): by methods that allow gene change or exchange.
An organism may lose its susceptibility to an antibiotic during the course of treatment, so it is
unpredictable. This may be due to:
a) Chromosomal resistance: Which develops as a result of spontaneous mutation in a locus that
controls susceptibility to a given antimicrobial drug.
➢ Spontaneous mutation occurs with a frequency of 10-8 to 10-12 and thus is an infrequent cause
of the emergence of clinical drug resistance in a given patient.

ANTIGENS AND ANTIBODIES
ANTIGENS (Ags)
•
•
•

An Ag is any foreign substance which when introduced into the body stimulates a specific
immune response in the form of antibody formation or cell mediated immunity.
it must be recognized by the body as being foreign or non-self.
An Ag is usually a protein or polysaccharide of a higher molecular weight.
•

Pure lipids or nucleic acids are not antigenic while lipopolysaccharide, lipoproteins,
nucleoproteins are antigenic.

Types of Antigens:

A. Incomplete antigens:
Hapten: is a protein free chemical substance,
incapable by itself of producing an Ab, but
when it binds to the body protein it becomes
antigenic and stimulates Ab production.
e.g: penicillin, aspirin, sulfa,
tranquillizers and formaldehyde.

cosmetics,

when a hapten is introduced into the body for the second time, it will react with the previously formed
Ab leading to reaction.

B. Complete antigens:
1. Iso-antigens (Human tissue antigens):
These are Ags present on the cells of the body of different members of the same species.
eg:: the "ABO or ABH" and the "Rh" factor.
Human leucocytic antigen (HLA) is iso-antigen present in all nucleated tissue cells mainly leucocytes.
•

HLA are of vital importance in organ transplantation.

2. Auto-antigens:
Normally an individual does not react with his organs, but due to infection or inflammation the antigenic
structure will change (recognized as non-self), resulting in the production of autoantibodies as in some
autoimmune diseases.

3. Heterophile antigens:
Ags shared by different species, e.g. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) shares Ags with sheep and horse RBC's.

 The antibodies formed in infectious mononucleosis
(caused by EBV) agglutinate sheep or horse blood cells
in the monospot test.

4. Superantigens:
•

•

•
•

active at a very low concentration, they can
activate a large number of T-cells nonspecifically.
They are mostly of bacterial origin and include the
staphylococcal enterotoxin (responsible for some
types of acute food poisoning), toxic shock syndrome
toxin, exfoliative dermatitis toxin and streptococcal
pyrogenic exotoxin.
some viral proteins as well as some antigens of
certain mycoplasma species act as superantigens.
They are termed superantigens because they bind
directly, i.e. unprocessed to the variable regions of Bchains (VB chains) of antigen receptors on certain
subsets of T- cells and cross-link them to the major
histocompatibility complex «MHC» class Il of antigenpresenting cells (APCS). İ.e. act as a clamp between the
two, providing a signal for T helper activation .

Adverse effect of superantigens is the systemic toxicity of the massive cytokine/ lymphokine release of
IL1, IL2 and TNF that results from the simultaneous stimulation of a large subset of T-cells.

ANTIBODIES
Antibodies or immunoglobulins are glycoproteins expressed as:
✓ Soluble molecules present in serum and tissue fluids, or
✓ Membrane bound receptors on the surface of B cells.
Contact between the B cell receptor and the antigen it recognizes results in B cell activation and
differentiation to generate plasma cells which secrete large amounts of antibody.
The secreted antibody has the same binding specificity as the original B cell receptor.

text:
THE COMPLEMENT SYSTEM
•

a complex group of serum proteins, present in low concentration in normal serum, that interact
with each other in a cascading fashion to protect against infectious agents.

Membrane-bound proteins are also included in the complement system.

Synthesis:
by several cells: hepatic parenchymal cells, monocytes, macrophages and intestinal epithelium.

Nomenclature of Complement Proteins:
- designated by the letter "C" followed by a number, which is related to the order of its discovery :C1,
C2, C3. etc.
-On cleavage of a complement component,
•

the large fragment is given the suffix "b" eg.:C5b

•

and the smaller fragment is given the suffix "a" e.g. C5a.

✓ Components of the alternative pathway are designated with a capital letter
e.g. factor B, factor D etc.
Pathways of Complement Activation:
•
•
•

The activation of complement components takes place in a sequential fashion, each component
activating its successor protein in the cascade.
Many components are pro-enzymes which must be cleaved to form active enzymes

•

There are three complement pathways the classical ,the alternative and lectin.
Complement pathways lead to the formation of a complex enzyme (C3 convertase) capable of
binding and cleaving a key protein C3, common to pathways.

•

C3 activation is the common central event .

•

After that, the three pathways proceed in the same fashion together through binding of the lateacting components to form a membrane attack complex (MAC) which is C5b6789 which becomes
inserted in the lipid bilayers of foreign membranes, ultimately causing cell lysis.

•

The classical pathway is typically initiated by Ag-Ab complexes, in solution or on the surface of a
cell thus it is triggered after the generation of specific Ab to a particular Ag.

 •

the alternative pathway occurs by microbial surfaces and it can proceed in the absence of Ab, and
thus helps in the first line of defense against microorganisms (innate immunity) and mediates an
inflammatory response.

•

the lectin pathway bypasses antibody and uses a lectin, mannose binding lectin (MBL) to initiate
events.

•

Biologic Functions of the Complement System:
1. Cell lysis: Insertion of the MAC (C5b6789) into the cell membrane leads to lysis of many types of
cells, including bacteria, tumour cells, erythrocytes, protozoa and enveloped viruses.
2. Opsonization: Cells, antigen-antibody complexes, and other particles are phagocytosed much more
efficiently in the presence of C3b bound on their surfaces,because of the presence of C3b receptors
on the surface of many phagocytes eg. monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils.. etc.
3. Inflammatory function: i.e. the generation of peptide fragments that regulate the features of the
inflammatory and immune response:
A. Chemotaxis: C5a attracts phagocytic cells, mainly polymorphs to the site of inflammation and
increases their activity.

 B. Anaphylatoxins: C3a and C5a can produce degranulation of mast cells with release of
histamine, serotonin and other mediators which cause increased vascular permeability and
smooth muscle contraction.

Regulation of the Complement System:
In order to avoid constant complement activation, a regulatory network exists to terminate
complement activity. Several serum proteins regulate the complement system at different
stages.

Transplantation :practice of grafting tissues or organs from one person to another or from one place to
another in the same person.

the presence of tissue antigens that differ from one individual to another and stimulate the immune
response which causes the rejection.
These tissue antigens are called Human Leucocytic Antigens(HLA) or Major Histocompatibility Complex
(MHC) or Transplantation antigens.

•

The virus is a cytolytic virus that infects epithelial cells of the skin
or mucous membrane.

liberated and can be transmitted to the other individuals.

vesicular lesions. In general, oropharyngeal HSV-1 infections

sacral ganglia.

AND ANTIBODIES
Prof. Maha El-Gharbawy

 IMMUNOGENS AND
ANTIGENS

 An Immunogen is any foreign substance which when
introduced into the body stimulates a specific immune
response in the form of antibody formation or cell mediated
immunity.
For a substance to be immunogenic, it must be recognized
by the body as being foreign or non-self.
An immunogen is usually a protein or polysaccharide of a
higher molecular weight.

 An antigen is a molecule that can bind to the
components of the immune system, including
antibodies, T and B cell receptors.
Antigenic determinants (Epitopes):
Epitopes are the chemical features on the antigen
molecule that physically bind to antibody (on B cells)
or T cell receptors. An antigen can have one or more
epitopes.

text: TUTORIAL 2 Lectures 4-6 Discussion Viral structure and classification Why do some viruses infect many kinds of cells or many hosts whereas some viruses infect only a particular kind of cell in a host? 1 This depends on the interaction between virus attachment protein VAP and host cell receptor . Viruses that use receptors that are present on different kinds of cells can infect those cells whereas viruses that require receptors that are found on limited types of cells can infect those cells only. This results in what we call virus tropism or virus affinity . 2 Which type of virus is more resistant to environmental conditions and why, enveloped or non-enveloped viruses? Naked viruses are more resistant because: Capsid can withstand harsh conditions. They generally resist dryness, acid, detergents, bile. Most of them can be transmitted by the fecal-oral route and can endure transmission in sewage. Whereas, enveloped viruses : Are environmentally labile Can be readily disrupted by drying, acids, detergents and solvents (e.g. ether) which result in inactivation of the virus. That is why enveloped viruses cannot survive harsh conditions as that of GIT. They are transmitted mainly in fluids and secretions. 3 Why do we call enveloped viruses: ether sensitive? Envelope contains lipids and ether is a lipid-solvent. When ether dissolves the lipid, the envelope structure is disrupted and the virus becomes inactivated. Thus it is sensitive to ether. In the intracellular state of a virus, it needs its: VAP Capsid Nucleic acid Envelope 4 Nucleic acid In the extracellular state of a virus, we can describe it as its: (more than one answer can be correct) Infectious virus particle Virion Nucleic acid 5 Infectious virus particle Virion Why do some viruses encode many proteins whereas other viruses encode only few proteins? 6 This depends on the amount of genetic material of the virus Why do cells have receptors for viruses? 7 These receptors perform functions needed for the cells, but viruses use these rec e ptors to enter the cell. Viruses lack the capacity to produce energy and cannot make their own proteins or replicate their genome independently of the host cell. text: Sampling for Microbiological Diagnosis The diagnosis of microbial etiology of an infectious disease includes the following steps Assessment of clinical and epidemiologic features. Anatomic localization of the infection site with the aid of physical, and radiologic examination. Some routine laboratory investigations may suggest bacterial or viral infection Collection of the appropriate specimens to be processed by microbiology Lab. Some routine laboratory investigations may suggest bacterial or viral infection: Complete blood picture— a bacterial infection often raises the white cell count with neutrophilia. Viral infections on the other hand induce lymphocyte activation and undifferentiated lymphocyte proliferation. C-reactive protein (CRP) & Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) — are markers of inflammation and are elevated in all inflammatory conditions whether bacterial or viral Procalcitonin — is another marker of generalised sepsis due to bacterial infection The best results are obtained when communication between the clinician and laboratory is maximal. Failure of proper specimen collection is the most common reason for Failing to establish an etiologic diagnosis, or worse, Suggesting a wrong diagnosis In the case of bacterial infections, the primary problem lies in: Distinguishing resident or contaminating normal floral organisms from those causing the infection. Proper Specimen SITE 1. Collect the sample when indicated from the correct anatomic site and before antibiotic intake . 2- Samples should be collected in sterile leak-proof containers , aseptic technique and sterile equipment , sufficient volume and transported as quickly as possible to the Microbiology Lab. 3- All specimens must be labeled appropriately: Patient name Type of sample & site A complete request form must accompany all specimens 4- Specimens should be delivered to the lab as soon as possible and within a maximum of 2 hours . If any delay is anticipated, samples must be stored in the refrigerator (4°C) EXCEPT: Blood culture bottles, fluid aspirates and pus should be kept at room temperature . CSF samples should be kept at 37°C (in an incubator if available) or at room temperature . 5- Specimens for viral isolation should be kept cool (4°C), or frozen (preferably at -60°C or colder) if there is more than 24 hours’ delay in bringing it to the laboratory. Viral transport media contain proteins to stabilize the viral agents and antimicrobials to prevent overgrowth of bacteria and fungi. 6-Specimens should be processed in a Biosafety Cabinet whenever possible. MICROBIOLOGICAL SAMPLES Blood Cerebro-spinal fluid (CSF) and other biological fluids (peritoneal, pleural..) Urine Sputum Throat swab Pus / pus swab / wound swab Stool Fungal specimens Swabs for molecular assay 1. Blood culture Blood culture is done when bacteremia or fungaemia is suspected. For adults, 20 ml of blood should be collected per venipuncture. Less blood is required for children . Steps of specimen collection: 1- Remove blood culture bottle cap and decontaminate exposed rubber stopper using 70% ethyl alcohol and allow drying. 2. Select the vein and prepare the arm using 70% alcohol in a concentric manner i.e. starting at the center of the site (for 30 sec), then disinfect the site a second time in the same manner with povidone iodine (betadine), allow to dry (3-5 min). Finally, use a 70% alcohol pad to remove the iodine (30 s). Do not touch the venipuncture site after preparation. 3- Decontaminate hands with an alcohol hand rub and wear gloves. Collect blood (20 ml) using a syringe. Aseptically inject blood through the central ring of the rubber stopper. Gently mix bottles by inversion. Dispose the syringe appropriately. Remove gloves & Decontaminate hands again. 2. CSF and other biological fluids ( pleural, pericardial, peritoneal,..) CSF is submitted for microbiological analysis when: meningitis or encephalitis is suspected. Obtained by: lumbar spinal puncture . Steps of specimen collection 3. Urine culture Steps of specimen collection Steps of specimen collection Sterile container 4. Sputum culture Steps of sputum collection 5.Throat swab culture 1. Depress tongue with a tongue depressor. 2. Sample the posterior pharynx, tonsils, and inflamed areas with a sterile swab. DO NOT TOUCH the tongue with the swab. Unless otherwise indicated, a throat swab will only be evaluated for the presence or absence of Group A Streptococci . 6. Pus / pus swab / wound swab Open wounds : Wash the wound with a jet of sterile saline to remove all surface contaminants. Aspirate if possible or pass a swab deep into the lesion to firmly sample the lesion’s “fresh border.” Samples of the base of the lesion and abscess wall are most productive. 2. Closed collection aspiration : 7.Stool culture 8. Fungal specimens a . Skin scraping : The skin should be cleaned with 70% alcohol to reduce bacterial contamination, then a sterile blunt scalpel is used to scrap the active periphery of the inflamed area. The sample is collected in a sterile glass petri dish. 8. Fungal specimens b. Nail pieces : Friable nail material should be removed from under the nail and collected in a sterile petri dish. 8. Fungal specimens c . Hairs : Infected hairs should be removed by plucking with epilating forceps and never by cutting which fails to remove the area most likely to harbor the fungus. 9.Swabs for molecular assay Swabs used must be compatible for the specific molecular assay for which they are intended. The wrong type of swab can produce false-negative results. Wooden-shafted swabs are toxic to some viruses . Cotton-tipped swabs are toxic to some bacteria , including chlamydiae .

text: DECONTAMINATION The process by which organisms are Removed or Destroyed in order to render an object safe to handle, use, or discard. The Choice Of The Method Of Decontamination Depends On : 1. The Nature of the object to be decontaminated 2. Its Tolerance to the process of decontamination 3. Its Microbial Load 4. The Risk it Carries in transmission of infection to patients or staff in contact with the object There are three levels of decontamination Levels of Decontamination The physical removal of visible soil, organic and inorganic material from objects and surfaces. -Removes some microorganisms (all vegetative bacteria except tubercle bacilli, all enveloped and some non-enveloped viruses, some fungi, but not bacterial spores). Levels Of Decontamination Levels of Decontamination Spaulding classification A strategy developed by Dr. Earle H. Spaulding for reprocessing contaminated medical devices . The system classifies devices as Critical, Semi Critical, or Noncritical based on The degree of risk of infection when A contaminated device is used Policy For The Decontamination Of Reusable Equipment And Devices According To The Spaulding Classification Risk Category Recommended Level Of Decontamination Examples Of Medical Devices/Items Low (non-critical) Items in contact with Intact Skin Disinfection (low -Intermediate-level disinfection preferred) Noncritical patient care items: Blood pressure cuffs, stethoscopes,,,, . Noncritical environmental surfaces: of medical equipment, bed rails, floors,……… Policy for the Decontamination of Reusable Equipment and Devices According to the Spaulding Classification Risk Category Recommended Level of Decontamination Examples of Medical Devices/Items Intermediate (Semi-critical) Items in contact with Mucous Membranes or Body Fluids Disinfection (high level) Respiratory equipment Non-invasive flexible endoscopes laryngoscope Risk category Recommended level of decontamination Examples of medical devices/items High (critical) Items involved with: A break in the skin or mucous membrane or Entering a sterile body cavity Sterilization Reusable items; Surgical instruments Rigid endoscopes Implants/prostheses Syringes, needles (single use) Policy for the Decontamination of Reusable Equipment and Devices According to the Spaulding Classification I. CLEANING I. CLEANING Definition This is accomplished using water with detergents with or without enzymatic products. Note Thorough cleaning is required before intermediate or high-level disinfection and sterilization Because, Inorganic and Organic Materials that remain on the surfaces interfere with the effectiveness of these processes. DISINFECTION II. Disinfection I- Disinfection By Moist Heat At Or Below 100° C Pasteurization Destroy all pathogenic microorganisms (Except bacterial spores) The time-temperature used = ~70°C for 30 minutes . Used as alternative to chemical disinfection for: Respiratory Therapy Equipment Anesthesia Equipment UV radiation Low energy non-ionizing radiation Has poor penetrating power (does not penetrate through glass or liquids) Lethal to microorganisms under optimum conditions. Restricted to disinfection of previously cleaned surfaces such as laboratory safety cabinets some piped water supplies ii-Disinfection By Ultraviolet Radiation III-Disinfection of Air by Filtration HEPA filters ( H igh- E fficiency P article A rrester ) Rapidly free large volumes of air from infectious particles of 0.5μ size achieving efficiency of 99.99%. Principles Of Chemical Disinfection 1-Disinfectants must always be used at the correct concentration referred to as: “Use Dilution or Working Dilution”. 2-The life of a disinfectant varies with its formulation and many disinfectants deteriorate when diluted with water. Note: Working dilution should be: Prepared daily OR Renewed based on Manufacturer recommendation Principles Of Chemical Disinfection 3-Disinfectants take time to act. This varies according to Microbial load Presence of organic material Temperature PH The nature of exposed surfaces Presence of resistant bacterial spores. 4- Disinfectants should not be mixed with other disinfectants or cleaning solutions. 5. Disinfectants do not act in the presence of organic matter except phenols . Direct detection methods: ( Light Microscopy) The role of Gram stained smears in diagnosis of bacterial infections Classify bacteria according to whether they retain crystal violet stain ( gram-positive—violet ) or not ( gram-negative—red ) Highlight cell morphology (e.g., bacilli, cocci) and cell arrangement (e.g., clumps, chains, diploids) Identify polymorphonuclear leukocytes , indicating bacterial infection rather than colonization Data from Gram stained smears examination can guide antibiotic therapy pending definitive bacterial identification (only in normally sterile samples CSF, Blood). The specimen material is fixed on a slide by heating. stained by sequential exposure to: Gram crystal violet Iodine Decolorizer (95% ethyl alcohol) Counterstain (safranin). Gram Smear II) Direct Antigen detection These tests use antibodies to detect antigens of the pathogen in the patient’s specimen. e.g : Latex agglutination, IF, ELISA, Lateral flow immunochromatography. The advantage of these tests , that they can be rapidly performed and are relatively inexpensive. ELISA Lateral flow immunochromatography Latex agglutination III) Nucleic acid detection of microorganisms in clinical samples II- Bacterial isolation (Culture) & Identification CULTURE MEDIA We routinely attempt to isolate the causal organisms of a disease from clinical samples. CULTURE MEDIA are used to provide the physiological requirements and nutrients to allow growth of bacteria. TYPES OF CULTURE MEDIA LIQUID MEDIA SOLID MEDIA LIQUID MEDIA Dispensed in screw-capped tubes. Growth is recognized by turbidity in the fluid. It is used when low count of bacteria is expected in certain samples as blood, since it enhances bacterial growth. SOLID MEDIA Dispensed in plastic disposable plates or sterile glass dishes. Solid media are solidified fluid media. The solidifying agent is agar. Growth of bacteria on solid media is in the form of colonies. Method of inoculation This is important for : • Accurate identification for proper antibiotic testing. • Quantitation to differentiate contamination from true infection. • Accurate antibiotic susceptibility testing for proper treatment. The main types of culture media I. Basal or ordinary media Simplest type of medium Includes the basic nutrients sufficient for growth of non-fastidious bacteria e.g. staphylococci. It includes: a-Fluid media e.g. Nutrient broth. b-Solid media e.g. Nutrient agar. II. Enriched Media Fastidious organisms (e.g. Streptococci) are unable to grow on ordinary media as they require special growth promoting factors (blood, serum, albumin) Media containing such substances are called enriched media . Examples: A. Blood agar B. Chocolate agar A.BLOOD AGAR Nutrient agar + 5-10% blood Uses: 1-Growing delicate fastidious organisms. 2- Discriminating organisms according to their hemolytic action (complete or partial haemolysis) B. CHOCOLATE AGAR A fter adding the blood to the melted agar, the temperature is raised for ten minutes, then the medium is poured as plates. Uses: T he culture of Haemophilus spp . and Neisseria spp. III. Selective media They contain inhibitory substances that inhibit organisms not desired to grow, while the organism under study will be able to grow. Examples: A. Mannitol salt agar B. MacConkey’s agar A. Mannitol Salt Agar Selecting agent: NaCl (10-15%)  it allows the growth of staphylococci, while it inhibits other organisms. Sugar: Mannitol is fermented by Staphylococcus aureus, other Staphylococci are non-mannitol fermenters Staphylococcus aureus O ther sp p of Staphylococci B. MacConkey’s agar The selecting agent: B ile salts inhibits Gram positive. Sugar : Lactose F ermented by some Gram-negative species as E.coli and Klebsiella giving pink colonies. Not fermented by others as Proteus, Salmonella and Shigella giving pale yellow colonies. IV . Anaerobic media These media are used to grow anaerobic organisms in certain infections: gas gangrene and closed abscesses. V. Transport medium Used for the preservation of delicate pathogens during transit to the laboratory. BACTERIAL IDENTIFICATION METHODS FOR BACTERIAL IDENTIFICATION A. Morphological identification Macroscopic appearance of colonies b. Microscopic examination of films taken from isolated colonies. Gram +ve Cocci Gram –ve Cocci Gram + ve Bacilli Gram –ve Bacilli B. Biochemical identification The conventional biochemical tests include Fermentation or oxidation of carbohydrates Use of carbon sources Presence of specific enzymes , Production of volatile fatty acids. Conventional biochemical tests Rapid identification panel (API 20 E system) Extensive databases exist that allow the identification of most clinically important bacteria.
