text: SEROLOGICAL TESTS SEROLOGICAL TESTS These tests analyze different samples for the presence of antigens (direct) and/or antibodies (indirect) to help diagnose diseases and check immune status. Scheme for using serological tests for lab diagnosis of infectious agents SEROLOGICAL TESTS Indirect diagnosis of a recent infection depends on the following criteria: Detection of IgM : indicates a recent primary infection. Rising titer : Increase in the IgG antibody level at least a fourfold between the serum obtained during the acute phase of disease and that obtained at least 2 to 3weeks later during the convalescent phase. High stationary titer : If the IgG titer of antibody is considerably higher than that found in the general population. SEROLOGICAL TESTS Advantages: Newer generations have high sensitivity and specificity. Do not require organism to be isolated in pure culture. Can be done to non-culturable bacteria. Rapid and cost effective. SEROLOGICAL TESTS The result of the serological reaction can be seen by naked eye as clumps in agglutination reactions (Ag is particulate ), precipitation (Ag is soluble ) or labeled signal detection ( i.e Ab labelled techniques). Agglutination: Haemagglutination. Latex agglutination. Antibody ( Ab )– labelled serological assays Immunofluorescence (Fluorescent-antibody assay). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Lateral flow immunochromatographic assays. SEROLOGICAL TESTS Agglutination 1) Haemagglutination Some viruses for example influenza virus have haemagglutinin spikes on their surface that are capable of haemagglutinating RBCs. This character can be used in a haemagglutination inhibition test to identify viruses or to detect viral antibodies . 2) Latex agglutination Particles such as latex beads could be conjugated to antibodies and used for agglutination of antigens in solutions for the rapid identification of pathogens. 2) Latex agglutination It is also possible to conjugate latex particles with the Ags and use it for detecting antibodies in patients’ sera or other body fluids. 2) Latex agglutination Antibody(Ab)–labelled serological assays 1) Immunofluorescence (Fluorescent-antibody assay) Immunofluorescence Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) Antigens may be detected in smears or tissues by adding a fluorescein labeled specific antibody. The slide is then examined by an ultraviolet microscope (uses ultraviolet lamps which excite fluorescent dyes to emit light in the visible range). The bound fluorescein Ab appears apple green against a dark background. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) For Ag detection , a second fluorescein labeled anti-species antibody used to detect the primary antibody attached to the antigen. The indirect IF is more sensitive than the direct method, and it gives more magnification to the reaction. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) Indirect IF assays can be also used for the detection and quantitation of antibody . Pathogen-infected cells (usually on glass microscope slides) are used as a matrix to capture antibodies specific for that pathogen. Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) Serial dilutions of test serum are applied to individual wells of the cell substrate ( primary antibody). A second fluorescein labeled antispecies antibody is used to detect the primary antibody attached to the antigen. Antibody–labelled serological assays 2) Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay or Enzyme Immune Assay (ELISA, EIA) ELISA Can be used to detect and quantitate antigens or antibodies in a patient’s sample. ELISA Principle of the test: Based on two facts Antigen or antibody can be attached to a solid phase (plastic surface), but still it retains its immunological activity. Antibody can be linked to an enzyme such as alkaline phosphatase or peroxidases and the complex retains both immunological and enzymatic activity. Variations of EIAs differ in the way in which they capture or detect antigen: Direct ELISA for Ag detection The soluble antigen is captured by an antibody immobilized on a solid phase (plastic surface or bead). After unbound components are washed away, it is then detected with a different antibody (the detector antibody ) labeled with an enzyme (horseradish peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase). After a washing step, an appropriate organic substrate for the particular enzyme is added. Direct ELISA for Ag detection Indirect ELISA for Ag detection Indirect EIAs to detect Ags are widely used because of their greater analytical sensitivity . In this test format, the detector antibody is unlabeled and a second labeled (species specific) anti-immunoglobulin is added as the “ indicator ” antibody. Indirect ELISA for Ag detection Indirect ELISA for Ag Indirect ELISA for Ab detection They are the serologic assays of choice for the qualitative (positive or negative) or quantitative determination of antibodies because they are rapid and cost-effective. In the EIA test format for antibody detection, antigen is bound to a solid phase. Serum is added and, if antibodies to the antigen are present in the sample, they bind to it. The bound antibody is detected by an anti-species antibody tagged with an enzyme . With addition of the enzyme substrate , a color reaction develops that can be assessed with a spectrophotometer . Indirect ELISA for Ab detection Antibody–labelled serological assays 3) Lateral flow immunochromatographic assays Lateral flow immunochromatographic assays A paper-based platform is used for the rapid detection of antigens (within 15 minutes). For this system, two types of specific antibodies against antigen are used. One of the antibodies is labeled with colloidal gold and the other is immobilized on the chromatographic paper Lateral flow immunochromatographic assays Sample pad: It receives the antigen-containing fluid. The sample continues to flow along the membrane by capillary action to the second conjugate pad. text: LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF VIRAL INFECTIONS Why to diagnose a viral disease? Screening for viral infections e.g. blood donors, pregnant women. Diagnosis and identification of etiological cause of viral infection. Institution of proper antiviral therapy (e.g. HIV, HCV). Detection of etiological agent of epidemics (e.g. Influenza). Detection of antigenic variation of viruses to help in vaccine production. I. Direct detection methods: 1.Microscopy: i . Histopathological and cytological Examination Direct microscopic examination of stained smears or tissue imprints The most important cytological changes of viral infection are the formation of syncytia or multinucleated giant cells and the detection of inclusion bodies. ii. Direct microscopic examination by Electron microscopy (EM) Recognition of viral morphology and ultrastructural details of virus-infected cells by EM is the basis of viral identification. 2. Direct viral antigen detection: Immunofluorescence seen by ultraviolet microscope ELISA Lateral flow immunochromatography 3. Detection of viral nucleic acid either DNA or RNA PCR for DNA genomes, reverse transcriptase (RT)-PCR for RNA genomes. Simultaneously detection of different microbial genomes (multiplex PCR) is now available. Real-time PCR for identification and quantification of RNA or DNA (measurement of viral load) Nucleic acid sequencing: determination of pathogen genome sequence. Isolation in cell culture 1-Primary cell lines : Obtained by dissociating specific animal organs with trypsin, cells obtained ( fibroblast or epithelial ) are then suspended in nutrient fluid. In test tube cultures, cells attach and grow as monolayers on the walls of test tubes (e.g. primary rabbit kidney cell line ). Normal tissue culture cell line Tissue culture flasks and plates 2-Diploid ( Semicontinuous ) cell lines: Cultures of a single cell type (usually fibroblasts) derived from embryonic tissue that are capable of being passed a large number of times (up to 50) before they undergo a significant change in their characteristics. 3- Continuous cell lines: Usually initiated from human or animal tumors consist of single cell type that can be passed indefinitely e.g. HeLa and Hep2 cell lines. Normal tissue culture cell line 1. Cytopathic effect (CPE) Cell degeneration or death which is recognized by: Rounding, shrinkage, ballooning As the cell dies, it is detached from the glass. Multi nucleated giant cell or syncytia. Inclusion bodies Cytopathic effect 2. Viral interference Some viruses produce NO cytopathic changes e.g. rubella but it prevents ( interferes with ) the replication of another virus normally causing CPE virus. Haemagglutination 3. Haemagglutination Done on fluid of tissue culture to detect haemagglutinating virus No Haemagglutination Detection of viral antigens eg Direct or indirect immunofluorescence 2. Detection of virus specific genome (PCR) Virus Growth identification Immunofluorescence PCR gel electrophoresis 3. Neutralization test for cytopathic viruses Virus identification Antibody inhibition assays 4. Haemagglutination inhibition (HI) for haemagglutinating viruses Confidence versus accessibility to viral tests N.B. 1. Serological tests and PCR are the most commonly used tests to diagnose viral infections. 2. Antigen detection assays for viruses are less sensitive than the viral culture methods and Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). A) Labelled assays: IIF Indirect Enzyme immunoassays Serological Diagnosis Indirect Immunofluorescence Indirect ELISA B) Antibody inhibition assays Use the specificity of an antibody to prevent infection (neutralization) or other activity ( hemagglutination inhibition) to identify strain of infecting virus, or to quantitate antibody responses to a specific strain of virus. C) Immunoblotting techniques Western blot Timing of infection Laboratory test Few days after symptoms Ag detection IgM PCR Viral isolation Later in the course After recovery IgM or IgG IgG (convalescence) Retrospectively in deceased patients Histopathology PCR Viral isolation Choice of method (s) for laboratory confirmation of a viral infection Depends on the stage of disease. Many viruses are most readily isolated during the first few days of illness, while diagnosis by antibody tests is often not confirmed until convalescence.

text: LABORATORY DIAGNOSIS OF FUNGAL INFECTIONS Presumptive Clinical Diagnosis of Mycosis Must Be Confirmed By a Laboratory Diagnosis : I. Direct detection methods 1. Direct microscopic examination (Light Microscopy ) - Fragments of skin, hair and nail are examined directly using 10-30% KOH solution on a glass slide and a coverslip is applied. The purpose of the alkali is to digest the keratin surrounding the fungi so that the hyphae and spores can be seen. - Pus, sputum or other exudates are examined by placing a small proportion of the sample on a microscopic slide and covering it with a coverslip. -Examine the specimen with low power and then with high power lens. The demonstration of septate mycelium, chains of arthrospores and free arthrospores permits a diagnosis of dermatophyte fungal infection. Budding yeast cells mixed with pseudofilaments are indicative of a yeast-like fungus i.e. Candida Visualization of capsulated organisms: When fresh preparations are mixed with a negative stain (such as India Ink), the background field, rather than the organism itself, is stained, making any capsule around the organism visible as a halo. This technique is mainly used to examine CSF samples for Cryptococcus neoformans. 2. Histopathological Examination Many fungi can be seen with H&E in tissue sections, some are not stained at all by this method. Special stains for fungi: a . Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS): red fungus against green background b. Gomori Methenamine Silver Stain (GMS): black fungus against green background c. Mucicarmine stain: demonstrates the mucopolysaccharide in the capsule of Cryptococcus Histopathological Examination PAS GMS Mucicarmine 3. Antigen detection: Fungal polysaccharides or proteins may be shed into body fluids during the course of infection. Glucuronoxylomannan (GXM), the major capsular polysaccharide of Cryptococcusi s shed in large amounts into blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) during the course of cryptococcal meningitis, is detected by latex agglutination and lateral flow immunoassay (dipstick) format. Galactomannan (GM) : polysaccharide present in the cell wall of Aspergillus spp . ELISA test for serum GM is now used for diagnosis of invasive aspergillosis. β-Glucan (BG) : a polysaccharide component of most fungal cell walls . Assay for BG is used for presumptive diagnosis of invasive fungal infection (IFI). BG does not appear in blood from patients with infection by Cryptococcus spp. or the Mucorales. 4. Molecular diagnostics: Molecular methods have the power to identify the increasing numbers of fungi found to produce disease in humans, e.g.: PCR, DNA hybridization II. Fungal isolation and identification A. Culture: II. Fungal isolation and identification Macroscopic Examination: The texture and color of the colony are examined on its front and back sides, the presence of diffusible pigments in the medium should be noted. The type of colony is observed, yeast-like or filamentous. Yeast-like colonies of Candida on SDA B. Identification: Filamentous colonies on SDA. A. Dermatophyte. B. Aspergillus fumigatus . C. Aspergillus niger . D. Zygomycetes Microscopic Examination: For filamentous colonies , a “Needle Mount” is made using lactophenol cotton blue . Points to be noted are size, shape, septation, color of spores or the type of specialized structures upon which spores are borne. b) For yeast-like colonies : Gram stain is performed. A B Identification tests of Candida albicans: i . Germ tube test A rapid method for the identification of C. albicans is to incubate the unknown yeast in serum at 37 o C for three to four hours. Only C. albicans form germ tubes . ii. Rice-Agar-Tween test (RAT): The unknown yeast is streaked by a cut into the media of RAT. The plates are incubated at 27 o C for 48 hours. Only members of genus Candida form yeast together with pseudomycelium . If chlamydospore s are formed also, then the organism is Candida albicans . iii. Fermentation and Assimilation tests: Several commercial laboratories have developed a battery of fermentation and assimilation tests for the identification of different species of candida. The most popular of this is the API 20C system . germ tubes chlamydospores API 20C III. text:
Genetic Engineering
Q1. Restriction enzymes cut DNA at:
A. Random locations
B. Ribosomal binding sites
C. Specific recognition sequence sites
D. Start codons only
Answer: C. Specific recognition sequence sites

Q2. A cloning vector is usually:
A. Ribosome
B. Plasmid or bacteriophage
C. Endospore
D. Teichoic acid fragment
Answer: B. Plasmid or bacteriophage

Q3. Recombinant DNA is formed when:
A. A plasmid replicates independently
B. Pieces of DNA from different sources cut with same RE are joined
C. A transposon integrates into chromosome
D. Conjugation occurs between bacteria
Answer: B. Pieces of DNA from different sources cut with same RE are joined

Q4. In recombinant vaccine production, HBsAg gene is inserted into:
A. Endospore coat
B. Expression vector (plasmid)
C. Bacterial ribosome
D. Outer membrane protein
Answer: B. Expression vector (plasmid)

Q5. Viral vector vaccines (e.g., Vaccinia) work by:
A. Killing bacteria directly

 B. Carrying antigenic genes into a harmless virus to trigger immune response
C. Attaching plasmids to ribosomes
D. Altering host chromosomes permanently
Answer: B. Carrying antigenic genes into a harmless virus to trigger immune response

Bacterial Genetics – Basics
Q6. Bacterial chromosomes are typically:
A. Linear DNA
B. Circular double-stranded DNA
C. Circular RNA
D. Linear single-stranded DNA
Answer: B. Circular double-stranded DNA

Q7. Plasmids do NOT usually code for:
A. Antibiotic resistance
B. Toxin production
C. Sex pilus formation
D. Ribosomal RNA
Answer: D. Ribosomal RNA

Q8. Episomes are:
A. Plasmids integrated into chromosome
B. Transposons with resistance genes
C. Ribosomal RNA operons
D. Defective bacteriophages
Answer: A. Plasmids integrated into chromosome

Q9. Transposable elements (“jumping genes”):
A. Replicate independently of chromosome
B. Move within or between DNA molecules
C. Code only for ribosomal proteins
D. Exist only in eukaryotic cells
Answer: B. Move within or between DNA molecules

 Q10. Phenotypic variation differs from genotypic variation because:
A. Phenotypic is permanent, genotypic is reversible
B. Phenotypic is non-heritable, genotypic is heritable
C. Phenotypic requires mutagens, genotypic does not
D. Phenotypic only occurs in plasmids
Answer: B. Phenotypic is non-heritable, genotypic is heritable

Mutations
Q11. A mutation induced by UV light is:
A. Spontaneous
B. Induced
C. Transduction
D. Transformation
Answer: B. Induced

Q12. Insertion mutation is most often caused by:
A. Transposon integration
B. Exotoxin release
C. Plasmid replication
D. Ribosomal frameshift
Answer: A. Transposon integration

Genetic Transfer
Q13. Transformation is best described as:
A. Uptake of free DNA fragments from environment
B. DNA transfer via bacteriophage
C. Plasmid transfer via pilus
D. Gene integration via mutation
Answer: A. Uptake of free DNA fragments from environment

Q14. Which process requires a sex pilus?
A. Transformation
B. Conjugation
C. Transduction

 D. Transposition
Answer: B. Conjugation

Q15. In conjugation, a cell carrying the F-factor is called:
A. F+ cell
B. F- cell
C. Competent cell
D. Lysogenic cell
Answer: A. F+ cell

Q16. In generalized transduction:
A. Any bacterial gene may be transferred
B. Only specific genes adjacent to prophage are transferred
C. DNA is taken up directly from environment
D. Requires F plasmid
Answer: A. Any bacterial gene may be transferred

Q17. Specialized transduction differs because:
A. Transfers only specific bacterial genes
B. Requires plasmid
C. Involves uptake of naked DNA
D. Transfers antibiotic resistance only
Answer: A. Transfers only specific bacterial genes

Q18. For genetic transfer to be successful, foreign DNA must:
A. Form a spore
B. Enter nucleus
C. Undergo recombination with host DNA
D. Remain unintegrated
Answer: C. Undergo recombination with host DNA

Q19. Abortive genetic transfer means:
A. DNA enters cell but is not replicated
B. DNA integrates and is expressed

MCQs on Staphylococci (20 Questions)
Q1. Staphylococcus aureus is best described as:
A. Gram-negative rods
B. Gram-positive cocci in clusters
C. Gram-positive diplococci
D. Gram-negative cocci in chains
Answer: B. Gram-positive cocci in clusters

Q2. Which feature differentiates staphylococci from streptococci?
A. Beta hemolysis
B. Catalase production
C. Coagulase production
D. Capsule formation
Answer: B. Catalase production

Q3. On Mannitol salt agar, Staphylococcus aureus produces:
A. Pink colonies due to non-fermentation
B. Yellow halos due to mannitol fermentation
C. No growth because of high salt
D. Green colonies with alpha hemolysis
Answer: B. Yellow halos due to mannitol fermentation

Q4. Staphylococcus aureus is resistant to:
A. 2% NaCl
B. 5% NaCl
C. 7.5% NaCl
D. 10% NaCl
Answer: D. 10% NaCl

 Q5. The most important test to differentiate S. aureus from other staphylococci is:
A. Catalase test
B. Oxidase test
C. Coagulase test
D. Urease test
Answer: C. Coagulase test

Q6. Clumping factor in S. aureus acts by:
A. Binding fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin coat
B. Binding IgM molecules
C. Breaking down hyaluronic acid
D. Binding complement proteins
Answer: A. Binding fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin coat

Q7. Protein A in S. aureus binds to:
A. Fc portion of IgG
B. Fab portion of IgM
C. Fc portion of IgA
D. Variable region of IgE
Answer: A. Fc portion of IgG

Q8. Which enzyme allows S. aureus to survive inside phagocytes?
A. Coagulase
B. Catalase
C. Lipase
D. DNAse
Answer: B. Catalase

Q9. Which toxin is responsible for staphylococcal food poisoning?
A. TSST-1
B. Enterotoxin
C. Exfoliative toxin
D. PVL toxin
Answer: B. Enterotoxin

 Q10. Staphylococcal enterotoxin is:
A. Heat-labile
B. Heat-stable

Answer: B. Heat-stable

Q11. Scalded skin syndrome is caused by:
A. TSST-1

Answer: C. Exfoliative toxin

Q12. Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) acts as:

Answer: B. Superantigen

Answer: B. Custard pastries, potato salad, canned meats

text:
MCQs Set 4 (Viral Replication, Bacteriophage, Bacterial
Genetics)
Viral Replication
Q1. A productive viral infection is best defined as:
A. No infectious progeny formed
B. Few viral genes expressed without progeny
C. Production of new progeny virus in permissive cells
D. Viral genome integrated but not expressed
Answer: C. Production of new progeny virus in permissive cells

Q2. Abortive viral infection occurs when:
A. Virus integrates into host genome
B. Cell is non-permissive or virus is defective
C. Virus replicates fully
D. Viral genome is latent
Answer: B. Cell is non-permissive or virus is defective

Q3. Latent viral infection is characterized by:
A. Destruction of the host cell
B. No expression of viral genes at all
C. Few viral genes expressed, genome persists
D. Production of large amounts of virions
Answer: C. Few viral genes expressed, genome persists

Q4. Site of replication for most DNA viruses is:
A. Cytoplasm
B. Nucleus
C. Mitochondria
D. Ribosome
Answer: B. Nucleus

 Q5. Single-stranded negative-sense RNA viruses must carry which enzyme?
A. DNA polymerase
B. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase
C. Reverse transcriptase
D. DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Answer: B. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase

Bacteriophages
Q6. Which bacteriophage cycle leads to immediate lysis of the host cell?
A. Lysogenic cycle
B. Prophage cycle
C. Lytic cycle
D. Abortive cycle
Answer: C. Lytic cycle

Q7. A prophage is best defined as:
A. Viral particle inside cytoplasm
B. Integrated phage DNA in bacterial chromosome
C. Capsid protein of bacteriophage
D. RNA bacteriophage genome
Answer: B. Integrated phage DNA in bacterial chromosome

Q8. Lysogenic conversion of Corynebacterium diphtheriae is important because:
A. Provides resistance to antibiotics
B. Encodes the diphtheria toxin gene
C. Enhances capsule synthesis
D. Produces IgA protease
Answer: B. Encodes the diphtheria toxin gene

Q9. Generalized transduction differs from specialized transduction in that:
A. Transfers only specific genes
B. Transfers any bacterial gene
C. Requires F plasmid
D. Requires direct cell contact
Answer: B. Transfers any bacterial gene

 Q10. Which of the following is NOT a use of bacteriophages?
A. Phage therapy
B. Phage typing of bacteria
C. Genetic mapping
D. Capsule formation
Answer: D. Capsule formation

Bacterial Genetics – Chromosome & Plasmids
Q11. Bacterial chromosomes are usually:
A. Linear double-stranded DNA
B. Circular double-stranded DNA
C. Circular single-stranded RNA
D. Linear single-stranded DNA
Answer: B. Circular double-stranded DNA

Q12. Plasmids are:
A. Essential for bacterial survival
B. Extrachromosomal circular DNA molecules
C. Always integrated in chromosome
D. Coding only for ribosomal RNA
Answer: B. Extrachromosomal circular DNA molecules

Q13. R plasmids are responsible for:
A. Antibiotic resistance
B. Spore formation
C. Capsule synthesis
D. Endotoxin production
Answer: A. Antibiotic resistance

Q14. F plasmid in Gram-negative bacteria is important for:
A. Transformation
B. Transduction
C. Conjugation

 D. Sporulation
Answer: C. Conjugation

Bacterial Genetics – Transposons & Mutation
Q15. Transposable elements are also called:
A. Mutagens
B. Jumping genes
C. Conjugative plasmids
D. Episomes
Answer: B. Jumping genes

Q16. Which statement about transposons is TRUE?
A. Can replicate independently of chromosomes
B. Always encode toxins
C. Can move within or between DNA molecules
D. Require F factor for movement
Answer: C. Can move within or between DNA molecules

Q17. A spontaneous mutation is defined as:
A. Induced by chemical mutagens
B. Induced by UV radiation
C. Occurs naturally without external agents
D. Occurs only in plasmids
Answer: C. Occurs naturally without external agents

Genetic Transfer
Q18. Uptake of free DNA fragments by bacteria is:
A. Conjugation
B. Transformation
C. Transduction
D. Translation
Answer: B. Transformation

Q5. An infant with recurrent pyogenic infections is found to have a deficiency in
complement C3. Which immune process is most impaired?
a) Antigen presentation
b) Opsonization
c) NK cell cytotoxicity
d) Isotype switching
Answer: b) Opsonization
Q6. Which complement pathway is triggered directly by bacterial endotoxin (LPS)?
a) Classical pathway
b) Alternative pathway
c) Lectin pathway
d) Mannan pathway
Answer: b) Alternative pathway
Q7. A renal biopsy shows immune complex deposition with C3 consumption. Which
complement pathway is likely activated?
a) Classical
b) Alternative

 c) Lectin
d) Both classical and alternative
Answer: a) Classical
Q8. Which MHC molecule presents endogenous viral peptides to CD8+ T cells?
a) MHC-I
b) MHC-II
c) MHC-III
d) Both I and II
Answer: a) MHC-I
Q9. A patient with recurrent viral infections but normal bacterial clearance is likely
deficient in:
a) Complement C3
b) NK cells
c) B lymphocytes
d) Neutrophils
Answer: b) NK cells
Q10. A cytokine storm in COVID-19 patients is mainly due to excessive production of:
a) IL-2
b) IL-6 and TNF-α
c) IL-4
d) TGF-β
Answer: b) IL-6 and TNF-α
Q11. Interferon-α therapy is used in chronic hepatitis B. What is its main antiviral action?
a) Neutralizing virus particles

 b) Blocking viral entry receptors
c) Inducing antiviral proteins in neighboring cells
d) Directly lysing infected hepatocytes
Answer: c) Inducing antiviral proteins in neighboring cells
Q12. Which cytokine is essential for differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells into Th1 cells?
a) IL-4
b) IL-12
c) IL-10
d) IL-17
Answer: b) IL-12
Q13. A newborn presents with recurrent bacterial infections despite normal antibody
levels. Genetic testing reveals defective Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling. Which immune
function is most impaired?
a) Recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)
b) Antigen-specific B cell response
c) Class-switch recombination
d) Antigen presentation by MHC-II
Answer: a) Recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)
Q14. Which of the following is a key distinguishing feature of innate immunity compared to
adaptive immunity?
a) Specific recognition of epitopes
b) Immunological memory
c) Rapid response within minutes to hours
d) Dependence on clonal expansion
Answer: c) Rapid response within minutes to hours

Active immunity
In the active immunity, the host cells learn to
respond to foreign material, and the host actively
produces the Abs, so they last longer than the
readymade Abs given for immediate protection.
Its
major disadvantage is its slow onset especially
the primary response.
a) active natural cell
It is the state of resistance built up in an
individual following effective contact with foreign
Ags
(microorganisms or their products). The contact
can be the result of clinical or subclinical
infection.
b) Active Artificial Immunity:
Through injection of killed or attenuated
organisms, toxoids, or recombinant peptides i.e.,
immunization by vaccines.
1. Antigen presenting cells: such as dendritic cells,
macrophages and B-lymphocytes.
a-Macrophages: They are phagocytic cells which are
concerned with processing and
presentation of protein Ags to the lymphocytes.
b-Dendritic cells: They are known as the most effective
antigen presenting cells for activating
T cells. They capture, process and present antigens to Tcells,
thus initiating an adaptive immune
response.

These include:

a. CD4 effector cells:
I. Th1 cells:
- Are stimulated by intracellular pathogens and secrete
cytokines mainly IL-2 and IFN-Y.
- IL-2 acts on CD8 positive cells to enhance their
proliferation and differentiation.
- IFN-Y amplifies Th1 response and activates
macrophages.
II. Th2 cells: are activated in response to large
extracellular pathogens or allergens and
produce cytokines e.g. IL4, IL5, IL13 which promote
humoral immunity.
- The cytokines released from T helper cells can cause B
cells to isotype switch to IgG, IgA and
IgE depending on the cytokine released.

2. T lymphocytes or T- cells:

Cells involved in the specific immune response

- They originate from a stem cell in the bone marrow, mature
in the microenvironment of the
thymus where they acquire cluster of differentiation (CD)
molecules, differentiate into
committed cells expressing specific T cell receptors (TCRs).
- The thymus begins to shrink after puberty and its capacity to
produce immune cells gradually
reduces, but may not completely diminish. Also, while the
majority of T-cells mature in the
thymus, there have been reports of T-cells maturation in the
liver and intestines.

Passive immunity
Immunity is temporary, and it gives immediate
protection because of receiving preformed Abs.

- lymphocytes are important in defense against intracellular
microbes.
- Several different subsets of T cells have been described,
each with a distinct function.

text:
Classification
Streptococci can be classified by their haemolytic
activities on blood agar into:
- Alpha (α) Hemolytic streptococci: cause partial
destruction of red blood cells. Examples:
Viridans streptococci and Streptococcus
pneumoniae.
- Beta (β) Hemolytic streptococci that cause
complete lysis of the red blood cells in blood agar
resulting in a clear zone around the colonies.
Those are further grouped on the basis of their
cell-wall carbohydrate into serogroups (A-H) and
(KU).
- Non-Hemolytic streptococci are unable to
hemolyze red blood cells.

Cultural characters
Facultative anaerobe, optimum temperature for growth
37ºC.Fastidious i.e. does not grow on nutrient agar. Grows on
blood agar. Clear often wide zone of β-hemolysis surrounds
colonies on blood agar.
Biochemical activities
Like all streptococci, they are catalase negative. They are
sensitive to bacitracin which could be used for its identification
in place of antigenic study. Susceptibility to bacitracin is
determined by placing a disc saturated with bacitracin onto a
plate inoculated with Streptococcus pyogenes, after overnight
incubation, zone of inhibition of growth around bacitracin disc
will be detected.
Antigenic structure
In addition to its carbohydrate (C Ag) group A; Streptococcus
pyogenes has and three surface protein antigens (M, T and R)
that are useful in serotyping. Of these three, M protein is the
most important. M protein acts as a virulence factor by
inhibiting phagocytosis. Immunity to infection with group A
streptococci is related to the presence of type specific
antibodies to M protein. Because there are many, perhaps 150
types of M protein, a person can have repeated infections with
Streptococcus pyogenes of different M types

Toxins and enzymes and their role in virulence
1-Streptokinase (fibrinolysin)

Streptococci

It transforms the plasminogen of human plasma into plasmin,
an active proteolytic enzyme that digests fibrin and other
proteins. This enzyme works to break up and dissolve blood
clots which can block blood vessels. It can be used to lyse
thrombi in the coronary arteries of heart attack patients.
2-Hyaluronidase (spreading factor)
It splits hyaluronic acid, an important component of the
ground substance of connective tissue.
Thus, hyaluronidase facilitates the rapid spread of
Streptococcus pyogenes in skin infections (cellulitis).

3-Streptococcal deoxyribonucleases
These enzymes can depolymerize free deoxyribonucleic acid
(DNA) present in pus. This process reduces the viscosity of the
abscess material and facilitates spread of the organisms.
4-Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins
Among these is the classic erythrogenic toxin which is
associated with the rash in scarlet fever.
5-Haemolysins e.g. Streptolysin O (SLO)
It is antigenic and antibody to streptolysin O develops after
infection. Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
serum levels higher than 200 Todd are suggestive of recent
infection with Streptococcus pyogenes. It also helps in the
diagnosis of rheumatic fever.

I. Pyogenic infections
a. Localized infections:
- Streptococcal pharyngitis and tonsillitis
- Streptococcal pyoderma: local infection of superficial layers
of skin, especially in children, is
called impetigo.
b. Invasive infections:
1.Erysipelas: If the portal of entry is the skin (through minor
cuts or even scratches), erysipelas
results, with massive brawny edema and a rapidly advancing
margin of infection.
2.Cellulitis: Streptococcal cellulitis is an acute, rapidly
spreading infection of the skin and
subcutaneous tissues. It follows infection associated with mild
trauma, burns, wounds, or surgical
incisions. Pain, tenderness, swelling, and erythema occurs.
3.Necrotizing fasciitis (streptococcal gangrene): there is
extensive and very rapidly spreading
necrosis of the skin, tissues, and fascia. Bacteria enter a
wound, such as from an insect bite, a burn,
or a cut.
4.Puerperal fever: If the streptococci enter the uterus after
delivery, puerperal fever develops,

 GENERAL INTRODUCTION TO MEDICAL PARASITOLOGY
Parasitology is the area of biology concerned with the phenomenon of dependence of one living
organism on another.
A parasite is defined as a eukaryotic organism which lives on, or within another organism called
the host at whose expense the parasite obtains food and protection. Usually, the parasite causes
injury to its host.
Medical Parasitology is the subject which deals with the parasites that infect man, the diseases
they produce, clinical picture and the host responses against them. It is also concerned with the
various methods of their diagnosis, their treatment and finally their prevention and control.
Types of Parasites
Parasites can be divided on the basis of their location into:
Ectoparasites which are found attached to the skin or superficial tissues of their hosts, causing
infestation, e.g., lice, fleas and ticks.
Endoparasites which live inside their host body causing infection, as all helminths and protozoon
parasites. They either live intracellular as Toxoplasma gondii and Leishmania species or
extracellular as Ascaris lumbricoides and schistosoma species.
Endoparasites can be further subdivided according to their host relation into the following
types:
1. Obligatory parasites are those which cannot exist without a host (completely depend on the
host), e.g., Ascaris lumbricoides.
2. Facultative parasites are those which can change its life style between free-living in the
environment (soil or water) and parasitic according to the surrounding conditions, e.g.,
Strongyloides stercoralis.
3. Accidental or Incidental parasites are those which enter accidentally and can live in a host
different from their original one (unnatural host), e.g., Fasciola species in man.
4. Erratic parasites or aberrant parasites are those which wander into organs in which they are

Introduction
Medical parasitology (‫(علم الطفيليات‬: the since that is concerned with the study of
parasite that affect man directly or indirectly, the disease they produce , clinical picture and
the response against them , it is also concerned with various method of diagnosis and
treatment and finally prevention and control.

Parasite)‫)الطفيل‬: an organism which live in or within another organism called (host) for
nutrition and protection.

Parasite are classified into 3 groups:
1. Helminthology (‫)الديدان‬: study of flat and round worm

2. Protozoology (‫)وحيد الخلية‬: study of one cell parasite

1

 Module 8- parasitology (dr. shoroq)

3. Entomology (‫)الحشرات‬: study of arthropods

Types of parasites

according to relation to
host

according to habitat

A. According to habitat :
1). Endoparasite (‫)طفيليات تعيش داخل جسم االنسان‬: live inside the
body of the host e.g: tape worm (‫ )الديدان الشريطية‬live inside small intestine
of man. ‫وتسمى االصابة بهذه الحشرات‬infection

2

 Module 8- parasitology (dr. shoroq)

2). Ectoparasite (‫)طفيليات تعيش خارج جسم االنسان‬:
Live on the body surface of the host e.g: ticks (‫ )القراد‬- lice (‫)القمل‬. ‫وتسمى‬
‫االصابة بهذه الحشرات‬infestation

B. According to relation with the host
1). Obligatory parasite: completely dependant on the
host and can’t exist without it e.g hookworms ‫الديدان الخطافية‬
‫طفيل مجبر على التطفل على كائن اخر وال يمكنه الحياة بدونه‬

2). Facultative parasite: are those which are able to exist
independently of their host, leading a free living life in soil or
water e.g strongyloid stercoralis. ‫طفيل‬
‫قادر على الحياة داخل جسم االنسان ويستطيع ايضا ان يعيش حر وبمفرده‬

3

 Module 8- parasitology (dr. shoroq)

3). Accidental or Incidental parasite:
are those which enter accidently and can live a host different
from their original one . ‫طفيل تتطفل عن طريق الخطأ على كائن غير العائل‬
‫االساسي الخاص به‬

4). Opportunistic parasite (‫)طفيليات انتهازية‬: are those
of low pathogenicity and become highy pathogenic in patients
with a defective immune system. (can produce disease in
immuno-compromised host e.g AIDS – Cancer but in immunocompetent hosts it becomes latent or produce self limiting
disease)
‫طفيليات تنتهز فرصة نقص المناعة وتهاجم الجسم بشدة ولكن في االصحاء ال تسبب‬
‫أعراض شديدة‬

Types of host
1. Definitive host: (‫ )العائل االساسي‬is the host in which the adult stage of the
parasite lives, or in which sexual reproduction takes place. ‫العائل الذي يحتوي بداخلة على‬
‫المرحلة الناضجة من الطفيل ويحدث داخلة التكاثر الجنسي‬

2. Intermediate host: ) ‫ )العائل الوسيط‬is the host in which the immature or
larval stage of the parasite are found, or in which the parasite multiples asexually.
‫العائل الذي يحتوي بداخله على المراحل غير الناضجة من الطفيل (اليرقات) ويحدث داخلة التكاثر الالجنسي‬

3. Reservoir host: (‫ )العائل الذي يخزن المرض‬is an animal host which has the
same stages of the parasite as man. They play the same role in parasite life cycle as
man, thus help to maintain parasites existence in nature. ‫حيوان غير االنسان يحتوي‬
‫بداخله على نفس المراحل من الطفيل التي يحتويها االنسان ويلعب نفس الدور الذي يلعبه االنسان في دورة‬
‫حياة الطفيل وبالتالي يحافظ على الطفيل من االنقراض‬

4. Vector: (‫ )هو اي حشرة تنقل المرض الى االنسان‬it is an arthropods host that
transmits parasites from one host to another (vector may be definitive or
intermediate host).

text: Introduction to Medical Protozoology What is the definition of protozoa ? Unicellular microorganisms of different sizes and forms Free-living or parasitic Capable of performing all functions of life Q. Which of the following is NOT true for protozoa? a. They are unicellular microorganisms. b. They may be free-living or parasitic. c. They are capable of performing all functions. d. They are totally pathogenic organisms. Answer: (d) What are the general characteristic features of protozoa ? What are the functions of the ectoplasm and the endoplasm of protozoa ? Ectoplasm :  Movement, ingestion of food, excretion, secretion, respiration and protection. Endoplasm :  Digestion and reproduction. What are the contents of the protozoan endoplasm? Nucleus Food vacuoles Stored food material in the form of glycogen . Contractile vacuoles for regulation of osmotic pressure as in ciliates and free-living amoebae. What are the types of nuclei in protozoa ? In the vesicular nucleus: chromatin granules are concentrated in the karyosome (nucleolus). They may be also dispersed on the nuclear membrane. In compact nucleus: the chromatin granules nearly fill the nucleus with minimal nucleoplasm. What is the classification of protozoa? Ciliophora ( Ciliates ) Apicomplexa ( Coccidia ) Sarcomastigophora   Sarcodina Mastigophora Cilia No organ of locomotion Pseudopodia Flagella How is movement in protozoa carried out? By pseudopodia as in sarcodina ( amoebae) By flagella as in mastigophora (flagellates) By cilia as in ciliophora (ciliates) Some protozoa engulf solid material using pseudopodia (amoebae). Some have a slit-like mouth opening (ciliates). Others feed by diffusion of food particles through the cell membrane ( flagellates) . How does food ingestion occur in protozoa? Diffusion through the ectoplasm (flagellates) How does excretion occur in protozoa? By the aid of contractile vacuoles (ciliates) Pigment granules deposition in the endoplasm ( Plasmodium ). How does secretion occur in protozoa? Secretion of histolytic enzymes for tissue penetration ( Entamoeba histolytica ) Secretion of the cyst wall for protection and transmission to another host ( Entamoeba histolytica & Giardia lamblia ). How does reproduction occur in protozoa?  Asexual reproduction : Binary fission: - Random as in amoeba - Longitudinal as in flagellates Multiple fission ( schizogony ) as in Plasmodium . The nucleus divides repeatedly before division of the cytoplasm leading to many daughter cells  Sexual reproduction: The fusion of male & female gametes to form the zygote as in Plasmodium. Q. Which part of the protozoa is responsible for the vital functions ? Cytoplasm Nucleoplasm Protoplasm Endoplasm Answer: (c ) Q. Which of the following is not true regarding the function of the protozoan ectoplasm? Movement and ingestion of food Excretion and secretion Respiration and protection Reproduction Answer: (d) Q. Which of the following is true regarding the vital activities of the protozoan endoplasm? Excretion and protection Digestion and reproduction Movement Ingestion of food Answer: (b) Q. Protozoa are divided into three phyla according to which of the following factors? The number of nuclei The organs of locomotion The secretory substances The metabolic activities Answer: (b) Q. How does excretion occur in flagellates? By the aid of contractile vacuole By diffusion By deposition of pigment granules By pseudopodia Answer: (b) Q. How does food ingestion occur in Sarcodina ? By pseudopodia By slit like opening By diffusion By the aid of contractile vacuole Answer: (a) What are the characters of sarcodina ? Life cycle of a Sarcodina ( Entamoeba histolytica ) Transmitted directly ; do not require an arthropod vector. Man can be infected by ingestion of mature cysts in contaminated food or drink. Q. What is the organ of locomotion in sarcodina ? Pseudopodia Flagella Cilia Apical complex Answer: (a) Q. To which of the following categories does Entamoeba histolytica belong? Apicomplexa Mastigophora Sarcodina Ciliophora Answer: (c) Q. What is the infective stage of Sarcodina ? Mature cyst Promastigote Oocyst Trophozoite Answer: (a) Q. Which of the following parasitic stages is responsible for the pathological lesions in Sarcodina ? Cyst Trophozoite Egg Larva Answer: (b) Q. How can Sarcodina be transmitted? Ingestion Inhalation Sexually Skin penetration Answer: (a) What are the characters of Mastigophora (flagellates)? Where do mastigophora (flagellates) live in their definitive hosts? The small intestine (Intestinal flagellates as Giardia lamblia ) The genito-urinary tract ( Trichomonas vaginalis ) * Both are transmitted directly without a vector Blood and tissues: (tissue and blood flagellates as Leishmania spp.) *They require arthropod vectors for transmission. Life cycle of an intestinal flagellate ( G. lamblia ) Genito -urinary flagellates ( Trichomonas vaginalis ), are sexually transmitted . life cycle of a blood and tissue flagellate ( Leishmania species) Q. Leishmania species belong to which of the following categories? Apicomplexa Mastigophora Sarcodina Ciliophora Answer: (b) Q. What are the infective stages of tissue flagellates ( Leishmania species)? Larvae Mature eggs Mature cysts Promastigotes Answer: (d) Q. The amastigote is a morphologic form of which of the following protozoa? Apicomplexa Blood and tissue flagellates Amoebae Intestinal flagellates Answer: (b) Q. What are the diagnostic stages of intestinal flagellates? Larvae Mature eggs Mature cysts Promastigotes Answer: (c) Q. How can tissue and blood flagellates be transmitted? Ingestion Inhalation Direct skin penetration Skin penetration through arthropods Answer: (d) Ingestion Inhalation Sexual relation Skin penetration Answer: (c) Q. How can genito -urinary flagellates be transmitted? What are the characters of Ciliophora ? What are the characters of Apicomplexa (coccidia )? text: MYIASIS What is Myiasis? What is the cause of Myiasis? Which of the following is the cause of myiasis? Adult flies Eggs of flies Larvae of flies Pupae of flies In myiasis, can maggots pupate in infested human tissues? Yes No How can we classify myiasis? Obligatory (Specific) Specific (Obligatory) Myiasis The fly larvae are obliged to live and develop on or in living tissue. Female flies deposit their eggs on dry soil or sand contaminated with human urine or excreta. They can also lay their eggs on soiled clothes or clothes that were left to dry outdoors. Once these clothes are worn without ironing, eggs hatch and the larvae, aided by their powerful oral hooks , bury themselves completely under the skin except for their posterior spiracles . Larvae can penetrate healthy tissues and unbroken skin, especially in children Specific myiasis Cordylobia and Dermatobia flies Facultative (semi-specific) myiasis Adults feed on decaying flesh, and eggs (or larvae) are deposited there. However, they can develop in a host if their entry is facilitated by the presence of a wound, ulcer or by inflamed eyes and ears as they are attracted by their offensive discharge . Larvae feed on wound exudate Sarcophaga, Calliphora and Lucilia flies Accidental Myiasis Eggs or larvae of higher Diptera are deposited on food material such as cheese and vegetables and these are then accidentally ingested leading to intestinal myiasis. Accidental Myiasis Eggs can be deposited around the anal canal or urogenital orifice and the larvae can travel up these passages leading to intestinal or urogenital myiasis. Musca domestica fly Which of the following can be infested in obligatory myiasis? Skin ulcers only Inflamed eyes only Intact healthy skin Dead bodies only What is the type of myiasis in which a fly deposits its larvae around the urethra, and they find their way up the genito urinary tract? Semi-specific Specific Accidental Creeping What attracts flies in facultative myiasis? Colour of the skin Offensive discharges Blood Blood and offensive discharge Which of the following attracts Cordylobia fly? Urine-soaked clothes Blood-stained clothes Offensive odour of pus Animal carcasses Which fly causes obligatory myiasis? Dermatobia Musca domestica c. Sarcophaga d. Lucilia How can we classify myiasis? What is the mechanism of intestinal myiasis? Flies deposit their eggs or larvae on human food and the larvae find their way to the intestine facilitated by lowered gastric acidity. Flies can deposit eggs or larvae on the anus (during sleep or defecation in open latrines). Maggots will be found in stool or vomitus. Common in children in rural areas. Musca domestica , Lucilia , Calliphora & Sarcophaga What is urogenital myiasis? Larvae may enter through the urinary and genital orifices or through lesions on these orifices. Inflammation with pus, mucous and blood in urine can happen, and obstruction to the urine flow with pain can also occur. Maggots could be found in urine. Musca domestica , Calliphora & Sarcophaga How can we classify cutaneous myiasis? Flies deposit their eggs or larvae on neglected wounds or ulcers . Sarcophaga , Calliphora & Lucilia flies Traumatic (Wound) Myiasis Larvae invade intact skin (near hair follicles) producing itching, severe pain, boil like swelling and serous exudate. Cordylobia & Dermatobia flies Furuncular Myiasis Larvae accidentally invade unbroken skin of ( unnatural host ) and wander in the dermal tissue forming serpentine lesion with papules and pustules. Creeping Myiasis Hypoderma & Gasterophilus flies Ocular, Nasopharyngeal & Aural Myiasis Maggots can invade the conjunctiva causing severe pain in the eye followed by conjunctivitis, corneal ulcers or even panophthalmitis . Maggots may find their way to the nose and cause obstruction with persistent bloody purulent discharge. Eggs or larvae of flies are deposited in external auditory meatus cause otitis externa. Later, larvae invade middle ear, inner ear or even mastoid sinuses. External: Ocular, Nasopharyngeal & Aural myiasis CEREBRAL MYIASIS Sarcophaga , Calliphora , Lucilia & Musca domestica flies Ocular, nasopharyngeal or aural myiasis are considered as semi-specific myiasis if the flies are attracted to offensive inflammatory discharges in these sites. However , if the larvae of adult flies invaded healthy, non-inflamed eyes, nose and ears, the type of myiasis in these cases is considered specific myiasis. Which myiasis happens when flies deposit their eggs or larvae on human food or the anus? Urogenital Aural Nasopharyngeal Intestinal Which myiasis could be prevented by protection of food from flies? Nasopharyngeal Intestinal Aural Urogenital When a child sleeps exposed outdoors in a rural area, which myiasis is the result? Intestinal Urogenital Aural Intestinal, urogenital and aural Which describes creeping myiasis? Skin is invaded by larvae of animal flies Skin is invaded by larvae of human flies A hair follicle is invaded by the larva of human flies A body orifice is invaded by the larvae of animal flies What type of myiasis involves an invasion of the hair follicles? Traumatic Creeping Furuncular Aural Which myiasis can lead to cerebral myiasis? Nasopharyngeal Furuncular Creeping Aural Nasopharyngeal and aural Is lowered gastric acidity a risk factor for intestinal myiasis? Yes No Do dysuria and haematuria constitute main symptoms in patients with urogenital myiasis? Yes No Can any site on skin surface be infested with furuncular myiasis? Yes No Diagnosis of myiasis Diagnosis Treatment of myiasis Removal of the larvae by Surgical removal. Stimulation of the larva to leave the wound by Vaseline. Larvae in body openings can be removed by applying chloroform/ether. Treatment Intestinal myiasis can be treated by colonic wash using a cathartic agent. Albendazole , mebendazole and levamisole can be effective in certain cases. Urogenital myiasis can be treated by increased water intake, urinary antiseptics and antibiotics. Prevention of myia

text: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم I. Direct Methods for Diagnosis of Parasitic Infections Mention the various samples to be examined in the parasitology laboratory . Collection of samples should be in a wide-mouthed container with a screw top. The sample should not be contaminated with urine or water, since: urine  can destroy some parasites water  may contain ciliates which can cause false diagnosis. - No antibiotics or barium enema, both will mask any parasitic infection. - Three stool samples should be examined as one sample every other day. Principle: Most helminthic eggs and protozoal cysts are heavier than the suspending liquid and so they sink and concentrate at the bottom of the tube i.e sediment , which is taken and examined. Sedimentation techniques Principle: This involves the use of solutions that have higher specific gravity than the organisms to be floated so that the organisms rise to the top and the debris sinks to the bottom giving a cleaner preparation. Floatation techniques The floatation procedure permits the separation of protozoan cysts and eggs of some helminths by using concentrated saline or zinc sulphate solution 33%. The main disadvantage is that heavy eggs and operculated eggs do not concentrate well with this technique. These can be used for identification of intestinal protozoa Additional Techniques Used for Identification of Intestinal Parasites The correlation of egg production with adult worm burden is possible in intestinal nematodes , e.g., Ascaris lumbricoides . Estimation of intensity of infection of schistosomes as a test of cure after treatment is also important. a. Pigment granule

12. Which of the following is not typically involved in protozoan metabolism but rather

a. Chromatoid body

c. Glycogen vacuole
d. Residual body

a. Mechanical
b. Cyclodevelopmental
c. Propagative
d. Cyclopropagative
Answer: c. Propagative
17. Which type of transmission is characterized by the passive transfer of a parasite
from one host to another without any development or reproduction occurring in the
vector?
a. Cyclodevelopmental
b. Propagative
c. Mechanical
d. Cyclopropagative
Answer: c. Mechanical

b. Miracidium

 d. Encysted metacercaria

‫)‪ )Second intermediate host‬لحد ماٌٌجى البنى ادم ٌاكل السمك دى ‪‬‬

‫الجنسٌا وده بٌكون فى ال ‪Intermediate Host‬‬

text:
Antimicrobial drugs are groups of synthetic, semisynthetic, or naturally occurring chemicals
that selectively inhibit specific organisms causing infectious diseases. Antimicrobial drugs are
intended to eliminate foreign organisms from healthy tissues of the patient without effects on the
normal tissue cells of the host. This essential property of these drugs is called selective toxicity,
which is relative, rather than absolute, requiring that the concentration of the drug be carefully
controlled to attack the microorganisms while still being tolerated by the host.
In the following chapters, the indicated topics will be covered:
 Antibacterial Drugs
 Antifungal Drugs
 Antiviral Drugs
 Rational use of antimicrobial agents

ANTIBACTERIAL DRUGS

Specific Urinary Antiseptic Drugs

I.

CELL WALL SYNTHESIS INHIBITORS

Figure 1 :Classification of cell wall synthesis inhibitors

 Beta-lactam Antibiotics
General features of Beta-lactams:
 They all have a β-lactam ring in their chemical structure, that makes them effective
antimicrobials.
 None of beta-lactams has activity against Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
(MRSA), except Ceftaroline (5th generation cephalosporin).
 None of them has activity against atypical intracellular organisms.
 They exhibit time-dependent killing: Their efficacy depends on the duration during which
the drug concentration is above the MIC.
 All are bactericidal.

A. PENICILLINS
Penicillins are among the most widely effective and the least toxic antibacterial drugs. Members
of this family differ from one another in their source, antimicrobial spectrum, stability to
stomach acid, and susceptibility to bacterial degradation enzymes
(Β-lactamases).
Classification:

(natural penicillins)

and

Table 1: Classification of penicillins
Pharmacokinetics:
- Penicillins distribute well throughout the body, but they penetrate poorly into CSF and serous
cavities, however infected serous membranes are more permeable, e.g. in meningitis,
penicillins penetrate well.
- All penicillins cross the placental barrier, but none have been shown to have teratogenic
effects. They can be safely used during pregnancy. Penicillins enter breast milk in small
amounts. Their use is usually considered compatible with breastfeeding.
- The primary route of excretion is renal, therefore, patients with impaired renal function must
have dosage regimens adjustment according to creatinine clearance.

 - Nafcillin and oxacillin, are primarily eliminated by non-renal routes, namely hepatic
inactivation and excretion in the bile, dose adjustment is not required in patients with renal
insufficiency.
1. Narrow spectrum beta-lactamase sensitive penicillins (Natural penicillins)

They include penicillin G and penicillin V.
Spectrum:
They are effective against Gram-positive cocci, Gram-positive bacilli, some Gram-negative cocci
(Neisseria meningitides), non-beta lactamase producing anaerobes, and Treponema palladium.
Many bacterial species become resistant either by producing beta lactamases (e.g.,
Staphylococcus aureus) or alteration of penicillin binding protein (e.g., Streptococcus
pneumoniae).

text:
Disorders of the Gall
Bladder
By
Prof. Mona Abdel-Hadi

 • Disorders of the biliary tract are extremely
common. Over 95% of them are directly
attributed to gall bladder stones, or
cholecystitis.

 Cholelithiasis
• They affect 10-20% of all adult populations in
developed countries.
• Types:
* Cholesterol stone: they constitute more than
80% of gall stones, they are either pure
cholesterol stones (rarc) or mixed stones (most
common constituting about 80% of gall stones).
+ Pigment stones: They constitute about 20% of
gallstones.

 Risk factors
Cholesterol stones
•Bile formation is the only significant pathway for climination of
excess cholesterol from the body, either as free cholesterol or as bile
salts. Cholesterol is rendered water soluble by aggregation with bile
salts and lecithins. When cholesterol concentrations exceed the
solubilizing capacity of bile (supersaturation), cholesterol can no
longer remain dispersed and crystallizes out of solution.
• They result from either
• Increased cholesterol level or
* Decreased bile salts in bile

 MRDICIVE ‫ايح ةيلك‬
EXCELTY OF
Nephrotic syndrome (NS)
It is a clinical presentation characterized by:
• Heavy proteinuria (23.5 gram protein /24 hrs in adults)
• Hypoproteinemia
• Generalized edema
• Hypercholesterolemia
• Lipiduria

 MRDICIVE‫ايح ةيلك‬
EXCELTY OF
Pathogenesis:
• Heavy proteinuria: due to initial derangement of the glomerular capillary wall which result in increase in capillary
permeability with daily heavy loss of protein in urine.
• Hypoproteinemia: is secondary to daily heavy loss of protein
• Generalized edema: is due to decrease in serum protein (hypoproteinemia) with subsequent decrease in plasma osmotic
pressure. This will lead to escape of fluid in the interstitial tissue (edema) with subsequent hypovolemia and diminished
glomerular filtration rate. This will lead to compensatory secretion of aldosterone leading to salt and water retention
(generalized edema).
• Hyperlipidemia: is due to the triggering effect of hypoalbuminemia leading to increase synthesis of lipoproteins in the liver
• Lipiduria: is due to increase GBM permeability to lipoproteins

 MEDICI٧E/ ‫بطا ميلك‬
Cause of nephrotic syndrome:
• There are many causes of glomerular injury that clinically leads to
nephrotic syndrome.
• Some of them the target is primary glomerular (primary glomerular
causes) others are due to systemic diseases that affect the
glomeruli as well as other tissues in the body (Secondary systemic
diseases)

HAEMATEMESIS (Vomiting of Blood)
The blood is dark brown, mixed with food, its pH is acidic. The brown colouration is due to acid hematin.

Causes:
1. Oesophageal causes:

a. Oesophageal varices in portal hypertension. It is the most
frequent cause in the oesophagus.
b. Carcinoma of the oesophagus.
c. Reflux oesophagitis with ulceration.
d. Oesophageal perforation (traumatic or post endoscopic).

2. Gastric causes:

3. Duodenal causes:
a. Peptic ulcer.
b. Duodenal malignancy.

4. Generalized diseases:

a. Chronic gastric peptic ulcer — most frequent gastric cause. a. Bleeding disorders.
b. Acute gastritis with ulcers.
d. Tumours of the stomach, especially gastric carcinoma.

NTESTINAL BILHARZIASIS
Infective granuloma caused by Schistosoma mansoni.

Pathogenesis and tissue reaction:





Lesions heaviest in rectum; decrease upward.
Submucosa most affected (rich blood supply).
Pathology due to deposition of Schistosoma eggs.
Eggs induce granulomatous inflammatory reaction (cell-mediated immunity).

Morphology:
1. Oedema, hyperemia, pinpoint hemorrhages due to escape of ova or toxic injury.
2. Bilharzial nodule: smallest lesion; coalescence of granulomas.
3. Sandy patches: calcified eggs in submucosa; surrounded by fibrosis; mucosa becomes atrophic;
dirty yellow patches like sandpaper.

3. Bilharzial polyps:
Most common at rectum; due to large egg deposition.
May be sessile, pedunculated, branching, or simple.

4. Bilharzial ulcers:
Due to:


Atrophy of mucosa over sandy patches (ischemic necrosis).

 

Sloughing of mucosa over polyps.
Ulcers are multiple, superficial, small, irregular; dirty floor; moth-eaten appearance.

5. Bilharzial mass:
Large ova deposition in subserosa → bilharzial mass → granulomatous reaction.
Mass may mimic cancer colon but does not obstruct (subserosal).

Complications of intestinal bilharziasis:
1. Chronic blood loss → anemia.
2. Bilharzial Hepatic Fibrosis (BHF): ova/worms → portal circulation → portal tracts of liver.
3. Lesions are not precancerous.

INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE (IBD)
IBD = Crohn disease + ulcerative colitis.

Etiology and pathogenesis:

Loss of balance between:
1. Activators of immune system (microbes, dietary antigens).
2. Host defenses that regulate inflammation.
Exact cause unknown. Theories:
1. Genetic predisposition (family history in 40%).
2. Abnormal mucosal structure → ↑ permeability, altered mucoproteins.
3. Abnormal immune reactivity → inappropriate activation by luminal antigens.
4. Inflammation final pathway → chronic tissue damage.

Definition:

A transmural granulomatous inflammatory disease that may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract but
most often involves the small intestine and colon.

Epidemiology:




More common in western developed populations, rare in Asia and Africa.
Age incidence: any age; peak in teens & 20s + minor peak in 50s–60s.
Women are more affected than men.

Any part of the GIT , but most common sites are:
1. Ileum and caecum 50%.
2. Small intestine alone 15%.
3. Colon alone 20%.
4. Anorectum 15%.
Two main features characterize Crohn disease:
1. Inflammation is transmural (all layers of
bowel wall).
2. Inflammation is discontinuous (skip lesions).

In the diseased bowel segment:
1. Mesentery: thickened, edematous, sometimes
fibrotic.
2. Mesenteric lymph nodes: enlarged, firm.
3. Mesenteric fat: wraps around surface (creeping
fat).
4. Serosa: granular, dull gray.
5. Intestinal wall: rubbery & thick due to edema,

6. Intestinal lumen: narrowed (x-ray string sign).

 Spared mucosa becomes nodular → cobblestone appearance (oedema + surrounding fibrosis).
 Deep fissures → adhesions → fistulae or sinus tracts → free perforation or abscess can occur.

text:
**DISEASES OF THE STOMACH

GASTRITIS: Inflammation of gastric mucosa may be acute or chronic.

I) Acute gastritis:

It is an acute transient inflammation of the gastric mucosa.

Pathogenesis (causes):

Imbalance between mucosal damaging and
defense factors.
1- Heavy and chronic use of non-steroidal antiinflammatory drug (NSAID) particularly
aspirin.
2- Excessive alcohol consumption.
3- Heavy smoking.
4- Cancer chemotherapy & irradiation.
5- Infections.
6- Ischemia and shock.
7- Ingestion of acid and alkali.

Morphology:
Grossly:

Diffuse edema + hyperemia of the gastric mucosa, with or without
superficial erosions/ulcerations.

Microscopically:


In mild cases, the gastric mucosal surface is intact. The lamina
propria is edematous, congested + infiltration by acute
inflammatory cells.



In severe cases, additionally, multiple erosions (loss of surface
epithelium that does not cross the muscularis mucosa, not an ulcer)
+usually hemorrhage → "acute erosive hemorrhagic gastritis".

Clinical features:



Epigastric pain with nausea and vomiting.
Occasionally, it may present by hematemesis, melena, or even fatal
blood loss.

2) Chronic gastritis

Damage of the gastric glands and mucosal atrophy + intestinal metaplasia, usually in the absence of erosions.
→ dysplastic and → carcinoma, i.e. it is a precancerous condition.

Etiologic classification:
I-Type A: Autoimmune gastritis associated with pernicious anemia. 10%
II-Type B: Associated with chronic infections especially Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori).90%

 Type A: Immunologic (autoimmune) gastritis
Epidemiology:

More common in western communities.

Site: body and fundus with sparing of the antrum.
Cause and pathogenesis:

Immune-mediated damage →CD4+ T cells →B cells → anti-parietal cell and anti-intrinsic factor antibodies.
+ Cytotoxic T cells damage parietal cells.

Morphology:

Chronic inflammatory infiltrate around parietal cells →
progressive loss → replaced by mucous cells.
→ atrophic mucosa and intestinal metaplasia.
Early: readdened and coarse + thickened rugae
Late: atrophied , thinned and flattened

Complications:

1- Loss of parietal cells → reduced HCl → G-cell hyperplasia
→ high gastrin.
2- High gastrin → ECL hyperplasia → ↑ neuroendocrine
tumors.
3- Intestinal metaplasia → ↑ gastric adenocarcinoma.
4- Vitamin B12 deficiency → pernicious anemia.

Type B: Chronic gastritis or H. pylori gastritis
Epidemiology: developing countries; persists throughout life.
Pathogenesis:

The bacillus adheres to gastric mucosal surface and does not invade the mucosa. It leads to damage as it:
1- Proinflamatory cytokones (IL-1 + TNF)→ Recruits neutrophils → toxic chemicals.
2- Induces chronic mucosal inflammation, by bacterial enzymes and toxins (proteases and urease).
3- Retards healing of damaged gastric mucosa and induce hyperacidity

Morphology:

It starts in the antrum → progressively involves the body and fundus → pan-gastritis.

Grossly:

The mucosa: reddened and has a coarser texture than normal.
The inflammatory infiltrate → thickening of the mucosal folds.
With long-standing → atrophic → thinned and flattened.

Microscopically:





In early cases: lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltrate the superficial part of the gastric mucosa.
Active infection → neutrophilic infiltration of both the lamina propria and antral mucosal glands.
Late cases: inflammation involves the deep mucosa.
Lymphoid follicles with reactive germinal centers in the deeper layers of the gastric mucosa.
Deep mucosal involvement is associated with destruction of the antral glands, with replacement
fibrosis and intestinal metaplasia (Chronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia).

 Effects and complications:

1- Gastric lymphoma (H. pylori induced lymphoid tissue proliferation).
2- Gastric adenocarcinoma (arising from dysplasia of metaplastic epithelium).
3- Increased incidence of gastric peptic ulcers and delayed peptic ulcer healing.

Leukoplakia

Precancerous lesions of oral cavity

Definition:

▪ A white patch or plaque that cannot be scrapped off and cannot be
characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease and
(defined by exclusion) of other known white or red lesions.

Clinical Picture:

▪ Oral leukoplakia is uncommon, less than 1% of adults.
▪ Associated with high tobacco use, such as Southeast Asia, usually in males above 40 years of age.
▪ Usually asymptomatic and are initially noticed by a dentist during a routine examination.

Morphology:
Grossly:

- Solitary or multiple white patches often with sharply demarcated borders.
- Anywhere in the oral cavity (favored locations are the buccal mucosa, floor of the mouth, ventral
surface of the tongue, palate and gingiva).

Microscopically:

- There is hyperkeratosis ( ↑ keratin or new keratin) and
acanthosis (↑brickle layer)
- The hyperplastic epithelium → benign or dysplastic →
carcinoma in situ.
- The underlying subepithelial tissue (no invasion) but
chronic inflammatory cells.

Prognosis:

4 -17% → squamous cell carcinoma within 20 years.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Benign tumours:
▪ Squamous cell papilloma (from surface epithelium).
▪ Angioma: might be hemangioma (blue) or lymphangioma (colorless).might cause

diffuse enlargement of the lip (macrocheilia)

 Squamous cell carcinoma:

Malignant tumours:

▪ Squamous cell carcinoma→ The commonest malignant tumour of the oral cavity
▪ Aggressive tumour →90% of oral malignancy , 95% of H&N cancers and 6th most common
neoplasm worldwide
▪ It arises anywhere, but is especially noticed on the lips and lateral borders of the tongue.

Pathogenesis: [predisposing factors]:multifactorial:
A. Tobacco smoking: the risk is magnified in alcoholics
B. Human papilloma virus infection (HPV 16) ‫هام‬: 50% of oropharyngeal cancers,tonsils, the base of
the tongue
C. Family history of head and neck cancer.
D. Actinic radiation (sunlight) and pipe smoking (the lower lip).
N.B: chronic irritation of the mucosa by ill-fitting dentures, jagged teeth could act as a "promoter "of
oral cancer in much the same way as alcohol does (not direct oncogenic or initiator).
Sites:

▪ SCC may arise anywhere in the oral cavity.
▪ Favored locations:
- Ventral surface of the tongue.
- Lower lip.
- Floor of the mouth.
- Soft palate.
- Gingiva.

Morphology:
Grossly:

- Starts as a painless ulcer that becomes painful.
- It has raised everted edges, hard indurated base, necrotic floor.

Microscopically

- well diffrentiated SCC with keratin pearls up to poorly
diffrentiated SCC with pleomorphic cells
- precursors as dysplasia and carinoma in situ are also seen
- The stroma is desmoplastic + chronic inflammatory cells.
▪ HNSCC is an aggressive epithelial malignancy.

Spread:

• Local spread: to the surrounding oral structures.
• Lymphatic spread: To submental, submandibular and
cervical lymph nodes (may be occult)
• Blood spread: Rare and late to the lung.

Causes of death:

• Inhalation bronchopneumonia from sepsis.
• Cancer cachexia and starvation.

 Prognosis:

survival→ less than 50% in the past 50 years.
▪ So, the early detection of all premalignant lesions is critical for the long-term survival.

 Inflammation of the Breast
1- Acute Mastitis "Diffuse"& Breast Abscess "Localized":
Def: acute inflammation of the breast commonly occurring during lactation.
Causes: nipple cracks & fissures during early weeks of nursing.
Pathogenesis: Obstruction of duct system by inspissated secretions
 stasis of milk  good media of 2ry infection  suppuration.

Organisms: * Staph. aureus  localized abscess "single, multiple".
* Streptococci  diffuse inflammation.

Gross: Swollen, red breast.
Microscopic: diffuse infiltration by acute inflammation cells.
Or localized cavity filled by pus + surrounding fibrous tissue.

Treatment: appropriate antibiotics, rarely surgical drainage.
Fate:

1- Resolution  no or little fibrosis.
2- Fibrosis  retraction of skin & nipple.

(DD)

2-Chronic Mastitis:
(Mammary duct ectasia – Plasma cell mastitis)
Def: Dilation of the main collecting ducts in the sub-areolar region which filled
with secretions  inspissated  obstruction  chronic inflammation
 rupture  fibrosis.

Incidence: multiparous pri-menopausal ♀ 5th or 6th decade.
Microscopic:

Ducts  dilated, contains debris & lipid-laden macrophage.
♣ If rupture  peri-ductal inflammatory cells "P,L" & fibrosis.

C/P: nipple discharge + hard mass & retraction dt fibrosis. (DD)

-1-

 3-Fat necrosis:
Def: inflammatory reaction dt rupture of fat cells & spill of fat  palpable mass.
Causes:

- Trauma

- Surgery

- Radiation therapy.

Gross: ill defined nodule, firm, grayish white with chalky white foci of calcification
 surrounded or replaced by fibrosis.

Microscopic: - Center: necrotic fat cells.
- Surrounded by lipid laden macrophages, PNL, lymphocytes, FBGC.
- Fibrosis & dystrophic calcification.

C/P: Solid irregular hard mass + nipple retraction.

(DD)

4- Granulomatous Mastitis:
1- A part of systemic granulomatous dis as TB, sarcoidosis.
2- Granulomatous lobular mastitis = idiopathic G. M.
▪ Uncommon
▪ Only in parous ♀.
▪ Multiple granulomas within breast lobules.
▪ Contain lipid vacuoles surrounded by neutrophiles.
▪ Treatment by antibiotics + steroids.

-2-

 Benign Epithelial Lesions
3 Groups with different risk for malignant transformation.

(1) Non Proliferative Breast Changes
Fibrocystic Changes of the breast
Def: A spectrum of macroscopic & microscopic changes in the ♀ breast,
characterized by cysts formation, fibrosis & adenosis.

Cause: Exaggerated response of breast tissue to cyclic hormonal (estrogen)
changes stimulations that occurs in the normal menstrual cycle.

Incidence:
- The most common cause of palpable masses in the ♀ breast.
- Age: reproductive life 20-50y &↓ after menopause.

Site: Bilateral & multifocal but one breast may be more diseased than the other.
Microscopic:
a- Cyst formation:

♦ Different size & shape
 Small cysts lined by cuboidal or columnar epithelium.
 Larger cysts lined by flattened or atrophic epithelium.
 Apocrine metaplasia in many cysts:
Lined by large polygonal cell with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm.
 Calcification is common.

b- Fibrosis:

 Cysts rupture  material release into adjacent stroma  chronic inflammation
with lymphocytic infiltration  Fibrosis.

c- Adenosis: ↑ No. of acini within some lobules.
Gross:
 Bilat & multifocal (Why ?).
 Involved area  ill defined with ↑ nodularity = Masses:
 Firm, Irregular & Whitish dt fibrosis.
 Contain cysts variable sizes from mm to several cms.
 Filled with serous turbid fluid.
 Unopened cysts are brown to blue "blue dome cysts".
 The secretions in the cysts may calcify
 micro-calcifications in Mammogram.

 Thyroid Gland
Goiter
Def: Enlargement of the thyroid gland.
Causes: 1- Simple

Simple Diffuse Colloid goiter (Non Toxic)
Def: Diffuse enlargement of thyroid, not associated with ↑or ↓ function (normal)
& dt enlargement of follicles which are filled with colloid called "colloid goiter"

Pathogenesis:
Absolute or relative dietary iodine deficiency
Or any condition interfere with T3 & T4 synthesis

Impaired synthesis of thyroid hormone

Compensatory TSH increase

Hypertrophy & hyperplasia of gland's follicles
Goiter

↑ hormones up to normal

Types:
1- Endemic colloid goiter: ▪ Absolute I2 deficiency in soil, water & food.
▪ Affecting > 10% of population.

2- Sporadic colloid goiter:

(less common)
▪ Associated with conditions interfere with hormones synthesis:
a- Idiopathic.
b- Hereditary enzymatic defects
c- Intake of goitrogentic substance "cauliflower, cabbage, turnip or cassava".

▪ Also, more common in ♀ & during puberty or pregnancy dt ↑ physiologic demand

Morphology:
1- Hyper plastic stage:
Gross: diffuse symmetrical enlargement.
Microscopic: * Newly generated follicles "↑ no. - small - scanty colloid"
* Follicular cells  columnar
2- Colloid involution stage:
Gross: marked diffuse enlargement,
Cut section: gelatinous, glistening dt accumulation of colloid.
Microscopic: * Enlarged follicles filled with dark colloid "not uniformed"
* With flattened epithelium.

Clinical features: most imp if:
♠ Prolonged repeated simple colloid goiter  simple multi- nodular goiter.
-1-

 Simple Multi-nodular Goiter
In all long standing simple diffuse cases, with repeated cycles of hyperplasia
& involution  Nodules "varying size".
With generation of new follicles with ↑↑ colloid accumulation  tensions
 rupture of follicles & vessels  hemorrhage, scaring or calcification.

Types: Endemic or sporadic.
Gross: Gland: Asymmetrically enlargement with multi-nodularity.
Microscopic: ▪ Follicles: variable sized, filled by colloid with cystic areas.
▪ Follicular cells: flat, cuboidal or columnar.
+ irregular scarring + focal hemorrhage + focal calcification.

C/P:
1- Mass effect:
► Esophageal compression  Dysphagia
► Tracheal compression  Dyspnea
► SVC compression  Obstruction
2- Hemorrhage  sudden painful enlargement +↑↑ mass effects.
3- 2ry toxic manifestations  Toxic Multi-nodular Goiter "in < 50% of cases".

Toxic Multi-nodular Goiter
Hyper activity of one or more of simple nodules.
DD with Grave's
 Older age
 No infiltrative ophthalmopathy or dermopathy
 Mild toxicity "variable elevations in T3 & T4".
 More prominent CVS manifestations "TC, AF, CHF".

-2-

 Diffuse 1ry Toxic Goiter
"Grave's Disease"
* Most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.
Characterized by triad:
1- Thyrotoxicosis dt hyper functional diffuse goiter 100%
2- Infiltrative ophthalmopathy with exophthalmous. 40%
3- Infiltrative dermopathy "pertibial myxoedema" 5-10%

Incidence:
♦ Age: young adults, peak 20 - 40y
♦ Sex: ♂: ♀ 1: 7
♦ Familial tendency.

Pathogenesis:
Autoimmune Disease
Defect in suppressor T cell function

Activation of CD4 T helper cells against TSH receptors

Stimulate B cells lymphocytes

Ab formation against proteins of TSH receptors

Binds with Thyroid cell membrane (TSH receptors)

Have actions similar to TSH, So called "LATS"

Activate the gland

↑↑ T3, T4 & ↑ size

Suppression of ant pituitary & ↓↓↓ of TSH
Anti TSH- receptor Ab:
 TSAb "TS-Ig"  stimulate function of thyroid epithelial cells.
 TSH binding inhibitor Ig  same TSH action  stimulate thyroid epithelial cells.
 TGS Ig  proliferation of follicular epithelial cells & gland growth.
Also, Ab:
 Bind with retro-orbital Ag especially in extra ocular muscles 
Infiltrative ophthalmopathy.
 Bind with sub-cutanous tissue  Infiltrative dermopathy.

Carcinoma of Cervix Uteri
Types:

2- Invasive cervical carcinoma.

Pathogenesis:
Most of cervical carcinomas are related to oncogenic strains of HPV which are either:
1- Low risk viruses: not associated with cervical neoplasia.
2- High risk viruses (HPV 16,18): oncogenic  cancer.
♦ Most of infections are eliminated by host immune response.
♦ Few cases develop persistent infection  virus integrates its DNA into host cell
genome  genetic mutations  CIN  invasive cervical carcinoma.

Site: the most susceptible part.
Immature epithelium of squamo-columnar junction "transformation zone"

1- CIN (Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia)
Def: Precancerous dysplastic changes of cervical squamous epithelium, that precede
development of invasive cervical carcinoma by many years/ decades.

Grades:
CIN I : involve lower 1/3 of epithelium  Reversible.
CIN II : involve lower 2/3 of epithelium  Reversible.
CIN III: involve Full thickness of epithelium by immature atypical anaplastic cells
"No surface differentiation" but the basement membrane is intact.
 Irreversible. Carcinoma in situ - pre invasive carcinoma

Recently 2-tiered system:
► The precursor lesions are named Squamous intraepithelial lesion (SIL)
1- Low grade (LSIL) = CIN I  commonly regress spontaneously
but small % progress to HSIL
2- High grade (HSIL) = CIN II & CIN III  high risk progress to cervical carcinoma.

Gross: No mass.
Microscopic:

- Dysplastic epithelial changes.
- Basement membrane is intact.

C/P: Asymptomatic.

* Was one of the most frequent ♀ cancers.
* One of the major causes of cancer deaths in ♀ in developing countries.

▪ Early diagnosis & treatment of CIN lesions by screening tests

4- Cigarette smoking.

early
