 Diseases of Oral Cavity
Precancerous Lesions
Leukoplakia
Def: A white, mucosal patch or plaque, caused by epidermal thickening or hyperkeratosis.
♠ Can't be scrapped off. Vs (Thrush stomatitis = Oral candidiasis)
♠ Can't be characterized clinically & pathologically as any diseases.
♠ Diagnosed by exclusion of other white lesions.

Incidence: uncommon, < 1% of adults.
↑ risk in: ▪ communities & races with high Tobacco use as Southeast Asia
▪ Males > 40Y.

Causes: Chronic irritation.
Sites: Any where in oral cavity, but commonly:
▪ Buccal mucosa
▪ Floor of mouth
▪ Gingiva.

▪ Hard & soft palates.
▪ Ventral surface of tongue.

Gross: Single or multiple
White patches
Sharply demarcated borders.

Microscopic: Hyperplastic epithelium
Hyperkeratosis & Acanthosis.
which might be normal or dysplastic + CIS
with chronic inflammatory cells below them.

C/P: Asymptomatic & noticed accidently during routine examination.
Prognosis: Malignant transformation 4-17% (Sq.C.C.) within 20y.

Tumours
I- Benign:

 Epithelial: Squamous cell papilloma.
 Mesenchymal: Angioma (hemangioma, lymphangioma).

II- Malignant:

 Epithelial: Squamous cell carcinoma 90 % "Commonest malignant".
 Mesenchymal: Sarcomas.
-1-

 Squamous Cell Carcinoma of Oral Cavity
Incidence:
♦ 95% of H&N cancers are SCC (HNSCCs), arise commonly in the oral cavity.
♦ 6th most common neoplasm worldwide.
♦ One of the aggressive epithelial malignancies.

Risk factors: multi-factorial;
1- Tobacco smoking & alcohol.
2- HPV 16: 50% oropharyngeal cancers "tonsils, base of tongue".
3- Family history of H&N cancers.
4- Actinic rays (sunlight).
5- Pipe smoking.
↑ risk for lower lip.
♣ Prolonged irritation as sharp tooth edge, ill fitting dentures or chronic infections
are not a direct cause to oral cancers but could act as Promoter.

Sites: Any where in oral cavity but commonly:
▪ Ventral surface of the tongue.
▪ Floor of the mouth.
▪ Lower lip.
▪ Soft palate.
▪ Gingiva.

Gross: Malignant ulcer. (+++) ‫أوصف‬
Microscopic:
► Precursor: Progressive hyperplasia & hyperkeratosis  dysplasia  CIS.
► Ranges from well differentiated SCC with keratin pearls
to poorly differentiated SCC with pleomorphic cells.

Spread: 1- Local: to surrounding oral structure.
2- Lymphatic: submental, submandibular & cervical LN. + Occult cancer.
3- Blood: rare, to lungs.

Cause of death: ▪ Inhalation bronchopneumonia from sepsis.
▪ Cancer Cachexia & starvation.

Prognosis: Aggressive tumours, despite advanced treatment the long term
survival is less than 50%
-2-

 Diseases of Salivary Glands
Tumour of salivary glands
Benign
1- Pleomorphic adenoma 50%
2- Adenolymphoma 5-10%
3- Basal cell & canalicular adenomas 5-10%

Malignant
1- Muco epidermoid carcinoma 15%
2- Adenoid cystic carcinoma 5%
3- Adeno carcinoma 10%
4- Malignant mixed tumour 3-5%
5- Acicic cell tumour 5%
6- Other carcinoma 1%

A- Pleomorphic adenoma
(Mixed S.G. Tumour)
Incidence:
* Most common tumour of major & minor Salivary glands.
* Mostly affect parotid.
*♀>♂
* Age: 4th - 5th decades

Gross:

adenoma "mass"
 Usually single & Unilateral.
 Rounded
 2-5 cm diameter
 Firm in consistency
 Encapsulated "incomplete"  difficult removal.
 Lobulated.
 Bosselated = tongue like protrusion.
 Cut surface: solid, grayish white with bluish semi translucent areas.

Microscopic:

variable histological patterns
 Epithelial & myoepithelial cells arranged in sheets, strands, ducts, acini.
 Abundant mesenchymal stroma of mucoid, myxoid, chondroid & bony tissue.

Prognosis:
- Benign tumour, recurrent if incomplete removal in 25 %
- Malignant transformation (rare)  malignant mixed SG tumour.

-3-

New Edition
By:

2025

Dr. Hassan A. Soliman
01001592680

Royal Med - 2028
01020172375
-0-

 Hepatitis
Def: Diffuse inflammation of the liver parenchyma.
Causes:
1- Infectious Micro- organisms: bacteria, viruses, parasitic, fungi & protozoa.
2- Alcohol.
3- Chemicals & Toxins.
4- Drugs as methyldopa - acetaminophen.
5- Radiation.
6- Immunologically as autoimmune diseases.
7- Genetic.

Viral Induced Hepatitis
a- Hepatotropic viruses: HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV, HEV = primary.
Most common causes of hepatitis. (prototype)
b- Systemic viruses that can involve the liver as = secondary.
EBV, CMV, HSV-1, Rubella, yellow fever virus.
N.B: the term viral hepatitis is restricted to hepatotropic viruses.

Viral Hepatitis
Most imp. ---------- World wide ---------- Sporadic or endemic

Pathogenesis of viral hepatitis:
H.V are not hepatotoxic (not cytopathic) but induce the immunological reaction
of CD8 cytotoxic T cells  damage the viral infected cells  lethal effects.
"Is this damage useful or useless??

Mode of transmission:
► Feco-oral: HAV - HEV.
► Blood: HBV - HCV - HDV.

Complications of VH:
1- Post hepatic cirrhosis.
2- Hepatic failure & encephalopathy.
3- ↑ Risk of hepatocellular carcinoma "HBV - HCV only".

Clinico-Pathological Syndromes: (C/P)
Depend on: Type of virus & host immune response  variable clinical features.

1- Sub clinical Infection
A/E: any type: many of HAV, 60% of HBV & 75% of HCV cases.
C/P: Asymptomatic, incidentally discovered.
Serology: minimal ↑ serum transaminases (AST,ALT)
+ve serological tests "antiviral Ab or viral Ag".
-1-

 2- Acute Viral Hepatitis
A/E: any type of hepatotropic viruses.
C/P: 4 phases, regardless the type of the virus.
a- Incubation Period:

 Asymptomatic period & variable duration with different viruses.
 It's last days & early days of acute c/p show the peak of infectivity.

b- Preicteric Phase:

 Non- specific constitutional symptoms as: malaise, general fatigability,
nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, loss of wt & low grad fever.
 ↑ liver enzymes.

c- Icteric Phase:

 Jaundice dt ↑ level of bilirubin mainly conjugated type.
 ↑↑↑↑ liver enzymes.

d- Convalescence: Several few weeks or months.
Microscopic picture:
1- Inflammation:

 Infiltration of PT by mixture of inflammation cells.
 Hyperplasia of Kupffer cells.

2- Cell injury:

 Ballooning degeneration
 Fatty change.

3- Necrosis:
 Drop out.
 Bridging necrosis of adjacent lobules.
Portal to Portal (P-P), Central to Central (C-C), Portal to Central (P-C).
No role of biopsy in diagnosis of acute viral hepatitis

3- Chronic Viral Hepatitis
Def: symptomatic, biochemical & serological evidence of persistent inflammatory
hepatic disease with histological documentation without improvement for > 6M.

A/E:

mainly HCV, HBV, HDV.

Never HAV & HEV

C/P: highly variable.
Microscopic picture: markedly variable.
1- Inflammation:
 Mild: cellular infiltration with in portal tract.
 Sever: infiltration spill over adjacent parenchyma interface hepatitis.
-2-

 2- Cell injury = Degeneration:
 Cellular ballooning.

 Fatty change.

3- Necrosis:
 Focal drop out

 Bridging.

4- Fibrosis: "Hallmark of irreversible liver damage"
 Early: Limited to portal tract.
 Later: Peri-portal fibrosis  bridging fibrosis.
Liver biopsy is very imp. & routine to show & monitor pathological changes

4- Carrier State
Def: an individual can transmit the virus but without any clinical manifestations.
A/E: ► HBV "commonest"
► Rare with HCV, HDV.
► Never HAV & HEV.
Healthy carriers: have normal liver enzymes
& no significant inflammation or necrosis in liver biopsy.

5- Fulminant Hepatitis

 Enlargement of Lymph Nodes
"Lymphadenopathy"
I- Non Neoplastic "Reactive Lymphadenitis"
A- Acute Lymphadenitis
1- Localized: LN draining of infected focus.
E.g.: Tonsillitis, tooth infection  cervical LN enlargement.

2- Generalized: associated with systemic infection "viral – bacterial".
E.g.: measles, infectious mononucleosis.

Gross: LN  enlarged, swollen, soft, red, engorged + abscess formation.
Microscopic:

acute inflammation

● Congestion.
● Germinal centers: large, ↑↑ mitotic figures.
● Neutrophiles infiltration. "around the follicles- within the sinuses".
● Extension to peri-nodal tissue (peri-adenitis).
● + Suppuration = abscess.

C/P: LN: enlarged, painful, tender "useful sign", mobile & soft.
Overlying skin: red, hot & odema + abscess with draining sinus.

Fate:

♦ Resolution  back to normal, when infection is controlled.
♦ Destruction  scarring.

B- Chronic Lymphadenitis
1- Specific:

"Granulomatous Lymphadinitis"

E.g.: TB, Syphilis, sarcoidosis, toxoplasmosis & cat scratch disease.

Gross: LN  enlarged, discrete (matted together in TB), firm, gray tan.
In TB: C.S  caseation.

Microscopic:
● Distorted LN architecture.
● Multiple, variable sized granulomas:
▪ Aggregation of epithelioid, histiocytes + MN giant cells.
▪ Non caseating (sarcoidosis) or caseating (TB).
▪ Surrounded by lymphocytes & fibrosis.
▪ Suppuration & neutorphilic infiltration as in cat scratch dis.

-1-

 2- Non specific: chronic from the start or on top of acute.
3 patterns:
a- Follicular Hyperplasia:
Chronic infections by organisms activates B-cell & enlarges the germinal center
which bulge against the surrounding collar small B-lymphocytes.
= infections needs humoral immunity.
G.C.  lymphocytes in varying stages of maturation (blast)
& ↑↑ no. of histiocytes containing phagocytosed pathogens & cellular debris.
► As chronic non specific infection, rheumatoid arthritis.

b- Para cortical lymphoid hyperplasia:
By organisms that stimulate T-cells.
Para follicular T-cell proliferation  pressure on lymphoid follicles.
► Viral infection.
► Drug reaction.
► Post vaccination.

c- Sinus Histiocytosis:
Distention of lymphoid sinusoid dt infiltration with histiocytes
& marked hyperplasia of lining endothelial cells.
► In LN daring cancer or its toxic products.

C/P: enlarged, firm, painless & not tender - no sings of acute inflammation.
Commonly in Axillary & Inguinal LN.
N.B.: the 3 pattern may occur in combination.

 Diseases of Testis
Tumours
Incidence:
The most common & imp cause of firm, painless enlargement of the testis.

Etiology: Unknown.
Risk factors:
1- Cryptorchidism = undescended testicles in 10% of cases.
2- Testicular dys-genesis as feminization & Klinefelter's Syndrome.
3- Genetic & familial factors.

"WHO" Classification of 1ry Testicular Tumours
I- Germ Cell Tumours (95%):
► All are Malignant, Except ……….

A- Tumours of one histologic pattern:
 Seminoma
 Embryonal carcinoma
 Yolk sac tumour
 Chorio-carcinoma
 Teratoma: a- Mature
b-Immature
c-With malignant transformation of somatic elements.

B- Tumours of more than one histologic pattern:
 Embryonal carcinoma & Teratoma = teratocarcinoma.
 Choriocarcinoma & other germ cell tumours.
 Other combinations.

II- Sex Cord- Stromal Tumours (5%):
► More Benign.
► Associated with endocrine abnormalities.

A- Well Differentiated:
 Leyding cell tumour
 Sertoli cell tumour
 Granulosa cell tumour

B- Mixed Forms.
-1-

 ** Seminoma**
Incidence:
* The most common germ cell tumour in adults.
* 30% of testicular germ cell tumours.
* Age: peak in 4th decade.
* The counterpart of dysgerminoma in ♀.

Gross:

Mass
Large - soft - solid- well demarcated- homogenous- bulging cut surfacegray white - confined to testis = intact tunica albuginea,
if large  foci of necrosis.

Microscopically:
♦ Cells: large - distinct borders - clear glycogen rich cytoplasm, rounded nuclei
with prominent nucleoli.
♦ Arranged in: small lobules.
♦ Stroma: fibrous tissue + lymphocytic infiltration.

C/P: Painless enlargement of testis.
Presented by: considerable size mass, confined to testis without metastasis.

Spread:
1- Direct.
2- Lymphatic "Early"  para-aortic & iliac LN.
3- Blood "Unusual & late".

Clinical Staging:

By: Physical Examination, Radiology & Tumour markers.
I: Tumour confined to testis.
II: Metastasis limited to retro-peritoneal LN below the diaphragm.
III: Metastasis out side the retro-peritoneal LN or above the diaphragm.

Prognosis:

Better than non seminomatous germ cells tumours.
dt later metastasis & radio-sensitive.

** Embryonal Carcinoma**
♠ More aggressive than seminoma.
♠ Peak incidence 20-30y.
Gross:
Mass
Ill defined - invasive through tunica albuginea into epididymis or spermatic cord
- areas of hemorrhage & necrosis

Microscopically:
♦ Cells: large primitive with large nuclei.
♦ Arranged in: sheets.
-2-

 ** Yolk Sac Tumour**
"Endodermal Sinus Tumour"
♠ Most common testicular tumour in infants & young children.
♠ In adults it occurs mixed germ cell neoplasm.
♠ Tumour marker: α feto protein.
Gross:
Mass
Non capsulated - homogenous - yellow white.

Microscopically:
♦ Cells: cuboidal to columnar, with eosinophilic hyaline globules.
♦ Arranged in: sheets, glands, papillae & microcysts.
♦ Schiller Duval Bodies = like primitive glomeruli.

** Chorio Carcinoma**
♠ Highly malignant.
♠ Peak incidence 20-30y.
♠ Forming mixed germ cell tumour.
♠ Highly vascular  widespread hematogenous metastasis  lungs & liver.
♠ Tumour marker: human chorionic gonadotropins.

Gross:
Small mass - extensive areas of hemorrhage & necrosis.
Microscopically: ♦ Cells: proliferating trophoblasts.

** Teratoma **
Def: group of neoplasms arising from tottipotent germ cells which have the ability
to differentiate to any of the 3 germ lines: "Ecto, Meso, Endo".

Age: Any age.
♦ Mature: common in infants & children. (Considered malignant in adults).
♦ Immature: any age, also, considered malignant, especially in adults.
♦ Malignant transformation: Adults.

Gross: Variegated appearance, firm in consistency, C.S: cysts & cartilaginous areas.
Microscopic:

3 variants "according degree of differentiation"

1- Mature Teratomas: fully differentiated tissues
Ectoderm  skin, it's appendages, neural tissue.
Mesoderm  muscles, cartilage, fat, lymphoid & blood cells.
Endoderm  gut, bronchial epithelium & glandular elements.

Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
Upper

Lower

Pyelonephritis

Cystitis – Urethritis

Def: infection involving the bladder "cystitis" & urethra
or kidney & collecting system "pyelonephritis" or both.
♠ The majority of cases of pyelonephritis are associated with LUTI.
♠ LUTI may remain localized without kidney affection.

Modes (Routs) of infection:
♠ Ascending: starts from LUTI then ascend to affect kidney. "most common"
♠ Haematogenous: starts from UUTI then descend to bladder. "less common"

Causative Organism:
1- Ascending: enteric gram -ve bacilli.
E coli > proteus, klebsiella, enterobacter , strept faecalis & pseudomonas.
2- Hematogenous: staphylococci.

Risk Factors:
1- Sex: Females. Dt:
▪ The uretheral opening is close to rectum  facilitate colonization.
▪ Short urethra  facilitate delivery of bacteria to UB
▪ Trauma of sexual intercourse facilitate entry of bacteria to UB
2- Instrumentation: catheterization or cystoscopy (older ♂).
3- Urinary tract obstruction  stasis  multiplication of bacteria.
 Congenital valves in ureters or urethra.
 Acquired as stones, BPH, tumours or pregnancy.
4- DM dt ↓ body resistance  ↑ susceptibility to infection.
Neurogenic bladder "dysfunction"  stasis.
5- Incompetent valves as:
 Congenital incompetent of vesico- ureteric valve  VUR
 Renal papillae  intra-renal reflux.
6- Immuno-suppression "drugs or diseases".
-1-

 Pathogenesis:
1- Ascending infection:
♦ Bacterial colonization in distal urethra & introitus in ♀.
(Bad hyagin).
♦ Moving to the bladder against urine flow.
(Instrumentation in ♂- ♀ features).
♦ Introduced to UB & ↑ multiplication dt incomplete emptying & ↑ residual urine.
By (urine obstruction at UB- UB dysfunction).
 LUTI "Cystitis"
♦ Up to ureter  renal pelvis by:
(a) vesico- ureteric reflux "congenital or acquired dt persistent ↑ in IV "
or (b) urine flow obstruction & stasis.
 retrograde flow of urine to renal pelvis by ↑ intra-vesical  during micturation.
♦ Spread to kidney parenchyma through intra renal reflux at papilla.
 UUTI "Pyelonephritis"

2- Haematogenous:
♦ During septicemia & infective bacterial endocarditis  seeding of bacteria.
Which facilitated by use of immune-suppressive drugs.
(Septic emboli  Pyemic abscess).

Pyelonephritis (PN)
Def: inflammation of renal parenchyma "tubules, interstitial tissue" & renal pelvis.
Types:
1- Acute PN

2- Chronic PN "specific or non-specific"

** Acute Pyelonephritis (APN):
Def: acute suppurative inflammation of renal parenchyma & pelvis by bacterial infection
& characterized by abscess formation.

Gross:

 Unilat or Bilateral kidneys affection.
 Size: normal or slightly enlarged - Swollen & Odematous.
 Capsule: strips easily.
 The cortex & medulla not differentiated from each other.
 Renal pelvis & calyces: hyperemic with hemorrhagic & yellow purulent foci.
 External surfaces: multiple abscesses which
* Yellowish
* Raised
* Discrete
* Arranged haphazardly or coalase as single large area of suppuration.

Microscopic:
 Glomeruli: not affected.
 Tubules: destructed & filled by pus  WBC’s casts in urine.
 Interstitium: abscesses + inflammatory cellular infiltration.
-2-

 Fates:
A- Appropriate treatment  benign course  healing by fibrosis (pyelonephritic scar)
 depressions in kidney surface & pelvi-calycial system deformities.
B- Inadequate treatment or persistent risk factors.

Complication:
1- Chronic pyelonephritis dt recurrent infection.
2- Papillary necrosis "Necrotizing papillitis" mainly in "DM or UTO"
Rare form – poor prognosis
3- Pyonephrosis: Pyelonephritis associated with complete obstruction of the ureter
leading to accumulation of pus

text:
Dr Mostafa Shmeila

9th lec. Handout

Inflammatory diseases of The urinary tract
Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
Classification:
1- Site: - Upper urinary tract infection (Pyelonephritis)
- Lower urinary tract infection (Cystitis, Urethritis)
2- Course: Acute or Chronic
Risk factors:
1- Urethral instrumentation:
- Catheterization, Cystoscopy (older males)
2- Female gender:
- The urethra is close to the rectum, Colonization of urethra by enteric bacteria
- The urethra is short, bacteria enter the urinary bladder due to trauma to the urethra during
sexual intercourse
3- Outflow obstruction or bladder dysfunction:
- Stasis
- Bacteria can multiply in the bladder freely
- Without being flushed out, or destroyed by the anti-microbial properties of the bladder
mucosa
4- Diabetes:
- Increase susceptibility to infection
- Neurogenic bladder dysfunction, leading to urinary stasis
5- Immunosuppression, Immunodeficiency

Pyelonephritis
Definition:
Inflammation of kidney parenchyma, Renal pelvis
N.B. - Kidney parenchyma: Tubule + Interstitium
- Pelvis = Pyelo
Cause:
Bacterial infection

Course:
Acute or Chronic
9th lec. Handout Page 1

 Dr Mostafa Shmeila

Acute or Chronic
Pathogenesis:
- Ascending infection (from the lower urinary tract) or Hematogenous infection (through the
blood stream)

1- Ascending infection
Incidence:
- The most important, frequent route
Pathogenesis:
- Bacteria reach the kidney from the lower urinary tract
- Combination of: a- Urinary bladder infection
b- Vesicoureteral reflux: - due to incompetence of vesicoureteral orifice
- Maybe congenital of acquired
c- Intrarenal reflux
Organisms:
- E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter
2- Hematogenous spread:
Incidence:
- Far less common
Pathogenesis:
- Occur in the course of septicemia or infective endocarditis
Organisms:
- Staphylococcus, E. coli

Acute Pyelonephritis
Definition:
- Acute suppurative inflammation of the kidney, renal pelvis
- Characterized by abscess formation
Cause:
- Bacterial infection
- Most commonly E. Coli
Morphology:
Grossly:
- One or both kidneys maybe involved
- Kidney surface: - Discrete, yellowish, raised abscesses
- Maybe scattered or coalesce to form a single large area of suppuration
- Renal pelvis, calyces: - Hyperemic
9th lec. Handout Page 2

 Dr Mostafa Shmeila

- Renal pelvis, calyces: - Hyperemic
- Hemorrhagic, suppurative foci
- Healing: - fibrosis
- Pyelonephritic scar

Microscopy:
- Renal Parenchyma: Abscess formation (the characteristic histologic feature)
- Tubules, collecting ducts: - Intratubular neutrophils
- frequently extent into the collecting ducts
- Characteristic leukocytic casts in urine
Glomeruli: Typically not affected
Complication:
1- Pyonephrosis:
- in case of prominent obstruction
- the pus doesn't drain, may fill the renal pelvis, calyces, ureter
2- Papillary necrosis:
- Rare form, with poor prognosis
- Ischemia, suppurative necrosis of the renal papillae
- Predisposing conditions: - Diabetes
- Urinary tract obstruction
- Sickle cell anemia
3- Perinephric abscess:
- Extension of suppurative inflammation through the renal capsule into the perinephric tissue

Chronic pyelonephritis
Characteristics:
- Tubulointerstitial inflammation + Renal parenchyma scarring + Pelvicalyceal gross scarring,
deformity
- Important cause of chronic kidney disease
Forms:
1- Chronic reflux-associated pyelonephritis
2- Chronic obstructive pyelonephritis
N.B. Both can be unilateral or bilateral
1- Chronic reflux-associated pyelonephritis:
Incidence:
- The most common cause of chronic pyelonephritis
Pathogenesis:
- Congenital vesicoureteral reflux + Intrarenal reflux
9th lec. Handout Page 3

 Dr Mostafa Shmeila

- Congenital vesicoureteral reflux + Intrarenal reflux
- UTI superimposition
2- Chronic obstructive pyelonephritis
Pathogenesis:
- Obstruction predisposes the kidney to infection
Pathogenesis of Chronic Pyelonephritis:
- Recurrent infections superimposed on VUR
- Or obstruction lead to recurrent bouts of renal inflammation, scarring

 C. Squamous cell carcinoma

text:
MCQs — Liver Cirrhosis, Viral Hepatitis, Bilharzial Fibrosis,
Portal Hypertension
(Answers at the end)

1. Cirrhosis is characterized microscopically by all of the following EXCEPT:
A. Diffuse fibrous septa
B. Regenerating nodules
C. Loss of normal lobular architecture
D. Predominant fatty change without fibrosis
E. Chronic inflammatory infiltrate

2. The primary cell responsible for fibrosis in cirrhosis is:
A. Kupffer cell
B. Ito cell (stellate cell)
C. Cholangiocyte
D. Endothelial cell
E. Hepatocyte

3. In chronic viral hepatitis, “interface hepatitis” is best described as:
A. Kupffer cell hyperplasia
B. Neutrophils filling the sinusoids
C. Inflammatory cells spilling from portal tracts into periportal hepatocytes
D. Bridging fibrosis only
E. Ballooning degeneration

4. Bridging necrosis in chronic viral hepatitis refers to necrosis that connects:
A. Hepatocytes to bile ducts
B. Central vein to central vein
C. Portal tract to portal tract or portal tract to central vein
D. Sinusoids to space of Disse
E. Bile ducts to hepatic artery

5. A patient with chronic HBV has variable zones of inflammation, fatty change,
and portal fibrosis. Which finding indicates IRREVERSIBLE damage?
A. Ballooning degeneration
B. Kupffer cell hyperplasia
C. Bridging fibrosis between lobules
D. Focal necrosis
E. Mild inflammatory infiltrate

 6. In cirrhosis, portal hypertension is MOSTLY caused by:
A. Increased portal inflow only
B. Compression of sinusoids by nodules + fibrosis
C. Decreased hepatic artery flow
D. Increased lymph formation
E. Vitamin K deficiency

7. Which of the following is a PRE-hepatic cause of portal hypertension?
A. Cirrhosis
B. Budd–Chiari syndrome
C. Schistosomiasis
D. Portal vein thrombosis
E. Constrictive pericarditis

8. A patient with portal hypertension develops massive splenomegaly. Which
complication may follow?
A. Hypercalcemia
B. Hypersplenism → pancytopenia
C. Hyperaldosteronism
D. Polycythemia
E. Leukemoid reaction

9. Esophageal varices occur due to formation of:
A. Intrahepatic shunts
B. Portosystemic shunts between left gastric vein → esophageal veins
C. Increased lymph flow
D. Hepatic artery aneurysm
E. Anastomosis between portal vein and hepatic veins

10. In ascites secondary to portal hypertension, the fluid is typically:
A. Exudate rich in protein
B. Transudate with <3 g/dL protein
C. High in amylase
D. Chylous fluid
E. Purulent fluid

11. Bilharzial hepatic fibrosis is characterized by:
A. Loss of architecture with regenerative nodules
B. Granulomatous reaction around schistosoma ova
C. Fatty degeneration with ballooning hepatocytes
D. Widespread hepatocellular necrosis
E. Diffuse Kupffer cell hyperplasia

 12. Which finding differentiates bilharzial hepatic fibrosis from cirrhosis?
A. Presence of fibrosis
B. Presence of portal hypertension
C. Preserved lobular architecture
D. Portal tract expansion
E. Risk of HCC

13. Acute viral hepatitis MOST commonly shows which microscopic change?
A. Bridging necrosis
B. Ballooning degeneration + Councilman bodies
C. Regenerative nodules
D. Fibrous septa
E. Portal tract granulomas

14. Complication MOST specific to chronic viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV):
A. Hepatocellular carcinoma
B. Splenic sequestration
C. Hyperbilirubinemia
D. Cholecystitis
E. Pancreatitis

15. In portal hypertension, hemorrhoids occur because of shunting between:
A. Splenic vein → azygos vein
B. Superior rectal vein → middle & inferior rectal veins
C. Portal vein → hepatic vein
D. Left gastric vein → esophageal veins
E. Cystic vein → umbilical veins

1. A 45-year-old obese woman presents with biliary colic after fatty meals. Ultrasound reveals
multiple faceted stones. These stones are most likely composed of:
A. Pure cholesterol

D. Calcium carbonate only

A. Mixed stone
B. Pigment stone
C. Pure cholesterol stone
D. Calcium bilirubinate stone
E. Struvite stone

commonly:
A. Bacterial infection of the gallbladder mucosa
B. Ischemic necrosis of the gallbladder wall

A. Mucocele
B. Empyema
C. Hydrops
D. Phlegmonous cholecystitis
E. Hemorrhagic cholecystitis

 5. A 62-year-old man has massive ascites and a large liver mass. AFP is elevated. Histology
shows trabecular arrangement and bile canaliculi. Most likely diagnosis:
A. Cholangiocarcinoma
B. Metastatic colon cancer
C. Hepatocellular carcinoma
D. Hepatoblastoma
E. Angiosarcoma

regresses after stopping OCPs. Diagnosis:
A. Hepatocellular carcinoma
B. Fibrolamellar carcinoma
C. Liver cell adenoma
D. Hemangioma
E. Focal nodular hyperplasia

A. High-fat diet
B. Chronic hemolysis
C. Obesity
D. Female sex
E. Pregnancy

cm, most likely:
A. Hemangioma
B. Angiosarcoma
C. HCC
D. Focal nodular hyperplasia

A. Elevated AFP in most cases

A. HCC

A. HCC
B. Cholangiocarcinoma
C. Hepatoblastoma
D. Metastatic tumors
E. Angiosarcoma

A. Hypoglycemia
B. DIC
C. Severe cachexia
D. Cardiac tamponade
E. Massive GI variceal hemorrhage

A. Smoking
B. Alcohol
C. Gallstones
D. Viral hepatitis
E. OCP use

A. Early symptoms with weight loss
B. Severe jaundice early on

D. High AFP

A. Hepatocellular carcinoma

Nutshell Summaries

Nutshell
CNS Drugs
Telegram: @Nutshell_AFM_28

Summary
Nutshell

Pharmacology
1

 Nutshell Summaries

Sedative-Hypnotics & Anxiolytics
They are used for anxiety disorders, insomnia, and seizure control. They are also drugs of abuse.
Subclasses:
- Benzodiazepines
- Non-Benzodiazepine
= Selective Anxiolytics
= Non-benzodiazepine GABA receptor antagonists “Z Drugs”
- Barbiturates
- Melatonin Receptor Agonists
- Orexin Receptor Antagonists
Benzodiazepine (BZDs)
- Short-acting: Midazolam,
Triazolam
- Intermediate-acting:
Lorazepam, Alprazepam
- Long-acting: Diazepam,
Clonazepam

- Lipophilic, Penetrate easily to the CNS and placenta (crosses BBB) + CYP450 dependant
- Binds to GABAA receptor = increases GABA inhibitory effect (hyperpolarization due
to Cl- influx) = Inhibition of neuronal action potential
Used for:
- Anxiety disorders
- Short-acting = sleep onset insomnia |||| Intermediate-acting = sleep-maintenance insomnia
- Clonazepam as anti-epileptic
- Diazepam as muscle relaxant in case of MS or cerebral palsy
- Used as pre-anesthetics => Midazolam for induction of general anesthesia
- They cause sedation, dizziness, confusion, ataxia, and respiratory depression.
- They cause physical and psychological dependace = withdrawal symptoms.
Benzodiazepine Antagonists (Flumazenil): used to reverse benzodiazepines and nonbenzodiazepines toxicity and severe adverse effects, such as coma/respiratory depression.
- Competitive BZD antagonists = require repeated IV adminstration

Selective Anxiolytics (nonBZDs)
Buspirone
Non-BZDs GABA Receptor
Antagonists (Z-Drugs)
- Short-acting: Zolipidem,
Zaleplon
- Intermediate-acting:
Esczopiclone
Barbiturates
- Long-acting: phenobarbital
- Short-acting: Secobarbital

- Partial agonist to serotonin 5-HT1A receptors = reduced anxiety without sedation
- Weak dopamine antagonism effect + No GABAergic effect (no muscle relaxant action)
- Used to tread Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
- Used along with antidepressants in Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)
- CYP450 dependant = hepatic elimination = dose adjustment in hepatic impairment
- Selective GABAA-alpha1 agonism = less muscle relaxant and anticonvulsion effects than
BZDs
- Short-acting = sleep onset insomnia |||| Intermediate-acting = sleep-maintenance insomnia
- Nex-day residual effects with intermediate acting = drowsiness, dizziness, headache
- Cause complex sleep disorders like sleepwalking, but less risk of dependance
- They prolong GABAA receptor opening = augment its activity + non-selective in high dose
- Treatment of seizures = Phenobarbital
- They are used for induction of anaesthesia. Cause sedation, diziness, respiratory depression
- Tolerance and Dependance.
- They lack antidote for their toxicity (so they are less used in comparison to BZDs)

9

 Nutshell Summaries
Melatonin Receptor
Antagonists = Ramelteon
= Used for Insomnia
Orexin Receptor Antagonists
= Suvorexant
= Used for Sleep
Maintenance Insomnia

- Melatonin normally promotes sleepiness (augment its receptors’ action: MT1/MT2)
- Doesn’t cause rebound insomnia, dependance, or withdrawal symptoms.
- May cause fatigue.
- Orexin normally promotes wakefullness (blocks its receptors: OX1/OX2). Not
GABAergic
- May cause next-day residual effect: somnolence and drowsiness
- Low risk of dependence, BUT: it’s controlled substance (Schedule IV)

10

 Nutshell Summaries

Antidepressant Drugs
Subclasses:
- Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)
- Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs)
- Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs)
- Atypical Antidepressants
- Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAO Inhibitorss)
Selective Serotonin Reuptake
Inhibitors
Fluoxetine, Paroxetine,
Sertraline, Citolopram

Serotonin-Norepinephrine
Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs)
Venlafaxine, Duloxetine

- CYP450 dependant = hepatic elimination = dose adjustment in hepatic impairment
- Well absorbed Orally
- Long half-lives = once-daily dosing. Fluoxetine has even longer t½ (active metabolites).
- Block

I. Drugs for Acid-Related Disorders

DRUGS FOR ACID-RELATED DISORDERS
Acid-related disorders occur when the caustic effects of aggressive factors (acid,
pepsin, bile) overwhelm the protective mechanisms of the gastrointestinal mucosa
(mucus, bicarbonate secretion, prostaglandins, blood flow, and epithelial
regeneration), leading to mucosal erosions or ulceration.
1.1. Acid Suppressive Therapy

Summary
Nutshell

1

 Nutshell Summaries

Drugs for Acid-Related Disorders
Mechanisms of Acid Secretion by Parietal Cells

Gastic acid secretion is controlled by one of the following intracellular mediators:
1. cAMP = Stimulated by Histamine (H2 Receptor))
2. Intracellular Calcium ions = Stimulated by Ach (M3 Receptor) and Gastrin
Gastric acid (HCL) is secreted as H+ ions and Cl- ions indvidually, and they unite within the lumen.
Acid secretion can be manipulated by:
1. Blocking the vagal stimulation (not studied here)
2. Blocking Histamine receptors
3. Manipulating H+ ion secretion by:
a) Irreversibly inhibiting the Proton Pump (Proton Pump Inhibitors)
b) Blocking the K+ site within the proton pump
The effect of acid can be neutralized, to an extent, by the use of Antacids.

2

 Nutshell Summaries
H2 Receptor Antagonists
Any drugs that ends with
“-tidine”.
Most famous: Cimetidine

- Renal elimination, needs dose adjustment in renal insufficiency
- Works om reducing intracellular cAMP + reversable action
- Suppress nocturnal acid secretion
- Used for GERD, Peptic Ulcer Disease (gastric ulcer/duodenal ulcer), Stress Ulcer
- Prophylaxis of: NSAIDS-induced ulcers, stress ulcers, aspiration pneumonitis during
surgeries (pre-anesthesia acid reduction)
Adverse Effects:
- Tolerence
- Cimetidine makes you like cement (decreased libido, gynecomastia, galactorrhea, reduced
sperm count. It also inhibits CytP450 complex. May also Cause cognitive impaitment (old
age and renal impairment are risk factors)

Potassium-Competitive Acid
Blockers
Vonoprazan

Proton Pumb Inhibitors
They all end with “-prazole”.
Omeprazole, pantoprazole

- Reversible inhibition of H+/K+ counter-transport by binding to Potassium site, thus
inhibiting the pumb.
- Predictable in efficacy (CYP independant)
- Faster, stronger, give sustained acid suppression compared to other classes, so it’s
preferred with erosive esophagitis that result from GERD or H. Pylori
- Limited safety studies.
- Hepatic elimination, need dose adjustment with hepatic impairment.
- Administred on empty stomach. Has short half-life with long duration of action
(irreversable inhibition of H+ pump)
- Used for GERD Erosive Eosophagitis, Peptic Ulcer Disease, Zolinger-Ellison
Syndrome (ZES = Gastrinoma), Eosinophilic Esophagitis.
- Prophylaxis of: NSAIDS-induced ulcers, stress ulcers, functional dyspepsia.
Adverse Effects:
- Rebound Acid Secretion
- Vit. B12 and Iron deficiency, and decrease Ca+ absorbtion = osteoporosis.
- Altered gut microbiotal and increased risk of C.diff + Community-aqcuired Pneumonia
- Acute intestinal nephritis (rare)
- Omeprazole inhibits CYP => toxicity of other drugs (phenytoin, warfarin, clopidogrel)
- Reduce absorbtion of ferrous sulfate iron and some antifungals.
- Increase the risk of methotrexate toxicity

Antacids
- Aluminum-based
- Magnisuim-based
- Clacium-based
- Sodium-based
- Combination

- Aluminum (AluMINIMUM STOOL = constipation), slower prolonged effect
- Magnesium = Diarrhea, fast action but short duration
- Mixure => synergism + balanced adverse effects (constipation and diarrhea)
- Clacium-based = rebound secretion
- Sodium-based = Metabolic alkalosis
- Reduced absorbtion of: tetracyclin, iron, thyroid hormones, -azole antifungals
- Altered excretion or toxicity (e.g. digoxin)

3

 Nutshell Summaries
Mucous Protective Agents
- Protect the mucosa from gastric acid in order to treat: peptic ulcer, NSAID-induced ulcers, GERD
- Part of the combination treatments against H. Pylori
- They are: Prostaglandins analogues, Sucralfate, Bismuth compounds

Misoprostol: Methyl
analogue of PGE1

- Rapid oral absorption.
- Short t½ (<30 min). Dosed 3–4x daily.
- Inhibits gastric acid, ↑ mucus/bicarbonate/intestinal electrolyte secretions/uterine
contractions, ↑ mucosal blood flow.
Uses: NSAID ulcer prophylaxis, cervical ripening/postpartum hemorrhage.
Adverse Effects: Diarrhea,

text:
CONCEPT 3

CNS DISORDERS

CNS 4
Dr. Mohammed Raouf
Tel: 01147140909
Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 1

 -Psychosis
…Is a disorder in which the patient is out of touch with reality ''the patient live in his
own imagination ‫ ''مشغىل بعبلمه الداخلى‬and subjected to hallucinations.

-Schizophrenia:
…Chronic deterioration of the whole mind ''thought , behaviour , affect ‫''المزاج‬
-Affect 1% of people "adults 18- 21 years" , males more, mainly Genetic.
-Schizophrenia results from increase dopamine & Serotonin in limbic system

*Symptoms of Schizophrenia:
a- +Ve symptoms: Paranoid delusions ‫ اوهبم العظمة‬, hallocinations ‫تهيئبت‬, thought disorders.

b- --Ve symptoms:
...inability to pay attention , loss of will power , loss of concentration , apathy, blunted
emotions , social withdrawal ‫منعزل‬

-Treatment:
…block D2 rec & 5HT2 rec in limbic system
-Antipsychotic drugs: = Neuroleptic drugs = Major tranquilizers
→ drugs used to treat schizophrenia / bipolar mania / Agitation.

*Pharmacokinetic:
-Metabolism: in liver by CYP450 enzymes → then elimination in urine
-T1/2: long → once/day.
-Parenteral forms are available → for rapid initiation & depot treatment.

*Classification of antipsychotics: {regarding receptor affinity & side effects}
1-Typical antipsychotics = 1st generation

2-Atypical antipsychotics = 2nd generation

-Chlorpromazine

-Thioridazine

-Clozapine -Risperidone -Aripiperazole

-Fluphenazine

-Haloperidol

-Olanzapine -Quetiapine

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 2

 1-First Generation Antipsychotics: FGAs {Typical}:
*Classification:
1-High potency: Strong D2 rec blockade + More Extrapyramidal SE {EPS}
-Ex: Fluphenazine & Haloperidol
2-Low potency: broader rec effect + More sedation & Anticholinergic effect.
-Ex: Chlorpromazine & Thioridazine

*Mechanism of action:
-They act as Competitive D2-receptors antagonists in limbic system
→ Antipsychotic effect.

*Pharmacological actions:
1-They block D2 receptors in limbic system → Antipsychotic effect.
{treat + Ve symptoms + minimal effect on –ve symptoms}
2-Low potency FGAs: block α1-adrenergic receptors , muscarinic receptors , histaminic
receptors → SE.

*Therapeutic Uses:
1-Reduce +Ve symptoms with Minimal effect on –ve symptoms.
2-In acute agitation → IM Haloperidol and Lorazepam.
3-In delirium ‫ اضطراة ذهنى‬/‫ → هزيبن‬Haloperidol.

*Side effects of Typical antipsychotics:
A-Common:

1-Extrapyramidal Symptoms {EPS}:
-Cause:
...blocking of D2 receptors in nigrostriatal pathway "responsible for fine motor
coordination" → ↓ activity of dopamine → relative ↑ in Ach ''cholinergic'' activity.

Pharmacology

Dr/Mohammed Raouf

Page 3

 a-Acute dystonia: sudden sustained muscle spasm in face & neck "neck twisting & tongue
protrusion"
-Treated with Anticholinergic as Benztropine.
b-Akathisia: inner restlessness & Compulsive movements {pacing , leg shaking}
→ inability to sit still.
-Treated with: Beta blocker Propranolol or BZD or ↓ dose
c- Pseudoparkinsonism: parkinsonism-like symptoms "Drug induced parkinsonism"
…bradykinesia , rigidity , tremors
-Treated with: ↓ dose & switch to 2nd generation atipsychotics or add anticholinergic.

2-Antihistaminic effect: sedation {low potency FGAs}.
3-Anti-adrenergic effect: α1- rec blockers → Postural or orthostatic hypotension.
4-Anti-cholinergic "anti-muscarinic" effect = Atropine like action.

B-Serious:

1-Irreversible Tardive dyskinesia:
-It is a late appearing {delayed onset} EPS.
-Characterized by: abnormal involuntary orofacial movements → tongue writhing , lips
smacking "rabbit syndrome".
-due to supersensitivity & increase number of D2 receptors in nigrostriatal pathway.
-Treated with: switch to 2nd generation atipsychotics.
2-Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome {NMS}
3-Thioridazine → prolong QT interval

2-Second Generation Antipsychotics: SGAs {Atypical}:
*Classification:
1-D2 & 5HT2A rec blockers: Risperidone , Olanzapine , Quetiapine.
2-Partial agonist on D2 receptor: Aripiprazole , Brexpiprazole

Pharmacology

Dr/Mo

-Mechanism: drugs enhance the coordinated GI motility & the transit of GIT contents

1-Metoclopramide: It is a having double actions:
1-Antiemetic action → D2-rec antagonist.

- Uses:
1-Gastroparesis (Diabetic Gastroparesis )
2-GERD in combination with anti-secretory agent.
3-Pre-anesthsia & before labor for stomach empting.
-Side effects:
1-Because metoclopramide extrapyramidal adverse effects are both dose-dependent and
cumulative → its use for GERD or Gastroparesis should not exceed 12 weeks and
ONLY when the benefits outweigh the risk.
2-Increased prolactin release with gynecomastia + Diarrhea with long-term use.
2-Domperidone: a similar drug to metoclopramide, but with no extrapyramidal
manifestations, it is called for removal from the market because of increasing incidence of

- Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease primarily targeting synovial joints.
-Characterized by inflammatory synovitis + cartilage & bone destruction + systemic complications.
-Pathogenic Mechanisms:
1-Autoimmunity Trigger: Genetic and environmental factors as smoking and infections.

-Adaptive immunity: Th17 cells → promote inflammation.
4-Hyperplastic synovium "pannus": invades cartilage and bone + Osteoclast activation
-DMARDs are agents that modify the disease course of autoimmune rheumatic disorders as rheumatoid arthritis,
psoriatic arthritis by targeting underlying immune dysfunction.

 Drugs for Gout
-GOUT:
-Gout is a metabolic disorder caused by hyperuricemia → deposition of monosodium urate
(MSU) crystal in joints→ cause acute and chronic joint inflammation (pain/hot/red/peripheral joints)
-Pathogenesis of gout: (remission & flare up)
1-Hyperuricemia (the primary driver) caused by:
a-Decrease renal excretion (90% of cases) due to genetic variants, drugs as thiazides, loop
diuretics, cyclosporine, aspirin low dose or chronic kidney disease (CKD).
b-Increased uric acid production due to purine-rich diet as red meat, seafood, increased cell
turnover (tumor lysis) or enzyme effects.
2-Monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition:
-Is triggered by low pH, low temperature, trauma
-It occurs at the joints, extra-articular tissue, tendons, kidneys (urate nephrolithiasis).
3-Acute Gout Flare:
...MSU crystals are phagocytosed by macrophages → Macrophages release IL-1B
→ stimulate neutrophils → Neutrophils release proteases, reactive oxygen species, PGs → which
cause pain and swelling → more inflammation & more urate crystal deposition.
4-Chronic Gout (Tophi and Joint Damage = Tophaceous gout):
...Macrophages fail to clear MSU leading to granuloma-like structures and bone erosions.
-Classification of Drugs Used in Treatment of Gout:

-Non-pharmacological treatment
-Pharmacological treatment of gout includes:

synthesis → reduce Pain & inflammatory reactions & swelling.
-N.B:
....Aspırin is not suitable for treatment of acute gouty attacks because aspirin at low doses
(<2.6 g/day) causes renal retention of uric acid by competing with uric acid excretion in
the renal tubules.

-Pharmacokinetics:
-Absorption: rapidly absorbed after oral administration.
-Metabolized in the liver + undergo enterohepatic circulation.

1-Colchicine binds tubulin protein in neutrophils and disrupts synthesis of

2-It reduce release of inflammatory mediator IL-1B.
3-It reduce phagocytosis of MSU crystals.

text:
DEPARTMENT OF INTERNAL MEDICINE

E. Book
Clinical Examination

 History Taking
1. Introduction:
The Importance of History Taking
History taking is the **most critical component** of the medical
examination process.
Benefits of Effective History Taking:
1. Focuses Attention: Directs the clinician to the affected body system(s).
2. Assesses Severity & Progression: Provides insight into the severity and
temporal evolution of the illness.
3. Enables Diagnosis: Can be sufficient to diagnose specific conditions (e.g.,
epilepsy, migraine, renal colic) based on symptomatology alone.

2. The Art of History Taking: Communication as a Foundation
History taking is a specialized form of communication that initiates the
doctor-patient relationship.
Key Principles for Effective Communication:
1. Establish Rapport: Put the patient at ease and encourage open dialogue.
2. Demonstrate Attentiveness: Make it clear the patient has your undivided
attention.
3. Show Respect: Greet the patient, using their name if possible.
4. Maintain Professionalism: Do not display anger or shock at the patient's
disclosures.
5. Allow Patient Narrative: Let patients tell their story in their own words and
sequence.

 6. Observe Non-Verbal Cues: Pay close attention to body language (facial
expressions, eye contact, posture, clenched fists, etc.).
7. Be an Active Listener: Listening is as important as questioning.

3. The Standard Structure of a Medical History
A complete medical history should systematically cover the following
components:
1. Personal Data
2. Chief Complaint
3. History of Present Illness
4. Past Medical History
5. Drug History and Allergies
6. Social History
7. Family History
I. Personal Data
This section provides essential contextual information about the patient.
1. Name: For identification and rapport.
2. Age: Certain diseases are age-specific (e.g., childhood infectious diseases,
congenital anomalies).
3. Sex:
● Some diseases are sex-linked (e.g., hemophilia in males).
● Some diseases show sex predilection (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis and
systemic lupus erythematosus are more common in females).
4. Occupation: May expose individuals to specific hazards (e.g., infections in
healthcare workers, radiation exposure, occupational lung diseases like
asbestosis).

 5. Residence/Geographic History: Can indicate risk for endemic diseases (e.g.,
schistosomiasis in rural dwellers in certain regions).
6. Habits: Document smoking history (pack-years), alcohol intake, and other
substance use.
7. Marital Status & Number of Children: Relevant for social support.

text:
Approach to patients with different symptoms
Patients in pain
Definition
The International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) proposed the
following definition (1979): ‘Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional
experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage or described in
terms of damage’. This definition has important implications: pain is not
necessarily or always associated with ongoing tissue damage; it is a subjective
experience and has an emotional as well as a sensory component and is always
unpleasant.
Pain is notoriously difficult to describe. It is difficult to assess and even
harder to quantify. Nevertheless, pain assessment is crucial in order to evaluate
its impact on the sufferer and also to plan a treatment strategy. It has been
termed ‘the 5th vital sign’ and is mandated as part of routine assessment of
patients in hospital. In 2004 the IASP declared that the relief of pain should be a
human right.

Classification of pain
Pain is commonly classified according to the following:
▪ Etiology and underlying condition.
▪ Mechanism.
▪ Duration.

 Etiology/underlying condition
▪ Trauma – an acute response to an injury.
▪ Surgery.
▪ Medical illness such as myocardial infarction or appendicitis.
▪ Physiological conditions such as menstruation and labour.
Mechanism
▪ Inflammatory/Nociceptive – pain generated and maintained by inflammatory
mediators (such as prostaglandin E2), secondary to an ongoing disease
process. Examples include inflammatory arthritis or mechanical back pain.
▪ Neuropathic – Neuropathic pain is generated in malfunctioning nerves and is
defined as ‘pain arising as a direct consequence of a lesion or disease affecting
the somatosensory system’. This type of pain has special clinical features as
described below and may arise from injury or dysfunction of the central or
peripheral nervous system. Examples include painful diabetic neuropathy and
post-stroke pain.
▪ Mixed pain – This includes features of both nociceptive and neuropathic pain,
such as back pain with radiculopathy (radiating leg pain due to nerve irritation
or compression).
▪ Psychosomatic – Purely psychosomatic pain is rare. However, pain, especially
chronic pain, almost invariably has an emotional and behavioral component.
Duration
▪ Acute – most commonly a physiological response to an injury. It resolves with
the disappearance of a noxious stimulus or within the time frame of a normal
healing process.
▪ Chronic – it can either be associated with an ongoing pathological process,
such as rheumatoid arthritis or malignancy, or be present for longer than is
consistent with a normal healing time. Pain is arbitrarily described as chronic

 if it persists for longer than 3 months. Chronic pain is often associated with
disability, mood and sleep disturbance and a significant behavioural response.
It is sometimes subdivided into pain associated with cancer and pain
associated with non-malignant conditions.

Figure 1 Spinal withdrawal reflex with pain.

 Figure 2 Pain pathway

As with any other branch of medicine, careful and meticulous assessment
of a patient’s symptoms and signs is fundamental. Two key questions should be
considered when dealing with a patient in pain:
▪ Is the pain a symptom of ongoing tissue damage or of another condition that
needs to be dealt with by another medical professional?
▪ What is the optimal treatment strategy: to either abolish the pain altogether
or reduce it to a more bearable level?
Unfortunately, no single standardized approach will allow assessment of
pain in every situation. Pain is essentially a subjective experience. Therefore,
what the patient describes as his experience is of paramount importance. As in
most areas of medicine, the history is the most useful tool in assessment and
diagnosis.

text: BLOOD PRESSURE M.Zeitoun Patient Preparation No acute anxiety, stress or pain. No caffeine, smoking in the preceding 30 minutes. No use of substances containing adrenergic stimulants such as phenylephrine or pseudoephedrine (may be present in nasal decongestants or ophthalmic drops). Patient Preparation Bladder and bowel comfortable. No tight clothing on arm or forearm. Quiet room with comfortable temperature. Rest for at least 5 minutes before measurement. Patient should stay silent prior and during the procedure. Posture The patient should be calmly seated with his or her back well supported and arm supported at the level of the heart. His or her feet should touch the floor and legs should not be crossed. Posture The seated BP measurement is the standard position to determine diagnostic and therapeutic treatment decisions. The standing blood pressure is used to test for postural hypotension, if present, which may modify the treatment. Posture Mercury Myth Mercury sphygmomanometers have been banned? Fact Mercury sphygmomanometers are mercury sphygs are still the gold standard. Sphygmomanometers Automatic monitors: Not suitable for use in diagnosis of hypertension. Not suitable for patient with arrhythmias. Aneroid monitors: Aneroid dial gauges easily prone to damage from dropping, causing significant errors. Cuff size A cuff that is too small may contribute to a falsely elevated blood pressur measurement. Recommended Technique for Measuring Blood Pressure Locate the brachial pulse and centre the cuff bladder over it . Position cuff at the heart level . The manometer should be positioned at the health care practitioner’s eye level. Recommended Technique for Measuring Blood Pressure Cuff Placement: The cuff should be placed on a bare arm, approximately 2 cm above the elbow crease. It should fit but should still allow for two fingers to slide under the cuff. Recommended Technique for Measuring Blood Pressure To exclude possibility of auscultatory gap, increase cuff pressure rapidly to 30 mmHg above level of disappearance of radial pulse. Place stethoscope over the brachial artery. Recommended Technique for Measuring Blood Pressure Appearance of sound = systolic pressure. Disappearance of sound = diastolic pressure. Take at least 2 blood pressure measurements, 1 minute apart. Recommended Technique for Measuring Blood Pressure Recommended Technique for Measuring Blood Pressure For initial readings, take the blood pressure in both arms and subsequently measure it in the arm with the highest reading. Thereafter, take two measurements on the side where BP is higher . Normally, there may be a difference in pressure of 5 mm Hg and sometimes up to 10 mm Hg . In the lower limb : the SBP is higher by 10 – 30 mm Hg. M.Zeitoun Respiratory rate M.Zeitoun Respiratory Rate The normal rate of respiration in a relaxed adult is about 14-16 breaths per minute in male and 16-18 breaths per minute in female . Tachypnea is an increased respiratory rate observed by the doctor. Apnea means cessation of respiration. M.Zeitoun Respiratory Rate Causes of Tachypnea: 1. Fever & anxiety. 2. Pulmonary edema. 3. Metabolic acidosis. M.Zeitoun Respiratory Rate Examine the patient with chest and upper abdomen fully exposed and evenly illuminated. Count the number of breaths in a full minute by observing the chest movements with the fingers held on the pulse. M.Zeitoun WHY? Basic Principles for Taking Respirations Respirations are partially under voluntary control. Pts may breathe faster or slower when they are aware respirations are being counted. Important to keep pt unaware of this procedure. Do not tell pt you are counting respirations. COUNTING RESPIRATIONS Count pulse first, then count respirations while holding wrist Respiratory Rate M.Zeitoun 1 inhalation + 1 exhalation = 1 respiration. Tachypnea : abnormally rapid breathing. Bradypnea : abnormally slow rate. Hyperpnea : abnormally deep breathing. Kussmaul’s : abnormally rapid deep breathing (seen in cases of metabolic acidosis. Temperature M.Zeitoun ROUTES TO MEASURE TEMPERATURE Oral: By mouth Rectally: By rectum Axillary: Under the arm in the armpit Temperature The normal range of body temperature (measured orally) of the healthy person is 36.7 º C – 37.3 º C.. M.Zeitoun Temperature Rectal temperature is usually about 0.5 C higher than that in the mouth, which in turn is 0.5 C higher than in the axilla. Body temperature is best recorded either beneath the tongue, which is convenient or in the rectum which is reliable. M.Zeitoun Oral Temperature Shake thermometer down to 35 °C or below. Insert it under the tongue. Instruct the patient to close both lips. Wait for 3 minutes. Then read the thermometer. M.Zeitoun Temperature Taking oral temperatures is not recommended when patients are unconscious, restless or unable to close their mouths. M.Zeitoun Temperature Fever (or pyrexia) refers to an elevated body temperature. Hyperpyrexia refers to extreme elevation in temperature, above 41.1°C. Hypothermia refers to an abnormally low temperature below 35°C rectally. M.Zeitoun Temperature Causes of fever include: Infection. Trauma (such as surgery or crush injuries), Malignancy. Blood disorders (e.g. acute hemolytic anemia). Drug reactions. Immune disorders (e.g. collagen diseases). M.Zeitoun Temperature Causes of hypothermia: ( < 35°C) 1. Shock. 2. Myxedema. 3. Advanced heart failure. M.Zeitoun THANK YOU M.Zeitoun

text: History Taking The Art of History Taking History taking in medicine is the most important aspect of the medical examination. Good and effective history taking can: 1- Focus the attention to the system or systems affected. 2- Give a better judgment of the severity and progress of the case. 3- Largely diagnose some diseases (e.g. epilepsy, migraine, and renal colic) The Art of History Taking History taking is a special form of the art of communication: this is the beginning of the good doctor-patient relationship: 1- The patient should be put at ease and encouraged to talk freely. 2- Make it clear that the patient has your whole attention. 3- Common things towards good communication is to greet the patient, by name if possible. The Art of History Taking 4- Don't be angered or shocked by anything he/or she says. 5- Patients must be allowed to tell their story in their own words and in their own way. 6- When the patient telling his story always watches his body language (e.g. face expression, eyes, clenched fist, etc.). 7- Be a good listener Medical History Taking Personal data Chief Complaint. History of Present Illness. Past Medical History. Drug history and allergies. Social history. Family history. I. Personal data 1.Name. 2.Age: Certain diseases are more common in special age groups (e.g. infectious fever and congenital anomalies in childhood). 3.Sex: •Certain diseases are related to sex (e.g. hemophilia in males). •Certain diseases are more common in certain sex (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus are more common in females). Personal data 4.Occupation: certain jobs may expose the individual to certain hazards (e.g. infection in medical staff, physical factors like radiation, and some occupational lung diseases). 5.Residence: e.g. Shistosomiasis in country-side indwellers. 6.Habits: e.g. smoking and alcohol intake. 7.Marital state and number of children. II. Chief or present Complaint These are the symptoms that make the patient come to the doctor. Try to define the main complaint and its duration. Most patients with long history tend to date them by events rather than by years. Multiple symptoms should be arranged chronologically (old to most recent). In patient's own words III. History of Present Illness Ask the patient to tell you the story from the beginning, ideally without interruption. Your goal is: To find out how exactly symptoms began. In what setting they arose How symptoms have evolved since initial onset. History of Present Illness So, the history of the present condition should include: 1. Mode of onset 2. Course 3. Duration. 4. Negative data. 5. Review of other systems. History of Present Illness So, the history of the present condition should include: 1. Mode of onset 2. Course 3. Duration. 4. Negative data. 5. Review of other systems. History of Present Illness Types of onset: •Sudden onset: seconds to minutes (e.g. vascular disease). •Acute onset: hours to days (e.g. infections). •Sub-acute onset: 1-2 weeks (e.g. chronic infections) •Gradual and insidious onset: months to years (e.g. malignant diseases). History of Present Illness Types of courses: •Progressive: e.g. malignant and degenerative diseases. •Regressive: e.g. self-limited (common cold), or response to treatment (acute infection and vascular accidents). •Stationary: e.g. hereditary diseases. •Paroxysmal attacks: e.g. bronchial asthma. •Fluctuating (remissions and relapses: e.g. some chronic inflammation. History of Present Illness Negative data : These negative information are sometimes more important than positive information. Review of other systems: other systems should be evaluated for evidence of any disturbances related to the present illness. IV. Past Medical History 1- History of previous illnesses: - History of rheumatic fever in heart disease. - History of parasitic diseases like Schistosomiasis . - History of high blood pressure. 2- Trauma and surgical operations. 3- Hospitalizations 4- Blood transfusion. 5- Pregnancies. 6- History of travel abroad. V. Drug history and allergies 1- Details of drugs taken: name, dosage, frequency, and length of usage. 2- Certain drug families known to cause problems (e.g. Aspirin for ulcers, steroids, etc.) 3- Adverse effects to any drug. 4- Allergic reactions to any drugs: e.g. to penicillin or sulpha . 5- Herbs and Herbal Medicines these can interact with many drugs 6- Traditional Medicines. VI. Social history The social environment may affect the patient's health or may be affected by it. 1-The exact nature of his or her occupation. 2-His domestic and marital relationships. 3-His home surroundings. 4-Use of alcohol or tobacco. 5-Economic condition. VII. Family history Certain diseases run in families (secondary to hereditary or environmental factors): 1-History of similar conditions or diseases in the other family members. 2-History of consanguinity. After this thorough history taking and analysis of symptoms, we should have provisional diagnosis / differential diagnosis of the patient. Built & Posture Notice any abnormal movements such as tremor (in alcohol withdrawal, for example), dystonia (perhaps as a side effect of neuroleptic therapy) or chorea (jerky, involuntary movements, characteristic of Huntington’s disease). Abnormalities of posture and movement can also be a clue to the patient’s overall wellbeing, and may represent pain, weakness or psychological or emotional disturbance. The physical examination begins as soon as you see the patient. Start with a rapid assessment of how unwell the patient is, since the clinical assessment may have to be adjusted for a deteriorating or dying patient, and any abnormal physiology may need to be addressed urgently before the actual diagnosis is found . Observe the patient before the consultation begins. Do they look generally well or unwell? What is their demeanour ? text: Abnormal coloration of the skin & Mucous membranes Mohammed Zeitoun MD, PHD Lecturer of Internal Medicine Diabetes Unit Alexandria University Agenda Pallor. Cyanosis. Jaundice. Pallor Pallor may be due to anaemia or to vasoconstriction. Pallor Pallor Pallor Agenda Pallor. Cyanosis. Jaundice. Cyanosis A bluish cast to the skin, that is easily seen in the tip of the nose, lips, cheeks, oral nucosa , conjunctivae, tongue , and the nail beds. Cyanosis In general, cyanosis becomes apparent when the mean capillary concentration of reduced hemoglobin exceeds 5g/dL. It is the absolute rather than the relative quantity of reduced hemoglobin that is important in producing cyanosis. P atients with severe anemia and even marked arterial desaturation do not display cyanosis. Clinical Classification & Etiology True Cyanosis (increased amount of reduced Hb) — Central Type — Peripheral Type — Mixed Type Cyanosis due to abnormal Hb derivatives — Methemoglobinemia — Sulfhemoglobinemia Cyanosis may be subdivided into central and peripheral types . In the central type, the SaO 2 is reduced or an abnormal hemoglobin derivative is present, and the mucous membranes and skin are both affected. Peripheral cyanosis is due to a slowing of blood flow and abnormally great extraction of O 2 from normally saturated arterial blood . It results from vasoconstriction and diminished peripheral blood flow, such as occurs in cold exposure, shock, congestive failure, and peripheral vascular disease. Cyanosis Central cyanosis: Cyanosis Central cyanosis: Colour of the tongue is a more reliable indicator of central cyanosis. Central cyanosis may occur in: COPD. Pneumonia. Bronchial asthma. Pulmonary infarction. Pulmonary fibrosis. Cyanosis Of Cardiac Origin Cyanosis of cardiac origin is usually caused by: Pulmonary oedema. Congenital heart disease: The presence of cyanosis implies the development of a right –to left shunt. The resultant cyanosis is not corrected when breathing 100% oxygen. Usually associated with finger clubbing. Impaired pulmonary function 1. Airway obstruction 2. Pulmonary diseases 3. Pleural diseases Right-to-left shunting of blood Tetralogy of Fallot Central Cyanosis Peripheral Cyanosis Caused by increased oxygen consumption in peripheral tissue . Vasoconstriction Low cardiac output Exposure to cold air or water Slowing of blood flow Right heart failure Agenda Pallor. Cyanosis. Jaundice. Jaundice Yellow discoloration of sclera, skin, mucous membranes due to deposition of bile pigment Clinically detected with serum bilirubin 2 2.5mg/dL Jaundice Jaundice is the result of excess bilirubin circulating in the blood. In jaundice, the sclerae , mucous membranes and skin are lemon-yellow in colour . Most bilirubin originates from the catabolism of haemoglobin in the reticulo -endothelial system. Jaundice Haemolytic jaundice: Unconjugutcd hyperbilirubinacmia such as in haemolytic anaemia . Urine looks normal. Jaundice Hepatocellular jaundice: Characteristic symptoms include anorexia with impairment of taste, nausea, vomiting and upper abdominal pain (often associated with hepatic tenderness). Common causes include viral hepatitis und chemical hepatitis. e.g. alcohol abuse and drug therapy. Jaundice Obstructive jaundice: Typical symptoms include itching ( pruritus ). dark urine and pale stools. Obstruction of the biliary tract is usually extra-hepatic in origin and caused by either gall stones or pancreatic carcinoma. Gall stones are suggested by a history of fever, rigors or biliary colic. Pancreatic carcinoma is suggested by chronic persistent back pain aggravated by recumbency, and palpable enlargement of the gall bladder may occur. Jaundice Obstructive jaundice: Intrahepatic obstruction is most often due to alcohol abuse, drug therapy and primary biliary cirrhosis (a disorder of middle-aged women often preceded by marked pruritus ). Jaundice Obstructive jaundice: In hepatocellular and obstructive jaundice, the urine is dark and the stool is pale. Jaundice

text: Vital signs Vital signs Pulse. Arterial blood pressure. Temperature. Respiratory rate. Signs & Symptoms Signs are observed or measured. Symptoms are told to you by the patient. When to measure vital signs? On admission to health care facility. In a hospital on regular hosp schedule or as MD ordered (q8hours, q4 hours, etc). Before and after procedures (surgery, invasive diagnostic procedures). Before, during, and after blood transfusions. When patient’s general condition changes (nursing judgment). You should report VS when: VS above the normal range VS below the normal range Any VS that has changed from a prior measurement Vital Signs Accuracy is essential: Abnormal vital signs are often the first indication of a disease of abnormality. Never guess or report an inaccurate reading. If you have difficulty obtaining a correct reading for any vital sign, ask for help ARTERIAL PULSES The arterial pulse should be examined in all 4 limbs and both sides of the neck. Comment On Arterial Pulses Rate. Rhythm. Force. Volume. Character. Vessel wall. Equality of both sides. Other pulses. + Radial Pulse حفظ Radial Artery - Anatomy The radial pulse is readily felt just lateral to the tendon of the flexor carpi radialis muscle. Apply three fingers over the radial pulse at the right wrist. Radial Pulse Lateral aspect of the lower forearm just proximal to the wrist joint. Feel the bony prominence. Move fingertips medially. Tips of fingers drop into a groove in which lies the artery. Examine the pulse by compressing the artery backwards against the bone, using the finger tips. Compress the radial artery gradual until a maximal pulsation is detected. Safety Alert DO NOT take a pulse with the thumb, since it has a pulse of its own You could mistake the pulse in your thumb for the person’s pulse TECHNIQUE DO NOT use thumb. DO NOT squeeze. If irregular, count for 1 full minute or take apical pulse for 1 minute. Radial Pulse - Rate If the pulse is regular: Count the pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by four to obtain pulse rate in beats per minute (b .p .m ). If the pulse is irrigular: Count over 1 minute. Normal resting pulse rate = 60-100 bpm . Bradycardia is defined as a rate of < 60 b.p.m . Tachycardia is a rate > 100 b.p.m . Radial Pulse - Rate Radial Pulse - Rate Radial Pulse - Rate Radial Pulse - Rhythm The interval between each pulse wave and the other. By regular rhythm we mean that the interval between each 2 consecutive beats are equal. Radial Pulse - Rhythm Normal rhythm is called sinus rhythm because it originates from the sinoatrial node. Sinus rhythm is seldom completely regular; because the heart speeds up during inspiration & slows at the beginning of expiration. This sinus arrhythmia is most obvious in children, young people and athletes. Radial Artery - Rhythm Radial Pulse - Rhythm حفظ Radial Pulse - Rhythm Pulsus bigeminus Radial Pulse - Rhythm Atrial fibrillation causes a totally random heart rhythm leading to a pulse which is irregular in both timing and volume, this is often described as 'irregularly irregular' rhythm. Radial Pulse - Force Amount of external pressure required to obliterate the pulse. Proportional to the systolic blood pressure. حفظ Radial Pulse - Force Distal finger is used to occlude the collateral circulation Middle finger feels the pulse Proximal finger occlude the artery حفظ Radial Pulse - Volume Amount of expansile pulsation of the arterial wall = amount of elevation of the palpating finger at arrival of each pulse wave. Term used to indicate the movement imparted to the finger applied gently to the pulse. Proportional to pulse pressure = systolic blood pressure – diastolic blood pressure. The pulse pressure is about 30-40 mmHg. Radial Pulse - Volume Causes of Large volume pulse: Aortic regurgitation Vasodilatation: Exercise, heat and pregnancy. Fever, thyrotoxicosis , anaemia . Causes of low volume pulse: Reduced stroke volume (E.g. heart failure). Peripheral vascular disease. Radial Pulse - Character Character describes the impression of the pulse waveform gained by palpation. Considerable experience is required before characteristic waveforms call be recognized with confidence. Radial Pulse - Character Water-hammer Pulse Sharp upstroke. Large amplitude. Rapid down stroke. Short duration. Wide pulse pressure. > 60 mmHg حفظ Causes of Water-hammer Pulse Most commonly in aortic regurge . Large arteriovenous fistula. Hyperkinetic states: thyrotoxicosis or anemia. حفظ How to examine for Water-hammer Pulse? Why do we raise the patient arm? To exaggerate the phenomena. حفظ To feel for a collapsing pulse, raise the arm while feeling across the pulse with the fingers of the other hand. Plateau Pulse Pulsus Parvus et Tardus (weak and delayed) Slow upstroke. Small amplitude. Slow down stroke. Long duration. Small pulse pressure < 30 mmHg. Causes: Aortic stenosis. Pulsus Alternans Rare. Alternate variations in the size of the pulse wave (Alternating strong and weak pulses). The pulse rhythm is regular. Sign of severe myocardial disease & heart failure. Thready Pulse Weak and rapid pulse. Pulse Deficit Refers to the difference between ventricular frequency and radial pulse frequency. It is seen in atrial fibrillation when some contractions aren’t efficient enough to be transmitted to the periphery. Pulse Apex Deficit Diff b/w heart rate & pulse rate , when counted simultaneously for one minute. Diff b/w AF & Ectopics Features Atrial fibrillation Ectopics Pulse deficit > 10 / min < 10 / min On exertion Persists/increase Decrease rhythm Irregularly irregular Regularly irregular Condition of the Vessel Wall The proximal and distal fingers are applied to the radial artery while adherent to each other. Then the 2 fingers are spread from each other to empty the radial artery (Milking movement). The middle finger is then used to roll the empty wall. Felt vessel wall indicates marked arterioslecosis ( Monckeberg sclerosis) and may be seen in elderly individuals. Equality On Both Sides

DEPARTMENT OF INTERNAL MEDICINE
E. Book
Clinical Examination

1

 History Taking
1. Introduction:
The Importance of History Taking:
History taking is the most critical component of the medical examination process.

Benefits of Effective History Taking:
1. Focuses Attention: Directs the clinician to the affected body system(s).
2. Assesses Severity & Progression: Provides insight into the severity and temporal
evolution of the illness.
3. Enables Diagnosis: Can be sufficient to diagnose specific conditions (e.g., epilepsy,
migraine, renal colic) based on symptomatology alone.

2. The Art of History Taking: Communication as a Foundation
 History taking is a specialized form of communication that initiates the doctorpatient relationship.

Key Principles for Effective Communication:
1. Establish Rapport: Put the patient at ease and encourage open dialogue.
2. Demonstrate Attentiveness: Make it clear the patient has your undivided
attention.
3. Show Respect: Greet the patient, using their name if possible.
4. Maintain Professionalism: Do not display anger or shock at the patient's
disclosures.
5. Allow Patient Narrative: Let patients tell their story in their own words and
sequence.
6. Observe Non-Verbal Cues: Pay close attention to body language (facial
expressions, eye contact, posture, clenched fists, etc.).
7. Be an Active Listener: Listening is as important as questioning.

3. The Standard Structure of a Medical History
 A complete medical history should systematically cover the following components:
1. Personal Data
5. Drug History and Allergies
2. Chief Complaint
6. Social History
3. History of Present Illness
7. Family History
4. Past Medical History

2

 I. Personal Data
This section provides essential contextual information about the patient.
1. Name: For identification and rapport.
2. Age: Certain diseases are age-specific (e.g., childhood infectious diseases, congenital
anomalies).
3. Sex:
 Some diseases are sex-linked (e.g., hemophilia in males).
 Some diseases show sex predilection (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus
erythematosus are more common in females).
4. Occupation: May expose individuals to specific hazards (e.g., infections in healthcare
workers, radiation exposure, occupational lung diseases like asbestosis).
5. Residence/Geographic History: Can indicate risk for endemic diseases (e.g.,
schistosomiasis in rural dwellers in certain regions).
6. Habits: Document smoking history (pack-years), alcohol intake, and other substance
use.
7. Marital Status & Number of Children: Relevant for social support.

II. Chief Complaint




The symptom(s) that prompted the patient to seek medical care.
Definition: State the main problem(s) in the patient's own words.
Duration: Note the time frame (e.g., "chest pain for 3 hours").
Chronology: For multiple complaints, list them in order of occurrence (oldest to
most recent).

Grade I: Dyspnea on doing more than the usual daily effort.

Paroxysmal attack of dyspnea that usually occurs at night, wakes the patient 2–3
hours after sleep with marked inspiratory dyspnea, cough with frothy expectoration,
and fighting for air.
Common in congestive heart failure.
Mechanism: Aggravation of pulmonary venous congestion due to absorption of
edema fluid from ECS to the circulation, increasing venous return to the heart.
When associated with wheezes due to bronchospasm, it is known as “Cardiac
Asthma.”

text:
Approach to patients with different symptoms
Patients in pain
Definition
The International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) proposed the following
definition (1979): ‘Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated
with actual or potential tissue damage or described in terms of damage’. This definition
has important implications: pain is not necessarily or always associated with ongoing
tissue damage; it is a subjective experience and has an emotional as well as a sensory
component and is always unpleasant.
Pain is notoriously difficult to describe. It is difficult to assess and even harder to
quantify. Nevertheless, pain assessment is crucial in order to evaluate its impact on the
sufferer and also to plan a treatment strategy. It has been termed ‘the 5th vital sign’ and
is mandated as part of routine assessment of patients in hospital. In 2004 the IASP
declared that the relief of pain should be a human right.

Classification of pain
Pain is commonly classified according to the following:
▪ Etiology and underlying condition.
▪ Mechanism.
▪ Duration.

Etiology/underlying condition
▪ Trauma – an acute response to an injury.
▪ Surgery.
▪ Medical illness such as myocardial infarction or appendicitis.
▪ Physiological conditions such as menstruation and labour.

1

 Mechanism
▪ Inflammatory/Nociceptive – pain generated and maintained by inflammatory
mediators (such as prostaglandin E2), secondary to an ongoing disease process.
Examples include inflammatory arthritis or mechanical back pain.
▪ Neuropathic – Neuropathic pain is generated in malfunctioning nerves and is defined
as ‘pain arising as a direct consequence of a lesion or disease affecting the
somatosensory system’. This type of pain has special clinical features as described
below and may arise from injury or dysfunction of the central or peripheral nervous
system. Examples include painful diabetic neuropathy and post-stroke pain.
▪ Mixed pain – This includes features of both nociceptive and neuropathic pain, such as
back pain with radiculopathy (radiating leg pain due to nerve irritation or
compression).
▪ Psychosomatic – Purely psychosomatic pain is rare. However, pain, especially chronic
pain, almost invariably has an emotional and behavioral component.
Duration
▪ Acute – most commonly a physiological response to an injury. It resolves with the
disappearance of a noxious stimulus or within the time frame of a normal healing
process.
▪ Chronic – it can either be associated with an ongoing pathological process, such as
rheumatoid arthritis or malignancy, or be present for longer than is consistent with a
normal healing time. Pain is arbitrarily described as chronic if it persists for longer
than 3 months. Chronic pain is often associated with disability, mood and sleep
disturbance and a significant behavioural response. It is sometimes subdivided into
pain associated with cancer and pain associated with non-malignant conditions.

2

 Figure 1 Spinal withdrawal reflex with pain.

Figure 2 Pain pathway

3

 As with any other branch of medicine, careful and meticulous assessment of a
patient’s symptoms and signs is fundamental. Two key questions should be considered
when dealing with a patient in pain:
▪ Is the pain a symptom of ongoing tissue damage or of another condition that needs to
be dealt with by another medical professional?
▪ What is the optimal treatment strategy: to either abolish the pain altogether or reduce
it to a more bearable level?
Unfortunately, no single standardized approach will allow assessment of pain in
every situation. Pain is essentially a subjective experience. Therefore, what the patient
describes as his experience is of paramount importance. As in most areas of medicine,
the history is the most useful tool in assessment and diagnosis.

History

and making a diagnosis. Even in acute pain states, where pain represents a protective
