text: Basics of X-RAY AND ULTRASOUND ILOs Principle of X-ray. Radiographic densities. X-ray examinations of different regions. Advantages and disadvantages of X-ray. Key elements of radiation safety. Principle of Ultrasound. US examinations of different body regions. Advantages and disadvantages of Ultrasound. X-Ray X-RAY X-RAY X-rays are a form of electromagnetic energy formed when high-speed electrons bombard a tuhgsten anode target. X-rays Have shorter wavelength than visible light  allowing them to penetrate matter. X-RAY X-rays passing through the tissues depends on the energy of the x-ray and atomic number of the tissue Tissues in the body contain different elements that vary by the atomic number, so there are differences in body tissue densities .  The higher the atomic number, more likely to absorb/block the x-ray  the denser the element X-RAY So, specific shadows of internal body structures become visible because they contain different types of elements Example: when x-ray strikes Bone blocked and will appear white on X-ray image. Air (less dense) x-rays passed all through and will appear black on X-ray image. (ex. lungs and bowel gasses) X-RAY Basic Radiographic densities: Metal  bright white Mineral  white Fluid/soft tissue  Gray Fat  Dark Gray Air  Black X-RAY X-ray can be done on many parts of the body upon the requested part to be examined: Skull  AP and lateral views X-RAY X-ray can be done on many parts of the body upon the requested part to be examined: Spine (cervical, dorsal and lumbar)  AP and lateral views X-RAY X-ray can be done on many parts of the body upon the requested part to be examined: Chest  PA and lateral views Abdomen X-RAY X-ray can be done on many parts of the body upon the requested part to be examined: Parts of the Upper and lower limbs X-RAY Advantages: Cheaper technique Lower radiation than CT Can diagnose and guide treatment in some conditions; Bone fractures, foreign bodies, bone lesions , urinary stones, Mammography (Breast) Disadvantages: Not provide 3D information radiation exposure X-RAY Key elements of radiation safety: Time  limit the amount of time Distance  more distance (X-ray dose inversely proportional the distance squared) Shielding  covering the body parts by metallic shield (Aprons) ULTRASOUND ULTRASOUND -- Principle of Ultrasound. Principle of Ultrasound. What is US? How does US work? And how is an image created? US probes and examinations of different body regions. US safety considerations. Sound is a series of pressure waves propagating through a medium. One cycle of the acoustic wave is composed of a complete positive and negative pressure change The wavelength is the distance traveled during one cycle The frequency of the wave is measured in cycles per second or Hertz (cycles/s, Hz) ULTRASOUND -- Principle of Ultrasound. The ultrasound probe generates inaudible high-frequency sound waves. The waves are reflected off the body structures and are detected by the probe. Ultrasound waves are: Reflected by Solid and Gas: Bright Transmitted (not reflected) by Fluid: Dark This reflection or transmission causes an additional effect distal to it: Distal to a bright object: dark acoustic shadowing Ultrasound is high-frequency sound waves (exceeding the upper limit of human hearing which is 20,000 Hz ) Diagnostic US operates between 3.5 and 10 Million Hz (3.5 and 10 MHz). Biostatistics is the application of statistics in medical research; e.g.
epidemiology, clinical trials, pharmacology, clinical decision making, etc.

Biostatistics
includes two
major
sections, descriptive
statistics and inferential statistics. Descriptive statistics is concerned with
describing, presenting, and summarizing data, while Inferential statistics is
concerned with analyzing data, finding associations and causal relationships
between data, and driving conclusions or inferences.

Collection of data
Data are the basic building blocks of statistics, they are the individual values
measured or observed.

Data are classified into two main types:
Constant data: observations that do not vary among individuals (e.g.,
number of eyes)

Variables: observations that differ between individuals or groups (e.g.,
weight)

Research Proposal and data collection tools

1. Criticize the following title: "Knowledge, Attitude, and Practice Towards Antibiotics Use

Among Medical Sector Final-Year Students in Egypt, 2023"
…………………………………………………………………………………………………
…………………………………………………………………………………………………
Introduction:
Antibiotics play an essential role in reducing mortality due to infections [1]. However,
the indiscriminate and imprudent use of antibiotics has led to the emergence of
antibiotic resistance, which is now a serious global health concern [2,3,4]. Antibiotic
resistance contributes to increased rates of morbidity, mortality, and economic burden
[5, 6], making it a priority issue for the World Health Organization (WHO) [7]. The
WHO conducted online surveys about antibiotic resistance in developing countries,
where Egypt showed a low level of awareness about prudent antibiotic use and a high
frequency of inappropriate antibiotic use among the public [8]. This is exacerbated by
factors such as antibiotic self-medication (ABSM), the easy availability of nonprescribed antibiotics in community pharmacies, high medical consultation costs, and
inadequate awareness about antibiotic use [9]. Therefore, there is an increasing
consensus that new plans and strategies for preventing antibiotic resistance should be
developed [10].
Medical sector students, as future healthcare providers (HCPs), play a vital role in
combating antibiotic resistance by promoting public awareness through disseminating
public health education about the judicious use of antibiotics and how to minimize
resistance toward them [11]. To competently undertake these responsibilities,
undergraduate medical sector students should be well-educated about all the related
principles of microbiology, pharmacology, and infectious diseases and receive the
appropriate training about antibiotic use [12]. They should also be able to handle
patients’ requests for antibiotics [13]. Therefore, it is essential to provide adequate

 undergraduate education and training on antibiotics for medical sector students [14].
This cross-sectional study will investigate and compare the knowledge, attitude, and
practice (KAP) related to antibiotic use and antibiotic resistance among final-year
medical sector undergraduate students in Egypt. The study focused on students in four
medical specialties: medicine, pharmacy, dentistry, and nursing. The main objective
of the study is to evaluate the KAP levels among the students in these specialties that
could be useful for implementing more effective and suitable antibiotic control
intervention strategies to mitigate antibiotic resistance.

 Preface
This handbook has been prepared for third-year medical students of the Faculty of
Medicine, University of Alexandria as they begin their formal study of surgery. At this stage
of training, a clear understanding of the basic principles of surgery is essential before
moving on to specific diseases and operative techniques.
Surgery extends beyond technical skills. It is based on sound scientific
knowledge, careful history-taking and clinical examination, ethical practice, and proper
perioperative care. For this reason, Part I: Basic Principles provides the foundation upon
which further surgical learning is built.
The content follows the official curriculum of the Department of Surgery and is
presented in a clear, focused, and clinically relevant manner.
This handbook is the result of a collaborative effort by the staff of the Department
of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, University of Alexandria. Each chapter concludes with
multiple-choice questions to help students revise key topics and prepare effectively for
examinations.
Some of the information and illustrations in this handbook have been adapted
from well-known standard surgical textbooks, including Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of
Surgery, Browse’s Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease, and SRB’s
Clinical Methods in Surgery. In addition, selected photographs have been contributed by
staff members of the Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine, University of
Alexandria.
The illustrations and clinical photographs included in this handbook are intended
as an introductory visual exposure to surgical diseases. Their aim is to familiarize
students with the names and general appearance of common conditions and to
stimulate interest in surgery. Students are not expected to study these images in detail;
comprehensive coverage will be provided in Parts II and III of this series.

text: Chapter 1 Metabolic Response to Injury Core Concepts of Metabolism Metabolism Defined: A complex system of interrelated biochemical reactions and physiological responses required for maintaining life. Homeostasis: The foundation of normal physiology. It is an optimum metabolic state that maintains the stability and functioning of the body. Homeostatic Maintenance: This complex process involves the brain, nerves, heart, lungs, kidneys, and spleen. The Stress Response: A "damage control" system intended to maintain homeostasis and provide the necessary substrate for injury repair. Triggering Factors of the Stress Response Psychological & Sensory Stimuli: Pain, fear, anxiety, and agitation. Circulatory Changes: Direct trauma and significant changes in circulatory volumes. Biological Insults: Reperfusion injuries and infective sources, such as gastrointestinal (GIT) perforation. The Graded Response: The response to injury is proportional; more severe injuries result in a greater metabolic response. Overview of Physiological Phases Phase Division: The human metabolic response to injury is split into the "ebb" and "flow" phases. The Ebb Phase Timeline: Begins immediately at the time of injury and typically lasts 24 to 48 hours. The Flow Phase Timeline: Follows the ebb phase and can last for days or even weeks. Transition: Following proper resuscitation, the ebb phase evolves into the hypermetabolic flow phase. The Ebb Phase (Shock) Primary Objective: To conserve circulating volume and energy stores for future recovery and repair. Metabolic Characteristics: Marked by a decreased basal metabolic rate and reduced cardiac output. Clinical Features: Patients often exhibit hypovolemia, hypothermia, and lactic acidosis. Resuscitation: While proper resuscitation can attenuate the ebb phase, it cannot completely abolish it. The Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) Hormonal Regulation: The ebb phase is primarily regulated by catecholamines, cortisol, and aldosterone. The Cascade: The liver produces Angiotensinogen. The kidney releases Renin to create Angiotensin I. Lung-derived ACE converts this to Angiotensin II. Systemic Effects: This results in vasoconstriction and the reabsorption of NaCl and $H_{2}O$ by the kidneys. The Flow Phase (Hypermetabolism) Systemic Inflammatory Response: This phase corresponds to the Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS). Metabolic Surge: Characterized by an increased basal metabolic rate (hypermetabolism) and increased oxygen consumption. Cardiovascular & Physical Signs: Includes increased cardiac output, raised body temperature, and leukocytosis. Resource Mobilization: The body mobilizes energy stores to replace lost or damaged tissue. Catabolism vs. Anabolism The Catabolic Phase: Lasts approximately 3 to 10 days. Catabolic Mechanisms: Increased production of counter-regulatory hormones and inflammatory cytokines leads to significant fat and protein mobilization. The Anabolic Phase: Follows catabolism and may last for several weeks. Reprioritization: The body shifts limited resources away from peripheral tissues (skin, muscle, fat) toward key viscera like the liver and immune system. The Neuroendocrine Arm: Neural Control Pathway Components: Consists of a neural part (brain, spinal cord, afferent neurons) and an endocrine part (hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal glands). The "Fight or Flight" Response: Neural activation restores volume and triggers the sympathetic nervous system. Catecholamine Release: Sympathetic activation triggers adrenaline release from the adrenal medulla and noradrenaline from the nerves. Pancreatic Interaction: Sympathetic activation stimulates the Alpha cells of the pancreas to release glucagon. The Neuroendocrine Arm: Endocrine Control Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis: The hypothalamus releases Corticotrophin-Releasing Hormone (CRH), stimulating the anterior pituitary to release ACTH. Adrenal Action: ACTH acts on the adrenal cortex to increase cortisol secretion. Counter-Regulatory Hormones: Glucagon, glucocorticoids, and catecholamines work together to provide energy via gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and lipolysis. Energy Provision: These hormones are essential for fueling the healing process. The Inflammatory Arm: Cytokines Chemical Messengers: The inflammatory cascade is mediated by cytokines produced within the first 24 hours. Key Identified Cytokines: Includes Interleukins (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8) and Interferon (IFN). Primary Mediator: Tumour Necrosis Factor alpha (TNFα) is the main cytokine in the inflammatory arm. Cytokine Actions: Directly cause pyrexia (fever) by acting on the hypothalamus. Induce skeletal muscle proteolysis. Contribute to peripheral insulin resistance. Impact on Muscle and Glucose Metabolism Muscle Wasting: Results from increased protein degradation coupled with decreased synthesis, primarily in peripheral skeletal muscle. Clinical Asthenia: Muscle loss leads to weakness, fatigue, reduced functional ability, and higher mortality risks. Insulin Resistance: Postoperative hyperglycemia occurs because of increased glucose production and decreased peripheral uptake. Poor Glycemic Control: Injured patients often struggle with blood sugar because cytokines further increase insulin resistance. SIRS, MODS, and MOF SIRS Defined: The pathological extension of the stress response characterized by an exaggerated systemic reaction. SIRS Criteria: * Temperature: > 38 or < 36. Heart Rate: > 90 beats per minute. Respiratory Rate: > 20 breaths per minute. WBC Count: > 12,000/mm^3 or < 4,000/mm3. Progression to Death: SIRS  Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS)  Multiple Organ Failure (MOF)  Death. Clinical Management & Compounding Factors Surgical Strategy: Elective practice seeks to minimize the "primary insult" through minimal access surgery and "stress-free" perioperative care. Emergency Intervention: Requires artificial augmentation of homeostasis (resuscitation) and organ support (critical care). Factors Compounding

text: Shock, Haemorrhage, and Resuscitation Definition Pathophysiology: Cellular Changes Microvascular & Systemic Changes Classification of Shock Classification of Shock Clinical Features and Stages Haemorrhage: Definitions and Types Definition: Acute blood loss (external or internal/concealed). Chronological Types: Primary: Immediate bleeding after injury. Reactionary: Within 24 hours (clot disruption/technical failure). Secondary: 7-14 days post-injury (infection, necrosis). Surgical vs Non-Surgical: Surgical: Controlled by surgery. Non-Surgical: Caused by clotting disorders. Classification of Blood Loss (Adults) Class I (<15%): Minimal clinical changes. Class II (15–30%): Mild tachycardia. Class III (30–40%): Hypotension, tachycardia. Class IV (>40%): Severe hypotension, shock. Assessment of Response to Fluid Bolus: Responder: BP remains high; bleeding controlled. Transient responder: BP rises temporarily; ongoing bleeding. Non-responder: BP doesn't improve; urgent intervention needed. Resuscitation & The Lethal Triad Core Principles: Stop active bleeding and support circulation. The Lethal Triad: 1. Hypothermia: Impairs coagulation. 2. Acidosis: Decreases enzymatic activity, worsens clotting. 3. Coagulopathy: Exacerbated by shock and trauma. Note: Avoid excessive fluids during ongoing bleeding (prevents 'dilutional' coagulopathy). Damage Control Resuscitation (DCR) Rapid Hemorrhage Control: Pressure, tourniquets, packing, or surgery. Permissive Hypotension: Maintain MAP ~50–65 mmHg until bleeding is controlled. Balanced Transfusion: RBC, FFP, and platelets in equal ratios (1:1:1). Limit crystalloids. Correction: Use Tranexamic acid, platelets, or cryoprecipitate; rewarm the patient. Major Haemorrhage Protocol Activation: Immediate for life-threatening bleeding. Steps: 1. Rapid ABC assessment. 2. Large-bore IV access + crossmatch. 3. Emergency transfusion (Type O if needed). 4. Identify source (Surgery/Angio/Endo). 5. Bedside imaging (US/X-ray); full imaging only if stable. Fluid Therapy & Vasoactive Agents Fluid Matching: Blood loss: Use blood components. Other fluid loss: Use crystalloid solutions. Bolus: 250–500 mL and assess response. Vasopressors/Inotropes: Use ONLY after adequate volume resuscitation. Distributive: Noradrenaline, phenylephrine, or vasopressin. Cardiogenic: Inotropes (e.g., dobutamine). Monitoring in Shock Blood Transfusion & Products Complications of Blood Transfusion Haemostasis: Mechanical Methods Haemostasis: Thermal & Energy-Based Electrosurgery: Monopolar: Most common; current passes through patient to dispersive electrode. Bipolar: Current confined between forceps tips; no dispersive electrode needed. Vessel Sealing ( LigaSure ): Seals vessels up to 7 mm. Ultrasonic (Harmonic Scalpel): Vibration seals/cuts vessels up to 5 mm. Argon Plasma Coagulation & Lasers: Precise heat coagulation. Haemostasis: Chemical & Topical Pharmacological Agents: Epinephrine (vasoconstriction). Vitamin K (Warfarin reversal), Protamine (Heparin reversal). Tranexamic Acid (Lysine analogue). Topical Agents: Passive: Surgicel ® (Cellulose), Gelfoam ® (Gelatin). Active: Thrombin products. Flowables : Combined passive/active (e.g., FloSeal ®). Endpoints of Resuscitation Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP): 65–90 mmHg. Urine Output: >0.5 mL/kg/hour. Central Venous Pressure (CVP): 5–10 cm H2O. Central Venous Oxygen Saturation: >70%. Biochemical: Lactate return to normal, resolution of base deficit. MCQ 1. Shock is best defined as: A. Inadequate tissue perfusion leading to insufficient oxygen and glucose delivery B. Sudden drop in blood pressure C. Failure of the cardiovascular system D. Loss of circulating blood volume 2. A key biochemical marker of tissue hypoxia in shock is: A. Serum potassium B. Serum lactate C. Hemoglobin level D. Blood urea 3. Anaerobic metabolism during shock primarily results in: A. Respiratory alkalosis B. Metabolic alkalosis C. Metabolic acidosis D. Hyperglycaemia 4. Failure of the sodium-potassium pump in shock leads to: A. Cellular dehydration B. Potassium loss from cells C. Cell shrinkage D. Cellular swelling 5. Hypoxia-induced endothelial injury mainly causes: A. Vasoconstriction B. Capillary leakage and tissue edema C. Increased oxygen delivery D. Reduced coagulation 6. Initial compensatory tachycardia with peripheral vasoconstriction is seen in all types of shock EXCEPT: A. Hypovolemic B. Cardiogenic C. Obstructive D. Distributive 7. Which condition is a cause of obstructive shock? A. Severe burns B. Myocardial infarction C. Cardiac tamponade D. Septicemia 8. Early septic shock is typically characterized by: A. Low cardiac output B. High or normal cardiac output C. Bradycardia D. Severe hypothermia 9. Neurogenic shock differs from other types by the presence of: A. Severe tachycardia B. Hypertension C. Cold extremities D. Hypotension with bradycardia 10. The compensated stage of shock is characterized by: A. Loss of consciousness B. Normal blood pressure with tachycardia C. Anuria D. Irreversible organ failure 11. The refractory stage of shock is defined by: A. Full recovery B. Reversible organ dysfunction C. Irreversible organ failure D. Mild hypotension 12. Reactionary haemorrhage typically occurs: A. Immediately after injury B. Within 24 hours C. Between 3–5 days D. After 2 weeks 13. A transient responder to fluid resuscitation indicates: A. text: Surgical Ethics and Law Introduction to Surgical Ethics Surgery, ethics, and law are fundamentally linked. Nature of Surgery: Involves deliberate intervention, causing tissue injury. Surgeon vs. Criminal: Distinguished by therapeutic intention. Justification: Harm is incidental; justified if performed competently in patient’s best interest. Patient Trust: Creates moral, professional, and legal obligations. Foundations of Surgical Ethics Definition: Derived from 'ethos' (character); moral principles guiding behavior. Professional Conduct: Ensures technical skill is guided by ethical standards. History: Hippocratic Oath (patient benefit) and Thomas Percival. Modern Focus: Patient-centered care, rights, and autonomy. Core Principles of Medical Ethics (I) 1. Autonomy: Respecting the patient’s right to self-rule and informed decisions. Competent adults can refuse even life-sustaining treatment. 2. Beneficence: The duty to act in the patient's best interest and promote well-being. Core Principles of Medical Ethics (II) 3. Non-maleficence: The duty to 'do no harm'. Unavoidable harm must be proportionate to the benefit. 4. Justice: Fairness in distribution of resources and treatment. Avoidance of arbitrary prejudice. Informed Consent: The Basics Respect for Autonomy: No surgery without valid consent (except emergencies). Process vs. Event: It is a continuous dialogue, not just a signature. Documentation: Discussion must be recorded in medical notes. Requirements for Valid Consent 1. Patient’s Own Decision: Made by the patient themselves. 2. Full Understanding: Comprehension of information and implications. 3. Voluntariness: Free from pressure or coercion. 4. Capacity: The mental ability to make the decision. Information Disclosure Diagnosis and natural history of the condition. Proposed treatment details. Potential risks and benefits. Reasonable alternatives (including no treatment). Expected outcomes. Emergency Surgery Doctrine of Necessity: Treatment proceeds if delay causes serious harm/death. Conditions: - Patient is incapacitated/unconscious. - Delay risks death or permanent harm. - Procedure is clearly in the patient's best interests. Consent in Children Minors (Under 18): Generally, require parental consent. Gillick Competence: Children under 16 can consent if they fully understand. Gillick competent decisions cannot be overridden by parents. Best Interests: Parents must act in the child's best interests. Adults Lacking Capacity Best Interests Principle: Decisions based on the patient's welfare. Relatives: Cannot legally consent but provide insight into patient preferences. Legal Tools: Advance directives and legal proxies must be respected. Life-Sustaining Treatment Withholding/Withdrawal is acceptable if: - Treatment is futile (won't achieve physiological goal). - Death is imminent and irreversible. - Permanent loss of consciousness (e.g., PVS). Must be fully documented and in patient’s best interest. Pain Relief, Double Effect, and Euthanasia Double Effect: Strong analgesia is ethical if primary intent is pain relief, even if it shortens life. Active Euthanasia: Deliberately causing death to relieve suffering. Legality: Illegal in most countries, including Egypt. Confidentiality General Rule: Patient information is private and essential for trust. Exceptions: - Required by law/court order. - To prevent serious harm (self/others). - Public interest (e.g., infectious diseases). - Sharing within the healthcare team. Ethics in Surgical Research Patient welfare is paramount over research goals. Requirements: Informed consent, Ethics Committee approval, risk-benefit balance. Vulnerable groups: Require extra protection. Innovation: Distinguish minor improvements from major research. Maintaining Professional Standards Competence: Operate only within your area of expertise. Lifelong Learning: Continuous education and regular audits. Honesty: Being transparent regarding medical errors. Conclusion The Dual Duty: Protecting life while respecting autonomy. Core Applications: Consent, confidentiality, research, and standards. Overarching Principles: Fairness, justice, and ethics in practice. MCQ 1. Which principle of medical ethics emphasizes respecting a patient’s right to make informed decisions? a. Beneficence b. Autonomy c. Non-maleficence d. Justice 2. Which of the following is a requirement for valid informed consent? a. Patient signature only b. Voluntariness c. Presence of a witness d. Legal representation 3. The surgeon prefers a specific technique d. Consent is not documented 4. Gillick competence refers to: a. Adults refusing life-sustaining treatment b. Children under 16 who can legally consent if they understand treatment c. Patients with advanced directives d. Surgeons assessing ethical risk in research 5. It is documented in research protocols 6. Which of the following is NOT a condition under which confidentiality may be breached? a. Required by law or court order b. To prevent serious harm c. text: Surgical Infection Microbiology: Gram-Positive Pathogens Streptococci: S. pyogenes (cellulitis), S. faecalis (post-bowel surgery). Treat with Penicillin. Staphylococci: S. aureus (major wound pathogen, MRSA), S. epidermidis (biofilms on prosthetics). Clostridia (Anaerobes): C. perfringens (gas gangrene), C. tetani (tetanus), C. difficile (colitis). Microbiology: Gram-Negative & Others Gram-negative Bacilli: E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus (gut-related), Pseudomonas (burns, urinary tract). Bacteroides: Anaerobes causing intra-abdominal abscesses. Fungi: Candida (common in immunocompromised or post-antibiotic patients). Risk Factors for Wound Infection Host Factors: Diabetes, obesity, malnutrition, steroids, smoking. Pathogen Factors: Virulence and bacterial load. Tissue Factors: Poor blood supply, low oxygen, hematoma, dead tissue. Foreign Material: Sutures, drains, prosthetic implants. Technique: Poor handling of tissue, excessive cautery. Classification of SSI Superficial SSI: Involves only skin and subcutaneous tissue. Deep SSI: Involves deep soft tissues (fascia, muscle). Requires drainage and systemic antibiotics Organ/Space SSI: Involves any part of the anatomy opened or manipulated during surgery. Secondary SSI: Occurs in a wound either left open or reopened. Specific Surgical Infections Abscess: Localized pus requiring drainage , heals with secondary intention Cellulitis: Non-suppurative spreading infection (Streptococci). Necrotizing Fasciitis: Rapidly spreading, high mortality, requires radical debridement. Boil/Carbuncle: Staphylococcal infection of hair follicles. Gas Gangrene Causative organism: Clostridium perfringens — Gram-positive, anaerobic,spore -forming bacilli found in soil and feces. Risk factors: Immunocompromised, diabetic, cancer patients; wounds with necrotic tissue or foreign material; high-energy military wounds. Pathophysiology: Anaerobic conditions promote bacterial growth. Bacterial toxins cause rapid tissue destruction, oedema, and systemic toxicity. Clinical features: Severe local pain Crepitus (gas in tissues, sometimes visible on X-ray) Thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate Rapid progression to systemic illness: circulatory collapse, organ failure Prevention: Antibiotic prophylaxis for high-risk wounds (e.g., amputations with necrotic ulcers). Treatment: Prompt, aggressive surgical debridement High-dose intravenous penicillin Tetanus Organism: Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic, Gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium found in soil and manure. Mechanism: Produces the exotoxin tetanospasmin, which afects the nervous system. Clinical features: Facial muscle spasms (trismus) Progression to generalized muscle spasms, opisthotonus Respiratory arrest and high mortality in severe cases Prevention: Tetanus toxoid vaccination (most efective measure). Treatment: Wound debridement Intravenous benzylpenicillin Muscle relaxants Ventilatory support in severe disease Sepsis & Management Bacteraemia : after deep SSI and prosthetic infections SIRS: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome. Sepsis: Infection + SIRS. MODS: severe organ dysfunction from uncontrolled SIRS Sepsis Six (to be done in 1 hour): 1. High-flow Oxygen | 2. Blood Cultures | 3. IV Antibiotics 4. IV Fluids | 5. Check Lactate | 6. Measure Urine Output Prevention and Management • Aseptic technique: sterile operating theatre, scrubbing, draping • Antiseptic technique: skin prep before incision • Prophylactic antibiotics: indicated in high-risk wounds (contaminated/dirty or prosthetic surgery) • Delayed primary / secondary closure: for heavily contaminated wounds Sepsis management: The Sepsis Six is the name given to a bundle of medical therapies designed to reduce mortality in patients with sepsis. The components of the Sepsis Six are: Give three to patients: (1) intravenous fuid challenge, (2) intravenous antibiotics, (3) oxygen and monitor urine output; Take three from patients: (4) blood cultures, (5) full blood count, (6) lactate. Viral Infections: HIV & COVID-19 HIV/Hepatitis: Risk of needle-stick injury. Use universal precautions (double gloving, masks). COVID-19: High perioperative risk of pneumonia and death. Management: Delay elective surgery if infected; preoperative screening; vaccination. Prevention: Operating Theatre Laminar Flow: Clean air directed over the wound. Normothermia: Keeping patient warm reduces infection risk. Supplemental Oxygen: High FiO2 post-surgery aids healing. Hand Hygiene: Alcohol gels (>70%) for routine disinfection. Preoperative Preparation Hospital Stay: Shorten stay to reduce MRSA colonization. Shaving: Avoid shaving night before (increases risk). Use clippers in theatre. Skin Prep: Alcohol-based chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine. Scrubbing: 2-3 minutes of antiseptic scrub for the surgical team. Antibiotic Prophylaxis Indications: Clean surgery with prosthesis, Clean-Contaminated, or Contaminated cases. Timing: Give at induction of anesthesia (0-60 mins before incision). Repeated Dosing: For long surgeries (>4 hours) or high blood loss (>1.5L). Review MCQs 1. Which organism is most commonly responsible for non-suppurative spreading cellulitis? a. Staphylococcus aureus b. β- haemolytic streptococci c. Clostridium perfringens d. Bacteroides fragilis 2. Which pathogen is classically associated with gas gangrene? a. Clostridium tetani b. Staphylococcus epidermidis c. Clostridium perfringens d. Pseudomonas aeruginosa 3. Which factor most strongly predisposes a wound to infection? a. Good vascularity b. Absence of dead space c. Presence of foreign material d. Early wound closure 4. Superfcial surgical site infection (SSSI) is characterized by: a. Organ cavity involvement b. Musculofascial infection c. Requirement for mandatory drainage d. Infection limited to skin and subcutaneous tissue 5. Which organism commonly causes pseudomembranous colitis after antibiotic use? a. Clostridium dificile b. Clostridium tetani c. Enterococcus faecalis d. Klebsiella pneumoniae 6. A key clinical featu

text: Basic Surgical Skills Importance of Patient Positioning Why It Matters Ensures safe anaesthesia Provides optimal surgical exposure Prevents nerve injury and pressure sores Reduces risk of respiratory and circulatory compromise Responsibility: Shared between surgeon, anaesthetist , and theatre team. Poor positioning may cause: Peripheral nerve damage Pressure ulcers Compartment syndrome DVT Respiratory problems Common Surgical Positions Supine Most common in general surgery Variations: Trendelenburg (head down) → Pelvic surgery, shock Reverse Trendelenburg (head up) → Upper abdominal surgery Prone Position Used for spinal and perineal surgery Requires: Careful padding Airway protection Eye protection Lateral Position Used in thoracic surgery Used for perianal abscess drainage Kidney Position Table flexed to increase space Used in renal surgery Lithotomy / Lloyd-Davies Position Used for: Gynaecological surgery Colorectal surgery Urological surgery Risks: DVT Compartment syndrome Peroneal nerve injury Preparation of the Surgical Site 1. Remove Metal Objects Prevents burns (diathermy) Reduces infection risk 2. Hair Removal (Only if Necessary) Best method → Electric clippers Avoid razor shaving → micro-abrasions → infection 3. Skin Antisepsis Alcohol-based chlorhexidine Povidone–iodine Allow to dry fully before draping 4. Draping Establish sterile field Avoid contact with non-sterile areas Theatre Etiquette & Sterile Technique 1. Surgical Hand Preparation Wash fingertips → hands → forearms → elbows Dry from fingers toward elbows 2. Sterile Gowning Touch only inside surface Keep hands inside cuffs Assistant ties gown 3. Closed Gloving Hands remain inside cuffs Keep hands above waist and within sterile field 4. Sharps Safety Never handle needles/blades directly Use needle holder or forceps Pass sharps in kidney dish Dispose immediately in sharps container Surgeon responsible for team safety 5. Equipment Checks Before incision: Confirm instrument function Check diathermy Check laparoscopic equipment 6. Surgical Ergonomics Table adjusted to forearm height Maintain balanced posture Prevent fatigue Skin Incisions Principles Scalpel perpendicular to skin Avoid oblique cuts (edge necrosis risk) Apply skin tension with non-dominant hand Common Blade Uses Blade 22 → Abdominal incisions Blade 15 → Minor surgery Blade 11 → Arteriotomy, abscess drainage Elliptical Incisions Used for circular lesions Rule: Length = 3 × width Remove dog ears for better cosmesis Abdominal Surgical Access Open Surgery Incision Types: Midline Transverse Oblique Flank Midline Laparotomy Fast Easily extendable Preferred in emergencies Minimal bleeding Laparoscopic Surgery 1. Open (Hasson) Technique Umbilicus (10–12 mm port) Controlled entry Reduced bowel/vessel injury Previous scars? → Use Palmer’s point (3 cm below left costal margin, mid-clavicular line) Closed (Veress Needle) Technique Spring-loaded needle Blunt tip deploys inside peritoneum Reduces injury risk Benefits of Laparoscopy Less pain Smaller scars Faster recovery Shorter hospital stay Fewer adhesions Magnified anatomical view Robotic Surgery Advanced minimally invasive surgery Surgeon operates from console 3D high-definition vision Wristed instruments (articulate like human wrist) Greater precision Improved ergonomics Useful in narrow pelvic spaces Suture Techniques 1. Interrupted Sutures Each stitch tied separately Secure Failure of one does not affect others Continuous Sutures Faster Even tension required Finished with Aberdeen knot Mattress Sutures Vertical or horizontal Strong Used for tension Promote eversion Subcuticular Sutures Within dermis Cosmetic closure No suture marks Drains in Surgery Purpose Remove blood, pus, bile, air, serous fluid Prevent collection Therapeutic or prophylactic Types 1. Open Drain Example: Penrose High infection risk No output measurement 2. Closed Passive Drain Gravity system Measurable output Lower infection risk 3. Closed Suction Drain (Active) Example: Redivac Negative pressure Most common Accurate measurement Lowest infection risk General Principles Do NOT use routinely Use only if clearly indicated Remove early Prolonged use → infection risk

text:
General Principles
• • Careful observation starts from the first
encounter.
– • Note posture, gait, breathing, colour, and
general state.
– • Give full attention and introduce yourself
properly.
– • Allow free speech; guide without dominating.
– • Explain actions clearly during the process.
– • Ask simple, open, non-leading questions.
– • Ensure privacy, especially for sensitive issues.

 • Patient Identification – personal details and date.
– Presenting Complaint (PC) – in patient’s own words.
– History of Presenting Complaint (HPC) – chronological
narrative.
– Past History – illnesses and previous operations.
– Drug History – medications and documented allergies.
– Family History – hereditary diseases and deaths.
– Habits – smoking and alcohol intake.

 Why History Taking is Critical in Surgery
• • 70% of diagnosis comes from history
– • Identifies urgency and red flags
– • Guides examination and investigations
– • Assesses operative and anaesthetic risk
– • Builds patient trust and rapport

 Structured Surgical History
• 1. Personal Data
– 2. Chief Complaint
– 3. History of Present Illness (HPI)
– 4. Past Medical & Surgical History
– 5. Drug & Allergy History
– 6. Family History
– 7. Social History
– 8. Review of Systems

text: Preoperative and Postoperative Care Surgery is a controlled trauma that triggers a massive physiological shift. Hypermetabolism: Oxygen demand rises by 40% . Hormonal Surge: The "Stress Response" releases catecholamines (adrenaline) and cortisol , which can lead to high blood sugar and increased heart rate. Inflammation: A cascade of cytokines can cause systemic swelling and organ strain. Clotting Risk: The body enters a "pro-thrombotic" state, making DVT/PE prevention a priority. The Body’s Response to Surgical Stress Preoperative Optimization The goal is to identify and fix issues before the patient reaches the operating table. Assessment: Evaluating "functional reserve" (the heart and lungs' ability to handle the 40% stress increase). Medication Adjustments: * Anticoagulants: Usually stopped 1–5 days prior (except Aspirin for high-risk cardiac patients). Diabetics: Stop oral meds; switch to IV insulin for major cases. Fasting (NPO): 2 hours for clear liquids; 6 hours for light meals to prevent aspiration. Preoperative Planning and Fasting Objectives: Collect medical data, optimize patient, and select surgical approach. Fasting Guidelines (NPO) to prevent aspiration: - Clear Fluids: 2 hours. - Breast Milk: 4 hours. - Light Meal (toast/biscuits): 6 hours. - Fatty Meal/Meat: 8 hours. Anticoagulants and Antiplatelets Aspirin: Usually continued for secondary prevention (MI/Stroke) , bleeding causes by aspirin is usually manageable but if there is severe risk stop for 5-7 days Clopidogrel: Stop 5–7 days before unless high stent risk. Warfarin: Stop 5 days before; target INR < 1.5. Bridging: LMWH only for high thrombotic risk (e.g., mechanical valves). DOACs (Apixaban/Rivaroxaban): Stop 1–2 days before surgery. Diabetics & Steroid Management Insulin: Long-acting (1/2 to 2/3 dose); Short-acting (Omit morning dose). Major Surgery: Use Variable Rate Intravenous Insulin Infusion (VRIII). Metformin: Stop on day of surgery. SGLT-2 Inhibitors: Stop 3 days before to avoid ketoacidosis. Steroids: Do NOT stop; give 'stress dose' hydrocortisone at induction. Preoperative Assessment History & Examination: Respectful, clear, and chaperoned when needed. Airway Assessment: Critical for safe anesthesia. Investigations (ASA guided): CBC, U&E, LFTs, Coagulation. ECG: Recommended for age > 65. Cross-match: Only if significant blood loss is anticipated. Postoperative care Once surgery is complete, the focus shifts to monitoring and complication prevention. The PACU: Immediate recovery focusing on airway, "Sepsis Six" protocols if needed, and stable vitals. Pain Management: Crucial not just for comfort, but to allow the patient to breathe deeply and move early, which prevents pneumonia and clots. Wound Watch: Most wound failures (dehiscence) happen between Days 5 and 8 . Postoperative Monitoring Vital Signs: Pulse, BP, Respiration, O2 Sat, Temp, Consciousness. Urine Output: Key indicator of renal perfusion and fluid status. Pain Control: Essential for early mobilization and respiratory health. Thermal Care: Maintain normothermia to reduce infection/cardiac risk. Post-op Systemic Care Respiratory: Oxygen initially; prevent complications with physio and mobilization. Cardiovascular: Monitor for hypotension (Hypovolemia vs Sepsis). Myocardial Ischemia: High risk in elderly; ECG monitoring required. Renal and Urinary Care Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): High mortality; prevent by maintaining hydration. Avoid Nephrotoxic Drugs: Caution with NSAIDs/Gentamicin. Urinary Retention: Prompt assessment and catheterization if needed. VTE Prophylaxis and Wound Care VTE (DVT/PE): Major cause of mortality; requires risk assessment/prophylaxis. Wound Inspection: Check for infection, hematoma, or dehiscence. Wound Dehiscence: Most common on postoperative Days 5–8. Nutritional Support Enteral (Preferred): Maintains gut integrity; reduces infection risk. Routes: Nasogastric (NG), Nasojejunal (NJ), or Gastrostomy. Parenteral (TPN): Used if gut fails; requires central venous access. Starvation Response: Decreased resting energy expenditure; switch to fats. WHY NUTRITION AND FLUIDS MATTER IN SURGERY Adequate nutrition and fluid balance before and after surgery are essential for: Proper wound healing Immune function Maintenance of muscle mass Reduction of postoperative complications Faster recovery and shorter hospital stay Many surgical patients are already malnourished due to: • Chronic illness (e.g. cancer, inflammatory bowel disease) • Reduced intake (pain, dysphagia, nausea) • Malabsorption • Increased metabolic demands Surgery itself worsens nutritional status through: • Fasting • Stress hormone release • Insulin resistance • Increased protein breakdown Effects of Intestinal Resection The impact of removing segments of the small intestine depends heavily on the location and the length of the remaining bowel. Jejunum: Resection is generally well-compensated by the rest of the small intestine. Ileum: Loss is much more significant because the ileum has specialized functions. Resection leads to: Bile salt malabsorption and Steatorrhoea (fatty stools). Vitamin B12 deficiency . Short Bowel Syndrome (SBS): Occurs when less than 200 cm of small bowel remains. Symptoms: Diarrhoea, dehydration, and malnutrition. Critical Threshold: If less than 100 cm remains, fluid loss becomes severe, often requiring lifelong Parenteral Nutrition . Artificial nutritional support Nutritional intervention is indicated if a patient has had no intake for 5 or more days or suffers from severe pre-existing malnutrition. Enteral Nutrition (The Preferred Method) This involves feeding via the gastrointestinal tract. It is preferred because it maintains gut integrity and carries a lower infection risk than IV feeding. Routes: Oral supplements, Nasogastric (NG) or Nasojejunal (NJ) tubes, Gastrostomy, or Jejunostomy. Complications: Aspiration, diarrhoea, tube blockage, and Refeeding Syndrome . Parenteral nutrition This is used only when the "gut cannot be used." Administ

response to

Dr Laila Ellebishy assistant lecturer

 ◤

Introduction to Metabolic Stress

▪

Definition: The body’s natural response to stress caused by
surgery, trauma, sepsis, or burns.

▪

Primary Goal: To maintain homeostasis and support survival.

▪

Key Principles:

▪

▪

The magnitude of the response is proportional to the severity of the
injury.

▪

Influenced by genetic and environmental factors.

The Double-Edged Sword: While initially adaptive for survival, an
excessive or prolonged response can lead to organ dysfunction and
mortality

 ◤

Mediators of the Stress Response

▪

The Innate Immune System: Triggered by tissue injury, leading to Systemic
Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS).

▪

Key Pro-inflammatory Cytokines:

▪

▪

Interleukin-1 (IL-1)

▪

Interleukin-6 (IL-6)

▪

Tumor Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α)

The Neuroendocrine Response: Simultaneous activation of stress hormones:
▪

Cortisol, Catecholamines, and Glucagon.

▪

Function: Mobilize energy substrates but promote catabolism and insulin resistance.

Phase

Ebb Phase

Flow Phase

Phases of the Response
Timing

Characteristics

First 24–48 hours

Hypovolaemia, reduced
cardiac output, decreased
metabolic rate (Energy
Conservation).

Hypermetabolism, protein
breakdown,
gluconeogenesis,

text: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair Department of Surgery Faculty of Medicine University of Alexandria 2026 Contents Normal Wound Healing in Skin GIT healing versus skin healing Acute Wound Failure (Abdominal Wound Dehiscence) Abnormal Wound Healing Types of Wound Healing Classification of Wounds Wound Management Principles Normal Wound Healing in Skin The immediate response to injury is haemostasis which is then followed by 3 overlapping stages: Inflammation Proliferation Remodeling Normal Wound Healing in Skin Haemostasis B lood vessels damage > constriction > exposing the subendothelial extracellular matrix > platelets adherence, activation and aggregation > platelet plug > reduces blood loss > release proteins including cytokines and growth factors > support extracellular matrix deposition + cell movement (chemotaxis) + epithelialization + new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis) T issue factor > + coagulation cascade > producing thrombin Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin + stabilizing platelet plug + providing a scaffold for infiltrating cells Normal Wound Healing in Skin Inflammation E arly inflammatory phase (days 1–2): platelet activation > attracts inflammatory cells, especially neutrophils (crucial for reducing bacterial contamination) Platelets and injured tissues release histamine and serotonin > increasing blood vessel permeability + helping immune cells enter the wound L ate inflammatory phase (days 2–3): monocytes arrive and transform into macrophages . Macrophages clean debris, produce proteolytic enzymes + release cytokines and growth factors that stimulate fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis . Normal Wound Healing in Skin Inflammation L ate inflammatory phase Signs: R ubor (redness) T umor (swelling) C alor (heat) Dolor (pain) Normal Wound Healing in Skin Inflammation L ate inflammatory phase Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are also released during inflammation and later remodelling to break down old collagen; excess MMP activity, such as in chronic wounds or infection, can delay healing. Platelets release cytokines and growth factors early, and macrophages in the late inflammatory phase. Normal Wound Healing in Skin Proliferation The proliferative phase (day 3 to 2–4 weeks): Fibroblasts > extracellular matrix, including glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans, as well as collagen. Angiogenesis and re- epithelialisation occur during this phase. The new tissue formed is called granulation tissue , which is pink and granular. Fibroblasts eventually differentiate into myofibroblasts, which contract the wound edges. Wound tensile strength gradually increases as collagen accumulates. Normal Wound Healing in Skin Wound contraction: centripetal movement of the wound edges, in which the surrounding skin is pulled toward the centre to reduce the wound size. It is an active, energy-consuming process, therefore it depends on an adequate blood supply. The activity occurs in a “picture-frame zone” located 3–8 mm beneath the wound edges all around the wound. In this zone, fibroblasts transform into myofibroblasts, which pull the wound edges toward the centre . Normal Wound Healing in Skin Wound contraction Stopped or impaired by: o Infection o Corticosteroids (cortisone) o Chemotherapeutic drugs Time course o There is a lag period of about 4 days before contraction begins. o Contraction then continues for 3–6 weeks, depending on the wound site and the care provided. Normal Wound Healing in Skin Wound contraction Clinical importance o Procedures that stop contraction ▪ Early split-thickness skin graft (before day 4) ▪ Full-thickness skin graft (at any time) ▪ Flaps o If a split-thickness graft is applied late, contraction continues and graft shrinkage occurs. Normal Wound Healing in Skin Remodelling The remodelling phase: starts 2–3 weeks after injury and may last a year or more. Type III collagen , abundant in the proliferative phase, is replaced by stronger type I collagen , which becomes cross-linked and aligned. Tensile strength peaks at around 80% of normal skin strength by 12 weeks. Normal Wound Healing in Skin GIT healing versus skin healing Key differences • Intestinal wounds gain strength much faster than skin wounds. • In the GIT, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts both produce collagen . • Collagen synthesis in GIT and skin wounds is regulated differently. GIT healing versus skin healing Critical period in intestinal healing • Day 4 after surgery o Collagenase activity is highest o Collagen levels drop to the lowest level o This is the highest risk period for anastomotic leakage • Sepsis increases collagenase activity, reducing tissue strength and suture holding capacity. Acute Wound Failure ( Abdominal Wound Dehiscence ) Definition • Acute wound failure is post-operative separation of the abdominal Musculo aponeurotic layers. • It usually occurs within the same hospital admission and requires intervention. Timing • Average day of occurrence: Post-operative day 7. • Can occur anytime from day 1 to >21 after surgery. Acute Wound Failure ( Abdominal Wound Dehiscence ) Clinical presentation • May occur suddenly without warning. • Evisceration → diagnosis is obvious. • In most cases, serosanguinous discharge from the wound precedes dehiscence (important warning sign). Acute Wound Failure ( Abdominal Wound Dehiscence ) Prediction of Acute Wound Failure Patient risk factors Local factors 1. Age > 65 years 2. Obesity 3. Pulmonary disease (chronic cough/ Smoking) 4. Hypoproteinaemia / malnutrition 5. Uraemia 6. Haemodynamic instability 7. Malignancy 8. Increased intra-abdominal pressure/ Ascites 9. Chronic diseases (e.g., diabetes, connective tissue disorders) 10. Immunosuppression (e.g., HIV/AIDS, immunosuppressive drugs) 11. Chemotherapy/ Steroid therapy 1. text:
Surgery, Ethics, and Law
• Surgical practice is not purely technical; it is
deeply connected with:
• Ethical principles
• Legal responsibilities
• Professional conduct
• Surgery requires trust between the patient
and surgeon, and ethical frameworks guide
surgeons in making difficult clinical decisions.

 Introduction
• Ethics and law are inseparable from surgery.
• Surgery deliberately invades the human body, which naturally
involves:
1. Pain
2. Tissue injury
3. Risk of disability
4. Risk of death
• Under normal circumstances, causing such harm would be illegal or
unethical.
However, in medicine this harm is accepted because it aims to
treat disease.
• So surgery is ethically justified only when it is done for therapeutic
benefit.

 Therapeutic Intent in Surgery
• The main factor that distinguishes surgery from assault
is therapeutic intent.
• The surgeon operates with the intention to:
1. Cure disease
2. Relieve suffering
3. Preserve life
4. Improve function
• Even though surgery causes harm temporarily (incision,
tissue damage), the ultimate goal is benefit.
• Therefore:
Intent + benefit to the patient = ethical justification.

 Ethical and Legal Justification
• Surgical procedures are ethically and legally
justified only when certain conditions are met:
• Competence
– Surgeon must have adequate training and skills.

• Best interest of the patient
– Surgery should improve health outcomes.

• Professional standards
– Procedures must follow accepted medical guidelines.

• Failure in these areas may lead to medical
negligence or malpractice.

rel: y3/MED 309 - Surgery/General/Surgery/Round ppt/wound_healing_slides.pdf
text:
Normal Wound Healing in Skin
• Wound healing in skin is traditionally divided
into three overlapping stages:
• • Inflammation
• • Proliferation
• • Remodelling
• An initial phase called haemostasis occurs
immediately after injury.

 Haemostasis
• When blood vessels are damaged, they
constrict, exposing the subendothelial
extracellular matrix.
• This causes platelets to adhere, activate, and
aggregate to form a platelet plug, which
reduces blood loss.
• Platelets release proteins including cytokines
and growth factors.

 Role of Platelet Factors
• These factors support:
• • Extracellular matrix deposition
• • Cell movement (chemotaxis)
• • Epithelialisation
• • New blood vessel formation (angiogenesis)

 Coagulation Cascade
• Tissue factor triggers the coagulation cascade
producing thrombin.
• Thrombin converts fibrinogen into fibrin
stabilizing the platelet plug.
• Fibrin provides a scaffold for infiltrating cells.
